But the conjecture of some other, to me, seems more probable; who conceive the Hebrew, *To,* or *Tho* (for that is the name of it, both here, and in Moses,) to be the same with that, as in name they agree, which the Greeks, and from them, the Latins call *Thos,* reported to be a kind of *wolf,* longer tailed, but shorter legged, and yet swifter; because nimbler; than the ordinary wolf, living by prey, not of himself prone to set on man, though not fearing him neither; but fighting with dogs, and lions, Aristotle, l. 2, c. 17 & l. 6, c. 35 & l. 9, c. 44, Pliny, l. 8, c. 34 & l. 10, c. 74. Oppian adds in his *hunting treatises,* l. 3, and in his *fishing treatises,* l. 1, that they are a mongrel kind, bred between a *wolf,* and an *ounce;* and do prey much upon deer.

*{in a net*} The word signifies a *net,* or *toil,* set to take beasts in, Psalm 141:10, the preposition is wanting, as Psalm 35:7.

*{they are full of the fury of the Lord*} Hebrew, *being full of heat,* or *wrath of the Lord.* See on verse 17, that is, of calamities, thence proceeding, chapter 9:19, Romans 2:8,9.

*{of the rebuke of thy God*} See on chapter 50:2.

**V. 21.** *{Therefore*} Or, *Notwithstanding.* So the course of the context necessarily requires it to be rendered. Notwithstanding this your forlorn, helpless and hopeless estate, that in man's eyes may seem altogether irrecoverable, yet the Lord will alter your condition, and raise you up out of it, and restore you to your former luster again. See the like use of this particle, chapter 30:18, Jeremiah 16:14 & 30:16.

*{hear now this, thou afflicted, and drunken, but not with wine*} Not drunk, at present, with ordinary wine, or strong drink, as your people had too much wont to be, when they reveled it in the times of your better estate, chapter 5:11,12 & 22:2,13 & 28:1,3,7, Hosea 4:11. What time you were drunk also, as well with pride and security proceeding from the height of your prosperity, chapter 29:9,10, Jeremiah 2:31 and 22:21, as you are now, with anguish and vexation of mind and spirit, arising from the depth of your adversity, Lamentations 3:15,19, but with that strong potion, in God's cup of wrath, verse 17, and the dismal effects of it, which makes all that drink deep of it, as you with others have done, not drunk only, but even mad drunk, and to fare as persons distracted, Jeremiah 25:16 & 51:7, Ezekiel 23:33,34.

**V. 22.** *{Thus saith the Lord, the Lord and thy God, that pleadeth the cause of his people*} Whom, being their sovereign Lord, he has undertaken to protect. See chapter 49:14 & 50:7,9,10. Hebrew, *will plead.* So chapter 49:25, Jeremiah 50:34, not, by a mere verbal, or vocal; but by a real, and active plea, as Ezekiel 38:22, a defect of the relative, as verse 18.

*{Behold,*} A note prefixed, to stir up not attention only; but admiration, upon consideration, and contemplation, of the strange change and alteration that was now to ensue. So chapter 10:33.

*{I have taken out of thine hand*} Or, *I will take out of thine hand:* that which I put formerly into your hand, Jeremiah 25:17,18. I will do that for you, that none of yours can do, verse 18,20. I will alter your condition.

*{the cup of trembling*} Whereof, see on verse 17.

*{even, the dregs of the cup of my fury:*} Or, *with the dregs of my cup of wrath.* See verse 17, that is, together with the dregs thereof: the noun repeated for the pronoun, as Jeremiah 2:4, 2 Timothy 1:18, the former particle supplied, as chapter 5:9, this latter, as chapter 34:15 and 35:4.

*{thou shalt no more drink it again*} Hebrew, *thou shalt not add to drink it further;* that is, either *thou shalt drink it no longer,* as chapter 23:12. Or, *thou shalt not drink it any more;* as Genesis 8:21. See chapter 54:9. But the former rather.

**V. 23.** *{But I will put it into the hand of them that afflict thee*} I will remove my wrath from you; and I will pour it out upon them, that have been your oppressors, chapter 49:26. See Lamentations 4:21.

*{But*} Hebrew, *And;* which may also be here retained.

*{that afflict thee*} Or, *vex thee;* as Job 19:2. Or, as some, *oppress thee;* supposing it to be the same with that, chapter 49:26, altered only by a small slip of the scribe's pen: but there is no need to question, or alter the reading, the word whereof it comes regularly being oft used for *to vex,* or *afflict,* Lamentations 1:5,12 & 3:32.

*{which have said to thy soul*} That is, *to thee,* as Psalm 3:2 and 11:1.

*{Bow down, that we may go over*} That have trodden you down, and trampled upon you as a despicable people: an allusion to the insolent usage of those eastern kings, to set their feet upon the necks, backs, and bodies, of conquered persons, and to make them, as their footstools. See Joshua 10:24, Psalm 66:12 & 110:1, chapter 10:6, Jeremiah 12:10.

*{go over*} Or, *go over thee:* the pronoun supplied as chapter 49:7 and 58:9.

*{and thou hast laid thy body as the ground*} Or, *and lay* (the words still of her insolent masters; the future, as oft, in an imperative notion, so 1 Samuel 2:3.) *thy back* (as chapter 38:17 & 50:6, Proverbs 10:13 & 19:29 & 26:3.) *as the ground,* for us to tread on. See Psalm 44:25 & 119:25, chapter 52:2.

*{and as the street to them that went over*} Or, *as the street to passengers:* that we may as freely tread upon you, and go over you, as men go along the streets.

### CHAPTER 52

**V. 1.** *{Awake, awake*} The former part of this chapter, unto verse 13, seems to be no other, than an appendix to the foregoing prophecy, or sermon, running all along in the same tenor, with the latter part of it, and very aptly closing with it.

*{Awake*} Or, *Arise.* The prophet calls upon Sion to do that herself here, which she had called upon God to do for her before, chapter 51:9, to wit, to rouse up herself, and pluck up her spirits. See chapter 51:12 & 60:1.

*{put on thy strength, O Zion*} Be of good courage, and make it to appear that you are so. See chapter 51:9.

*{put on thy beautiful garments, O Jerusalem*} Hebrew, *thy garments of beauty,* or *bravery;* as it is rendered, chapter 3:18. Put off your prison garments, your captive attire, your mourning weeds, your servile garb, lay aside now your wonted raiment, and put on your best and bravest apparel; your estate being clean altered, and changed for the better. See Genesis 27:15 & 38:14 & 41:24, Ruth 3:3, chapter 61:10, Jeremiah 52:33, Zechariah 3:4,5.

*{the holy city*} Hebrew, *city of holiness;* as chapter 48:2. Now being purged and refined, as having passed through the furnace, by the fire of affliction, to be restored to her former purity again, chapter 1:25 & 4:3,4 & 62:12.

*{from henceforth there shall no more come into thee the uncircumcised, and the unclean*} Hebrew, *there shall not add that shall come into thee,* or *against thee:* as the particle is used, Numbers 23:21,23. For the syntax, see the like chapter 29:1 & 47:5, Hosea 1:6. You shall no longer be possessed, nor shall any more be invaded by heathen people, as by the Syrians, Assyrians, Egyptians, and Chaldeans, you have been, 2 Kings 16,18,23,24,25, chapter 63:18, Lamentations 1:10. See chapter 60:18 & 62:8. Or, wicked ones shall not harbor with you, chapter 35:8 and 60:21 and 62:12, Revelation 21:27. But the former here rather.

**V. 2.** *{Shake thyself from the dust*} That you sat in before, as a mourner, Job 2:8 & 42:6. Or, lay along in, as a prisoner, or captive, that are wont to lie, disregarded, and ill entreated, on the bare ground, and in the dust, Psalm 7:5 & 44:25 & 119:25. Or, *shake the dust from thee,* which you have gathered, by lying flat on the ground while you were made, as a common footstool, for your proud, and stately lords, and masters to tread upon. See chapter 51:23, which this may well reflect upon; and there seems an *hypallage,* or, inversion in the words, *Shake thee from the dust,* for, *shake the dust from thee.* So in the next clause.

*{Arise, and sit down O Jerusalem*} Rather, *Arise, sit up, O Jerusalem:* for the copulative is not in the text, and the word of *sitting,* is here used, not for sitting down, but for *sitting up,* as Genesis 27:19, where Jacob to his father Isaac, that lay bedridden, *arise, sit up.* As Babylon is commanded, *to come down, and sit in the dust,* chapter 47:1, so is Jerusalem here willed, *to rise from the dust,* and *sit up.*

*{loose thyself from the bands of thy neck*} That is, *loose the bands from off thy neck:* an *hypallage,* as before, such bands, or chains, as prisoners, or captives, are wont to be fastened with, by the neck, to some post, or staple, or one to another, as beasts in a yoke. See Jeremiah 27:2,8,12 & 28:23,24, Lamentations 1:14. So Jeremiah 40:4, *I loose thee from the bands on thy hands,* for *I loose the bands from off thy hands;* or, them, from off you.

*{O captive daughter of Zion*} Or, *Daughter Sion.* See chapter 1:8.

**V. 3.** *{For thus saith the Lord, Ye have sold yourselves for nought*} I sold you not; but you sold yourselves by your sins, or *ye were sold for nought:* for the Hebrew text says no more: the Babylonians to whom you were sold, paid me, whose servants you were, nothing for you, not so much as thanks, Psalm 44:12, so that I gained nothing by the sale of you, but reproach from the hands, and mouths of those, unto whom you were sold, verse 5, Daniel 1:2 & 5:2,3,24.

*{and ye shall be redeemed without money*} Hebrew, *without silver,* as Exodus 21:11, chapter 55:1. I will require you back from them again, without ransom, chapter 45:13. So that God's argument runs thus; You were my people, I had interest in you; the Babylonians have gotten you into their hands; they pretend to hold you, as good purchase; but I had never aught of them for you: and there is no reason, therefore, but that you should be restored without ransom. Thus does God plead the cause of his people. See chapter 49:24,25 and 51:22.

**V. 4.** *{For thus saith the Lord God*} Hebrew, *the Lord Jehovah:* as chapter 50:4,9.

*{my people went down aforetime, into Egypt, to sojourn there*} In time of famine, Jacob went with his whole household thither, Genesis 46:6.

*{went down*} See chapter 30:2 & 31:1.

*{into Egypt*} The particle is wanting, as also in those texts.

*{and the Assyrian oppressed them without cause*} The interpreters do exceedingly dissent about the sense of these words: Some by *Assur,* here, would have Pharao understood, the Egyptian king, for his cruelty towards God's people, and his evil usage of them, termed *Assur;* because therein resembling the Assyrian king. Some of them proceed so far, as to affirm, that that Pharao, which oppressed God's people in Egypt, was no Egyptian; for he would there have known Joseph; but an Assyrian, Exodus 1:8. So the meaning should be. My people did not invade Egypt in warlike manner, but came thither to sojourn; and during their abode there, did them no wrong, but were beneficial to them, preserved them alive from perishing through famine, by their foresight, and built them divers cities, Genesis 47:19, Exodus 1:11, and yet they oppressed them, and dealt very cruelly with them, Exodus 1:13,14,16. But this exposition is built upon a very forced interpretation, and a mere groundless, yea, an improbable, conjecture. Others, by *Assur,* here, understand the king, or kings of Assyria, and some, Salmaneser, that had carried captive the ten tribes, 2 Kings 17:11. Some, Tiglath-Pileser, and Sennacherib, that pillaged and plundered the other two, 2 Kings 16:8,17,18 & 18:13–17, the one called in by Ahaz; the other indeed, because Ezekiah had at first revolted from him; yet after his submission, and composition made, contrary to his covenant, besetting, and distressing Jerusalem, chapter 33:8. Others again, by *Assur,* or the Assyrian king, understand the Babylonian, Nebuchadnezzar, so called, say they, because Babylon was sometime subject to the Assyrian, and the kingdom of Babylon, a branch of that empire. See 2 Kings 17:24, 2 Chronicles 33:11, and the Babylonian was afterward possessed of that monarchy, which the Assyrian kings had held before. Now again among them, there is some dissent about the connection of this latter branch of the verse, with the former: for some knit them together, as our version, with a copulative, so the first, they went down into Egypt, and Pharao causelessly wronged them: and so some of those also, that go with the latter branch, applying from the latter branch, what was implied, but not expressed in the former; the Egyptians, at first, wrongfully oppressed them, when they sojourned with them, and the Assyrians, and the Babylonians have of late done the like. Others give the copulative, an adversative notion; *and,* for, *but,* as chapter 29:13 and 53:5, and they conceive the context to run thus; My people did, of their own accord, sometime, go down into Egypt, where they had means afforded them, that kept them from perishing by famine, and were there seated in the best, and richest part of that land, Genesis 47:4,6,11,13,17. Now, by this means they became Pharao's subjects, and he might justly claim some interest in them, and refuse therefore to part with them; but you Assyrians, and Babylonians, can make no such claim; you have violently invaded them; by force transported them out of their own land, into your dominions. If I compelled them to deliver them, and plagued them, for their evil usage of them, Deuteronomy 26:5,6, I may much more justly both constrain you to re-deliver them, and that freely too; and take vengeance also upon you for the wrongs that you have done them, having, for nothing, without any just cause on their part given you, afflicted, and oppressed them: and it may indeed be so understood; for howsoever it be true, that God's people had, at his hand, deserved whatsoever at their enemies' hand they had endured; and that God had, for their sins justly given them up into their hands; yet they intended nothing less, whatsoever they might pretend, than the executing of God's judgment, or the righting of the wrongs done to him, whom they both otherwise, and even therein also, wronged much more themselves; they minded nothing but the satisfaction of their own ambitious humors, the wreaking of their wrath, and the exercising of their cruelty upon them, chapter 10:5–14 & 47:6, Jeremiah 50:7,17. So in the psalms, God's people complain to God, of their causeless sufferings, in regard of their enemies; because, though they had trespassed against him, yet, they had not trespassed against them, Psalm 7:3–5,8 and 25:18,19,21 & 35:7,12,24 & 41:4–9 & 69:4,5. Among this great variety, all circumstances weighed, I concur with those, who understand this latter of the Assyrians, as the words expressly give it; which I suppose may well comprehend the whole race of those kings above mentioned, with their issue, that had from time to time infested either house, as well that of Judah, as that also of Israel, as the like is thereby designed, Jeremiah 50:17. And I conceive, that the sufferings of God's people by the Egyptians, are intimated, as well in the former branch of the verse, as by the Assyrians in the latter: yet not so much the causelessness of the wrongs done them, as the fruitlessness of their sufferings, in regard of any gain that God got thereby, to be intimated in the word, *for nought:* as Psalm 44:12, *for nothing of wealth,* or *worth.*

**V. 5.** *{Now therefore what have I here saith the Lord, that my people is taken away for nought?*} The words are in the Hebrew word for word, *And now what to me here, that* (as Job 11:6, verse 6.) or, *when* (as Job 3:22, for the word may signify either) *my people is taken away freely?* Now this most interpreters take, as reflecting upon the words foregoing. Some expounding it, what should I do? should I sit still, and do nothing, when my people when my people are thus causelessly oppressed, and detained from me injuriously? Or, what should I do, but deliver my people, as formerly, in the like case, I have done? Others, what do I here, to wit, at Jerusalem, when my people are in Babylon, and do not rather haste thither to deliver them thence? Others, again, What do I here, to wit, at Babylon, as kept in captivity with my people, in a profane country, in a strange land, from my temple at Jerusalem, Psalm 137:4. I conceive this verse to be of a distinct subject from what was mentioned in the former: he had pointed at two several oppressions of his people, in the words foregoing, both past, and gone; the one by the Egyptian, the other by the Assyrian: he now passes on to the third, that was present, and concerning which he was dealing with his people, at present: for the prophecy is delivered, as to the people held by the Babylonian in captivity, assuring them of speedy deliverance out of it.

*{Now therefore*} Or, *And now:* as the Hebrew is; at this present.

*{what have I here,*} Hebrew, *what to me here?* what accrues unto me? what gain get I by this present oppression of my people, more than by either of the former?

*{that my people is taken away for nought?*} Or, *when,* or, *since that:* as Job 38:5. Or, as some, *for my people is taken away for nought:* and so the particle is taken, chapter 28:27, but I adhere rather to the former.

*{is taken away*} So the word signifies, Psalm 51:12, Hosea 4:11 and 13:11. Or, (for so it may very well be rendered,) *is led away,* or, *is carried away:* as Genesis 12:15, to wit, captive; as Jeremiah 48:46, opposed here, to their voluntary descent into Egypt, verse 4.

*{for nought*} As before, verse 3, my people are taken from me, and carried away, and I receive nothing at all for them. I have no more now from the Chaldeans, than from the Assyrians before.

*{they that rule over them, make them to howl saith the Lord;*} Their lordlike masters (chapter 26:13 and 49:7.) use them with extreme cruelty, chapter 47:6. They suffer much, and I receive nothing, for all the hard service my servants endure.

*{and my name continually every day is blasphemed*} That is all I had from the Assyrian before, chapter 37:4,6,17,23,24,29, and that is all I get from the Babylonian now, Daniel 3:15 & 5:23, chapter 14:13,14, Ezekiel 36:20,23, as my people suffer in their persons, so I myself, in my reputation, being deemed unable to deliver my people. Thus profane persons, by the sufferings of God's people take occasion to blaspheme, and to insult, even over God himself, Psalm 3:2 & 42:3 & 74:22,23 & 89:50,51.

*{every day*} Or, *all the day long:* and thus rather for the article as Genesis 6:5, Psalm 44:22, chapter 51:13, Romans 8:36, which is wanting; when it is, *every day:* as Psalm 7:11 & 140:2 & 145:2.

**V. 6.** *{Therefore my people shall know my name:*} I will no longer endure this loss and reproach: but I will make my power known, by the deliverance of my people, Psalm 106:8, chapter 49:26 & 63:14. It may seem to have an eye to God's words unto Moses, Exodus 6:3. I will make myself known to my people, by my name Jehovah, as I did to them in Egypt, by making my word good, by fulfilling my promises.

*{therefore they shall know in that day*} A supply from the former branch; as Genesis 1:16,30, 1 Kings 10:11.

*{in that day*} At that time, when this is effected; as chapter 26:1.

*{that I am he that doth speak: behold it is I.*} That is not Esay, or any other my messenger, but I the Lord, that speak by him; who now foretell and promise, what I will then fulfill and perform, chapter 42:9 & 48:3,5. *That it is I that do speak,* saying (supplied, as Psalm 105:14,15.) *Lo, here I am,* ready to do what I have undertaken, and by promise engaged myself to make good. See chapter 42:27 and 65:1. There is a trajection in the words, with a repetition of the particle intervenient, not unlike that, chapter 59:18.

**V. 7.** *{How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings.*} The joyous and gladsome entertainment of those that should bring tidings into Judea, and unto Jerusalem, of the dissolution of the Babylonian captivity, Nahum 1:15, and of those, much more, that should publish salvation, purchased by Christ, Romans 10:15, Galatians 4:15,16.

*{How beautiful*} Or, *comely,* or, *sightly,* as Proverbs 19:10 and 26:1, Canticles 1:5,10 and 2:14. Or, *delightful,* or *desirable,* Jeremiah 6:2, for that, the root it springs from, does first, and properly signify.

*{are the feet*} How welcome will such be when they come; *foot,* or *feet,* for the person himself, say some, as Psalm 38:16 & 119:59, Proverbs 6:18 & 7:11. Or, how welcome will their coming be? *foot,* and *feet,* for coming, say others, as Genesis 30:27, 2 Kings 6:32. Yet there seems here to be some emphasis in it, as if it were said, the very *feet,* of such, though sweaty, dusty and dirty with travel, yet will be deemed desirable and amiable unto God's people, in regard of the tidings they bring to them; and they ready to fall down at them, as ready even to kiss them. See Acts 10:25.

*{upon the mountains*} Alluding either unto such high places, on which beacons, and watchtowers, were situate, which those were wont to get up unto, thence, by some sign given, to call people together, that had some message, or tidings, to publish unto them, chapter 40:9. Or, to the mountains, rather, that Jerusalem was environed with, Psalm 121:1 & 125:2, and he seems to speak, as if he saw messengers coming over these hills, to bring tidings from Babylon to Jerusalem, of the captivity broken up. See the like chapter 13:4.

*{of him that bringeth good tidings*} The word *good,* should be in a different character; for the word is indefinite to good, or bad. See chapter 40:9. *of him that bringeth good tidings;* that is of the prophet Jeremy, says one, that defined the time of the captivity, Jeremiah 25:12 & 29:10, Daniel 9:3, but poor Jeremy found but very sorry entertainment among his people, for all that his determination: Nor is it probable, that people would be so much taken, and so deeply affected with a prediction of a deliverance, to come seventy years after, from a very calamitous captivity, that they were then suddenly to enter into. The word is rather taken collectively, and indefinitely, not aiming at, or pointing to, any one in particular; but intending any whosoever, one, or more, that should come with such tidings. See chapter 40:9 & 41:27, as in such cases men are wont to contend, to go one before another, and to strive who shall bring the good news first, 2 Samuel 18:19–23. See Jeremiah 50:8.

*{that publisheth peace*} Hebrew, *maketh to hear;* as Nehemiah 8:15. *peace,* that is prosperity and welfare; as chapter 48:18.

*{that bringeth good tidings of good,*} A superfluous repetition; it would be simply rendered; *of him that bringeth good* or, *glad tidings:* for the word here used signifies either, 1 Kings 22:8, Proverbs 15:15, Zechariah 9:17.

*{that publisheth salvation,*} Deliverance, corporal, by Cyrus; spiritual, by Christ, chapter 51:5. Hebrew, *that maketh to hear;* as before.

*{that saith to Zion, Thy God reigneth*} Your God has manifested, and magnified his royal power, by the destruction of his enemies, and the deliverance of his people; but chiefly, and principally, in his spiritual kingdom erected, and exercised by his Christ, Psalm 93:1 & 97:1 & 99:1, 110:1–7 & 146:10, Revelation 6:2 & 11:15 and 19:6.

**V. 8.** *{Thy watchmen shall lift up their voice*} Hebrew, *the voice:* the pronoun wanting, as chapter 49:22,23. Of another syntax, see anon. Your prophets and teachers, (chapter 60:10, Ezekiel 3:17 & 33:7, Hebrews 13:17.) shall with much joy, and loud voice, publish your deliverance. See chapter 40:9, an allusion, as there, and verse 7, so here as some think, to the manner of those that bring tidings, and tell them aloud, in high places, that as many as may be, may hear them; but the term of *watchmen,* suits not so well to such. I rather take it, to have an eye to those, that are placed upon watchtowers, to espy, and give notice of the approach, or coming afar off, of any that may be deemed to come for relief, in straits, or with good tidings after some great battle fought, conquest achieved, or the like. See 2 Samuel 18:24–27, as the former sort, the tidings-bringers are said to appear on the hills, not far distant from the city, verse 7, so the watchmen from the walls, and turrets, about the city, who either descrying them afar off, and by their gesture, or other signs, discerning that they come with good tidings, or receiving, as the usual manner is, the report of things first from them, shall, in the manner here mentioned, publish it to others. See 2 Kings 7:10,11.

*{with the voice together shall they sing?*} So chapter 51:11, *they shall come with song,* or *singing to Zion:* But the particle expressed there is wanting here; as chapter 33:5, and oft elsewhere. But some therefore thus render the context; *As for the voice of thy watchmen;* or, as others, *the voice of thy watchmen,* without aught else prefixed, (which I take to be the better, as Canticles 2:8, as if he heard the one now, saw the other before, verse 7, and were ravished at the hearing of the one, at the sight of the other;) *they lift up the voice, they sing together;* and this reading, the points, and pauses, in the Hebrew, incline to. Some think it has some reference, either to the singing and shouting of the priests and Levites, and others, at the founding of the temple, Ezra 3:10,11. Or, to their singing together afterward in the temple, at the dedication of it after it was built, Ezra 6:16, but they were works of a later date, than this here respected.

*{for they shall see eye to eye, when the Lord shall bring again Zion.*} They shall clearly, and evidently, behold those things fulfilled, that had before by them been foretold, these things performed that had been promised, 1 Peter 10–12.

*{eye to eye*} Numbers 14:14, *face to face,* Genesis 32:30, and *mouth* *to mouth,* Numbers 12:12. See Jeremiah 32:4.

*{when the Lord shall bring again Zion.*} So is the word generally rendered, both here, and Psalm 14:7 & 53:6 & 126:1, in all which places, yet it seems to be word for word in the text, *when the Lord shall return again to Zion,* with a want of the particle *to,* as, chapter 35:10 and 51:11, and it may well be so rendered also in those places of the psalms; *when the Lord shall turn to the captivity of his people;* and, *when the Lord turned unto the captivity of Zion:* when in mercy and favor, he turned again to them; as Numbers 10:36, Psalm 90:13, chapter 63:17. So the sense will be, *when the Lord shall return unto Zion again;* either to his people that had sometime held it, but had been dispossessed of it, and detained long from it, or, to the place itself, to take up his abode, and make his residence again there, as in former time he did, Psalm 132:13,14, chapter 31:9, for God is said to come along with his people, in the front of them, at their return, verse 12. They shall clearly see God himself returning, in conspicuous manner, together with his redeemed ones unto Zion. And this way the most of the Jewish commenters go: Nor can it be denied, but that the word, in the form here used, is commonly, almost generally, intransitive; and signifies, not *to reduce,* as in another form, but *to return.* Howbeit, some places there are, wherein it seems to require a transitive notion, as Job 42:18, *the Lord turned the captivity of Job.* & Nahum 2:2, *The Lord hath turned the pride of the excellency of Jacob;* and so without any supply, it may well be here as our version has it. See Jeremiah 30:3,18.

**V. 9.** *{Break forth into joy, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem:*} That have lain long ruined, but shall now be re-edified, chapter 44:28. Hebrew, *wastes;* as chapter 49:19 & 51:3. See chapter 14:7 and 35:1 & 44:23 & 49:13 and 45:1 and 55:12.

*{for the Lord hath comforted his people,*} Returning in mercy to them, verse 8. See chapter 51:3.

*{he hath redeemed Jerusalem.*} Set her at liberty again, verse 3. See chapter 44:23 & 48:20, Luke 1:68.

**V. 10.** *{The Lord hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations:*} Or, *hath stripped up his arm;* as alluding to the gesture of those, that strip up the sleeve of the arm, to strike the more readily with it. See Ezekiel 4:7, chapter 53:1. *arm,* for *power:* as chapter 51:9, which place this seems to reflect upon. The Lord according to your desire, and suit to him there has raised up himself and shows forth his might, in most conspicuous manner, in the sight of other people, as well as your own, that they cannot but take notice of his handiwork, both in your adversaries' destruction, and in your deliverance, Psalm 98:2, chapter 26:11.

*{holy arm*} Hebrew, *arm of holiness;* as Psalm 98:1.

*{in the eyes*} For, *in the sight,* Psalm 98:2, as, *in the ears,* for, *in the hearing,* chapter 36:11.

*{and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of the Lord*} Or, *that all the ends of the earth may see;* as chapter 41:20,22. Or, *so that all the ends of the earth have seen;* as Psalm 98:3, *the salvation of the Lord;* which he has wrought for his people, chapter 49:26, which shall be so remarkable, that notice shall be taken of it, even in the remotest parts of the world, on every side, unto the land's end, Psalm 67:8 & 98:3, Micah 5:4, Luke 3:6.

**V. 11.** *{Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence:*} Get you with all speed out of Babylon, you that have been hitherto detained in captivity there, chapter 48:20 & 62:10, Jeremiah 50:8 & 51:6, 1 Corinthians 6:17, Revelation 18:4.

*{touch no unclean thing,*} Keep yourselves pure and clean, free from heathenish and idolatrous defilements, 2 Corinthians 6:17 and 7:1, 1 Timothy 5:22, James 1:27, an allusion to legal pollutions, contracted by touch, Leviticus 11:24,39–44 & 22:4–6, Colossians 2:21.

*{Go ye out of the midst of her*} Or, *out of her;* as chapter 5:8, to wit, out of Babylon, as before: a double repetition redoubled.

*{be ye clean, ye that bear the vessels of the Lord.*} Either you that are to bear back the holy vessels, that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away to Babylon, being, by Cyrus, now restored, Daniel 1:2, 2 Chronicles 36:7, Ezra 1:7,8,11. See the charge, by Esdras, given unto them, Ezra 8:28. Or, you priests that are to handle them in your ordinary ministrations, Leviticus 21:6,23, Numbers 4:5,15 & 19:13,19, Ezekiel 22:26, Haggai 2:13,14, and so all Christians called to be spiritual priests, 1 Peter 2:5,9,13, Revelation 1:6.

**V. 12.** *{For ye shall not go out with haste,*} Or, *in haste;* hastily, as they were enjoined to eat the passover, Exodus 12:11, and as they are said to have gone out of Egypt, Exodus 12:33, so that they could not have time to provide themselves of necessaries, Exodus 12:39, Deuteronomy 16:3. But the word seems to import somewhat more than so here: you shall not make haste out of fear, as if you misdoubted, lest you should be intercepted and stayed again, by those that detained you before: for the word it comes from, properly signifies, *to tremble,* Deuteronomy 20:3, and consequently *to make haste out of fear,* 1 Samuel 23:26. It implies therefore, a *frightful* or, *trembling haste,* a making haste out of fear, Psalm 31:12 & 116:11.

*{nor go by flight,*} As if you fled; as they seemed to do out of Egypt, Exodus 14:5, and as those are wont to do, that steal away without the privity of those under whom, or, in whose power, they are, Genesis 31:20,21, and this therefore, and the former, *flight,* and *haste,* are, as here, so elsewhere, joined together, 2 Samuel 4:4, 2 Kings 7:7,16. You shall not go away hastily, out of fear, or by stealth; but you shall depart freely, peaceably, quietly, by commission from public authority, taking your own time, without tumult, noise, or fear of aught, chapter 55:12, 2 Chronicles 36:23, Ezra 1:3,4.

*{for the Lord will go before you; and the God of Israel will be your rereward*} Hebrew, *the Lord is walking,* or, *marching before you; and the God of Israel is gathering you up,* or, *closing you:* as Numbers 10:25, Joshua 6:9,13. You shall not need to fear aught, either in setting out, or on the way; for God will secure, and safeguard you, on every side, both before, and behind. It is an allusion to God's conduct of his people, in their departure from Egypt, and passage through the wilderness, by the the pillar of cloud, and fire; which sometime went in the front with them, and sometime also stood in the rear of them, as was most conducible for their protection and safety, Exodus 13:21 & 14:19,20. So chapter 58:8.

**V. 13.** *{Behold*} At this verse seems to begin a new sermon; certain it is, that they belong to the same subject, with the next chapter, and do together with it, jointly make up an entire prophecy, concerning Christ, his person, parentage, condition, manner of life, sufferings, humiliation, exaltation, benefit redounding thence to his, and honor to himself.

*{Behold*} So is the prophecy of his birth ushered in, chapter 7:14.

*{my servant*} This prophecy, the Jewish commenters themselves affirm to be very difficult; and howsoever their later masters strive all they can, to turn it from Christ, in hatred to whom, they strangely ring, and wrest the several passages of it, writhing, and wriggling them, sometime one way, and sometime another, (wherein I could wish, that some Christian writers had not too far concurred with them,) by, and in applying them, some to Moses, some to Esdras, some to Jesus the son of Josadak, some to Josias, some to Ezekias, some to Esay, some to Jeremy, some to Israel, in general, or the main body of the just ones returned from the captivity; (unto none of all which, the subject matter of it will agree) yet the Chaldee paraphrast expounds it of the Messiah; and so likewise some of them acknowledge upon the place, that their ancient doctors did. The title was before given unto Christ, chapter 42:1, and hereafter, chapter 53:11, so called by God the Father, who here speaks of him, because he did him service in the work of man's redemption, Luke 2:49, John 5:17,30 and 6:38 and 9:4 and 10:18 and 12:49 and 14:31 and 17:4 and 12:21, Philippians 2:7,8, for the deliverance of his elect from the thraldom of sin, and Satan, Matthew 1:21, Galatians 1:4 and 3:13, 1 Thessalonians 1:10, Titus 2:14, Hebrews 2:14,15.

*{shall deal prudently*} So the word seems to be used of David, 1 Samuel 18:30. Or, *shall prosper;* and so it is generally deemed to be used of the Messiah, descended from David, Jeremiah 23:5, of whom also it is said, chapter 53:10, that *the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in his hand.*

*{he shall be exalted, and extolled, and be very high.*} Divers terms heaped up, to express in part the transcendent, and unexpressible advancement of Christ, in regard of his human nature, assumed by his deity, the Eternal Word, to subsist in one person with it, John 1:14, Hebrews 2:16. For the Talmudists do but trifle, when they dream of three distinct degrees in the text; *exalted* above Abraham, *extolled* above Moses, and *advanced* above the angels; though the things themselves be true, John 8:53,56, Hebrews 3:3–5 & 1:4–7, but not so particularly here intended. Rather, as some of ours every way exalted, that men are ordinarily wont so to be; to wit, when raised from a mean estate to some honorable condition, or from a private life, to magistracy, and government, Genesis 41:14,40–44, Psalm 105:17–22 and 78:70,71 and 113:7,8, Ecclesiastes 1:14. Or, when furnished with such parts, and endowments of wisdom and understanding, as makes them admirable in the eyes of others, Genesis 41:39, 1 Kings 3:12 and 10:24, Daniel 1:19,20 and 5:11, and when enabled to perform and go through with great matters, whereby they become famous, and renowned, far and near, 2 Samuel 7:8,9, 2 Chronicles 26:5–8. In all which respects, our Savior was most eminently exalted, above all creatures in heaven, and earth; as by the Scriptures above pointed to, and those typical psalms, 2 and 45 and 72, 110, most evidently appears. See on chapter 53:4. See Ephesians 1:20–22, Philippians 2:9,10, Colossians 1:19 and 2:3,9, Hebrews 2:7,8 and 12:3.

**V. 14.** *{As many were astonied at thee*} The speech of the Father, not of Christ, as before; but unto Christ, whom he here directs his speech unto. The words some expound, of an astonishment at Christ, in way of admiration of him, in regard of the power of his deity, and his excellent parts, appearing, and manifesting themselves, partly, in his manner of teaching, and partly, in the miracles, and mighty works wrought by him, Matthew 7:28,29 and 8:27 and 13:54 and 22:33, Mark 1:22,27 and 6:2 and 7:37 and 11:18, Luke 9:43. But this sense suits not well with the course of the context. The word rather, according, both to the original, and the ordinary use of it, is here to be understood of such an astonishment as arises from the contemplation of some strange, uncouth, and rueful spectacle of desolation, deformity, misery, or the like. So is it used, Leviticus 26:32, where the notation of it also is expressed. So also, 1 Kings 9:8, 2 Chronicles 7:21, Jeremiah 18:16 & 19:8 & 49:17 & 50:13, Ezekiel 26:16 & 27:35 & 28:19, and no marvel, if many were astonished at the sight of our Savior's condition, in regard of those base, disgraceful, and despiteful usages, that were offered, and done, to him, in the time of his humiliation here on earth, when his followers were so amazed at the relation of them, when they were sometime foretold them, Mark 10:32–34.

*{(his visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men)*} Those that expound the foregoing branch, of men's wondering at Christ's excellencies, make these words the second member of the collation, which the note of similitude, prefixed to the former, shows, here to be intended: as if the text ran thus; As he was sometime highly admired for his powerful words and works; so he shall afterward be as much abused and disgraced again. But the reddition of the similitude, comes afterward in the next verse: this being inserted between both, by way of *parenthesis,* with a transition from person to person, in this prophet not unusual; (see chapter 1:29,30 & 2:9 & 3:25,26, and we need not therefore, with some of ours, either offer to alter the text, or understand the former, of one person; and the latter of another: that, of Israel, this, of Christ,) as rendering a reason, why at sight of our Savior, in time of his depression, many should be so astonished. Howbeit, the words are not so to be understood, as if our blessed Savior had, in regard of his bodily person, or presence, been some strange, deformed, or misshapen creature; but in regard of his outward estate, coming of mean, and obscure parentage, chapter 53:2, living in a low despicable condition, chapter 53:3, exposed to scorn, and contempt, and to much affliction, through the whole course of his life, chapter 53:2, and more especially, yet, in regard of what he was also in his personal appearance; through the base and despiteful usages, that he sustained at the hands of his malicious and mischievous adversaries, when they had gotten him into their power, Psalm 22:12–18 and 69:19–21 & 71:7, chapter 50:6 and 52:5,7,10, Matthew 26:67,68 and 27:16–44, Mark 14:65 & 15:15–32, Luke 22:44,63 & 23:26,33,35,39, John 19:1,5,16–18,23,29. A learned late writer would have this passage read by way of interrogation, as the words of those that wonder at the sight of Christ, thus rendering the text, saying, (as Psalm 105:15.) *is his visage in such manner corrupted,* or, *marred?* etc. But the former version seems the more familiar, and to come off more freely.

*{his visage was so marred*} His watching, dragging to and fro, from place to place, buffeting, scourging, carrying his cross, and other misusage, could not, but much alter the state of his body, and impair, yea, deface all the sightliness of it. Howbeit, the word *visage,* here, and *form,* in the next branch, seem to be taken more largely for all outward appearance, both of bodily shape and of state, or condition in general, as *sight* or appearance, chapter 11:3, John 7:24, and *form,* 1 Samuel 28:14, 2 Timothy 3:5, and *face,* or *person,* Deuteronomy 16:19, Romans 2:11. So chapter 53:2. Hebrew, *such the corruption of his visage more than,* or, *above a man:* for they seem wide here, who drawing the word from another root, would have it rendered, *the unction of his person above any man,* Psalm 45:2,7.

*{more than any man*} Hebrew, *than a man: a man* for, *any man,* or, *any one;* as chapter 4:11 & 40:26 & 50:2, so that he seemed rather as a worm, than a man, Psalm 22:6.

*{and his form more than the sons of men*} As if no form, or shape of a man, were left to be seen in him: as some render those words, Psalm 38:3, chapter 1:6, the same notion in other terms; as Job 25:6.

**V. 15.** *{So shall he sprinkle many nations*} The reddition, or latter part of the collation, concerning Christ's exaltation, opposed to the former, concerning his humiliation, verse 14, and further confirming and illustrating what concerning Christ's success, and advancement, was before delivered, verse 13.

*{sprinkle*} The Jewish commenters expound these words, some of them, of the slaughter that he should make of his enemies; *he shall sprinkle them,* that is, shed their blood; chapter 63:3, *their blood was sprinkled upon my garments;* some of them, of the reports that shall go abroad of his honor, and valor; for the term of *sprinkling,* or *dropping* rather, is, say they, used of speech, Deuteronomy 32:2, Ezekiel 20:46 & 41:2, Amos 7:16, Micah 2:6,11. So the meaning should be, he shall make them to *sprinkle,* or *drop;* that is, give them occasion to talk of him: but the word of *sprinkling,* is one, those of *dropping,* other: and this never found so used; though those are. Others of them again, but without example, likewise, would have the word taken, in a notion of *dispersion,* he shall, say they, grow strong, and drive away the horns of the heathen, that had formerly dispersed God's people, Zechariah 1:21. But these interpretations are groundless, and forced. Ours expound the words much to one effect; to wit, that Christ should bedew many nations with the doctrine of the gospel, by the ministry of his apostles, and thereby convert them to the faith, through the efficacy of the Spirit, accompanying the same, and working faith in them, chapter 59:10,21, Matthew 28:18, Acts 2:33,38,41, Romans 10:17, 2 Corinthians 3:6. Or, which comes all to one, that he should sanctify, and cleanse them with his Spirit, imparted to them, by the word, and with his blood, by faith applied unto their souls, Ezekiel 36:25,27, John 15:3 & 17:17, Acts 15:9, Galatians 3:2, Ephesians 5:26, 1 Peter 1:2, 1 John 1:7, Revelation 1:5 & 7:14, an allusion, as some think, to the water, and washing with it, used in the evangelical baptism, Matthew 3:11, John 3:5, Acts 2:38 & 21:16, 1 Peter 3:21, as others, to the the legal baptizings, or sprinklings, with water, or blood, or both mixed together; for the sanctifying of some, and cleansing of others, that were legally unclean, Exodus 24:6,8 & 29:4,20,21, Leviticus 13:6,7,8, Numbers 19:12–21, Psalm 51:7, Hebrews 9:10,13,14,18–22 & 10:8,10,22.

*{many nations*} As many persons astonished at him before; verse 14, so many people now taken with him, and converted to him, chapter 2:3, yet *many,* not *all;* as Matthew 28:18, because not accepted by some, though offered to all, Acts 2:41 and 17:11,18,32–34.

*{the kings shall shut their mouths at him*} *Kings* simply, (for there is no article in the original) or *even kings* (as chapter 51:12,22 and 60:10 & 62:2.) *shall shut their mouths* (Hebrew, *mouth* as, *tongue,* also, Job 29:10.) out of reverence and respect, out of another manner of astonishment at him now, than before, verse 14, to wit, out of admiration of his incomparable excellency. See Job 29:9,10. Or, being so convinced of the truth of his teaching, that they shall not be able, or dare once to contradict it, Luke 21:12,15. See Job 40:4,5, Psalm 107:42, Micah 7:17. But the former seems rather here chiefly intended. For the Jewish critic does but dally here who, to make this suit with his forced fancy, concerning the foregoing branch, would fasten upon this a double sense: the word here used, says he, has a twofold notion; of *opening,* and of *shutting;* of *opening,* as it signifies *to skip:* for in skipping, or leaping, the feet are opened, Canticles 2:8, of *shutting,* or *closing,* Deuteronomy 15:7, Job 5:16, here it may import both: they shall open their mouths to talk of him; and they shall shut their mouths, in way of wonderment at him. But this is to make a *Delphic* word of God's word. And yet such quirks are too many much taken with.

*{for that which had not been told them, shall they see; and that which they had not heard, shall they consider.*} *For,* Hebrew, *And;* as chapter 40:29. They shall see those things fulfilled, which their wizards could never foretell; nor had been told by any other, and they shall hear such mysteries, yea, not hear them only: but consider seriously of them, and understand them aright. (See chapter 1:3.) as they never had been made acquainted with, or had once thought on before, chapter 41:26 and 45:21 and 64:4, Romans 16:25,26, 1 Corinthians 2:8,9. Or, as others read, and render the words; *they to whom it had not been related,* or, *to whom nothing had been related of him, shall see: and those that had not heard; shall consider,* or, *understand.* So the ancient, both Greek and Latin, and of ours not a few. See chapter 65:1, Romans 15:20,21. I go rather with the former; the syntax seeming to me the more familiar, and the fuller. The same way go the Jewish commenters, save that some of them conceive it spoken, not simply, and absolutely, but comparatively; they shall see greater glory, and excellency in him, than ever they heard, or dreamed of; they shall find, and know his magnificence to go far beyond whatsoever they had been told, or could conceive of him before. See of Solomon, 1 Kings 10:6,7.

### CHAPTER 53

**V. 1.** *{Who hath believed our report?*} Or, *who believeth our report?* Or, *doctrine;* as chapter 28:19. Or, *preaching,* as some render it, Hosea 7:12. Hebrew, *hearing,* chapter 28:19, that which they hear from us; those glad tidings before mentioned, chapter 52:7. Some for the better connection of the ensuing discourse, with the former, prefix the adversative particle, *But;* rendering the words: *But who believeth our report?* that is, who, say they, of the Jewish people: the fewness of those that received the gospel among that people, being opposed to the multitudes of other nations, that should embrace it, and believe in Christ, chapter 52:15. So the words contain a complaint of the paucity, and small number of those, among the Jews, that gave any credit to the prophecies foregoing, concerning Christ, and the doctrine of his kingdom, and his glorious advancement, either in the times of this our prophet, and other his fellow messengers; or, in the time, that being exhibited in the flesh, he lived here upon earth: unto which times, we find these words applied in the gospel, John 12:37,38, Romans 10:16. See chapter 49:4, John 3:32 & 5:43,44 & 7:5,48, Acts 28:22. See for the form of speech, Psalm 90:11, chapter 50:10.

*{and*} Or, *or;* as, chapter 40:13,18.

*{to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?*} His mighty power working by, and manifesting itself in Christ, and in the ministry of his word, chapter 40:10 & 51:5 & 52:10, Romans 1:16, 1 Corinthians 1:18,24, which must from God be revealed, before it can be believed, chapter 54:23, Matthew 11:25 & 16:17, John 6:44,45, 1 Corinthians 2:9,12, Galatians 1:12. Hebrew, *upon whom;* which some taking hold of, thus render the text; *upon whom is the arm of the Lord stripped up,* or, *made bare?* that is, on whom has the ministry of his servants an efficacious work, for the converting of them unto God? a metaphor, say they, taken from workmen, who are wont, for the better expedition, to strip the arm up to the elbow, when they go about their work. See chapter 52:10. But this seems overcurious; nor will the Greek, in the gospel, bear it: and the particle, though it usually signify *upon;* yet is it also frequently used for *unto;* as Exodus 20:3, *to my face:* so the words there are, 2 Kings 18:27, compared with Esay 36:12, Psalm 13:6 & 18:41, chapter [unclear]:12, with verse 11.

**V. 2.** *{For he shall grow up before him, as a tender plant*} Hebrew, *And;* which both the old Greek, and Latin, and some other after them retain. Others, render it, *Indeed,* as chapter 30:20. Or, *Yet;* as verse 7, chapter 46:7, and others again, not a few, whom our version concurs with, *For;* as verse 11, chapter 52:15 & 64:5, as ushering in a passage, wherein the ground is discovered, and a reason rendered, how it came, or should come to pass, that so few of the Jewish nation should entertain Christ, as the Messiah, and their Savior, and give belief to the doctrine of the prophets and apostles, concerning him. They looked for a Messiah to come in princely state, with royal attendance, and secular power, that should reign and rule, as some mighty monarch, and set them free from the bondage of the Roman empire, and when they saw nothing less; but all clean contrary in Christ, hence came it to pass, that they were offended in him, and could by no means be induced to believe that such an one should be their Messiah, Matthew 13:55,57, Luke 24:21, John 7:27,41,52, 1 Corinthians 1:23.

*{grow up*} Hebrew, *ascend;* which some understand, of Christ's exaltation; as if it were said, that he should rise and grow great, for all this, that so few entertain him, and believe in him. And some of note, to this purpose, would thus join this verse with the latter part of the former; *And he, on whom the arm of the Lord shall be revealed* (to wit, Christ) *shall grow up:* but this offers too much violence to the context. And albeit, the word here used, does sometime import *a rising,* by advancement, and improvement of height, strength, stature, or state, chapter 40:31, Jeremiah 51:53, yet it is used commonly of plants, simply springing up, without any such special connotation, chapter 32:3, and all the circumstances of the text do carry it another way, as in the opening of the words will appear.

*{before him*} This small particle is very variously expounded. Some understand it, of God; that in the sight of God, he should be great, and highly esteemed, though mean, and of no account in man's eyes, as the like is said, in express terms, of John his harbinger, Luke 1:15, and, in effect, of Christ also, Luke 1:32. Or, that by his most wise, and powerful providence, he should be produced, and under his protection, having his eye perpetually upon him, grow up to a great height, chapter 52:13. Others, of the people, in whose eyes he should appear, and seem to be such, as is hereafter intimated. Others, of Christ himself, that he should be lowly, and of small esteem in his own sight; as it is said of Saul, 1 Samuel 15:17, and in the person of Christ, Psalm 22:6. Others, lastly, of none of all these; because no express mention of any of these, unto whom it may fitly be referred, but of the outward show that Christ should make, rendering the text, *for his appearance,* or *outward show,* or *state:* for the word *face,* in Hebrew, is very frequently so used; as was before showed, on chapter 52:14, and answers to the word *sight,* or, *appearance;* used afterward, in the last clause of this verse. *for sight,* as, *for height,* Proverbs 25:3, where the same particle is so used; and this best suits with the scope, and current of the context.

*{as a tender plant*} The word *tender* is not in the text; and true it is, that the term here used, is of a large extent in the ordinary use of it, comprehending branches of all sorts, without distinction of strength, or size. See Psalm 80:11, Hosea 14:6, Job 8:15,16,30 & Ezekiel 17:4, where, though our version renders it, *a young twig,* which would do very well here; yet the words, next before-going, control it there. The word properly signifies, *a suckling,* or *sucking child,* Numbers 11:12, Psalm 8:2, 1 Samuel 15:3 & 22:19, Jeremiah 44:7, Lamentations 2:11 and 4:4, and so the ancient Greek, and some after them, here take it; but the resemblance, here used, admits not that. In the next place, therefore, the word does signify sometime, *a branch,* or, *bough,* in general, because it sucks, and draws the sap and moisture, as milk, from the root, or stock, from whence it shoots up, or spreads out, Romans 11:17. Sometime, more specially, such a *plant,* or, *twig,* as resembles for its tenderness, and smallness of growth, some *suckling,* or *sucking child:* so is it used, Job 14:7, where it is not amiss rendered, *a tender branch;* and may well here (the circumstances of the place, not well admitting only, but requiring it) *a tender plant,* or *young twig,* as we use to say, *a sucker:* for so use we to term such young plants, as shoot up from the root of some elder tree, or stander. See chapter 11:1. This some understand of the mean beginnings of Christ's kingdom; though afterward wonderfully thriving and prospering, Matthew 13:31,32, Mark 4:27–32. Others, rather of Christ himself. See chapter 11:1.

*{and as a root out of a dry ground*} By *root,* some understand here, a *sprig,* sprouting out, or springing up from a root; as chapter 11:10, Revelation 5:5, but it may be here taken in its ordinary notion; the word, *sprig,* or *twig,* or *plant,* being supplied from the former branch, as is not unusual. See on chapter 51:8, and so the words may be rendered; *and as,* or *even as* (as chapter 1:6 & 40:30.) *the twig,* or *plant of a root, that riseth out of a dry ground.* Hebrew, *a ground of drought,* or *dryness,* as Psalm 63:1 & 68:6, where it is strange (says the Jewish commenter) that tree, or herb, should take root, and much more unlikely, that it should thrive, and bear fruit, as this plant was to do, chapter 52:13, verse 10. By this *dry ground,* some understand the Virgin Mary, Christ's mother, in regard of hope of issue, while she should so continue, as such. See chapter 56:3, Luke 1:34. Others, of the decayed stock of David, and mean family of Jesse, that then seemed to be a dry tree, or dead *trunk* of a tree rather; as being reduced to a far lower estate, than it was in at first. See chapter 11:1. But I suppose we need not appropriate this limb of the collation, unto either of these, albeit, the consideration of the mean, and low state and condition of both these (Joseph the Virgin's husband being also taken into them) come within compass of that, which is here aimed at; to wit, the mean condition of our Savior, which made him so despicable in the eyes of his own people, Luke 1:48 & 2:24 & 3:23, Matthew 13:55, Mark 6:3. It is sufficient, that by this resemblance is intimated, such a poor, and bare condition, without sightly show or state, as might well be compared to some sorry plant, that had, with much ado, shot up, and got above ground from some, almost sapless root, in some such waste and waterless place. See Jeremiah 17:6.

*{he hath no form, nor comeliness*} The former word applied to a plant, seems to import the sightliness, or comeliness of a plant, or tree in regard of the trunk, and body of it, its shape, proportion, straightness, smoothness, well coloredness, and the like: for it comes of a word, that signifies, *to delineate, draw out,* or *portray* aught, in its due shape and lineaments, Joshua 15:9,11 & 19:13, chapter 44:23, and applied to mankind, or womankind, signifies a person well composed, and complexion, well faced and featured, or well proportioned, and shaped, Genesis 29:17 & 36:6. So it is used also of beasts, Genesis 41:2, where, with its epithet, it is rendered, *well-favored,* and might as well be, *well-featured, and fat:* fatness bettering the feature of a beast, as leanness defaces it: the latter seems to have reference, in plants, to that sightliness of them, that proceeds from the leaves, and blossoms, and keys, and fruits, or other like verdure, wherewith such are wont to be arrayed and adorned. So it is used, Leviticus 23:40, where they are enjoined at the feast of tabernacles to take *the fruit,* (that is, *boughs,* or *branches,* as it is explained, Nehemiah 8:15. Or more specially *leafy boughs,* and *branches,* (for so the word there used, properly signifies. See Proverbs 11:28.) *of trees of sightliness,* or *goodliness,* that is, of *sightly,* or *goodly trees,* (as it is there rendered, of such trees, as were thick with leaves, and twigs, as in both places it is afterward expounded) to make them booths of. And hence applied to beasts, it is attributed to such, as are furnished, and garnished with goodly and stately heads or horns, Deuteronomy 33:17. Given to men, and women, it is used of such, as are attired and decked with goodly and gorgeous apparel, chapter 63:1, Ezekiel 16:10,14, where the word is also used. Hence those speeches in the Proverbs, *In the multitude of people, is the sightliness of a king,* Proverbs 14:28, as if he had said, not so much, in his rich and royal robes, as in the numerousness of his subjects; and Proverbs 20:29, *the bravery of young men is their strength; and the sightliness of old men is the gray head;* that is, vigor and valor, sets out, and adorns the one; and his gray hairs, the other; more than fine, and gay apparel does either. Now leaves and verdure, are to plants, as vestments and attire, unto man, or woman. Howbeit, some of the rabbines, on Genesis 29:17, where *beauty* in two distinct respects, is given unto Rachel, and use made of these two words, by the former, understand the *feature,* or *composure of the face,* by the other, the *clearness* of the complexion or countenance. But I suppose them not to be so strictly here taken. Howsoever, the mean estate of the Messiah, void of all show and luster, that is wont to draw men's eyes after it, is here very pithily and pregnantly, set forth, and deciphered, by the resemblance of such a plant, as has neither height nor strength, nor comely shape, nor leaves, or verdure, to make it any way sightly, or desirable. Or, if it shall be deemed, that in the former branch only, some plant is alluded unto, the person of man rather in this latter; such a party is here intimated, as for personage and state, may be compared unto such a plant, as by such notions has been described. See chapter 1:30.

*{and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him*} Hebrew, *and we shall see him, and no sight* (or *sightliness;* for so the word sounds, having an elegant consonance, with the term of *seeing,* whence it is derived, chapter 52:14, and comprehends both the former) *is* (to wit, *in him,* a defect of the pronoun, as Deuteronomy 3:12, chapter 35:9, the like syntax, see Proverbs 4:23, chapter 37:9,36.) Or (as it may be rendered; by supply from the former member, as Genesis 1:16, chapter 52:6.) we shall not *see* any *sightliness* in him; *and we shall desire him,* for *that we should desire him:* as chapter 40:25, Malachi 1:9, that is, for which or in regard whereof, we should have any desire, or affection unto him: neither is there any need, as some would, to supply the negative from the former branch, as Psalm 9:18, Proverbs 30:3, rendering the words, *and we shall not desire him,* there being as much implied without it. He that is styled, *the desire of all nations,* Haggai 1:7, (whence some are of opinion, that *Mechmed,* or *Mahommed,* borrowed his name, that he might be deemed as another Messiah) and who much better than Daniel, might be termed, *a man of desires,* Daniel 10:11,19, having all desirable things that can be; yea, all desirableness, treasured up in him, Colossians 2:3,9, in true beauty, and excellency, far exceeding and surpassing, not the sons of men only, Psalm 45:2,7, but the angels themselves, Hebrews 1:4, yet appears so stripped, and divested of all show of any such matter, Philippians 2:6,7,8, that his own people, when they see him, can discern nothing at all sightly, or desirable in him. See Ch. 52.14.

**V. 3.** *{He is despised, and rejected of men*} It was not enough to say of him, that he was not desired, ver. 2. but he adds further now, that he was, as some: not base only and despicable, but even vile, and abominable creature, both despised, and rejected. See Chap. 49.7. *despised*, as of Jeconiah, Jer. 22.28. *rejected of men*: or, as some, taking the word for a noun: *a rejection of men*; the abstract for the concrete; as 1 Cor. 4.13. But I conceive it rather to be a participle, found entire, Ezek. 3.27. but here contracted, because it rests on the word adjoined to it: and it is not amiss rendered by our translators, *rejected of men*; that is, as one of the Jewish commenters; either more abject than any man, as Chap. 52.14. (as so there should be a want of the preposition there used, as there is also, Chap. 20.7. & 32.2. and that in this very notion, also) Chap. 65.5. or, one *severed*, and *cast out* from the company and society of men; as scarce deemed worthy the name of a man, Psalm 22.6. and unworthy, therefore, to converse with men, or to have any communion with them. See of Paul; Act. 22.22. and this latter fits well with the Hebrew; for it is word for word, *leaving of men*, or, *ceasing from men*: as one that cannot be admitted to any society with them: the condition of the leper, Levit. 13.46. 2 Chr. 26.21. deemed in that regard, as *dead*, Num. 12.10,12,14. See Psalm 31.11,12. & 88.4,5–8. So rather, than as one, *the last*, or *lowest of men*: as Paul of himself, *the last, and least of the Apostles*; yea, *the least*, or (as the word imports, composed of a twofold degree of comparison) *less than the least of the Saints; not worthy to be called an Apostle*, 1 Cor. 15.8,9. Eph. 5.8. so here, as we would say the very list, or fag end of mankind, one, at whom the nature, and name of man ends; so mean, and so low, that the nature of man can hardly descend lower, and may therefore seem scarce worthy the name of a man. See Psalm 22.6. and what Agur of himself, Proverbs 30.2. But this seems to strain somewhat too far. Howbeit, Christ of himself says, that he was to be *made nought-worth*, or *nothing*, Mar. 9.12.

*{a man of sorrows*} Not *of sorrow* barely; but *of sorrows*: not a man *full of sorrow*, or *filled with sorrow* only; as the psalmist speaks *Our soul is exceedingly filled with scorn, and contempt*, Psal. 123.3,4. but, *a man of sorrows*, as the psalmist elsewhere; *My soul is full of evils*; with evil of all sorts, or all sorts of evil, Psal. 88.3. and as Solomon, *a man of wicked devices*, Prov. 12.2. a man, not wholly set upon, and addicted unto evil, only; such an one as Moses describes, Gen. 6.5. *all the device of whose heart*, (or whatsoever he devises) *is all day long only* (that is, continually nothing but) *evil*: but a man made up of evil, or wicked devices of all sorts; that devises nothing but evil, and refrains no device that is evil, Psal. 36.4. as if he consisted of nothing but such: so *a man of sorrows*, of sorrows of all sorts, so full of them, that he may seem to consist wholly of them to be made of no other mold: nothing but sorrow to be seen in him, (see Chap. 1.6.) and variety of sorrows, sorrows of all sorts; such sorrows, as for our sake he sustained, and for our sins, verse 4,5.

*{and acquainted with grief*} The participle here used, is by the Jewish critics diversely expounded. Some of them would have it signify *cut off*, or *destroyed with infirmity*, or *grief*. So they suppose the word whereof it comes, to be taken, Judg. 8.16. Prov. 10.9. & 14.33. Jer. 31.19. Ezek. 19.7. but these places are not so pregnant; and others of them, understand them as in another notion: the most of them therefore herein depart from them; and expound it according to the ordinary use, and sense of the verb: some *known by infirmity*; well known, or commonly known, to be much subject thereunto, and exercised therewith, one so encompassed with infirmities, as, Heb. 5.1. that they cannot but appear, and be seen in him by all that behold him: thus they take it, because the word is in a passive form, and is by most so taken, Deut. 1.13,15. but those passive forms have sometime an active, or a neuter notion, as in our languages, also, sometime the like: and so others of them, as most of ours, take this here, rendering it, *one knowing of infirmity*; as it sounds word for word, that is, knowing it experimentally: as it is said, *he that knew not sin*, 2 Cor. 5.21. that neither had drawn aught of it from any other, nor done any himself: and as the tree inhibited, was called *the tree of the knowledge of good and evil*, Gen. 2.9,17. not, as the devil suggested, because the fruit thereof eaten, had a singular power to give man a notional knowledge of good and evil, which before he had not: but because, upon the eating of it contrary to God's command, man should come to have an experimental knowledge of evil, as well as of good, which before he had not: yea, and in some sort, of the benefit and excellency of good also, being by the want, better; by the loss of it (which is yet more) best known, so we use to say, *such an one never knew what misery meant*, having lived free from it, and, *a man never knows what health is*, until he have had a fit of sickness: thus it might be rendered, *knowing of infirmity*, as *men knowing of the sea*, 1 King. 9.27. and, *knowing of the times*, Est. 1.13. and, *knowing of good and evil*, Gen. 3.5. (for so the words are in those places) that is, *skillful* in those things: and as we use to say, *a knowing man*, for one *skillful* in aught: or, to fit it better to the Hebrew form, *a man skilled in infirmity*, as both the ancient Greek, and some of ours, also, take the word for *skillful*, or *skilled*, in the place of Deuteronomy before pointed to: or, as the word *taught*, C. 54.13. does sometime imply, not only *learned*, and so skilled in aught, but one also *expert*, or *experienced in*, and *accustomed*, or *inured* unto aught, Jer. 2.24. & 3.23. and the word of *learning* is used by the apostle, both of himself, Phil. 4.11,12. and of Christ, Heb. 5.8. so the word here may be taken, one *inured to infirmity*, or *grief*, and *accustomed* thereunto; which by ours is very fitly rendered, *acquainted* therewith; as we use to say of those, who not only know one another by hearsay, or by sight, but that have familiarly conversed together. Or, lastly, as some render the word, both in Moses, and here, *known of it*: as those are said to be well known of us, that we have been frequently conversant, and familiarly acquainted with, Hos. 5.5. Amos 3.2. which, as it comes nearest to the ordinary acception, and construction of the terms in the original, so is it the same, in effect, with the last before proposed. Howsoever, the notice, or acquaintance, is attributed to the person, in the one; to the affection, in the other: both which, in substance, come all to one: and import thus much; That Christ, and human griefs, and infirmities, were to have great, and much acquaintance, the one with the other, he having had in his person, much experience of them, and they constantly keeping together with him: a great comfort to all those that have interest in him, Hebrews 4.15.

*{grief*} The word here used; (as the root also from whence it springs) has, in the first place, a notion of *disease*, or *sickness*, Chap. 38.1,9. in the next place, (because sickness usually brings pain, and weakness with it, they are either of them used, sometime, in a notion of *vexation*, and *grief*: as Eccl. 5.17. & 6.2. Jer. 5.3. Hos. 5.13. sometime, in a notion of *infirmity*, and *weakness*, as Judges 16.7,11,17. Chap. 14.10. and of either of these, proceeding as well from any affliction of body, or mind, as from any natural disease: in either of which latter notions, it may well be here taken, not so fitly in the first: because we read not of any peculiar *disease*, such as we usually appropriate that term unto, that our Savior was troubled with, all his life: and by some of the ancients, it is not improbably deemed, that he was not exercised with any such; it being not so suitable for him, to have any disease hanging on him, that showed his power constantly, in the healing of others; that it might not be objected to him, as in another kind, and upon another occasion, it was; *Physician heal thy self*, Luk. 4.23. *infirmity* for *infirmities*, collectively, as Heb. 5.2.

*{and we hid as it were our faces from him*} The words in Hebrew are both diversely read, and diversely resolved. For some make the first word a participle, *as one hiding*, or *one that hideth*: and the participle, in that flexion, is very commonly so framed. Others make it a noun verbal, *as an hiding*, and some verbals of that form are found. Again, some render the last, the particle with the pronoun *from us*, and that not a few embrace. Others, *from him*, and so the pronoun in that form, is most frequently used, yet in the other notion, also, not unusual, Gen. 3.22. Psal. 2.3. Hence arise variety of versions; Some render the words, *and he hid, as it were the face* (that is, his face, the pronoun supplied, as Chap. 59.2.) *from us*; or *he is as one that hideth his face*. Heb. *the face from him*, or *of him*: but of this latter construction, I find no suitable example. But whether of these two ways we read, or render the words, they import such a condition of dejection, and confusion, and of affection thence arising, as makes a man, like one ashamed of himself, to cover his face, as not enduring to look up, or to be seen, and to shun the sight of others: and so the meaning should be, he is one, who, as conscious to himself, either of the deformity, and loathsomeness of his person, or of his despicable and dejected estate, hides his face from human sight: the one was the leper's case, Levit. 13.45. the other, Babylons, Chap. 47.3,5. and hence, together with the help of another word in the next verse, have the Talmudists coined us a tale, how that one of their great masters met with their Messiah, at Rome, where he found him, lying among the lepers. But others render the words, *and as an hiding of faces*, or *of the face*, (for the word, though of a plural form, yet is ordinarily of a singular notion, as Prov. 25.23. Cha. 59.2.) *from him*, or *as he, from whom one would hide the face*, or *his face*; as before: that is, as one, whom men hide their faces from: this sense our version follows: and following it, it may seem that it should rather be rendered; *and as one, from whom the face is hid*, or *men's faces are hid*: for according to this reading, the words are more general, and indefinite; there being no *our*, in the text. Now *hiding the face*, proceeds, sometime, from a reverent respect, and awful dread, Exod. 3.6. 1 King. 19.13. sometime, from some glorious splendor, that dazzles the eyesight, Chap. 6.2. Exod. 34.30,33. 2 Cor. 3.13. sometime, from some strange passion of love, that with a kind of ravishment, affects the lover, upon the sight of his beloved, and casts him into fainting fits. Cant. 6.5. compared with Chap. 4.9. (for they, palpably abuse, both that Scripture, and the church's eyes, that is, her teachers, who thence would force a malignity intimated in them,) sometime from pity, and compassion; when men cannot endure to see some person dear unto them, or any of the same nature with them, cruelly dealt with, or otherwise, in some lamentable condition, Est. 8.6. sometime, out of extreme hatred, or at least, out of displeasure, indignation, or wrath, 2 Sam. 14.8. Psal. 10.1. & 27.9. Chap. 54.8. & 59.2. sometime, out of neglect, and disregard; as from one, whom we list not to look after, Chap. 58.7. sometime, out of detestation, as from some vile, loathsome, abhorred, and abominable creature, whom we cannot brook, or abide to behold, Chap. 1.13,14,15. and to this purpose, one of the Jewish commenters tells us, that there is a certain people that cannot endure the sight of a Jew, but turn the face from him, wheresoever they meet with any of them. But whether that be, or ever were so, or no, is not much material; not at all, to this text. Howbeit, in this last notion, wherewith some also take in two of the next before it, I conceive the words may well be here understood. See Chap. 49.7. yet not concurring with those that attribute this, *hiding of the face*, unto pity and compassion; because it crosses the main drift of the whole context: nor consenting with them, that suppose the covering of men's faces condemned to die, to be here pointed at; as Ch. 25.7. Est. 7.8. To which purpose, they draw in also the blindfolding of Christ, Luk. 22.64. but that is the covering of the party's own face by others, not the hiding of others from him. Howbeit, all things well weighed, I incline rather to the first, both reading, and rendering; because it both fits well the scope of the place, as importing a despicable and shameful condition, and that of one, who seemed to be divested of that magnificence, which formerly he had been possessed of. See Joh. 17.5. Phil. 2.6,7,8. Heb. 12.2. and flows most freely, without any force at all, from the terms used in the text.

*{he was despised*} Or, *he is despised* as in the beginning of the verse, Ps. 22.6. repeated again for the more emphasis. So Ch. 14.26,27. Psal. 68.22.

*{and we esteemed him not*} Or, *esteem him not*; (Phi. 2.7. *he made himself of no esteem*) or *regard him not*; as the word is rendered, Chap. 33.8. *he regards no man*, Psal. 144.3. the great contempt that should be offered unto Christ by the Jewish nation, being expressed here in a form of extenuation, but to be conceived in a notion of exaggeration, as if it had been said more fully. We shall not only, when he comes amongst us, afford him no respect, or regard; but shall very reproachfully, and disgracefully abuse him. See the like manner of speech, Prov. 10.2. *Treasure wickedly gotten shall not profit*; that is, shall do a man much mischief: and, *the father of a fool shall not rejoice*; he shall have no joy, but much grief, of him, Prov. 17.21. and, *It is not good to have respect of persons in Judgment*, that is, indeed, it is stark naught, Prov. 24.23. and, *If any man love not the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema, maranatha*; that is, accursed, without revocation, irrevocably, and irrecoverably accursed, 1 Cor. 16.22. a text by some, extremely tentered; meant of such, as out of mere malice alone against knowledge oppose Christ, and Christianity, such as our Savior speaks of, Matthew 12.32. and the apostle, Heb. 6.6. & 10.26,27,29.

**V. 4.** *{Surely he hath born our griefs, and carried our sorrows*} He took upon him, not our nature alone but the infirmities also of it; and became liable to such sorrows of affliction, and pains, as man's sinful nature is exposed, and subject unto, Rom. 8.3. Heb. 4.15. ver. 3. Or, the griefs and sorrows, that he is said to have been so abundantly exercised with, ver. 3. (for these words have apparent reference to the very same there used) he sustained for us: and are therefore called *ours*; because procured to him, by our sins; and sustained by him, for the discharge of our sins, unto the guilt whereof, out of love to us, undertaken by him, they were deservedly due, Heb. 9.29. 1 Pet. 2.24. & 3.8. Some would have the former word rendered, *he took away*, or *hath taken away, our griefs*, that is, our sins, the procuring cause of them, together with the griefs themselves, the effect of them: And it is true, that the word signifies, sometime, to take away, as Job 7.21. and that our Savior is said *to take away the sins of the world*, Joh. 1.29. but the sequel of the context carries it another way; tending to show here, rather the ground, and cause of his sufferings, than the end, or issue of them. This passage the evangelist makes use of, in relating Christ's practice, in the healing of corporal infirmities, not so much, as I conceive, thereby intimating that those bodily maladies, and the cure thereof, was, (as some would have it) a type of those diseases of the soul, that Christ came principally to free men from, and his deliverance of them from the same: but that by his tender pity, and compassionate affection towards persons so affected, and afflicted, he showed that he had assumed, together with our nature, the infirmities of the same; and had therefore a lively fellow-feeling of those pains and griefs, that did from the same proceed, in others.

*{yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted*} The reason why they so much disesteemed Christ, to wit, because they made no other account, but that all those afflictions that befell him, were, by God, for his own evil deserts, inflicted upon him, out of a disaffection to him, Phil. 22.7,8. & 71.11. Matth. 27.39–43.

*{yet*} Heb. *and*; as Ch. 50.7.

*{we esteemed*} The same word, by an elegant *antanaclasis*, is here repeated, that the prophet had made use of in the verse before-going, but in a different notion here, from that there: they did not *esteem* him, that is: made any account of him, because they *esteemed*, that is, accounted him to be one out of grace and favor with God, yea, to be one pursued by him, with those evils, for his sins. The very like conceit, that Jobs friends had of him, for his sufferings, Job 4.7,8. & 8.4. & 22.5–11.

*{stricken, smitten, and afflicted*} Three several terms used, to express the greatness, and grievousness of his sufferings; as three other of near nature, being joined together, to intimate the eminent, and incomparable height of his ensuing honor, C. 52.13.

*{stricken*} Or, *plagued*: so it is rendered, Psal. 73.14. now because the noun hence deduced, is used of the *stroke*, or *plague* of *leprosy*, Levit. 13.3,9,20. and very oft in that chapter; hence the Rabbines, some of them, abuse this place, to prove that their dotage before touched; that the Messiah should sometime be a *leper*: and the old Latin renders it, *as a leper*: which yet may bear a warrantable sense. See ver. 3. But that of the Talmudists, is a most ridiculous fancy, such as their rhapsodies are fraught with, not a few: the word is general, comprehending any *stroke*, *plague*, or *affliction* whatsoever: and they may as well prove, that Asaph, the author of that 73. Psalm, was for a long time a *leper*, from the passage therein pointed to, as from this, that the Messiah was so, or ever should so be. See V. 8.

*{smitten of God*} That is, as some would have it, most grievously smitten; it being the manner of Scripture, by such forms, to express the eminent greatness of any thing: as *Sinners of God*, for grievous sinners, Gen. 13.13. and, *a sleep of God*, for *a deep sleep*, 1 Sam. 26.12. See Jer. 2.31. But that he was grievously smitten, was conspicuous enough; nor did they deem amiss therein: their mistake was, that they thought him thus handled by God, in way of vengeance for his sins. So they wickedly and impiously deemed of Christ, when they saw what grievous things he suffered. And it is but an idle foppery of some popish writers, to require the words to be read, *God smitten*, as intimating the deity of Christ: because the word, *of*, is not expressly in the text: when as they cannot be ignorant, who know any thing in the Hebrew, that the course of the construction, of noun with noun, does necessarily imply it.
