Beside, that this reading directly crosses the prophet's intention; as intimating, that the Jewish people should acknowledge Christ, notwithstanding his sufferings, to be God; who, on the contrary, therefore condemned him, as guilty of impiety and blasphemy, and were enraged against him for it, because he professed himself to be the Son of God, one with the Father, and equal to God, Mat. 26.53–56. Joh. 5.18. & 10.31,33. & 19.7.

*{and afflicted*} To wit, by God, as before; for that have all the three words reference unto: as if all that befell him, came not from man's malice against him, but God's just wrath and displeasure.

**Verse 5.** *{But he was wounded for our transgressions*} Heb. *And*; the copulative, in an adversative notion, as Chapter 36.12. and 40.31. The right ground, and true cause of Christ's suffering, is, in this verse, and those following, related, in way of opposition, to that vain and fond conceit, that his own people had of him and them.

*{wounded*} So both the ancient Greek, and old Latin, render the word here used; and some, *smitten*, to have it answer to the latter end of verse 4. which comes, much in effect, to the same; as descending from a word, that signifies, *to smite, to wound, to thrust thorough, to slay*. Others, render it, *polluted*, or *profaned*, used, and dealt with, as some common, vile, or profane thing; as descending from the same root but in another notion; whereof see Psal. 89.39,44,45. Chap. 43.28. & 47.6. but the word deduced from that root in whether notion of the twain, is somewhat different from that, that is here used, as may be seen, Ezek. 32.26. I suppose, therefore, that the better reading is that in the margin of our Bibles; *He was tormented*, or *pained*: for the word comes regularly from a root, that signifies properly, *to be in pain*; as women, or other creatures, that bring forth, with pain, are wont to be, at the time of their travail, so Ps. 51.5. where, as the one word, there used, has in it a notion of the *heat* of delight, in conception, as Gen. 29.39,41. so the other, of sharpness of *pain*, in production, as Job 39.1,2,3. & 29.9. and it is used, commonly, of any grievous *torment*, or *pain*, proceeding from vexation, affliction, or fear, Job 19.20. Prov. 26.10. Chap. 13.8. & 26.18. and 51.9. Jer. 5.3. and this word, the prophet, delighting much in consonances, may seem the rather to have made choice of here; because it comes very near, in sound, to the word rendered *grief*, ver. 3,4.

*{for*} Heb. *from*; that is, *because of*, as Psalm 12.5. Chapter 48.4. Obad. 10. as importing the principal cause of Christ's sufferings, man's sins, Romanes 4.25. 1 Corinthians 15.3. so in the next branch.

*{our transgressions*} Or, *defections, revolts*, (as some not amiss render it, both here, and Chap. 59.12,13.) or, *rebellions*; for so the word it comes of, is commonly rendered, 2 King. 1.1. & 3.5,7. & 8.20,22.

*{he was bruised for our iniquities*} The word used again, verse 10. signifies properly, *to beat*, or *break*, or *crush to pieces*, or *grind to powder*. See Chap. 3.15. used ordinarily, of grievous oppression, and affliction: yea, such as tends to, and ends, if not stayed, in destruction: Job 4.19. & 6.9. & 19.2. and 22.9. Psal. 72.4. & 90.3. & 94.5. Lam. 3.24.

*{the chastisement of our peace was upon him*} He was chastised to procure our peace, by removal of our sins, that set God and us asunder, Chapter 59.2. the guilt thereof, being discharged with the price of his blood, 1 Peter 1.18,19. and to reconcile us unto him, Rom. 3.25. & 5.1,10. 2 Cor. 5.19,21. Eph. 2.13–17. Col. 1.19,20. 1 Pet. 3.18.

*{and with his stripes are we healed*} Heb. *by his stripe*, or *bruise*: for the word properly signifies, the mark, or *print of a stripe*, or *stroke*, remaining upon some part of the body, black and blue, by gathering and settling together of the blood there; from whence it has this name, Exod. 21.25. Prov. 20.30. and the same signifies the Greek word, whereby it is expressed, 1 Pet. 2.24. But it is used also for any sore, and grievous stroke, or hurt; such as those, by which the same is wont to be produced, Genesis 4.23. See Chap. 1.6. Jer. 30.12. and such, no doubt, our Savior, as well in the propriety of the term, as otherwise also, bare in his body, being not buffeted only, but scourged, as he was, Mat. 26.67. & 27.16.

**V. 6.** *{All we like sheep, have gone astray*} In these words is showed wherein those iniquities, and sins of ours, for which our Savior suffered, do consist.

*{All we*} By nature, none of us excepted, Ps. 14.3. Rom. 3.12,23. Eph. 2.2,3.

*{like sheep*} Or, *like lost sheep*; as more expressly, Ps. 119.176. So *clusters*, for *clusters left*, Chap. 24.13.

*{have gone astray*} As sheep stray, sometime scared and scattered, by dogs, or wolves, or thieves, or the like, Joh. 10.12. or forced to seek abroad, for want of pasture, Gen. 47.4. Jer. 14.5. sometime, again of themselves, out of a silly disposition. Luke 15.4. so it is with men also, in either respect, resembled by *sheep*. There is a *straying*, or *wandering*, enforced, when they are driven, by violence, from their wonted places of abode. Of which, see Psal. 119.176. Jer. 50.17. Ezek. 34.4,6. Zach. 13.7. Mat. 26.31. Mar. 14.27. But this is not the *straying* here spoken of; and there is a voluntary *straying*, (they are not willing only, but love to wander, Jer. 14.10.) a wandering out of self-will not a corporal, but a spiritual straying; by which, men, of themselves, wander from God, and go astray from the way of truth, and life; from those ways and courses, that God has prescribed them in his word; and directs them unto, by his Spirit. Of which, see Psalm 14.3. & 53.2. & 58.3. & 119.67. Rom. 3.12. 1 Pet. 2.25. James 5.20. and this is the *straying* here spoken of.

*{we have turned every one to his own way*} *We have turned the face* (to wit, away from God, and his ways, and) *looked after every one his own way*. So the Hebrew word used, both here, and Chap. 56.11. (a parallel place) as also, Jer. 2.20. (where the notation of it is) properly signifies: and because in so doing, the *face*, and whole body with it, are turned about; hence it comes to pass that the word is also used, for *to turn*, or *to return*, as Numbers 14.25. Deuteronomy 1.7,40. and 2.3. & 16.7. See Deut. 31.18,20. Jer. 7.24.

*{every one to his own way*} So Chapter 56.11. All agree in turning aside from the right way; but they herein disagree, in that each one has a byway of his own, which they turn unto; some running after one lust, or vice, or evil course, or idol, some after another, Ch. 55.7. & 57.17. Eccles. 11.9. 2 King. 17.30,31. Jer. 2.28. & 11.13.

*{and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all*} Heb. *hath made the iniquity of us all to meet on him* or *to light*, or *fall on him*, rather. Some of the Jewish doctors, to divert this place from being understood of Christ's satisfaction, by his sufferings, made for sinners; because the word here found, is sometime used of intercession by prayer, as Jer. 7.16. and here also, ver. 12. would fain turn the word that way; as if the party here spoken of, were, by prayer, only to have mediated, and pacified God's wrath, for the sins of some other, as Moses did sometime for his people, Exod. 32.12,14. Num. 14.19,20. Psal. 106.23. and because the word would not sound handsomely, if it should be said here, *the Lord interceded*, or *prayed*, as it is afterward; *he interceded*, or *prayed*; they would have it rendered; *the Lord made him to intercede*, or *to pray*: But neither produce they any instance of the word so used, nor will the syntax admit, or endure such a sense: For what a strange piece of nonsense were this; *the Lord made him to intercede the iniquity of us all upon him*? and both the words before, ver. 4,5. and those also following, ver. 7,10,12. do evidently hold out to any eye, not willfully winking, that satisfaction was made to God's justice, and his wrath pacified, towards those, that had interest therein; not by intercession, and prayer only, but by penalties, and sufferings. The word, therefore, is not amiss rendered by our interpreters, where they give it, word for word in the margin, *the Lord made to meet on him*, and it may well be, *to meet with him*, as our English phrase is wont to express the like. So Chap. 47.3. *I will not meet thee, as a man*, and *the revenger of blood, shall slay the murderer, where he meeteth with him*, Num. 39.19,21. (as Exodus 23.4. *if thou meet with thine enemies ox, or ass*.) Or, *where he lighteth on him*; as *he lighted on a place*, Gen. 28.11. which place, some of the Jewish masters themselves, also, refer us to, for the notion of the word, in this place: and so, here, it may more fitly be rendered; *he made the iniquity of us all to light upon him*: as, *the arm of God* is said (though another word be there) *to light upon Assur*, Chap. 30.30. or, which I conceive to be the fittest expression; *he made it all to fall on him*: for so the word is, in the first form, very frequently rendered, *fall upon him*, 2 Sam. 1.15. 1 King. 2.29,31. and, *fall upon the Priests*, 1 Sam. 22.18. and, *he fell upon the Priests*, ver. 20. and, *he fell upon him*, 1 King. 2.25,34,46. and, *he fell upon two men better than himself*, 1 King. 2.32. God made it to fall on him as man is wont to fall in hostile manner, with a weapon, on his foe. God inflicted on him, whatsoever was requisite, to the satisfying of his justice for all the sins of all his Elect ones, even of all that trust in him, Joh. 3.14,15,16. & 11.50,52. 2 Cor. 5.14,15. Heb. 2.9,14,15.

*{the iniquity*} Not the stain, or taint itself of sin; but, as the Jewish doctors themselves, well expound it, the guilt and penalty of it; a portion of punishment, in some regard proportionable, to whatsoever was due unto their sins, and to themselves for the same. So is the word taken, Gen. 4.13. Lev. 20.17,19,20. 1 Sam. 28.10. Lam. 4.6. which two latter places, the Jewish commenters here point us to. The Greek interpreters render this passage much in the same words, that the apostle uses, Romanes 4.25.

**V. 7.** *{He was oppressed; and he was afflicted*} A very pregnant place, for the satisfaction made by Christ's sufferings for our sins, were it fitly rendered, and rightly understood. The words are, word for word; *It was exacted, and he answered*. *It was exacted*; or, *It is exacted*; as some also well render it: that the former word does properly, and commonly, signify, *to exact*, cannot be denied. The Jewish commenters, themselves, observe on the place, that it is usually meant of *moneys*; directing us to that place, 2 King. 23.35. *he exacted the money*. So Chap. 58.3. *ye exact all your labors*; or, as some, *all your debts*: and, *of a stranger thou mayest exact it; but not of thy brother*, Deut. 15.2,3. hence the name of an *exacter*, so frequent in Scripture, Job 3.17. & 39.7. Chap. 3.12. & 9.4. & 14.2. & 60.17. Zach. 9.8. & 10.4. and that it is here a passive, the same writers here observe. The old Latin renders it, *He was offered*, as if the word were parallel to that other, from whence the *Corban* comes, mentioned, Mat. 15.5. and so the meaning should be, *he was made to approach*, or *offered* as a sacrifice, ver. 10. But this version arises from a twofold mistake: For, first, the word here used, and that other, of *approaching*, differ, as our Jewish critics tell us; as *Sibboleth*, and *Shiboleth*, Judg. 12.6. And secondly, this latter, in the passive form, carries always neutral; neither an active, nor passive sense: it signifies, *to approach*, not *to offer*, or *make to approach*, not yet *to be made to approach*, or *to be offered*. So Gen. 33.7. Exod. 20.21. Chap. 29.13. The word, therefore: is the same rather, with that, 1 Sam. 3.6. where it is said, *the people*, being in a *strait, were pressed*, or *distressed*: and so also, Chap. 14.24. save that there it is used, more metaphorically, here properly; there, personally, here, impersonally; as the words of the text evidently show: For there is neither noun, nor pronoun, before the first word of the verse; but a pronoun expressly before the next: which evidently controls their conceit, who expound it of the person, from whom it was exacted, and render the words, *He was exacted*, which yet they expound, it was demanded, or required of no other, but of him: the sense is sound, but the construction harsh, and not sorting well with the frame of the context. This the Rabbine himself saw, and thereupon expounds it; *It was exacted*, to wit, money says he, by way of tax, or assessment, as 2 King. 23.34,35. *and he was afflicted*, namely, the people of whom it was required, by stripes, or strokes, being beaten, because they paid not the sums required of them, as the people in Egypt were beaten, when they could not make up the full tale of bricks, Exod. 5.14. But the great doctor had no regard, to the current of the context: for that runs in a constant, and continued course and tenor, not as speaking of one, and the same party or parties, both sinning and suffering, or sustaining penalties, for their own defaults: but as one, suffering for the sin of another, and sustaining grievous penalties, for defaults made, and faults committed, by other persons. Some of ours therefore read it; *It is exacted, and he is afflicted*. Others, *It was exacted, and he was afflicted*. Or, *When it was exacted, he was afflicted*. Of which manner of syntax, see on ver. 2. that is, the penalty due to God's justice, for our sins, ver. 6. was exacted; and he sustained the same for us. For that which a learned late annotator suggests, who would have it rendered, *he was humble*, or humbly submitted himself, *not opening his mouth*, because of Pharao it is said, Exod. 10.3. *thou refusest to be humbled*: Neither does that place and this, suit well the one with the other: (It is one thing to be *humbled*; another *to be humble*.) and this interpretation seems to decline from the drift of the precedent discourse, whereupon this has dependence. The words, as formerly read, do sufficiently confirm the doctrine of satisfaction made to God's justice, by Christ's sufferings for our sins. But yet some further strength may be, from hence, added thereunto, if we consider the latter term a little more exactly: For howsoever it be true, that the word, here used, do in the passive form signify, *to be afflicted*, or *humbled*, as Exod. 10.3. Psal. 119.107. and so in a grave, or weighty form, it is used, ver. 4. which this may here seem to have reference unto: and that the word used in a notion of *answering*, be seldom found, but in an active form: yet, as in the notion of *affliction*, the word is used, sometime, in an active form passively, for, *to be afflicted*; Psal. 116.10. so in the notion of *answering*, it is sometime used actively, in the passive form, not *to be answered*, either verbally, as Job 11.2. or, really, as Job 19.7. Prov. 21.13. but, *to answer*; and that either verbally, or really, also. In the former sense, some understand that place, Psal. 119.167. *before I answered*, (that is, say they, before ever I was able to speak, as ver. 172. *my tongue shall answer*, that is, speak of, *thy word*,) *I went astray*; as parallel to that, Psal. 58.3. and having respect to inbred pravity: but the word seems to be there: as in an active form, so in a passive sense: and in a signification of *affliction*, and *humiliation*, as it is commonly expounded. Howbeit, the word is found elsewhere, in a passive form, with an active sense, and that without any question, in the notion of *answering*, Ezek. 14.4,7. as also the word of *speaking* is Psal. 119.13. Ezek. 33. 30. Mal. 3.13,16. And somewhat to this purpose, an author of good note expounds this text, thus rendering the words; *It is exacted, and he undertaketh*, (a term that some of the ancients also use, in the opening of this text) that is, says he, the penalty due to us, was in rigor of justice exacted; and he became a *sponsor*, or *surety* for us, by undertaking, in our behalf, the discharge of it. And though the word, says he, in Hebrew, be not found so used; yet in Latin, the word *respondere*, that is, *to answer*, comes from *Spondere*, that signifies *to undertake*; and the word, *to answer*, in the French tongue, is so commonly used. Hereunto may be added, that the old Latin seems to look this way, that renders the text, *He was offered of his own accord*, or *because he himself would*: which version, howsoever it fail much, in the former term, as has already been showed; yet it comes home to us, in the latter word; implying a voluntary undertaking, or *engaging of himself* (see Jer. 31.20.) unto God his Father, in our behalf, as a *Surety*, (so is he termed, Heb. 7.22.) for the payment of our debt. And, which is yet more than so, that albeit, the Hebrew be not found expressly, and directly used for such a *sponsion*, or *engagement*; yet that in this very form that here it has, it is twice used in the place of Ezekiel before pointed to; *I the Lord will answer him* (to wit, the man that repairs to me for advice, with an idol in his heart) and again, *I will answer him by my self*, and that in a notion, not of a verbal, but of a real *answering* and so I conceive it is to be taken here, *It was exacted, and he answered it*. (the particle being necessarily, as oft elsewhere, supplied, See Chap. 48.5,6.) that is, he not only undertook it, but discharged it. So we use the word commonly in our English tongue, *to answer a debt*, for *to discharge it*. And so of our Savior it is most true, that he *answered* our debt, and caused our bond to be, canceled, that it might not come to be put in suit, against us, any more again. See Joh. 19.30. Rom. 4.25. Col. 2.14. A singular comfort to every sincere Christian soul.

*{yet he opened not his mouth*} Heb. *And*; But so we had it before, V. 4. and it may well be here retained, if we keep to the received reading of being *oppressed*, and *afflicted*, as if it were said, having respect to his patience, for all the oppressions and afflictions, that he sustained for others, and that in regard of those, by whom he suffered them unjustly: yet was he silent, he neither murmured, or repined, at God's disposal of things in that manner, nor used any railing, or reviling speeches, against those that dealt so despitefully with him, but carried himself calmly, and quietly under them, Mat. 26.39,42. Mar. 14.36. Joh. 18.23. 1 Pet. 2.23. Howbeit, if we admit the sense in the second place propounded, and pressed, of *exacting*, and *answering*, that is, *undertaking*, or *discharging*, the copulative shall not need at all, to be altered: for the words will well go on in way of connection to the former: as if it were said; Having an eye to his voluntary obedience, and submission to the will of his Father, and agreement thereunto, he undertook willingly what his Father required of him, and as willingly when the time came, underwent it; neither hanging back, or opposing aught, in way of contradiction thereunto, when it was by his Father propounded to him, at first; nor afterward seeking to shift it off, when he was to perform what he had engaged himself unto, by pleading aught for himself, & the releasement of him, from their most unjust proceedings, in whose hands he then was. See Ch. 50.5,6. Mat. 26.62,63. & 27.12,14. Mar. 14.60,61. & 15.3,5. Luk. 23.9. Joh. 10.18. & 14.31. & 19.11. *to open the mouth*, an usual form, (the antecedent, put for the consequent) for, *to speak*. So Job 3.1. & 33.2. Psal. 78.2. Prov. 31.8,26. so *to open the lips*, Job 32.20. and on the contrary, *not to open the mouth*, for *to be silent*, not to say aught, Psalm 39.9. Proverbs 24.7.

*{he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter*} The Hebrew word is more general, and signifies a *sheep*; which word of ours, it comes near to in sound. and it is so rendered also, Act. 8.32. where this passage is related, Psal. 119.176. Jer. 50.17. and yet more largely, *lesser cattle*, Ch. 7.25. as parallel to another word used, V. 6. but, as more specially intending, *sheep* there, in regard of the silliness thereof; so here, in regard of the ordinary number of them, above any such other cattle, brought to the butchery, Ps. 44.22. Jer. 12.3. Zach. 11.4. Rom. 8.36. and their quiet carriage, in driving thither: the text may well be rendered, *as a sheep that is led to the slaughter*; as Jer. 11.19. As a sheep, that goes as quietly, to the shambles, or the slaughter-house, as if it were going to the fold, wherein it is usually lodged; or the field, where it is wont to feed. See Jer. 11.19.

*{and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb*} This latter word, whereof *Rachel* had her name, Gen. 29.6. is, by the ancient Greek interpreter, rendered; *a lamb*, and so Act. 8.32. Luke, retaining that translation, gives it. Howbeit, it signifies *an ewe*, as appears plainly, Gen. 31.38. & 32.14. where these *rachels* are distinguished from *rams*, as also, Cant. 6.6. where they are described with *twins* by their sides: and the word, though of a masculine form, yet is of a feminine gender, as is manifest, by the verb, or participle, joined with it: and he seems to mention the ewe, as the quieter of that kind, because the rams are sometime more unruly.

*{is dumb*} So Psalm 39.2,9. Or *tongue-tied*: for that seems to be the first notion of the root it comes of, *to bind*, or *tie up*, Ge. 37.7.

*{so he openeth not his mouth*} Heb. *and*; used here, for the note of similitude; as also, Psal. 1.3. and 109.17. Prov. 10.25. and 17.3. Ch. 10.26. and so it is rendered, Act. 8.37. Of the phrase, see before.

**V. 8.** *{He was taken from prison, and from judgment*} In the exposition of this passage, interpreters do exceedingly dissent, and that about every word, and particle, in it. Howbeit, they may in general be referred all to two heads, either of those, that understand them of Christ's humiliation, and oppression only, and the harsh, cruel, and unjust courses, whereby his life was taken from him, Mat. 27.18,24. Act. 2.23. & 3.14,15. & 13.28. Or, of those, that conceive them to be spoken of his deliverance out of those afflictions, and distresses, injuriously inflicted; and his advancement from them, to a glorious condition, Luk. 24.26. Act. 2.24,33,36. & 3.15,21. Phil. 2.8,9. 1 Tim. 3.16. Heb. 2.9. 1 Pet. 1.11.

*{taken*} That is, as some, *taken away*, put to death: as Psal. 31.13. Prov. 1.19. as others, *drawn away*, to wit, unto judgment, and to punishment, by death; as Prov. 24.11. but the structure is not here, and there alike: yea, as some, supposing the particular manner of his death here designed *taken up* to the cross, John 3.14,15. and 12.32,33. but of such use of the word, no instance is brought. Others, *he is taken up*, from hence, and received by God, into glory; as Gen. 5.24. Mar. 16.19. Luke 24.51. Act. 1.9,11. 1 Timo. 3.16.

*{from*} So the word most usually signifies; and so many here take it, as meant of being delivered, and set free from the matters here mentioned: as, *from work*, Gen. 2.2. *from enemies*, Psal. 44.4. *from bands*, Jer. 40.4. others take it, for, *by*, or *through*, as noting the means whereby, or the manner how, he was brought to his end. So Job 7.14. & 37.10. Jer. 10.14. Or, *for*; as implying the cause producing, procuring, or impellent. So Ps. 12.5. V. 5. C. 65.14. others, for *without*, without being imprisoned, or having any due course of judicature, taken with him: as the particle seems to be used, Ps. 109.24. Lam. 4.9. but neither are those places parallel; and one produced to that purpose, has a negative joined with it, Job 31.19. Others, lastly, for, *after*: after that he had passed those harsh, and unjust courses taken with him. So is the particle used, Dan. 11.23. Hos. 6.3.

*{prison*} Supposed to be so called, as a place of *coercion*, or *restraint* (see on Chap. 44.7.) for the verb, whence it comes, signifies *to shut up*, or *restrain*, Gen. 20.18. Deut. 11.17. yet, for a *prison*, the word is nowhere found to be used: nor was our Savior ever imprisoned; though that would stand well enough with their exposition, that render the particle *without*. Others, therefore understand by it, *restraint*, or *distress*: and this not unfitly agrees with the native signification of the word; used for *the shutting up* or, *restraint, of the womb*, (so the words are) Proverbs 30.16. that is, *the womb shut up*, or, *restrained*; as Jacob speaks to Rachel, Gen. 30.2. nor can it be denied, or doubt made, but that Christ was under *restraint*; and in *distress*, proceeding from such strict restraint. Others, of such *anguish*, and *anxiety* of mind, and spirit, as Christ's soul was possessed of, arising from the apprehension of God's wrath; both in his agony, Luke 22.44. and upon the cross, Mat. 27.46. Others render it, *dominion, power, tyranny, oppression*: and a term of the same stock, differing but in a vowel only from it, is used sometime for *power, authority*, or *magistracy*, Judg. 18.7. and the root they both spring from, for *to have power*, or *to prevail*, 2 Chr. 14.11. and this very word sometime for such power abused: for *oppression*, or *tyranny*. So Psal. 107.39. where it is also joined with the particle here used: and it suits well with the power, both of Jews, and Gentiles, unjustly exercised against Christ, Psalm 2.1,2. Act. 4.25–27. Others would have it to signify, here, *a congregation*, or *a multitude*: because another word of kin to this, is used for *a solemn assembly*. See on Chap. 1.13. and this some refer to the assembly of the Jewish rulers, wherein Christ was condemned, Mat. 26.57–66. Others, to the popular multitude, that were instant to have him crucified, Mat. 27.15–26. Mar. 15.8,15. Luk. 23.18–25. and to these therefore, as well as those, by whom they were incited, is the murder of Christ ascribed, Luk. 24.20. Act. 3.23,26. & 3.13,14,15. & 7.52. & 13.27. but neither is the word itself any where, as I conceive, so used; nor its kin, of other, than a solemn *assembly*, called together by authority; not of a confused, or disorderly multitude on their own heads gathered together.

*{and from judgment*} This some understand of *judgment*, in general, either, without which, or by which, or after which, exercised, and executed upon our Savior, he was, either taken away, or taken up. Some more particularly restrain it, either to the Jewish assembly's censure of him, Mat. 26.66. Joh. 19.7. or, to Pilates sentence passed upon him; Luk. 23.24. distinguished from the act of the rude multitude, which they conceive implied in the word before-going. Nor want they, that expound it of the *judgment* of God, and the torments by him inflicted upon him, implied in the word *curse*, Gal. 3.13. I concur with those, who by these two terms, understand *oppression*, and *judgment*, as comprehending all those harsh, and cruel courses, as under pretense of judgment, were exercised upon our Savior, whereby his life was taken from him, and himself taken away, for the time; or, from which, he was after a while freed, being, after the sustaining of them, taken hence, and taken up unto God, as Enoch, and Elia before him; of both whose assumption, the same term is used, Gen. 5.24. 2 King. 2.9,10. But I incline rather to the former, because the course of the context, both before, and after, as well in this verse, as in the next, runs still upon his sufferings.

*{and who shall declare his generation?*} Or, *who can declare?* for the indicative future, is oft potentially used. See Chap. 26.18. & 49.15. This passage, some understand of the generation of Christ, from eternity, in regard of his Godhead, Prov. 8.24,25. Others, of the production of him, and that of a virgin, without knowledge of man, in regard of his manhood, Luk. 1.34,35. and some, of both jointly; as also that, Psal. 2.7. Acts 13.33. Some by *generation*, here, understand neither of these; but, either, his continuance, reading the words, *but who can reckon his age?* living now to eternity, beyond all number of days, or years, Ro. 6.9. Heb. 7.3,8,15. Rev. 1.18. agreeable to that, *he shall prolong his days*, ver. 10. that, which they extend also to his body, the church, Psal. 125.1. Jer. 31.36,37. & 33.25,26. Mat. 16.18. Heb. 7.25. and for continuance of time, the word is commonly used; as Chap. 13.20. & 60.15. Or, of his issue, rendering the text: *who can count*, or, *reckon, his race?* his spiritual seed and issue, being a numberless multitude, Gen. 15.5. & 22.17,18. Jer. 33.22. Heb. 2.10,13. Rev. 7.9. as agreeable to that, *he shall see a seed*, verse 10. so is the word taken, Psal. 22.30. & 24.6. & 49.19. & 73.15. & 112.2. In the first sense, most of the ancient writers take it: & in the two latter, most of the latter. What the first should do here, cannot easily be made to appear; the latter if we admit, according to the former interpretation, at least of the foregoing branch, the copulative would be turned into an adversative, as ver. 10. *yet who can reckon his age*, or, *count his race?* But there want not those, that turn the words another way: and they conceive them to run in an abrupt, and passionate form of speech, as complaining either of the strangeness of the things that befell him: & they then read the words, *who would have said of his generation?* to wit, that such things should have, in his age, or time, befallen him? as, *Who would have said to Abram, that Sarah should give suck?* Gen. 21.7. or, of the monstrous impiety, and wickedness of them, that dealt in this manner with him, that came to save them: and then they render the words, *Who can utter*, or *describe, his generation?* or, *his age?* that is the wickedness of the men of his time, or the age he lived in: the verb signifies *to speak*, or *utter*, Job 12.8. Psal. 69.12. & 143.5. *his generation*, or *age*, for, the men of his time: as, *his generations*, or *ages*: for, those of the times wherein he lived, Gen. 6.9. So is the word very frequently used, Gen. 7.1. Deut. 32.5,20. Psal. 73.8. Mat. 11.16. & 12.39. & 16.4. and 17.17. And this sense seems not improbable; as well suiting, both with what ushered it in, and what attends on it. As for that of another, *Who could declare his stock?* that is, who would say, that he was begotten of God, or the Son of God, seeing him depressed, and abased so beneath the meanest of men? Chap. 52.14. it gains with me no acceptance; because I find not where the word is in that notion used. Besides, that the centurion, unto whom the execution was committed, seeing the manner of his death, and, in likelihood, observing his last words, recorded, Luk. 23.46. is, both by Matthew & Mark, reported to have broken out into those words, *of a truth, this man was a Son of God*, Mat. 27.54. Mar. 15.39.

*{for he was cut off out of the land of the living*} Or, as some read the words, (those especially, that expound the two foregoing branches, of his deliverance, and exaltation) *though he were cut off*: as the particle is used, Gen. 8.21. Josh. 17.18. Chap. 12.1. But what if we read it according to the exposition of the branch, next before, deemed not improbable; as continuing the sentence in a notion of wonderment, *that he should be cut off*, (so the particle was used before, ver. 5,6.) as a tree that was hewn down, 2 King. 6.4. that he should be thus taken away, by a violent death, from abiding and conversing on earth, among men, that there live, Psal. 27.13. & 52.5. and 116.9. Chap. 38.11.

*{for the transgression of my people was he stricken*} The words thus read, are the same in substance, with what was before said, ver. 5. See there. But some read them thus rather; *by the transgression of my people was he stricken*. Heb. *from*, but of the various use of that particle, see on the first branch of this verse: in this sense, the words conceived, the sentence may still be continued, and carried on thus, *that* (the particle supplied from the former; as 1 Sam. 24.30.) *by the transgression of mine own people he should thus be stricken*, Act. 2.23. & 3.13–15. & 13.28.

*{my people*} Either mine Elect, for whom he died: as Col. 1.24. 2 Tim. 2.10. or, those obstinate wicked, that pursued him to death, 1 Thess. 2.15.

*{was he stricken*} As ver. 4. Heb. *the stroke was upon him*: so the pronoun is found used in a singular notion, Gen. 9.26,27. Job 20.23. & 22.2. Psal. 11.7. & 28.8. Chap. 44.15. contrary to that which both some popish writers, to fasten willful corruptions upon the Hebrew text, affirm; and some Jewish doctors also, to divert this testimony from the Messiah, avow: both either of gross ignorance, or of mere malice; for other of the Jewish masters, and that of prime note, for grammar especially, observe the affix here used, to be as well singular, as plural: and the places above recited, whereof some also are by them alleged, do evidently evince as much. Howbeit others, and that of ours also render it, *they were stricken*; *the stroke was upon them*, taking the pronoun in a plural notion, as it is commonly used, Exo. 15.15. Deut. 33.29. Ps. 2.5. & 17.10. & 21.11. & 49.11. & 104.9. and so some understand it, of the Jewish people, upon whom; according to their own imprecation, Mat. 26.23. the stroke of God's wrath, shortly after, lighted and lies heavy, to this very day, for their crucifying of Christ, Mat. 21.39,41. & 23.37,30. & 24.22,23. Luk. 13.34,35. & 21.20–24. 1 Thess. 2.15,16. And some of those that go this way, knit this member thus to the former; *because he was cut off through the transgression* or, *wickedness of my people*; therefore, *shall they be smitten*, or, *they are smitten*; (for the prophet speaks of these things, as already in execution, and act) *the stroke shall be*, or *is, upon them*. But the course of the context carries it on, rather, the former way, and makes the passage clearer to what follows. For they seem to go further out of the way, who taking the affix in a plural notion, would have it understood, either of Christ, considered jointly with those, as one with him; for whom he suffered, 2 Cor. 5.21. or of those alone, whom the stroke was due to; rendering the text, *he was cut off from the land of the living, for the iniquity of my people, unto whom the stroke belonged, was due*, or, *was intended*; for this, the words will hardly bear.

**V. 9.** *{And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death*} Some writers of note, suspect these words to have been by some means transposed, and suppose, for the fitting of them, to the story of the gospel, concerning his death with malefactors, on mount Calvary, Mat. 27.33,38. Mar. 15.28. Luk. 22.37. and his burial, in Josephs sepulcher, Mat. 27.57,60. that the text ought thus to be read; *And his death shall be disposed of, with the wicked, and his grave with the rich*. The like thoughts have some other had of Psal. 35.7. and of Act. 7.16. but to give way to such conjectures, seems unsafe. To let that therefore pass, and take the words as we find them, at present, in the text; the expositions of them in the lump; may be referred to two heads: the one of those, which seems the more improbable, who understand the words, as concerning either the effect, or the efficacy of Christ's sufferings; to wit either, that those wicked ones, and rich ones, that had had an hand in the procuring of his death, should pay full dear for it; being given up to endure the like harsh and cruel usage, at the hands of others, as Christ, at their hands had sustained: as Chap. 43.3,4. or, that even wicked men, and those great ones too, who are wont to be most obstinate, should be subdued and made subject to the scepter of Christ, by the power and efficacy of his passion, Psal. 110.2. The other is, of those, who conceive them to be meant, wholly of his sufferings themselves, either, that the Jewish people should put him into the hands of heathen people, the Romans, and their ruler Pilate, Mat. 20.19,20. Joh. 18.35. who by that means, having condemned him, and dealt with him, as with a malefactor, should dispose of his death, and burial, at his pleasure, Mat. 27.2,57,58. Luk. 23.1,2,50,52. Joh. 18.28–32. & 19.6,11,12,38. Or that God should deliver him into the hands of wicked men, and rulers so to be disposed of by them, for either, as themselves pleased, Luk. 22.53. Act. 2.23. & 4.27,28. Howbeit, among the latter there are, who, together with his sufferings, conceive an intimation of some honor done him, concerning his burial; as if it were said, that though *his grave*, were, in ordinary course to have been *among malefactors*; yet it was *with the rich*: being buried in honorable manner, by Joseph, in his own tomb, Mat. 27.57–60. and that to show, that all penalty and shame for sin, were fully satisfied for, and had an end at his death; according to that, Joh. 19.40. Howbeit, that seems rather to have been manifested, at, and by, his resurrection, Rom. 4.25. & the reception of him, in soul first, (though that not so conspicuous) Luk. 23.43,46. and in the whole man, not long afterward, into heaven, Joh. 13.1. & 16.10. 1 Tim. 3.16. otherwise his abode in the grave, though a rich, and honorable man's grave, under the power of death, for a time, was a branch of his humiliation, and is reckoned, as a part of his passion, Act. 2.24,27. Nor want there here again some others, who would have hereby intimated, Christ's carrying of our sins, which in his body he bare on the cross, 1 Pet. 2.24. with him into the grave, and there burying them, that they may not appear any more in God's sight, as Gen. 23.4. Psal. 88.5. to which purpose, also, they hook in hither that of the apostle, Rom. 6.4. Col. 2.12. as also that of Dan. 9.24. *to shut up and seal up sin*, as they would have the words there read, with some reference to the shutting up of Christ in the sepulcher, and the sealing up of it, Mat. 27.66. And as this in the former branch, so the precious riches of his blood and death in the latter, 1 Pet. 1.19. Eph. 1.7,8,18. & 2.7. & 3.8. Col. 1.27. All which to make out, the two concretes in the text are presumed to be put for the abstracts, *wicked ones*, for, *wickednesses*: & *rich*, for *riches*: and the text is rendered, *He put wickednesses in his grave, and riches in his death*. But these things seem overmuch forced, and far-fetched. Nor seems it safe, or fit, to strain Scriptures thus, to wring points of faith from them: nor should I have mentioned them, but for the great note of their author.

*{And he made his grave with the wicked*} Heb. *And he gave*, or, *shall give the wicked*, or, *with the wicked, his grave*: which the old Latin swerves too far from, rendering it, *He gave the wicked for his grave*: Now some here, by *he*, understand God, by whose hidden counsels, and predetermination, these things were done; and without whom, men could not have had any such power over him, Mat. 26.53,54. Joh. 19.9,10. Others, the Jewish people, by whose hands they were acted and executed, See Act. 2.23. & 4.47,28. But others conceive, not amiss, that the words may well be taken indefinitely, and so rendered by a passive form; (of which manner of construction, See on Chap. 34.11. and the like to this, Gen. 40.15. *his grave was given to the wicked*, (as Levit. 13.49.) or, *was disposed of* (for so, the word of *giving*, oft signifies. See Chapter 41.2.) *by the wicked*, (as Chap. 7.17.) or, *with the wicked*: (as Chap. 28.15.) that is, as if he had been one of that rank, ver. 1. say some; or because in mount Calvary he was buried, say others, Joh. 19.41,42. where malefactors' corpses used to be laid. But this latter seems not so suitable to the tenor of the story. For albeit, the place of his burial was not far distant from the place of his execution; yet it was in a private garden, belonging to a man of eminent place, wherein he had cut a sepulcher out for himself, Mat. 27.57,60. Mar. 15.43,46.

*{and with the rich in his death*} Or, *and to the rich*; as before, for the particle is the same: by the *rich*, some understand Joseph, that begged, and buried Christ's body, called a *rich man*, Mat. 27.57. Others, Pilate, that had the power to dispose of Christ's corpse, and of whom Joseph begged it, Mat. 27.58. conceiving a rich man, to be put here for a *ruler*; as Ecl. 10.6,7,20. because those usually are such: thus they that expound it of some particular person, which may carry the better show with it; because the former word, *wicked*, was plural, this, singular. But many other conceive the word *rich*, here to be taken collectively, and the same persons to be meant by both; those that had an hand in the death of Christ, as well the baser sort of people, as the rich and wealthy rulers, whether of the Jewish nation, or the Roman state, whom (say those, that understand the place of the vengeance, by God executed, on either, for the death of Christ,) their riches should not ransom, nor relieve in the day of wrath, Prov. 11.4. Ezek. 7.19. as yet they are usually wont to do; Prov. 13.8.

*{in his death*} Or, *at his death*; as Job 27.19. *at their death*; though in another notion there, than here: for there it is said of some, that they *shall be buried at their death*: that is, in mean and base manner; their corpses being committed to the ground, as soon as their breath is out of their bodies, without further care or, cost; whereas, though our Savior's body was, shortly after his decease, disposed of, for burial, yet was it curiously shrouded, and richly embalmed before he was laid up in the grave, Mar. 15.46. Joh. 19.39,40. so the particle is used also, Ezr. 9.4. Est. 1.12. Heb. *deaths*; as Jer. 16.4. hence the Jewish doctors (whose expositions I meddle the less with, in this present prophecy, because they run most upon another ground) strive to wring this prediction awry, and to turn it, from the Messiah, or any other particular person, to the main body of their own people, who, though innocent, say they, yet were put to death, as malefactors, because they would not change their religion, Psal. 44.22. and, were made away, if rich, not for their wickedness, but for their wealth: & that some, by one kind of death some by another: some burnt, some slain, some stoned, and the like: but the word, though plural, is found elsewhere also, applied to one particular person, as to the King of Tyre, Eze. 28.8,10. where it is said of him, that he shall die *the death of the slain*; & *the deaths of the uncircumcised*: and so the apostle of himself, also *in deaths oft*, 2 Cor. 11.23. that is, not in hazards, and dangers of death only; but in afflictions, and vexations, as sore and painful, as death itself, and such as might well go, for as many deaths, 1 Cor. 4.9. & 15.31. Luk. 9.23. 2 Cor. 1.9. & 4.8–11. & 6.4,5,9. & 11.23–27. and the same might by the prophet, as well, yea, far better, be said of the Messiah, as of the Tyrian prince, by the prophet, in the one place: or, of himself, by the apostle in the other: besides, that the Chaldee paraphrast, renders it in the singular number. Nor can I condescend unto those, though of prime note, who, having put the word *people*, into the text, and set it in the front of the verse, render the words, *unto their own death*; as importing, that the Jews, by delivering up of Christ, brought destruction upon themselves: as having reference to the imprecation by themselves passed upon them, at the delivering up of him, Mat. 27.25. See before, ver. 8. There is another reading, that the Rabbines some of them, here exhibit; as if it were not made up of a servile particle, and a noun, with his affix; as both we, and themselves, also, commonly take it; but a noun only, with a pronoun affixed unto it, and so should signify *his high places*. Which I should not mention, save that some, not popish writers only, but ours also, and those of note, do not only take notice of it, but admit it, and press it, as intimating the stateliness of the sepulcher, wherein Christ's body was laid; as if Josephs monument were, as stately an one, as Shebna had built it for himself, Ch. 22.16. But this reading, the points, or vowels, in the original, refuse, and refute: nor do the doctors, that cite it, give any approbation of it; nor will this reading cohere handsomely with the rest of the context. I suppose, that as the latter part of the foregoing verse, so the forepart of this, run on in a continued series, containing matter of admiration, in this manner; *And that his burial should be at the disposal of wicked ones, and of rich ones*, or, *rulers, at his death*; that is, that wicked great ones should have such power given them over him, as not only to take his life away from him, by a violent and most cruel death; but after that perpetrated, to dispose of his dead corpse also for his burial, at their pleasure.

*{because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth*} This reading may stand, not amiss, with the expositions of those, that conceive the foregoing words to be understood, either of the revenging hand of God, upon the Jews, for the death of Christ, or of some honor done him, in, or at, his interment; or of the benefit that from his death and burial, accrue to the faithful: nor so well with theirs, that go the other way before mentioned; for the construction seems overmuch strained, when the meaning is made to be; because they envied him for his integrity, both in life and doctrine, Mat. 27.18. yea, though not only no man could convince him of sin, Mat. 27.19,23,24. Luk. 23.14,15. Joh. 8.46. but even the devil himself could find nothing amiss in him, Joh. 14.30. But the words would rather be read, as they sound, *not for any iniquity, that he had done, nor guile that was in his mouth*. So Job 16.17. where the very same form of speech, and words also, are found, *Not for any injustice* (so the word is there rendered) *that is in mine hands*; that is, *albeit he had done nothing amiss*, Mar. 7.37. Luk. 23.41. for the word rendered *violence*, is more general: and is used for any *wrong*, Gen. 16.5. Psalm 7.16. Jer. 51.35. and the Greek therefore gives it, *sin*, 1 Pet. 2.22. according to that, 1 Joh. 3.5. *in him was no sin*: so also, but there the negative only transposed, 1 Chron. 12.17. *without any wrong, that is in my hands*: for so it would be rendered, both in Job, and there; there being in either place, a defect of the relative, as also here; and the like, Chap. 50.9. and 51.12. Nor does that at all cross this exposition, which a learned writer objects, who having himself sometime rendered the text here, *although*, or, *when as yet, he had done no wrong*, does afterward revoke it, because never finds the particle here used, in such an adversative, but frequently in a causal notion, for it is plainly in a causal notion, when it is said, *not for*, or, *because of, any wrong he had done*: which is the very same, in effect, with what himself had before given, *albeit he had done no wrong*, and he had no cause therefore to reverse; his grammatical construction only, was not so exact.

*{neither was any deceit in his mouth*} Or, *nor for any guile, that was in his mouth*: a defect, of the particle; as Psal. 59.3. but supplied here from the former member of the distribution & of the relative, also, as before: it is rendered, 1 Pet. 2.22. *neither was guile found in his mouth*: *to be found*, for, *to be*; as Luk. 17.18. So Chap. 30.14. 51.3. There was nothing amiss with him, either in word, or deed.

**V. 10.** *{Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him, he hath put him to grief*} Or, *Yet the Lord being willing*, (as 1 King. 13.33.) or, *desiring*, (as Psal. 34.12. for the word seems to be here, as in those places, a participle,) *to break him, did put him to pain*, or, *torment*.

*{Yet*} Heb. *And*: as Ver. 4,7.

*{bruise*} Or, *break*. See on ver. 5. not, that his body was battered to pieces; or, that any bone of him was broken, Exod. 12.46. Psal. 34.20. Joh. 19.33,36. but as the psalmist of himself, *I am sore broken*, Psal. 38.8. and as we use to say, that a man is much *broken*, with age, sickness, grief of mind, evil usage, and the like: all which and much more, were together in Christ's sufferings.

*{put him to grief*} Or, as some, *suffer him to be put to pain*, or, *torment*; because this form, oft has in it, a notion of permission: as Psal. 37.33. & 119.10,116. Chap. 63.17. and true it is, that God did not incite, or instigate those wicked wretches, unto those vile, and cruel courses and carriages, that they offered unto Christ, Jam. 1.15. but yet that his sufferings were by God predetermined for the salvation of mankind, is expressly said, Act. 2.23. & 4.28. and of Absoloms wicked act, we know what is said, 2 Sam. 12.11,22. of the word, see on ver. 3,4. the pronoun, *him*, is wanting in the text; as Chap. 13.2. supplied here from the words before.

*{when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin*} So if it be read, it may well close with the foregoing branch, as implying such harsh, and hard usage of him, then put in execution, and exercised, what time he was made such a sacrifice. Otherwise, as if as most seem to take them, they relate to the after fruits and benefits, mentioned in the words ensuing, it would rather be rendered, *when thou shalt have made his soul an offering for sin*: as, Chap. 4.4.

*{when*} Heb. *if*. So Num. 36.4. Job 21.6. Chap. 28.25.

*{thou shalt make his soul*} As, 2 Cor. 5.21. a change of the person; the speech being turned to God; as Ch. 2.9. or, *his soul shall have made itself an offering*; for the second person masculine, and the third feminine, are in letters, and sound, the same, *his soul*; that is, *himself*: or, he himself, as Psal. 3.2. and as God made a sacrifice of him; so he made a sacrifice of himself, Eph. 5.2. Heb. 91.4,25,26. But the former seems the better.

*{an offering for sin*} Heb. *trespass*, or, *sin*. So Levit. 5.19. & 7.5. Zach. 14.19. and so of our Savior, 2 Cor. 5.21. *God made him sin*; that is, *a sin sacrifice*: a sacrifice *for sin*, Rom. 8.2. for the word *sacrifice*, is there also wanting; as Heb. 10.8. because he had undertaken for the guilt of our sins, ver. 7. and sustained for us, the penalty due thereunto, ver. 5,6. 1 Cor. 5.7.

*{he shall see his seed*} Heb. *a seed*; that is, issue, posterity, as Gen. 15.3. *thou hast not given me a seed*: and Gen. 4.25. *God hath set me a seed*: and, *so shall thy seed be*, Gen. 15.5. *his* is not in the Hebrew; but may be supplied: as oft elsewhere, ver. 3. Chap. 27.6. & 40.12. yet not greatly needful here: *a seed*, indefinitely, is sufficient. It is that which our Savior of himself, applying it to himself, and the fruit of his sufferings; *If the grain fall into the ground and die there, it fructifies, and multiplies; it brings forth much fruit*, Joh. 12.24,32,34. and so Christ by his death, brought *many sons to God*, Heb. 12.10,3. even a numberless progeny. See on verse 8. *who can reckon up his race?* as from Abraham and Sarah, that were esteemed, *a dead stock*, the one: and *no better than dead*, the others, Gen. 18.11,12. Rom. 4.19. Heb. 11.12. and from Isaac destinated unto death, & *received again*, in a manner, *from the dead*; sprung a numberless issue, Ge. 22.2,10. & 26.24. & Heb. 11.17–19.

*{see seed*} Live, and survive to see them; as Job *lived to see his sons, and sons' sons*, Job 42.16. and *thou shalt see thy children's children*, Psal. 128.6.

*{he shall prolong his days*} The pronoun is wanting; as before: in regard whereof, the words have a twofold sense given them, Some expounding them, of Christ himself, who, after his resurrection, should die no more; nor live a while here, and then die again; as some other, raised to life, for a time, 1 King. 17.22. 2 King. 4.35. & 8.5. & 13.21. Luk. 7.15. & 8.55. Joh. 11.44. but live, and reign, for ever, Act. 13.34. Rom. 6.9,10. Heb. 7.25. & 9.27,28. and Rev. 1.18. Others, of his issue, the race of Saints; (and the ancient Greek, and old Latin, go both that way) being to continue successively here on earth, to the world's end, and from thenceforth to live with him in glory for ever, Mat. 16.18. & 28.20. and 25.46. Joh. 25,29. & 11.25,26. & 14.19. 1 Thess. 4.17. and then it should be read, *he shall see a seed, that shall prolong its days*, with a supply of the relative; as Chap. 51.12. but the former seems more probable. Of the phrase, see Deut. 17.20. Prov. 28.16.

*{and the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in his hand*} Or, *the will*; as the old Latin gives it, according to that Joh. 4.38. and 6.38. Or, *the desire*, as the word is rendered, 1 Sam. 18.25. Or, *the purpose of the Lord*, as Eccl. 3.1,17. and 8.6. it has reference to the verb, from whence it comes, used in the first branch. That which God intended to effect, by giving him up, Rom. 8.32. V. 9. and for which he was well content, & pleased so to do, shall, by his means, and ministry (so the word *hand*, is ordinarily used, Chap. 20.3. and 37.24. & 6.4–7.) accordingly take effect. See ver. 11. 52,13.

**V. 11.** *{He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied*} Or, as some render it, *He shall see the fruit of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied*. That is, he shall receive, and enjoy that, as the effect, and issue, of all the pains that he has taken, and pain that he has endured; that shall give him full content.

*{shall see*} *To see*, is commonly used, for, *to perceive*, or *enjoy*; as, *to see good*, for, *to receive*, or, *enjoy good*, Ps. 34.12. Job 9.25. Jer. 17.6. *to see life*, for, *to enjoy life*, *to live*, Eccl. 9.9. Joh. 3.36. & it is used frequently, without any further addition, to behold, what one much desires, with great delight, Ps. 35.2. & 54.7. & Ch. 60.5. & 66.14. so here.

*{of the travail*} Heb. *from the travail*; as, *to eat of one's bread*, Lev. 22.13. Num. 15.19. and, *to drink of one's wine*, Dan. 1.5. Jer. 51.7. *travail*, for the fruit of his *travail*, as, *labor*, for the fruit of one's *labor*, Psal. 128.2. *thou shalt eat the labor of thine hands*; eat, and enjoy that, for which your hands have labored; or, *from the travail*, that which proceeds, and comes from it; as, *from the eater came meat, and from the strong, sweet*, Judg. 14.14. and the word rendered *travail*, signifies properly toilsome, troublesome, wearisome labor, Deut. 26.7. Job 5.7. Psal. 107.12.

*{the travail of his soul*} For, *his travail*, or, *his own travail*; as, *his soul*, for, *himself*, ver. 9.

*{shall be satisfied*} A metaphor taken, either from persons, that, having been much pinched, and pained with hunger and thirst, have food, or drink, afforded them now to their fill, which they so much wished for, and earnestly desired before, Psal. 107.5,9. Mat. 5.6. or, from the husbandman, that has his fill of those fruits of the earth, that he has taken much pains for; or, of trees, and plants, that he has taken much pains about, 2 Chron. 31.10. Joel 2.26. contrary to that, Hos. 4.10. Mic. 9.14. Hag. 1.6. See Prov. 12.11. and 28.19. 2 Tim. 2.6. But there are two other expositions, (to pass by the rest,) that carry some good show of probability with them, we have authors of good note for them. The former render the words thus, *When, he shall see his soul* (that is, *himself*, as before,) *freed from trouble* (having an end put unto all those troubles that he was here exposed unto, and exercised with) *he shall be satisfied*, that is, most abundantly filled with glory, being taken up into heaven, and set there at God's right hand, Psal. 16.11. & 17.15. The latter (that which to me seems the more probable of the twain) read the words thus; *For the travail of his soul, he shall see seed, and be satisfied*: *For the travail of his soul*, that is, *because he hath travailed*: as, *for my knowledge*, that is *because I knew*, Chap. 48.4. *he shall see a seed*: supplied from the verse before-going, as, Job 3.17,18,20,23. & 22.24. Chap. 52.26. *and he shall be satisfied*: that is, much refreshed, and gladded therewith: and the metaphor they suppose taken from women delivered of child, after hard, and long labor: which sense, and notion admitted, I should rather render the text *after the travail of his soul*; that is, *after his travail*: yet the word, *soul*, may be the better retained; because a feminine term, and that sex here alluded to rather: by whose *pangs*, in travail also, are Christ's sufferings deciphered, Act. 2.27. for so the word there used, properly signifies. *After* these therefore (for so the particle is oft used, as was before showed, on ver. 8.) past, and gone, *he shall see seed*: He shall not travail in vain, as those complain, that they did, as if they went but with wind, Chap. 26.18. and that the babe was come near to the breaking place, but no power to bring forth, Chap. 37.3. God would not cause to travail, and deny delivery, Chap. 66.9. but the fruit of his travail, so much desired, he should obtain, to wit, a numerous issue of faithful souls begotten to God, which he himself also should survive to see with much joy, (that which women oft in that case fail of, Gen. 35.17,19. 1 Sam. 3.18–21.) being so taken therewith, as a woman, that being safely delivered, after sore and sharp labor, forgets now all her forepassed sorrow, for joy of her much desired birth, Joh. 16.21. And this exposition, the words of the text do very well bear: though I adhere rather to the first.

*{by his knowledge shall my righteous Servant justify many*} These words are delivered, as in the person of God the Father, with whose words he began; Chap. 52.13. and the like passages from person to person, we oft meet with in this prophet, as Chap. 13.11. & 17.10. and 22.19. & 26.19. and they hold out unto us, the main fruit, and effect, of Christ's passion, before-mentioned, man's justification, and reconciliation, to God, Rom. 3.24,25. & 5.1,8,10. and the seed, or issue, that he should see, & rest satisfied in, for all the pains that he had undertaken, and for their sakes, undergone: the persons thus justified, and saved by those sufferings, whereby satisfaction was fully made unto God, for their sins, Heb. 2.10,13. The greatest satisfaction to his soul, is to see souls justified, by faith, in him; as the greatest joy, and contentment of mind, to his faithful ministers, to see souls won, and begotten, by their ministry, to him, 1 Cor. 4.15. Gal. 4.19. 1 Thess. 21.9,20. 2 Joh. 4. 3 Joh. 3.14.

*{by his knowledge*} Or, to make it more plain, and take away all ambiguity, *the knowledge of him*: not his *knowledge*, taken subjectively; his own knowledge, as some would here expound it: the knowledge, that he has himself, either of God, Mat. 11.27. Joh. 8.55. & 10.15. or, of them, Joh. 10.14,27. but his knowledge, taken objectively, that is, the knowledge, whereby they know him, Phil. 3.8. 2 Pet. 1.3. & 2.20. So Psal. 5.7. *thy fear*: for, *the fear of thee*, and, *my fear*, for *the fear of me*, Jer. 32.40. & Psal. 139.17. *thy thoughts*, for, *my thoughts of thee*: and, *my wrong*, for, *the wrong*, by others, *done to me*, Gen. 16.5. Jer. 51.37. Yet not, that the bare knowledge of Christ, is that, whereby we are justified: for the devils themselves, both know, and acknowledge him too, Mar. 1.24,34. Luk. 4.34,41. but by *knowledge of him*, is meant, *faith on him*, Act. 25.23. & 26.28. the antecedent, for the consequent, as Joh. 17.3. because the *knowledge* of him, is the ground of *trust*, and confidence in him, Rom. 10.14,17. 1 Joh. 5.20. as the *belief of him*, though not the justifying act of faith (for the devils, also, *believe and tremble*, Jam. 2.19.) yet, is put for *trust*, and *confidence, in him*, Act. 13.39. Rom. 10.9. 1 Joh. 5.1. for that act, whereby we are said to be justified, where the apostle states the controversy concerning justification, Rom. 3.25,26. and whereby the same is more fully expressed, and more precisely defined, Joh. 3.15,16,18,36. Act. 16.31. and 20.21. & 24.25. Rom. 10.14. Gal. 2.16.

*{my righteous Servant*} *My Servant*: because serviceable to God his Father; yea, unto the Elect of God also, in the work of man's redemption. See Chap. 42.1. & 52.13. Mat. 20.28. Mar. 10.45. Luk. 22.27. Rom. 15.8. Phil. 2.7. *righteous Servant*, as, *righteous Lord*, Psal. 11.7. (the adjective, before the substantive, not so usual in that language) called therefore *that righteous one*, Act. 3.14. & 7.52. and 22.14. because wholly free from all act, or taint, of sin, ver. 10. 2 Cor. 5.21. 1 Joh. 3.5. which unless he had been, he could not have been, either a fit priest, Heb. 7.26. or, a fit sacrifice, 1 Pet. 1.18,19. to make satisfaction to God, for the sins of others, having need to satisfy for his own sins, & for himself, Heb. 7.27. 1 Pet. 2.18.

*{shall justify*} Some would have the word, here used, to signify no other, than a converting of men to godliness and righteousness, by wholesome instruction, and religious institution: as the ministers of God, or teachers, are said *to make many wise, and righteous*, Dan. 12.3. for so, questionless, the word is there taken: and in a notion, near thereunto, Rev. 22.11. the term being used of inherent *righteousness*, as we usually speak, and as the Scripture, also, uses the word *righteous*, and *righteousness*, Mat. 5.20. & 6.31. Luk. 1.6,75. Eph. 4.24. or *sanctification*, as it is more distinctly, and specially termed in Scripture, Rom. 6.22. 2 Cor. 7.1. 1 Thess. 4.3,4. 2 Thess. 2.13. and true it is, that none are *justified*, but such as are withal *sanctified*, 1 Cor. 6.11. as also, that we have as well the one, as the other, from Christ, 1 Cor. 1.30. & 6.11. Heb. 9.14. & 10.10. 1 Pet. 1.2. Rev. 1.5,6. but yet that is not the notion of the word, in this place, but by *justifying*, is here meant, as also, through the whole discourse of *justification*, in Pauls epistles, Rom. 3.24,25,26,28,30. and 4.2,5,25. & 5.1,9,16,18. Gal. 2.16. 1 Cor. 6.11. (in which last place, also, *justification*, and *sanctification*, are expressly distinguished, the one from the other) to wit, of the discharge of men, from the guilt of sin, by making satisfaction unto God for the same: as evidently appears by the whole course of the context, and the main matter of the prophet's discourse in this place: as well by those passages before, that clear the way to this, ver. 5,6,7,10. as also, by the reason of it rendered, in the very words next ensuing: For being wholly discharged, of *all sin and all iniquity*: that is, of all guilt of sin, either for the omitting of aught, that they were bound to do (for that also makes guilty, and liable to the curse, Deut. 27.26. Gal. 3.10,13.) or, for the committing of aught, that they ought, not to have done; yea, or in regard of any the least warping, as well as swerving, by any obliquity of heart, or spirit from the law of God, the only strict, and straight rule of all righteousness (for that also comes within the compass of *sin*, and *iniquity*; 1 Joh. 3.4. and 5.17.) being thus (I say) discharged of all guilt of sin whatsoever, and of what kind, or name soever they must of necessity become, and justly be deemed (so far, as concerns any guilt of sin) perfectly *righteous*, Romanes 5.19. Phillip 3.9. and be consequently *justified*, that is, even in justice acquitted, and assoiled, whensoever they shall be cited to appear at God's tribunal, Romanes 3.26,30. & 8.1,33,34. But of this notion, and use of the word *justify*, see more on Chapter 3.25.

*{many*} So Matthew 20.28. and 26.28. Romanes 5.15,19. even, *all that trust in him*, Psalm 2.12. and 37.40. John 3.15,16,18,36. & 6.29,35,40. & 11.25,26. Act. 10.43. & 13.38,39. 1 Joh. 2.2. therefore *many*, because satisfaction made by him, for *many*, V. 12.

*{for he shall bear their iniquities*} Heb. *and he shall bear their iniquities*; but the copulative is oft used, in a causal notion; as implying the cause, or reason, rendered, of what was before said. So ver. 2. Psa. 75.1. & 95.9. & 108.12. Chap. 38.21. & 40.26. & 52.15. yet it may also be rendered; *whose iniquities he shall bear*: for the copulative oft supplies, also, the place of the relative; as Job 20.11. & 37.5. Ch. 4.6. & 17.2. & 28.1. whether way we here take it, either as rendering the reason, why he should *justify* so many; because he should *bear* the guilt of their sins, and thereby make full satisfaction unto God for them; (for by such bearing of them, 1 Pet. 2.24. he should take them away from them, Joh. 1.29.) or, as describing the persons, whom he should justify; not all promiscuously, but those only, whose sins he undertook to discharge, and for whom he laid down his life; that is, the faithful and penitent alone, unto whom, only, he promises to make good this favor, and assigns to share in the fruit of his intercession, and sufferings, Mat. 9.13. & 11.28. Mar. 1.15. Joh. 3.18. & 17.9,20. it will come, in effect and substance, all to one, & the result of all will be, that Christ justifies those, and those alone, that rely on him, and belong to him, by his sufferings for their sins, Rom. 5.8,9. See ver. 10.

**V. 12.** *{Therefore I will divide him a portion with the great; and he shall divide the spoil with the strong*} In this passage is related another fruit, and effect of the sufferings of Christ, and his service, exhibited unto God his Father therein; to wit, the multitudes of those, that God the Father would for the same bestow upon him, to the advancement of his honor, being adorned, and enriched with them, as a victorious conqueror, and triumpher, with rich spoils and booties, taken from those, whom by fight, he has subdued.

*{Therefore*} So the apostle: *Therefore also*, Philip 2.9. because he has done me and finished, this faithful service, refusing no pains, hardship, or evil usage, attending upon it, Ch. 50.5,6. V. 10. and in the next branch again. See Joh. 17.4,5. and the apostle Paul of himself, 2 Tim. 4.7,8. and of all the faithful, our Savior himself, Rev. 3.21.

*{I*} God the Father, who spoke before, V. 11. so Ps. 2.8. See John 6.37,39,44,65. Act. 2.47. & 11.21.

*{will divide him a portion with the great*} This some understand of a portion of honor and dignity, collated upon Christ, not as the *first-born* only, in one respect, Rom. 8.29. Col. 1.15. unto whom a double portion was due, Deut. 21.17. but, as the *only-begotten* also of the Father, in another respect, Joh. 1.14. far above all creatures, either men, or angels, Psal. 45.7. Eph. 1.21. Phil. 2.9. Col. 1.18,19. Heb. 1.3,4,6,9. and they suppose it to be taken from the division of inheritances, Josh. 14.1. Prov. 29.24. Luk. 15.12. in regard whereof, they insert the word *portion*, which is not in the text; as some other also who expound it by that, Psal. 2.8. *I will give the heathen for thine inheritance*; and *thou inheritest all nations*, Psal. 82.8. understanding it, as spoken of the great princes, and potentates of this world, that should be brought in, and made to submit, and stoop to the scepter of Christ, Ch. 49.23. & 52.13,15. & 60.3,10. Psal. 72.10,11. and to avoid ambiguity, lest any should seem to share herein with Christ, and yet in some kind and degree, some are said so to do, Ch. 49.23. & 60.10. Mat. 19.28. Joh. 17.22. Rev. 2.26,27. & 3.21. & 21.7.) they would have the words rendered, *I will divide him great ones for a portion*. Others, again, insert the word, *spoil*, supplied from the next branch, thus rendering the words, *I will divide great ones to him, for a spoil*; or *I will divide him a spoil of great ones*: whereby they understand those principalities and powers, of the kingdom of darkness subdued, spoiled and triumphed over, by Christ, Col. 2.15. an allusion to the distribution of spoils, after some great victory obtained, or conquest achieved, Judg. 5.30. Psal. 68.12. 2 Chr. 20.25. Chap. 9.2. & 33.23. Zach. 14.7. Heb. *I will divide to him, of*, or *in great ones*, or *many*: (for the word is ambiguous, and is used as ordinarily in the one notion, as in the other, of multitude, as of magnitude, whence the like ambiguity, Psal. 35.11. & 119.162.) Some therefore here render it, *I will give many to him*, or *bestow many on him*, and that with very good probability: For howsoever it be true, that the word, here used does signify, in the first place, *to distribute*, or *divide*, Josh. 22.8. Neh. 13.13. yet the word is used sometime, at the second hand, simply, for *to impart, bestow, give, assign*, or *attribute*, even where no distribution is necessarily implied, or, at least intended: because of division, and distribution, that is the ordinary end. So is the word deemed to be taken, Deut. 4.19. of the *Sun, Moon* and *Stars*, which the Lord has *imparted*, and *assigned, unto all Nations*, bestowed upon all alike, Deut. 29.26. *whom he had not given unto them*, Job 21.17. *he gives sorrows in his anger*, Job 39.17. of the *ostrich*: *he hath not imparted unto her understanding*: where the same particle is found before *understanding*, that is here, before *great*, or *many*. And it seems to be no other here, than there; but note only of the accusative case, as it is commonly termed; as also, Exod. 7.20. Lev. 24.16. Job 21.12. Eccl. 5.10. Lam. 1.17. Jon. 3.5. So the meaning should be no more than this, that God would bestow many upon him, or give many unto him, to be his subjects, whether with an allusion to a portion of inheritance; as Psalm 16.5,6. or, the distribution of spoils; as Genesis 49.27. it is indifferent.

*{he shall divide the spoil with the strong*} It is by the best interpreters acknowledged, that the same is in some other terms repeated here, that was intimated in the words foregoing: this difference only observe, that the Father's donation and appointment, was pointed to there; Christ's possession, and enjoyment of what was by his Father's donation assigned to him, here. Divers go the same way here, that our English does; *he shall divide the spoil with the strong*, (as Prov. 16.17. *to divide the spoil with the proud*; and Prov. 29.24. *to partake with a thief*; but another particle there:) that is, say some, he shall settle his kingdom, among the great and mighty kingdoms of this world; as sharing in some sort with them, Rev. 11.15. the old Latin reads it, *he shall divide the spoil of the mighty* that is, as some, the spoils that Satan, the *strong man*, had formerly been possessed of, Luke 11.21,22. but I find not yet, where this particle is used, as a note of the genitive case. Some render it, *that he may divide the spoil with the strong*: so the copulative was used before, ver. 2. see there; as if it were said, I will furnish him with all endowments, whereby he may be enabled to grapple with, conquer, plunder, and triumph over, all the enemies of man's salvation, Col. 2.15. to which purpose also, some other, *he shall divide the mighty as a spoil*. But in the last place some render it; (which to me seems most probable) he shall *obtain, receive, perceive*, or *possess*, very many *for a prey*: for as the word, that primarily signifies, *to divide*, or *distribute*, either inheritance, or prey, does signify, in the next place, *to impart, assign*, or *give*, and *bestow*, in general, in relation to the giver, so it is used also, in general, for *to inherit, receive, obtain*, and *possess*, in relation to the receiver. So Josh. 18.2. *those remained that had not yet received their inheritance*, Job 27.17. *He* (that is, the wicked man) *shall prepare it, but the just shall wear it; and the guiltless shall inherit, obtain, possess*, or *enjoy his silver*, Psal. 60.6. *I will obtain Sechem*, or *possess it*, make myself Lord of it: and for the word commonly rendered *strong*, it is very apparent, both that the verb, from whence it comes, has very usually a notion of multitude in it. (See on Chap. 31.1.) and the word itself is most frequently used, to signify *very many*; as Chap. 8.7. Gen. 18.18. Num. 14.12. Deut. 4.38. & 9.1. & 11.23. & 26.5. Josh. 23.9. Joel 2.5. Mic. 4.7. and, *for a prey*, the word so joined with *very many*, without any particle coming between, is also not unusual: for so it is said, Psal. 135.11. *he gave their land an inheritance*, that is, *for an inheritance*. So that the words, thus resolved, intimate the numerous or innumerable, rather, multitude of those that should be converted unto Christ (of which, see Act. 2.41,47. & 4.4. & 6.7. & 8.6,11. & 11.21. & 13.44,48. & 21.20.) whom he is said to obtain and possess, or enjoy, as a spoil or a prey: in allusion either to the choicest substance, jewels or garments especially, that were reserved, and set apart, for the general, or commander in chief, to wear; riding in triumph, Judges 5.30. 2 Samuel 12.30. or, to captives, great ones especially, taken in fight, or conquest, and following the conqueror, as an addition to his magnificence and honor, Chapter 45.14. and 49.18.

*{because he hath poured out his soul unto death*} Poured out, as water is *poured out*: so is the word used, Gen. 20.24. and so the psalmist of himself, in the person of Christ, Psal. 22.14. *I am poured out like water*: and so some expound the phrase here used; *pour not out my soul*, or *life*, Psal. 141.8. because when the soul departs, the life goes with it: *he poured out his soul*, or *his life*; (so the word is used, Psal. 26.9. & 31.13. & 35.4. and 56.6.) as if he had made no more reckoning of it, than of water: as it is said of the martyrs slain for him, that *they loved not their souls*, that is, *their lives, unto death*, Rev. 12.11. they parted with their lives, for his sake as freely, and as willingly, as if they valued, or loved them not, (which helps to explain that, Luke 14.26.) they did that in Christ's cause, that himself before, for them, to fulfill his Father's will, had done, Joh. 10.17,18. & 14.30,31. So the apostle of him; *He became obedient unto death*, Phil. 2.8. See Luke 23.46. of *pouring out of the soul*, in another sense, to wit, by prayer with tears. See 1 Sam. 1.15. compared with Ch. 7.6. Ps. 42.3,4. Lam. 2.19. and of our Savior somewhat near it, in that notion, Heb. 5.7.

*{and he was numbered with the transgressors*} Or, *with transgressors*: for there is no article in the text. He was reckoned, as such an one, as one of that rank; being put to the same death, that malefactors used to suffer, in the same place, where such were ordinarily wont to be executed; and at the same time, when some other also in the same place were to suffer: two notorious thieves; the one, crucified on his right, and the other on his left hand, he hanging in the midst between them, as the principal of them, Mat. 27.38. wherein the evangelist tells us, that this prophecy was fulfilled, Mar. 15.27,28. yea, he was not only reckoned among them, but cast behind them; or (if you will) for height of evil desert, preferred before them, when Barabbas, that notorious miscreant, was required to be let loose, rather than he should be let live, Mat. 27.16,17,20,21. Mark 15.7,11. Luke 23.18,19,25. Acts 3.14,15.

*{and he bare the sin of many*} The penalty of the sins of all that numerous, or numberless multitude, before-mentioned, that were, by the ministry of the gospel, so brought home to him, as sincerely to trust on him, verse 5,6. which, by bearing also for them, verse 4. 1 Peter 2.24. he took away from them; Joh. 1.29. and by discharging them of the guilt thereof, V. 7. brought them into a justifiable condition, even in God's sight; and at his tribunal, V. 11.

*{and made intercession for the transgressors*} For those very transgressors, or wicked ones, by whom he suffered Luk. 23.34. wherein Steven also imitated him, Acts 7.60. for the article, here emphatical, seems to point unto that special act, and those particular persons; but has relation, also, to Christ's intercession for sinners, that belong to him, and have interest in him, Rom. 4.5. & 5.6,8,10. which continues still, and shall do unto the world's end, Rom. 8.34. Heb. 7.25. & 9.24. 1 Joh. 2.1,2.

### CHAPTER 54

**Verse 1.** *{Sing, O barren*} This chapter some suppose to belong to the former sermon, or prophecy, beginning at Ch. 52.1. and proceeding on from thence, in a continued discourse, concerning the state of the church restored, unto ver. 12. which having been there interrupted, with a digression, concerning, either the Messiah, or some other, whom they suppose to be there meant, should, in this chapter, be returned unto again. But most take it to be a new prophecy, distinct from the former, though much of the same subject, and argument, with it: Howsoever, it has a good coherence with, and dependence upon, the latter end of the former: For that ended with mention, as has been showed, of those multitudes that should be converted to Christ: this begins with those swarms of people, that should be bred by, and brought into the church; and is wholly spent in predictions, and promises, of the enlargement and advancement thereof, together with the continuance of it in that estate.

*{Sing*} Or, *Shout*, for joy; as Ch. 12.6. Zeph. 3.14. Zach. 2.10. for there is also a crying out for grief, Lam. 2.19. where the same word is used.

*{O barren, thou that didst not bear*} A want of the relative; as Ch. 51.12. and so in the next branch. This some understand of the Jewish church and state, returned from captivity, which, during the time of that Babylonish bondage, seemed to be as a widow, or a lone woman, barren without hope of issue, ver. 4. See Ch. 49.21. Others, of the Gentiles, to be called in, by the ministry of the gospel, who had been before barren, and brought none forth unto God, being *without Christ, without God*, in the world, Eph. 2.1–3,12. It may well be understood of the church under the New Testament, consisting jointly of Jew and Gentile; though with reference unto that former, as a type of this latter. See Galatians 4.27.

*{break forth into singing, and cry aloud, thou that didst not travail*} The same thing repeated in other more emphatical terms, implying abundant matter of exceeding great joy. Of the terms, see on C. 12.6. & 14.7. & 55.1,2.

*{travail*} For *bear*, or *bring forth*, the antecedent for the consequent; as Ch. 23.4.

*{for more are the children of the desolate, than the children of the married wife, saith the Lord*} Heb. *many from*, or *in comparison of, them*, for, *more* in number than they; as it is rendered, Gal. 4.27. See the like use of this particle, Judg. 5.34. Psal. 45.7. Prov. 22.1. Eccl. 7.1. That is, as not a few: the Jewish state, that had been a long time desolate, shall abound in people much more than either herself formerly, in her flourishing estate, as some; or than other kingdoms and provinces, say others, that had enjoyed a continued succession of kings, (a king say they, being as an husband to a state) which she for a long time wanted; and cities inhabited, whereas their land had been depopulated, and their cities ruined: and they observe withal, that Jerusalem, even in her latter times, is reported, by Pliny, l. 5. C. 14. to have been the famousest, or fairest city, not of Jewry alone, but of all the eastern parts. But the most refer it to the spiritual estate of Sion, to the *Jerusalem, from above*, unto which more children were to be begotten, and bred again, by the ministry of the gospel, 1 Cor. 4.15. 1 Pet. 1.23. of the Gentiles, that were wholly barren before; than of the Jews, that were sometime fruitful, Rom. 9.23,26,30. Rev. 7.4,9. And there is thought to be in the words, some allusion to Sarahs case, though a long time barren; yet in issue afterward going beyond Hagar, Gen. 11.30. & 17.19. & 21.12. & 22.17. Gal. 4.27,31. or to Hannah, in regard of Peninnah, at first, barren, and yet afterward more fruitful than the other, 1 Sam. 1.5,6,20. & 2.5.
