**Ver. 2.** *{Enlarge the place of thy tent*} Heb. *widen*; as Cha. 5.14. Implying, that her issue and inhabitants, should so increase and multiply, that she should want room to receive them. See Chapter 49.20,21. and 60.4,5. it has reference to their ancient manner of dwelling in tents, Gen. 12.8. & 18.1. & 26.17. & 33.19. Hebr. 11.9.

*{and let them stretch out the curtains of thine habitations*} That is, *let the curtains* (of which their tents consisted, Exod. 26.1,12. Jer. 4.20.) *be stretched out*, for the verb is used impersonally. See the like. Ch. 33.1. & 34.11.

*{spare not, lengthen thy cords*} Or, *spare not to lengthen* (as, *multiply, wash me*, for *multiply to wash me*, wash me over and over, again and again, Ps. 51.2.) *thy cords*: wherewith those curtains were fastened, whereof their tents consisted, unto pins, or stakes, driven into the ground. See Ch. 33.20.

*{and strengthen thy stakes*} Make them strong, and sure; drive them fast into the ground, that they may be able to hold, and keep right, such a weight of curtains, of that length and breadth, that yours must be, being fastened to them, by those cords. See hereof also, Chapter 33.20.

**Ver. 3.** *{For thou shalt break forth on the right hand, and on the left*} The reason why the tent was to be enlarged; because her issue, that must dwell in it, would be multiplied, and room on every side, on either hand, was to be made for them. See Chapter 49.20.

*{break forth*} That is, bring forth, and propagate abundantly: so is the word used, both of mankind, and other creatures, Gen. 30.30,43. Exod. 1.12. 1 Chr. 4.38. Job 1.10. and it is a metaphor, taken, either, from the breaking forth of issue, at time of delivery, Gen. 38.33. See Ch. 37.3. or, from such plenty of any material laid up in a storehouse, as being more in quantity, than the place is able well to contain, breaks through the walls that enclose it, Proverbs 3.10.

*{on the right hand, and on the left*} That is, say some, to the south, and to the north, or, southward, and northward, as intimating which way the church should most propagate: because the face being turned eastward; (which part of the world, as placed before man, so situate, has its name. See on Ch. 2.6.) the south is on the right hand, (thence in Hebrew denominated. See Ch. 21.1. & 43.6.) and the north on the left. But this is too nice: the phrase, *on the right hand, and on the left*, is used for, on either side, Exod. 14.29. Num. 22.26. 2 Sam. 16.6. Ch. 9.20. In the phrase, there seems a defect, to be thus more fully made up; *thou shalt bring forth*, or, be delivered of those, that shall break out, (through the curtains of your tents, if it be not made the wider to hold them) both *on the right hand, and on the left*; as alluding to a storehouse, so unreasonably stowed, that the walls are enforced to give way, on either side. See Zach. 2.4.

*{and thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles*} This, some understand of the Jewish people, who, after their return from the captivity, did, in process of time, enlarge their territories, and encroached upon some parts of Moab, Edom, and Syria; according to that promise made by God, to Abraham, Gen. 22.17. *Thy seed shall possess their enemies gates*. But whatsoever was therein then done, was but a dim shadow of that which is herein principally intended: to wit, the inheritance which God would give unto Christ, and to his church together with him, by multitudes of faithful converts, in all parts of the world. See on Chap. 46.12. and 53.12. A work begun by the apostles; the children of the former church, and carried on by those, that succeeded them, in the spreading of the gospel, Mathew 28.19,20. Mark 16.15. Luk. 24.47. Acts 1.8. Romanes 10.18.

*{and make the desolate places to be inhabited*} They shall people the world, that lay as desolate before, with a new race of faithful people, V. 1. as after their return from the captivity, they reedified, and replenished their cities, and country again. Psalm 6.9.35. Ch. 44.26. & 49.8. & 51.3.

**V. 4.** *{Fear not*} Do not, out of a distrustful conceit, entertain groundless fears, as if the things, now foretold you, were matters incredible, and impossible to be performed. See Ch. 41.10,14. & 43.1. and 44.8.

*{For thou shalt not be ashamed*} Or, *blush*, Ch. 50.7. as one frustrate of his expectation, and failing of his hopes, Rom. 5.5. or, you shall not continue still in, or return again unto, that deserted, dejected, and reproachful condition, wherein, at present, you are, Ve. 6. See Chapter 29.22.

*{neither be thou confounded; for thou shalt not be put to shame*} The same thing repeated in other terms; to give the fuller assurance of the performance of the things promised, and add further strength to the feeble faith of his poor people, Ch. 35.3,4. So likewise, Chap. 29.22.

*{for thou shalt forget the shame of thy youth, and shalt not remember the reproach of thy widowhood any more*} Or, *but thou shalt forget*, &c. as the particle is expressed, Chap. 30.16. & 49.25. so great, and glorious shall your condition be, and your issue so ample, that it shall drown the memory, both of your mean and reproachful estate, which in your younger years, you sustained, in the Egyptian servitude, Jer. 2.2. Ezek. 23.3. and the like also, which you do now undergo, in your present Babylonian bondage, Ch. 49.21. Lam. 1.1. you shall no more regard them, (so great shall your joy be) than as if they had never been, Ch. 65.16. Joh. 16.21. See the like expressions, Gen. 41.30,31,51.

**Ver. 5.** *{For thy maker is thine husband, (the Lord of hosts is his name)*} Or, *Thy Maker (whose name is the Lord of hosts)* (as Chap. 51.15.) *is thine husband*. The Sovereign Lord of the whole world, who has all the creatures at his command, and who, at first founded you, Deut. 32.15,18. Psal. 149.2. Chap. 43.1. & 44.2. is joined in marriage unto you; and will again live and dwell, as an husband, with you, to make you fruitful in issue, and honorable in estate, as beseems the wife of such an one to be. See C. 65.2. Hos. 2.19,20. Eph. 5.25,27,32.

*{Maker*} Heb. *makers*; for the word is in the plural number; as Job 35.10. See the note there.

*{and thy Redeemer, the holy One of Israel, the God of the whole earth shall he be called*} Or, *and he, that is, thy redeemer, the holy One of Israel*; or *thy redeemer, who is the holy One of Israel, shall be called the God of the whole earth*. He that founded you, will now rescue, and restore you again, Chap. 49.7,26. and will not be only (*to be called*: for *to be*: as Ch. 4.3. & 56.7.) the God of Israel, as formerly he has been, Deut. 26.17,18. both the God of all nations, throughout the whole world, Ch. 56.3,7. Zach. 14.9. Mat. 28.19. Rom. 3.29,30. & 10.12,13.

**V. 6.** *{For the Lord hath called thee, as a woman forsaken, and grieved in spirit, and a wife of youth, when thou wast refused, saith thy God*} Or, as some render the words, *For the Lord will call*, or *revoke thee, as a woman that hath been forsaken, and grieved in spirit, & a wife of youth, though thou wast rejected, will thy God call*, or *name thee*.

*{the Lord hath called thee*} Or *will call*; or, as some, *will recall thee*: as, *out of Egypt I called back my son*, Hos. 11.1. God will reunite you again unto him, as a man his wife, that he had left for a time, Jer. 3.1,12. & 4.1.

*{as a woman forsaken*} By her husband, upon some dislike or difference, falling out between them; so seemed she to be, during the time of her captivity, Chap. 62.4. See V. 7.

*{grieved in spirit*} In regard of her barrenness, say some, that was reproachful in those times, 1 Samuel 1.6–8,15. See on Chapter 4.1. but rather in regard, that God her husband seemed to have forsaken her, Chapter 49.14. the word used here, is that from whence *Jabez* his mother gave him that name. 1 Chr. 4.9. there is an elegant consonancy between this term, and the former in the Hebrew, which our English cannot express.

*{and a wife of youth*} *a young wife*; or *a wife taken in youth*, Prov. 5.18. Mal. 2.14. as *an husband of youth*. Joel 1.8. you shall be as dear to me, as a young wife to her husband, Chapter 62.5. or as ever you were to me, in your younger days, at first, Jer. 2.1,2. Ezekiel 16.8.

*{when thou wast refused*} Or, *though thou hast been*, or *wast rejected*, or *cast off*; as it is rendered, Jeremiah 31.37. for so she seemed to be, during the time of her captivity, as a woman *divorced*; Chap. 50.1. *dismissed*, Jer. 3.1. and cast off: so she complains of herself, that God had *utterly cast her off*, Lam. 5.20. and further, that he had made her as *refuse*, among foreign people, Lam. 3.45. which word seems the rather here to be used, as implying the despicable estate that she had been in, while her abode was in Babylon. See Jer. 30.17. and for the use of the particle, see on Chap. 12.1.

*{saith thy God*} Says he, who continues still to be your God, and to mind you, and your good, Chap. 49.15,16. or, as some, who join this clause to those words, *a wife of youth*; enclosing, as in a parenthesis, those that lie between them; *a wife of youth will the Lord name thee*, or *call thee*. So the verb of *saying*, is found used in the participle, *O thou that art named*, or *called, the house of Jacob*, Mica. 2.7. and the pronoun, oft omitted, may well be supplied from the former branch. See Chapter 51.2,3. and 58.13.

**V. 7.** *{For a small moment*} For a very short time. God as he is slow to wrath, Exod. 34.6. Num. 14.18. Chap. 48.9. so short in wrath usually, and in the expressions of it, towards his, Psal. 30.5. & 103.8,9. Chap. 26.20. their seventy years' captivity, is reckoned but as a moment, not only in regard of God with whom, *a thousand years* are but as one day, Psal. 90.4. 2 Pet. 3.8. and man's life reckoned, at that rate, Psal. 90.10. less than a moment, as just nothing, Ps. 30.5. but in regard of that ensuing favor and goodness of God, that shall continue unto all eternity, and that exceeding mass of glory & happiness issuing from it; able not to weigh down only, but to swallow up, whatsoever foregoing afflictions and grievances, though never so great, and of never so long continuance, 2 Cor. 4.17,18. Rom. 8.18. Heb. 11.37.

*{have I forsaken thee*} So God seems to do, both to the sight of others, and to their own sense also, when he withdraws from his people, those outward expressions of his favor and love towards them, which they had formerly enjoyed: and more especially, when for some space of time he gives them up into, and leaves them in the hands of their enemies, Psal. 22.1. and 37.9. & 71.11.

*{but with great mercies will I gather thee*} Heb. *and* (for *but*, as Ch. 53.5.) *with great tender mercies* (for so the word is not amiss rendered, Psal. 103.4. importing an inward yearning, and working of the bowels, in a mother, towards the fruit of her womb, from whence the word comes, 1 King. 3.16.) *will I gather thee*, or *take thee up*: as it is well rendered, Psal. 27.10. as some left, lost, or forlorn creature. See Ch. 40.11. Yet there may be in the word, some hint had to their dispersion, in the captivity, into sundry parts, out of which they were to be recollected, before they could be reduced. See Ch. 11.11,12. Thus is God far more free, and full in mercies and goodness, than in wrath and anger, to his, Exod. 20.6. Psal. 30.5. & 63.3. & 86.5.

**V. 8.** *{In a little wrath, I hid my face from thee, for a moment*} The same thing, in other terms, repeated again; as before the like was observed, V. 4.

*{a little wrath*} Opposed to the *great mercies*, mentioned verse 7. The word rendered *little*, is nowhere else found; but seems to have some affinity with a word used, Job 4.12. & 26.14. that is deemed to signify *a ship*: and there is an elegant paronomasy (which our English will not yield) between it, and the word translated *wrath*; but signifying, properly, *a bubble*, Hos. 10.7. that is no sooner up, but is suddenly down again; and may the rather be here used, to imply the shortness of God's wrath. See Chap. 34.2.

*{I hid my face from thee*} So also is God said to do, when he withdraws and withholds the wonted expressions of his favor, from persons, and people; especially, when having so done, and they being now in straits and distresses, he answers not their suits, for relief and release according to their desires, Deuteronomy 32.20. Psal. 27.9. & 30.7. See Chap. 1.15. & 8.17. & 57.17. a speech borrowed from those, that refuse to admit unto sight, or to look upon one, whom they do really disaffect, or would seem at least to be displeased with, 2 Sam. 14.24,28,32. 2 Kings 13.14. See on Chapter 53.3.

*{for a moment*} As verse 7.

*{but with everlasting kindness will I have mercy on thee*} Heb. *and* (as before V. 7.) *with kindness of perpetuity*; opposed to that little, or short moment of displeasure before-mentioned. See Ps. 103.17. Jer. 31.3.

*{saith the Lord thy Redeemer*} As ver. 5.

**V. 9.** *{For this is as the waters of Noah unto me*} This covenant of grace, that I will now enter into with you, shall be as firm, and as sure to continue, as that which I made at the general deluge, never to drown the whole world, in that manner again, Gen. 9.9.11.

*{the waters of Noah*} As we use to say, *Noahs flood*, for the deluge in his days, concerning such a general inundation as then was: the note of similitude wanting; as Chap. 51.12. Yet the Jewish critics, some of them, have another reading here, which the Chaldee also exhibits, and the old Latin retains, rendering the text: *as the days of Noah*, as Mathew 24.37. but the former reading is the more received, nor do the Jews themselves approve the other.

*{For as I have sworn*} Heb. *which I have sworn*; or as some render it, *who have sworn*, as having relation unto the words next before, *unto me*. Others, *concerning which I have sworn*. But it may well be rendered, *As I have sworn*: for so is the relative used, Jer. 48.8. *as the Lord hath spoken*. Otherwise, if we retain our version here, the relative must stand for the conjunction causal, as 1 Samu. 15.15. and the note of similitude must be supplied, as before; which is oft also in the other particle included. See Chapter 55.9.

*{I have sworn*} Or, *did*, sometime, *swear*; where any formal oath, concerning this, was by God conceived, we find not. Howbeit, in regard that solemn covenants of great concernment, were wont to be confirmed by oath, Gen. 26.28,31. & 31.44,53. 1 Sam. 20.16,17,42. God therefore speaks here of his solemn covenant, made, with all mankind, to Noah, as if he had taken a formal oath, in precise terms, for the constant and inviolable performance of it; as to Abraham he did for the confirmation of his faith, Gen. 12.2. & 17.3,4. & 22.17. Heb. 6.13,14. and is said to have done the like unto Isaac, Psal. 105.9. though we read only of a promise made him without any new oath, to make good unto him the oath made formerly to Abraham, Gen. 26.3,4. Yea, so is God said to have sworn, to make David King of Israel, 2 Sam. 3.9. and to set of his issue on his throne for ever, Psal. 132.11. though we find not upon record any formal oath concerning either: only a solemn symbol, intimating the one, 1 Sam. 16.12,13. and a solemn message sent unto him, concerning the other, 2 Sam. 7.12,16. but God's promises are as firm and sure, as any oath is, or can be. God cannot lie nor fail in the least tittle of aught he says, or undertakes, Num. 23.19. 1 Sam. 15.29. Mat. 5.18. Tit. 1.2.

*{that the waters of Noah shall no more go over the earth*} That is, such an inundation, as was in Noahs time, to drown the whole world again, Heb. *from the waters of Noah passing over the earth*: as if he had said, I bound myself, as by oath, from causing or suffering them so to do. Of the phrase, see before, Chapter 17.1. & 23.1. & 24.10. So in the next clause, *from being wroth, and from rebuking*.

*{so have I sworn, that I would not be wroth with thee, nor rebuke thee*} I have bound myself by oath, from being so incensed against you, as utterly to cast you off, or to destroy you; for of such a kind of wrath, and such a kind of rebuke, Ps. 9.5. does God speak in this place. See on the next verse. Otherwise God is angry oft, even with the best of his, Exod. 3.14. Num. 12.7. Deu. 3.26. and rebukes those, and that sharply too, sometime, whom he loves best, 2 Sam. 11.27. & 12.10,11. Ps. 32.3,4. & 38.3. & 118.18. Heb. 12.6. Rev. 3.19. Of God's rebuke, not verbal, but real, see ch. 50.2. Many other resemblances, between the waters of Noah, and the state of Gods people, do some expositors, and other writers, here frame; which conceiving to be beside the intention of Gods Spirit in this place, I forbear either to refute, or relate.

**V. 10.** *{For the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed; but my kindness shall not depart from thee; neither shall the covenant of my peace be removed*} That is, sooner shall the one be, than the other. So Chap. 51.6. See Jer. 31.35–37. & 33.20,21,25,26. from which places, parallel to this, collated with this, may evidently appear, in what notion those terms of *wrath,* and *rebuke,* v. 9. are to be taken.

*{the mountains shall depart*} Not necessarily implying, that they shall so do: for many of them are like to stand as long as the world lasts, Psal. 65.6. but that they sooner may so do, (as also some, sometime, in earthquakes, have done, alluded unto, Hab. 3.6. Zach. 14.4. Rev. 6.14. and whole regions with them; whereof, see Seneca, in his *natural questions,* l. 6. c. 29. and Pliny in his *natural story,* l. 2. c. 81,85,86.) sooner than that should come to pass, that God says, and swears, here shall never be: this the people of God built upon, Psal. 46.3.

*{the hills removed*} As following, or going along with the greater; *mountains* and *hills,* are oft joined together, Chapter 30.25. and 31.4. and 40.4,12. and 41.15. and in the two verbs here used, *mut,* and *mush,* differing but in one letter, there is an harmony of sound, which our language cannot fitly express.

*{the covenant of my peace*} Or, rather, *my covenant of peace,* Ezek. 34.25. & 37.26. that is of reconcilement to you, and continuance at one with you, Rom. 5.1,10. & 8.35,38,39. or of welfare, prosperity, and safety, everlasting, and never to have an end; for that notion also, the word of *peace,* oft has, Genesis 33.18. Chapter 9.6. & 26.3,12. and 48.18. ver. 13. See Heb. 9.12. and 10.4. and 13.20. whether way we take it, a most sweet and comfortable consideration for every true-hearted soul to rely, and rest itself upon, chap. 50.10.

*{saith the Lord that hath mercy on thee*} So Ch. 14.1. implying, that it is all of mere mercy, whatsoever God, in this kind, does for any of his, Ps. 6.4. & 106.43. Eph. 2.4,5. Tit. 3.5.

**V. 11.** *{O thou afflicted, tossed with tempests, and not comforted*} Heb. *afflicted,* (chap. 51.21.) *stormed,* like Jonas his ship, Jon. 1.11,13. for the same word is used of either: such seemed their estate to be, forlorn, helpless, hopeless, during the time of their captivity. So God by Zachary using the very same word, says, that he had *stormed them,* that is, with a storm, or tempest, driven them out, as a ship, or a fleet of ships, forced out of the haven, or from their moorings, where they rode in harbor quietly, into the main ocean, Zach. 7.14. and there with boisterous winds distressed, weather-beaten, and without rudder, tackle, or anchor, tossed to and fro, Jam. 3.4. in which distracted and distressed estate, they seemed to continue, while their captivity lasted, both destitute of all help from man, ch. 51.17,18. Lam. 1.2,3,12. and seeming utterly forsaken of, and forgotten with, God, ch. 40.27. & 49.14.

*{behold, I will lay thy stones with fair colors, and lay thy foundations with sapphire*} God promises, not to raise her only, out of that dejected and distressed estate, wherein at present she was, but to advance her, to a most eminent, and glorious condition: the spiritual excellencies of the church, under the Messiah, being here described by an hyperbolical similitude of such a goodly, costly, stately structure, whether city, or palace, as here on earth, is scarce imaginable: whereof, see the like, Rev. 21.11–21. and the relation hereof, is therefore ushered in with a note usually prefixed before such matter, as may deservedly require, both serious consideration, and admiration in abundance. See Chapter 7.14. and 28.16.

*{lay thy stones with fair colors*} Heb. *I am making,* or *will make,* (as Chap. 3.1. *is taking away*) *to lie with puc,* or *phuc, thy stones,* about which the Jewish critics much puzzle themselves. Some would have it rendered, *I will lay thy foundation, and the stones shall be of puc,* or *phuc.* Other, *I will lay thy pavement, with stones of puc,* or *phuc:* and they tell us, some of them, that it is the name of a precious stone, of a sandy color. Others, that it is black, and the same with *nophec,* mentioned Exod. 28.12. which the most render, *a carbuncle,* there, as many also do this here. Howbeit, a carbuncle is not black, having its name, indeed, from a *coal,* but a quick, and burning coal meant, not a dead one, as being of a fiery and flamy color. See on ver. 12. The word certainly signifies a kind of *paint, tincture,* or *complexion,* (as we nowadays term it) wherewith women used to improve, or taint and corrupt rather, their native hue, 2 King. 9.30. Jer. 4.30. which, whether it were composed of the juice of some plant, or the matter of some mineral, is not among the Jewish doctors agreed: But hence it is not unlikely, that the Latin word, *fucus,* used in general, for all such stuff, accustomed to counterfeit with, had its original, from whence also, was one of Jobs daughters named, *the horn of paint,* or *complexion,* for the eminency of her beauty, Job 42.14. and the Chaldee Paraphrast, therefore, renders the words, *I will cover,* or *varnish thy stones with paint,* using a word that is acknowledged to signify such stuff, as was before described and so our late translators, as some others also before them, both here, and 1 Chr. 29.2. render it, where the text is, *stones of puc,* or *phuc.* The verb whose participle is here used, signifies, in its first form, *to lie down;* properly, as beasts do: distinguished from another appropriated to mankind: yet sometime it is used more generally, as Job 11.19. Chap. 14.30. in the form here used, it signifies, *to make to lie down,* or *to lay.* Whence some of the Jewish commenters here render it, by a word used, Cant. 3.10. (from whence another for *a pavement,* 2 Kings 16.17.) signifying *to pave;* as if he had said, *I will lay thy pavement,* or *pave thee, with painted stones;* or *make thy pavement stones of goodly colors;* that is, of such fair, and curious colors, as may seem to have had some artificial tincture used to them. Rev. 21.21. *the streets* of the new Jerusalem, are said to be *paved with pure gold, as transparent as glass.* The participle is here put for the verb: as ch. 3.1. and there may seem an inversion of the terms, *I will lay,* or *pave in,* or *with paint, thy stones,* for *I will pave thee with stones of paint:* as the words are, 2 Chr. 29.2. See the like inversion of terms, Judges 1.8. Psalm 74.7. Howsoever, I concur rather with those, that understand this branch of the pavement, than with those that refer it to the foundation; whereof, in the next.

*{and lay thy foundations with sapphires*} Heb. *found thee with sapphires* as before, *pave thee with painted stones.* This stone is found in the priestly breastplate, Exod. 28.18. as also, in the foundations of the *new Jerusalem,* Rev. 21.19. the Jewish doctors tell us, some of them, that it is a precious stone of a red color; and that they would prove from Lam. 4.7. Other of them, that it is of a white color; that which they would draw from Exod. 24.10. but neither with any probability of proof from those places, as we shall (God willing, and assisting us) show, if we shall be able to break through to the former of them. But our jewelers, and lapidaries, generally hold the right sapphire, to be of a sky color; though sometime found, as powdered with some golden spots. So Theophrast, *of stones,* Pliny, l. 37. c. 9. and Dennis, the Greek Geographer, who calls it therefore, *the Golden sky colored sapphire.* In regard hereof, it is in visions, and apparitions, so frequently mentioned, Exod. 24.10. Ezek. 1.26. & 10.1. and hence some read these words of God to Job, Job 38.37. *Who by his wisdom can make the sky of a sapphirine hue:* such as it shows, when the air is most clear, and free from clouds. The word is both in Greek and Latin, the same with the Hebrew.

**V. 12.** *{And I will make thy windows Agates*} The windows are of special use in a building, and in regard of their situation, very conspicuous. They are here styled by a term, not elsewhere found, derived from the *Sun,* (whence also *Samson* had his name) because the ordinary use of them, is to let in the daylight, that proceeds from the Sun. And this being a principal use of them, beside their eminency otherwise, gives just cause to doubt, whether the word *Cadcod,* be well rendered *an Agate,* the *Agate,* being a stone, neither of any esteem or reckoning near to a *sapphire;* nor transparent, as the *sapphire* is. Howbeit, in Theophrasts time, it seems by him, that it bore some price: and Pliny, l. 37. c. 10. informs us; that though, in his time, they were of no great value, yet were, some sort of them, commended for their *glassy perspicuity.* But they that render it an *Achate,* or *an Agate,* seem to have been led most thereunto, by the affinity of the sound, and the letters, in either term, interchangeable. Others render it, both here; as also, Ezek. 27.16. some, *a Pyropus,* as so termed, of sparkling like fire, Job 41.19. some, a *Chrysoprase;* some, *Pearl;* some, *Amber,* some *Crystal;* which with windows seems best to suit: for they go too low, that would draw it down to *glass;* whereof also, I suppose no mention to be, in the sacred records, left us, in the Hebrew. Some would have instead of *windows,* here, *turrets,* or *sentinels:* but the notation of the word speaks for the former.

*{and thy gates of Carbuncles*} Heb. *stones of Ekdah,* or *Ekdach:* as *Ahaz,* and *Achaz,* Chap. 1.1. a word nowhere else found in Scripture; but having its name from a word that signifies *to kindle fire,* and *to burn,* Chap. 50.10. & 64.2. from which root also comes another term, that denotes a kind of hot, burning, malady; as does also the word *Carbuncle,* both in English and Latin; and its parallel in Greek, imports as well a sore, or ulcer, so called of the inflammation it brings with it, as a rich stone, of its fiery, or flamy color; so termed. See on v. 11. the gates, Rev. 21.21. are said to be each of one entire pearl.

*{all thy borders of pleasant stones*} Heb. *all thy border;* or *thy whole border;* that is, say some of the Jewish commenters, all your cities; not Jerusalem alone, but all the cities within her territories, called *Jerusalems cities,* Jer. 34.1. as intimating, that they should be built with goodly rich stones, as well as she. But I rather conceive, with the ancient Greek interpreter, that by *border,* is here meant, the whole compass of her walls, so far, as the same should reach. See Chapter 60.18. Ezekiel 48.35. the foundation, the pavement, the gates, and windows, were before; there rests nothing, but the walls, that bound it, and the compass thereof therefore not unfitly termed, *her border.* By the foundation, some would have understood here, Christ our Savior, 1 Cor. 3.11. By the windows, the teachers, that let in light to the people, Dan. 12.3. By the gates, and walls, Gods protection, Ch. 26.2. & 60.12. But to descend to such niceties, I deem it both unsafe, and needless,

*{of pleasant stones*} Heb. *into stones of desire,* or, *delight: stones of delight;* for, *goodly, beautiful, delightsome stones;* such as are pleasing to the eye, and men delight to look upon: (see Psal. 102.14.) as *a city of desire* or, *delight,* for, *a delightsome city,* Mal. 3.12. for the syntax, both here and in the former branch, *I will put thy windows and border into such and such stones:* Some would have it to be an Hypallage, or Inversion of the words; for, *I will put such and such stones into thy windows, and into thy walls;* or, *in thy windows, and thy walls;* as Judg. 1.8. *They cast the city into the fire,* for, *they cast fire into the city.* Others, and so some of the Jewish critics, would have it to be, as if it were said, *I will turn the stones that thou wast at first built with, into such and such stones;* and so the terms of *windows* and *walls,* should be put for the materials whereof they were built: and they point us to Hos. 2.12. where it is said, (the same verb and participle, being both there used, that are here) *I will turn her vines and fig trees* (that is, the places wherein they grow, their vineyards, and orchards) *into a forest.* But this passage helps rather to put us into the right. For it is well there rendered in our version, *I will make them a forest.* And in such forms of speech, the particle seems oft to be superfluous, as, 2 Sam. 3.30. 1 Chr. 3.2. compared with, 2 Sam. 3.3. Jer. 40.2. See ch. 4.2. Jer. 12.11. or, if it shall be deemed to be of some special use, the words may be rendered; *I will make them to become a forest,* in the one place; and *I will make them to be such, and such stones,* in the other; which our version sufficiently expresses.

**V. 13.** *{And all thy children shall be taught of the Lord;*} Or, *made skillful, and learned, by the Lord.* See Chap. 8.16. & 50.4. For Gods teaching, is an effectual teaching unto those, whom, by the inward efficacy of his Spirit working together, with the external ministry of his Word, he instructs, Jer. 31.34. Joh. 6.45. 1 Cor. 2.10. 2 Cor. 13.3. Eph. 4.20,21. 1 Joh. 2.20,27.

*{and great shall be the peace of thy children,*} They shall enjoy abundance of prosperity and welfare, Psal. 37.11. and 119.165. Chap. 48.18. & 52.7. See on ver. 10.

**V. 14.** *{In righteousness shalt thou be established:*} You shall be settled again by righteous and faithful governors; such as were Zorobabel, Ezra, Jeshua, and Nehemy: *righteousness,* for *men of righteousness;* as chap. 1.21. & 41.2. So some: See Chap. 1.26,27. Others, by *righteousness,* understand Gods gracious goodness, whereby their state should again be established. So the word seems used, 1 Sam. 12.7. Psal. 36.10. ver. 17. Others Gods fidelity and faithfulness, in performance of his promises; as, Psal. 142.1,2. chap. 51.5. & 56.1. Heb. 6.10. 1 Joh. 1.9. But I conceive, the meaning to be, as the words plainly sound, (*righteousness* being opposed to *oppression*) that she shall be settled again in a constant tenor, and due execution of justice; with security, to enjoy quietly that condition, that God should restore her unto, (see chap. 1.27.) the continuance whereof, as settled on a sure groundwork, is implied in the term of *establishment,* Psal. 111.7,8. and 125.1. Mat. 16.18. Heb. 12.28. See chap. 2.2.

*{thou shalt be far from oppression,*} Heb. *be thou far from oppression:* though some would make it not a verb, but a verbal rendering it; *being far off from oppression;* but no instance is given of the like: the meaning is, either *be thou far,* for *thou shalt be far:* as, *live,* for, *thou shalt live,* Gen. 20.7. Prov. 4.4. and *dwell,* for, *thou shalt dwell,* Psal. 37.27. and so the Hebrew commenters expound it: or, *be far* from fear *of oppression:* fear it not; and so some of ours, supplying that term of *fear,* or, *dread,* from the words ensuing. See the like promise, chap. 60.18.

*{for thou shalt not fear,*} You shall have no need, or cause, to fear it; because your former oppressors shall be destroyed; and an utter riddance made of them, Chapter 16.4. and if any shall hereafter attempt aught against you, their designs shall be utterly frustrate, ver. 15–17. Some read the words, *that thou mayst not fear;* that you may be freed from those fears, that so much possessed, disturbed, and distracted you in times past, chap. 33.18. and 51.12,13. So is this particle used, Job 6.11. Chap. 52.5,6. and this reading suits well with the former exposition of the branch before-going.

*{and from terror,*} Or, *dread;* to wit, of oppression; whereof before: for the word is oft used for *consternation;* or, a quelling and dismaying dread, Jer. 10.2. & 17.17. & 48.39. but it may as well be rendered, *and from contrition,* or, *destruction,* or, *ruin:* for so also the word signifies; and is so rendered, Psal. 89.40. Prov. 10.14,29. and 13.3. & 18.7. such as formerly has befallen you, Jer. 4.20. Lam. 3.47.

*{for it shall not come near thee,*} Or, *that it may not come near thee;* as before, Psal. 91.7. Prov. 1.33.

**V. 15.** *{Behold,*} To give them fuller assurance of future safety, because they might have some thoughts within them, that though their former adversaries, and oppressors, were quelled and destroyed; yet some other rising up in their room, might again disturb them, and reduce them to their former sad condition, the Lord promises to frustrate whatsoever attempts shall, by any evil-affected, be at any time made against them; to incite, and stir them up to a more serious and sedulous consideration thereof, he prefixes this note, as requiring attention before it: whereof, See on verse 11.

*{they shall surely gather together,*} Heb. *he shall gathering, gather together:* so the word is used, Psal. 56.6. & 59.3. & 140.3. and the word, though singular, yet is in a plural, or collective notion; as speaking, not of some particular person, but of people: the gemination of the word, in this manner, does sometime imply, certainty; as Mic. 2.12. and so our translators here take it: and the meaning then is, that there shall undoubtedly be such, as will be attempting the disturbance and destruction of Gods people; as such formerly have ever been, Psal. 129.1. 2 Tim. 3.12. sometime, sedulity; as Exod. 19.5. Deut. 6.17. and taking it so here, the text may be rendered, *they may diligently gather together;* as not foretelling what shall be, but forecasting what may be; as if it were said, though people should never so sedulously, and in never so great multitudes, combine, and gather themselves together against you, Zach. 12.3. yet it shall be to no purpose, chap. 8.9,10. Those that that here conceive the word in a notion of *dwelling,* or *sojourning* (though it be most commonly so used) and expound the text of hollow-hearted proselytes, do swerve clean away from the genuine sense of the prophet.

*{but not by me:*} Heb. *not from me:* the adversative is wanting; as chap. 17.11. *from me:* not with any charge, command, or commission from me; as Sennacherib pretended, and God himself, in some sort, acknowledges: though that neither known to him, nor minded by him, chap. 10.6,7. and of Nebuchadnezzar the like may be said, Jer. 25.9. & 40.2,3. but it should not be so with these, who are therefore said to come not from him, because he should not go along with them, to make them successful, as with some of them he did. So Hos. 8.4. *they have set up Kings, but not by me.* The Jewish commenters expounding this passage of Gog and Magog, with their retinue, object, that God himself is said to bring them against his people, Ezek. 38.17. whereunto they answer not amiss, that God indeed is said to bring them: but that it is to their ruin, and to the benefit of his people. So Mic. 4.11–13.

*{whosoever shall gather together against thee shall fall for thy sake,*} Or, *whatsoever people shall gather themselves together against thee, to fight with thee, shall fall,* Psal. 59.3. & 140.3. or, *whosoever shall gather together, to fight with thee, shall fall before thee:* as the particle is used, Zach. 6.5. Exod. 20.3. Ps. 9.19. So, *they shall fall before you,* Levit. 26.7,8. All their attempts against you, shall tend to their own ruin, and end in their own destruction, Psal. 27.2. & 37.12–15. chap. 10.34.

**V. 16.** *{Behold,*} As before, ver. 15.

*{I have created the Smith that bloweth the coals in the fire, and that bringeth forth an instrument for his work:*} Both the workman, that makes weapons, and arms, and the warrior, that wears them, or makes use of them, are my creatures; and in my power therefore it is, to dispose both of them, and their arms, and weapons, as I please, Psal. 119.91. Job 10.11.

*{created the Smith*} Both made him a man, Job 10.8. Psal. 119.73. Jer. 1.5. and made him a smith; a man skillful in the work of his trade: for, skill in such things, is also of God, Exod. 31.3–6. of the word rendered *Smith,* see on chap. 40.19.

*{that bloweth the coals in the fire*} Or, *that bloweth the fire of coals.* Heb. *coal.* See chap. 44.12. thereby to melt or mollify the metal that he is to work upon: this is added to distinguish him from the carpenter that works in timber, and the mason that works in stone; and need not the help of fire so much, to make out their work; because the term here used, comprehends them all three. See on chap. 40.20. & 41.7.

*{and that bringeth forth an instrument for his work*} That is, if we so read it, a tool, for himself to use in his trade; which seems not to suit with the scope of the place, save that such tools, as he frames for his own use, may further him in the framing of arms. See chap. 44.12. Others, therefore, read it, *an instrument of his work:* as a *Psalm of David,* Psalm, 20. & 21, &c. That is, such an one, as he is wont to make: warlike weapons, being a great part of them, fruits of the forge, 1 Sam. 13.19. And this not amiss. Howbeit, I conceive, that it may as well be rendered, *that produceth instruments for their work;* that is, such weapons, as they must use, that intend aught against you, v. 15. for though the verb there be singular, yet the notion is plural, and so may also be here; as chapter 5.26–30. where though the text in the original run constantly in the singular; yet the words, because collectively used, are not amiss, all along rendered in the plural: and so it suits fitly, both with what went before, ver. 15. and with what follows verse 17. For I cannot concur with those that would have the words expounded, by way of inversion; *that bringeth his work out into an instrument.* But *instrument,* for, *instruments:* as Jer. 51.34. Zach. 11.15. so *coal,* for *coals,* before.

*{and I have created the waster to destroy*} To destroy those, whom my will is to have destroyed. It may be understood of wicked men, whose whole study, life, and practice, is to waste and destroy: for such also does God make use of, Chap. 10.6. and for such uses, has he made them, Prov. 16.4. to be executioners of his just wrath against other wicked, (so is that of Solomon to be understood) chap. 10.5. Ezek. 7.21,24. But I suppose, that by *the waster,* or *destroyer,* is understood the *warrior,* in general: whose work and employment is to waste and destroy, and whose arms are therefore termed *weapons,* or, *instruments of destruction,* from the word here used, Ezek. 9.1. Some would have the whole verse, to this effect rendered, *As I have created the Smith to produce warlike weapons: so have I made wasters* (I want no instruments myself) *to destroy* my enemies, and yours. But the former sense is more familiar, and agrees better with the context.

**V. 17.** *{No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper*} *That is formed to be employed against thee;* a form of speech defective, but in Scripture very frequent. See chap. 38.17,21. and of Gods turning back mens weapons, upon those themselves, that use them. See Jer. 21.4.

*{and every tongue that shall rise up in judgment against thee, thou shalt condemn*} There are two ways especially, whereby persons are wont to be oppressed, either by force or violence, as Urias was, Jer. 29.23. or, by pretense of law and right; as was Naboth, 1 Kin. 21.13. against the one, God in the former branch, had given them security; assuring them, that none, by hostile courses, should prevail against them: for no weapon, or engine used against them, should be able to do, either the enemy service, or them damage: against the other, he gives them security in these words, assuring them, that none should by false suggestions, and wrong information, any way impeach them in their right; but that they should have the better, at length, in the upshot, of all those, that by any means should attempt so to do. See chap. 49.24,25. and 50.8,9. & 51.22.

*{every tongue*} That is every person, that shall so use, or abuse rather, his tongue; as Psal. 12.3. *The Lord will cut off the flattering lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things;* that is, those that so use lips and tongue; because things are acted by the tongue, Psal. 52.2. whence, *a man of tongue,* for, a detractor, or slanderer, Psal. 140.11.

*{rise up in judgment against thee*} To accuse or charge you wrongfully, Deut. 19.16. as the devil did Job to God, Job 1.9,11. and his friends to himself, Job 16.20. & 22.5–10. or to lay claim to you, as pretending to have right to you, and power over you as their lawful captive, or slave, chap. 49.24. & 52.3–5.

*{shalt thou condemn*} They shall not cast you, Psal. 109.6,7,31. but you shall cast them: you shall be cleared, Psal. 37.6. and they shall be convinced of falsehood, and condemned accordingly to suffer, Deut. 25.1. & 19.17–19.

*{This is the heritage of the servants of the Lord;*} A solemn close of all before related, concerning the state of Gods people. The like whereunto, see concerning their adversaries, Chap. 17.14. and the wicked in general, Job 18.21. & 20.29. and concerning both the one, and the other, Judg. 5.31.

*{the heritage of the servants of the Lord*} The portion that God will vouchsafe to bestow upon his servants, for their fidelity and loyalty showed in his service; & the privilege, or benefit, that from thence shall accrue unto them. See Job 20.29. & 27.13. & 31.2. & it seems to allude to that of Solomon, concerning a wise and discreet servant, that he shall share in the *heritage* among the brethren, Prov. 17.2. that which the apostle also says of the faithful servant, that from God, he shall receive, as a *reward,* of his faithful service, the *inheritance,* that belongs to a son and heir, Col. 3.24. and God indeed makes all his servants, not sons only, but *heirs* also, 2 Sam. 7.14. Mat. 6.1,5,9,26,32. Luk. 12.32. Rom. 8.14–17. Rev. 21.7.

*{and their righteousness of me*} Heb. *from with me;* which some expound, *from before me,* or, *in my sight:* as it is said of Zachary and Elizabeth, Luk. 1.6. *they were both just in Gods sight:* that is, sincerely righteous; not in outward show and semblance only, as those, 2 Tim. 3.5. but in inward disposition of heart and soul: where, God only sees, 1 Sam. 16.7. as if the meaning were, in way of further description of the servants of God before-mentioned, *of whose uprightness I am well assured.* But, *from with me,* seems to be no more here, than simply *from me;* as Gen. 4.1. where the former particle is deemed to be understood; and Gen. 19.24. and Psal. 24.5. where both forms are used; the latter particle being expressed in one part of the verse, omitted in the other. Howbeit, the meaning is rather their *righteousness;* that is, the reward of their *righteousness:* as *my work,* for, the reward of my work, chap. 49.4. So Psal. 112.3,9. or, that *beneficence,* and blessing, which from my hand they shall receive: for so also, is the word *righteousness,* used: as the apostle also seems to expound that of the Psalmist, at least, so uses the word himself, 2 Cor. 9.9,10. So Psal. 24.5. fore-cited, *he shall receive the blessing from the Lord; and righteousness from God his Savior.* See ver. 14. or if it be deemed to have a peculiar respect, to the privilege in the last place, to wit, in the fore-part of this verse propounded; by *righteousness,* may be understood, Gods justification of them, and vindication of their righteousness, against all those, that shall wrongfully attempt to appeach them, and impeach it, Psal. 37.6. & 106.30,31. chap. 59.8,9. Rom. 8.33. 2 Cor. 5.21. See chap. 45.24,25. unto which place, if this be deemed parallel, it would rather be rendered, *and their righteousness is from the Lord.* But I take the former to be the genuine sense of the word, in this place.

*saith the Lord.* As ver. 10.

### CHAPTER 55

**V. 1.** *{Ho, every one that thirsteth, &c.*} In this Chapter is contained, a free invitation of all sorts of people, as well Gentiles, as Jews, to come in, unto Christ, and to yield themselves to him, to be instructed, and ruled by him, for their own good, ver. 1–5. together with a serious exhortation to repentance, and amendment of life, ver. 6,7. and a gracious promise of reconciliation, and restitution thereupon, ver. 8–13.

*{Ho*} Of the various acception of the particle here used, see on Chapt. 1.4. & 10.5. & 18.1. here it is without question, a note of compellation; and of invitation, and incitation withal; as also, Zach. 2.10,11.

*{every one*} Whether Jew, or Gentile, ver. 4,5. Joe. 2.32. Rom. 10.12. though some restrain it to the former; because some things, hereafter mentioned, ver. 12,13. seem more specially to concern them.

*{that thirsteth*} That is in distress, and being sensible of his distressed condition, is desirous of relief, that finding and feeling in himself a want of sincere grace, and sound comfort, is pained with the sense thereof, and earnestly desires a supply: for all these things concur in bodily thirst; a want of moisture in the inward parts; a sense of pain, and grievance, thence arising, and such an earnest desire of liquor to slake and relieve the same, as nothing can satisfy, but that alone, Psal. 42.1. Chap. 41.17,18. and a spiritual affection, proportionable hereunto, is required, in all those, that are invited to partake in the mercies and favors of God, here offered, to be found, and had, in Christ. So Mat. 5.6. & 11.28. Joh. 7.37. Rev. 21.6. & 22.17. and neither brutish worldlings therefore, that rest fully satisfied with worldly contentments, and carnal delights, Psal. 17.14. nor Pharisaical justiciaries, that are puffed up, with a fond and vain conceit of their own good parts and perfections, while they so continue, can have any share in the mercies here propounded, Luk. 1.53. & 18.9–14. Rom. 10.3. Rev. 3.17,18. Of this spiritual thirst, after God, and grace, and the enjoyment of his ordinances, and the comforts of his Spirit, see Psal. 42.1,2. & 63.1,2. & 84.2. Howbeit, under the name of *thirst,* is *hunger* here also comprehended; that which appears by the mention of *eating* here, of *bread,* or *food* in general, ver. 2. and both are expressed, Mat. 5.6. as also, Psal. 107.5. See the like, Chap. 5.13. but *thirst* is more frequently mentioned; partly, because that is the more vehement, and intolerable, of the twain: and partly, because those means that quench thirst, do in part also slake hunger; whereas, those that allay hunger, are not wont to abate thirst.

*{come*} The word signifies indifferently, either *go,* as Gen. 43.33. or, *come;* as Hos. 6.1. here it is rightly rendered in the latter notion; because they are called to return to God, the Fountain of living water, whom before they had forsaken, Jer. 2.13.

*{to the waters*} That is, as the most, to the waters of saving grace, and spiritual comfort, Chap. 12.3. Ezek. 47.1,2. Joh. 4.10,14. and 7.37,38. Rev. 21.6. & 22.17. But it seems to me, that, *to the waters,* here, is, as if he had said, *to the water side;* as Judg. 7.4,5. for it seems to be, not so much *water,* as other commodities, (yet such as supply the room of *water,* and in a more eminent manner, relieve, and refresh; do that, for which water is desired, and much more than it,) are those precious things, that they are invited to partake in: and the *waters,* or, water-side, the place whither they are willed to resort, there to furnish themselves with them: and I conceive it, to be an allusion to the manner of people dwelling in towns and cities, situate near to some river by which victuals & other wares are wont to be brought to them; who, upon the arrival of shipping there, with such provisions, are wont, after notice thereof given, to repair thither, for the storing of themselves with such necessary provisions, as they stand in need of, and are there to be had: it is like our Saviors invitation, to come unto him, with assurance of finding with him, and receiving from him, means of relief, and refreshment, Matt. 11.28. Joh. 6.35,37. in which place, he shows what manner of coming it is, that is required; not a bare corporal motion; but a spiritual access by faith, which is as well the foot of the soul, to bring us unto Christ, as the hand of the soul to lay hold upon Christ, Cant. 3.4. Mat. 9.11,12. See ver. 3.

*{and he that hath no money*} Or, *even,* (as chap. 40.30.) *he that hath no money.* Heb. *silver:* as Chap. 43.24. that is, say some, that has no merits; but merits none can any have. The meaning is, that is never so poor, that has nothing in this world, of any worth, or valuable consideration; implying, that Gods grace (which Simon the Sorcerer fondly supposed, might be bought with money, Act. 8.20.) is given freely without regard had to the wealth, or poverty of the party, that desires to partake of it, Mat. 11.5,25. 1 Cor. 1.26–28. Jam. 2.5. and without any matter of valuable consideration required of any, in lieu of it; Mat. 10.8. Rom. 3.24. Eph. 2.8.

*{come*} As before: and again in the next branch; and yet again, in the third verse, so oft repeated, as to show Gods forwardness to invite, and willingness to impart: so closely to tax mens natural backwardness to those things, that most nearly and deeply concern his own good. See the like, Ezek. 3.1. 18.30,31,32.

*{buy*} The word here used, signifies in the first place, *to break,* Chap. 14.5. & 30.14. and because in buying, and selling, especially by retail, the wares and commodities that are bought and sold, are wont to be *broken,* if solid bodies of large bulk; or to be divided, and made out into parcels: hence the word is, in the second place used, in one form, for *to buy:* as Gen. 41.57. & 42.5. and so here; in another form, for *to sell,* Gen. 46.6. Amos 8.5,6. But here may be a question moved, how they are called to *buy,* when no price is required; or, how the commodities here mentioned are freely conferred, when they are said to be *bought;* Hereunto it is commonly answered, that these things are said to be *bought;* because something is to be done by those, that desire to partake of them; for it is required of them, that they *come to the water,* that they have recourse to the place, where they are to be had; that they repair to him from whom they are to be had, *come unto me,* ver. 3. that they *hearken* to him, and be advised, and ruled by him, ver. 2,3. and again, because something must be parted with, for the achieving of them: for they must part with their corruptions, they must leave, and lay down their sins, ver. 7. yea, the case may so stand, that a man must be fain to part with all that ever he is possessed of, and his life itself also, or he cannot become owner of the commodities here mentioned. See Mat. 13.44–46. and 16.24,25. & 19.21. Luk. 14.26.23. and yet notwithstanding all this, the things offered may be truly said to be freely bestowed; as a Princes alms may be said to be freely given, albeit, it be required, that those that desire to share in them, do repair to his Almosyner, residing at his court; or as a scholar is said to have his learning freely given him, when no stipend is required for the teaching of him, albeit, that for the attaining of learning, he must frequent the school, and follow his book hard; or, as the physician may be said freely to have cured his patient of whom he demands no fee, for his visitation, and advice; although he require of him, to be ruled and ordered in all things by him, and to observe exactly what he prescribes. The rather here, notwithstanding all that is required to be done, or to be endured, to be parted with, or observed: because, first, nothing is required, that is any matter of gain to God, or whereby any benefit can redound unto him: he receives nothing from us, that can add aught to him, Job 22.2,3. & 35.6,7. Ps. 16.2. 2. All that is required of any, is for the good, behoof, benefit, of those of whom it is required, ver. 2,3. Deut. 5.29. & 6.24. and 10.13. & 30.16,19,20. Prov. 9.12. 3. All that is required of them, is no more, than they were bound in duty to have done, albeit, no such mercies, as are here typified, had been vouchsafed unto them, Luk. 17.10. and a kings pardon of a rebel, is not the less free, because granted under condition of loyal carriage for the future. 4ly, All that is necessarily required, for them to part with, is nothing but that, that is the very bane of their souls, and will at length so prove, if it be not timely avoided: it is, as the physician requiring to have the malignant humor purged out, with some pill, or potion; or the surgeons, to have the dead, or proud flesh eaten out with some corrosive: And lastly, whatsoever else may, upon occasion be parted with; besides, that it is Gods own, either lent us only, or, at most, not absolutely given us, but that God still retains a right to it, and interest in it, and may redemand it, when he pleases, 1 Chron. 29.11,12,14,16. Job 1.21. it is all as nothing, of no worth, of no valuable consideration, in comparison of that which, parting with it, we gain, Rom. 8.18. 2 Cor. 4.17,18. Phil. 3.7,8. not to add, that whatsoever it be, that is so parted with, is required *an hundred fold,* some way, or other, Mar. 10.29,30. All which considerations laid together, it may easily be conceived how, in some sense, these commodities may be said to be bought; and yet nothing thereby derogated from the freeness of the gift. Howbeit, I conceive that the readiest way of answer is, that the words of *buying,* and *selling,* are in Scripture oft used improperly, *to sell,* for *to give,* part with, or *deliver;* and so God is said sometime, to have *sold* his people, Deut. 32.30. Judg. 3.8. & 4.9. Psal. 44.12. sometime to have *delivered,* or *given* them up, Judg. 2.14. & 6.1. Psal. 106.41. into the hands of the heathen, their enemies, the latter term expounding the former. See chap. 50.1. & 52.3. and in like manner, *to buy,* is used for, *to get, gain, compass, receive,* or, *attain* aught. So *buy truth, but sell it not: buy wisdom, and instruction, and understanding,* Prov. 23.23. that is, *get wisdom, get understanding: forget it not: get wisdom, forsake her not; and with,* or *among, all thy getting, get understanding:* as it is well rendered, Prov. 4.5,6,7. Yet in another place, not amiss, *buy,* because opposed to *sell;* but taken improperly: *buy,* for, *get: sell,* for, *forsake, put away,* or *forget.* So our Savior, to the Angel of the Laodicean church: *I advise thee to buy of me;* that is to procure from me: for Christ sets not aught to sale. Thus the plain meaning will be; get, provide you, furnish yourselves: the word of *buying,* being only used to this purpose; because that is the ordinary, and most usual way, whereby men, that want such necessaries, are wont to supply themselves. See Chap. 1.3. yet here, as some suppose, also, to assure them, that they should as readily have it, without payment of aught, as if they were able, and willing, to lay down the full price for it.

*{buy and eat*} That is, *buy,* or get, that which you may *eat:* furnish yourselves with food; as they did, by going into Egypt, Gen. 41.57. & 42.5. *buy, and eat,* for, *buy, that ye may eat:* as, *do this, and live,* that is, *that ye may live,* Gen. 42.18. and *make haste, and go,* for, *make haste to be gone,* Gen. 45.9. and, *Balak arose, and warred,* for, *arose to war;* or, *that he might war against Israel,* Josh. 24.9. for, indeed he never durst do it, nor did, Judg. 11.25.

*{eat*} Or, *feed:* for it comprehends both *eating* and *drinking;* as, Gen. 31.46. Neh. 9.21. and has reference as well to *bread,* in the next verse, as to *milk,* and *wine,* in this.

*{yea, come,*} Or, *come, I say,* Heb. *and, come:* so chap. 44.15. and 49.6. of *coming,* see before: the same thing, for more vehemency, not doubled, but tripled, as chap. 51.9. & 52.11.

*{buy wine, and milk*} Of *buying,* before: *wine,* and *milk,* are here put, as two eminent, and principal kinds, and parts of nourishment, to comprehend, as whatsoever is necessary for the sustentation, refreshing, and cheering of the body; so typically, whatsoever is requisite for the support, relief, comfort, and delight of the soul, ver. 2.

*{wine*} Not *water,* (for it was to the water-side only that they were called to come, as well for the *wine,* as for the *milk;* nor was either to be found in the water, but at the water) but *wine:* not drink barely, but drink of more than ordinary excellency: drink reserved for feasts. See Ch. 25.6. such drink, as may not allay thirst only, but please and delight the palate, Cant. 1.2. & 4.18. & 7.9. cheer & glad the heart, Judg. 9.13. Ps. 104.15. Zach. 9.17. & 10.7. and make men forget their griefs, as drowned in it, Prov. 31.6. in regard whereof it is, that Christs blood, whereby remission of our sins is procured, and our reconcilement to God purchased, the main ground of all true joy, and sound comfort, Rom. 6.25. & 5.1,2,10. Eph. 1.7. is resembled by *wine,* Mat. 26.28,29. See also Prov. 9.2.

*{milk*} As not *water;* but *wine:* so not *water,* but *milk:* such as Jael gave Sisera, instead of water, as in a sweltering heat, having fled on foot, the less hazardous, and more comfortable, Judg. 4.19. & 5.25. *milk,* a food commended not for wholesomeness, and battling only, as appears in children that feed mainly, if not wholly on it, and thrive exceedingly with it; but for sweetness also, and delight, Cant. 4.11. it is put sometime, for the weaker sort of food that children are fed with, opposed to strong meat, 1 Cor. 3.2. Heb. 5.14,13. but it is here used more largely to comprehend all such kind of sustenance, as affords plentiful nourishment; and not children only, but men also, are wont to feed on with delight, Gen. 18.8. & 49.12. where *wine,* and *milk,* are joined together, as two principal, not stays only of life, but maintainers, where plenty is of them, of a cheerful life. So in a typical notion, and a spiritual sense, they are also found together. Cant. 5.1.

*{without money,*} Heb. *silver,* as before.

*{and without price.*} Freely, without any valuable consideration whatsoever; without any such expense, as wicked wretches would seem willingly to render unto God, therewith to purchase liberty for continuance in their sin, Mic. 6.6,7. So Chap. 45.13. the word is rendered *hire,* Mic. 3.11. and our English word comes very near to it.

**V. 2.** *{wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labor for that which satisfieth not?*} An affectionate expostulation, containing in it a gentle reproof, and compassionate complaint withal, of their folly, in being at great cost, and taking of much pains, about the procuring of such means, as were not able to relieve them, in their distressed condition, or to afford them such contentment, as they desired, and expected from them, chap. 30.4–7. & 57.9,10. Hos. 5.13.

*{spend*} Heb. *weigh,* as Jer. 32.9,10. because payments of money anciently were, for the most part, by weight, Gen. 23.16.

*{money*} Heb. *silver;* as ver. 1.

*{for that which is no bread*} Heb. *for not bread;* as *not wood,* chap. 10.15. *bread,* for, *food,* in general, as Neh. 5.18. chap. 3.1. for that which can no more feed you, than those husks could the hungry Prodigal, Luk. 15.16.

*{your labor*} *Weigh out your silver, and your labor;* for, *weigh,* or lay out your *money,* and spend *your labor:* for labor cannot be weighed out, as *silver,* or *moneys,* may: so 1 Cor. 3.2. *I gave you to drink milk, and not solid meat,* for, *I gave you milk to drink, and fed you not with solid meat;* and the word properly signifies, *wearisome labor,* Chap. 57.10.

*{for that which satisfieth not*} Or, *for that which cannot satisfy,* or, *wherewith ye cannot be satisfied.* Heb. *for not to be satiated;* or, *not unto satiety* (for it may be either a noun, or a verb) as Hag. 1.6. as, *not to profit,* chap. 30.5. & 44.10. for *that cannot profit.*

*{hearken diligently unto me*} Heb. *hearing hear,* as chap. 6.9. but there, in a notion of bare *hearing;* when, as we use to say, one *gives us the hearing,* but regards not what we say; but here rather, *hearkening hearken;* implying both attention to what is said, and obedience to what is thereby required. So Exod. 15.26. & 19.5. Deut. 11.13. & 15.5. Jer. 17.24. Zach. 6.15.

*{and eat ye that which is good*} Or, *and ye shall eat that which is good;* as chap. 1.19. Heb. *eat good: eat,* for, *ye shall eat;* as Gen. 45.18. Chap. 36.16. *good;* that which is both wholesome, and toothsome, also, as we use to say; comfortable, pleasant and delightful: for the Hebrew word comprehends as well the one, as the other, Gen. 3.6. Psal. 34.8. Prov. 13.2. & 24.13. Cant. 4.10.

*{and let your soul delight itself in fatness.*} Or, *and delight yourselves with that which is fat: your soul,* for, *yourselves;* as Jer. 6.16. and *your heart,* for, *yourselves,* Psal. 22.26. *let it delight itself;* Heb. *it shall delight itself:* and so it would be rendered; you shall be both abundantly and daintily fed, even as you yourselves would desire, Psal. 37.3,4. Job 36.11.

*{in fatness*} Or, *with fatness: fatness,* for that which is *fat:* fat meat, that is usually more pleasing to the taste, than that that is lean; and is the choicer sort of flesh, Neh. 8.10. So Psal. 36.8. & 63.5. See chap. 25.6.

**V. 3.** *{Incline your ear,*} So Psal. 45.10. & 73.1. A metaphorical speech, borrowed from those, that either bow down, or turn the head to the one side, to bring the better ear; if the one be quicker of hearing than the other, to listen to him, that speaks unto them; and is used here, in the same notion with that of *hearkening,* before, ver. 2.

*{and come unto me:*} As before, ver. 1.

*{hear*} *Obey;* as 1 Sam. 15.22,23. the principal matter that God requires of them, Jer. 7.22,23.

*{and your soul shall live:*} That is, *ye shall live;* as, *let my soul live,* (that is, *let me live*) *that I may praise thee,* Psal. 119.175. See before, on ver. 2. You shall not miscarry and perish, whether temporally, or spiritually, for want of such supplies, and supports, as, in vain, you seek for elsewhere, but shall assuredly, and abundantly, be furnished with either from me, Psal. 37.3,4. Chap. 33.16.

*{and I will make an everlasting Covenant with you,*} I will enter into a new gracious Covenant with you, that shall never be disannulled; chap. 54.10. Heb. *I will cut out unto them,* (a metaphor taken from that solemn rite of cutting, or cleaving the body of some beast asunder, at the making of such covenants, Gen. 15.9,10,17,18. Jer. 34.8,18. or from the strict and exact cutting out of articles, agreed upon, for mutual performance, by the Covenanters on either side: that which a word of the like notion with this imports. See on chap. 10.22,23.) *a Covenant of perpetuity,* or *eternity;* as Gen. 9.16. chap. 24.5. See the same promise, Chap. 61.8.

*{even, the sure mercies of David.*} Or, as some would have the words rendered; *the sure mercies of David* will I bestow on you, or, I will give you *the sure mercies of David;* because the apostle so cites the place, Act. 13.34. but it is not needful to thrust into the text, whatsoever the apostles in citing of a passage, or some small parcel of a passage, shall, for the fuller explication, or fitter application of it, to the present purpose, add, or annex thereunto. Otherwise, it would be necessary to insert some things, into the text, in other places likewise; as chap. 61.1. from Luk. 4.18. and elsewhere; yea, and to alter a word in the text here; because instead of *mercies* here, we have, after the Greek version, *holy things,* there. I should rather choose to render the words, *according to the sure mercies of David;* for that note of similitude, or correspondency, is very frequently omitted. See on ver. 8. & chap. 54.9.

*{the sure*} Or *firm,* as chap. 22.23. & 33.16. or, *faithful;* as Neh. 13.13. chap. 8.2. and as the apostle, from the Greek, the word may well signify either.

*{mercies of David*} Those that God had sometime promised unto David, and, by Covenant, solemnly engaged himself, to perform, and observe forever, 2 Sam. 7.13–17. Psal. 89.35–37,40. & 132.11,12. and there want not, that suppose the beginning of that 89. Psalm, to be here alluded unto, the Psalm itself, being commonly called, and known among the Jewish people, by that name, taken from the first word of it, (as divers books of Scripture are in like manner entitled with them) *The mercies of David,* as deemed the penman of that holy hymn. But this seems to be but a groundless conjecture: for neither does the Psalm begin with those words *The mercies of David;* but, *The mercies of the Lord:* nor is Davids name prefixed before it: nor does it appear that David was the composer of it; but *Ethan,* rather, whose name it holds forth in its front. And howsoever it be undoubtedly true, that this passage has, questionless, respect to the subject matter, and substance of that Psalm; yea, not improbable, that it may have some glance at the very words and terms also, wherein the same is there delivered, ver. 1–4,24,28,29,33–37. yet because I find the precise words here used, not there, but elsewhere, to wit, in the close of Solomons solemn supplication, 2 Chron. 6.42. concluded with these words, *Remember the mercies of David thy servant,* I suppose this form rather to have reference thereunto. Now according to this exposition, most commonly received, by the *mercies of David,* should be meant, mercies promised unto David, and covenanted with him; and that Solomon seems to have meant thereby, which some conceive to imply that the Covenant, which God promises to make this people upon their return to him, should be as firm, and as sure, as that which he had plighted with David concerning the perpetual succession of his seed. Others, that the Covenant should be the same in substance, with that, which God at first, made with Abraham, to be the God of him, and his seed, and that in his seed all the nations of the world should be blessed, Gen. 17.7. & 22.18. and afterward again, renewed, and ratified unto David: for that took in, and comprehended together with him, not his issue alone, that was to reign after him, but the body also of Gods people, that were to be ruled, and reigned over, by him, and them. See Jer. 31.36,37. & 33.24–26. and David the rather may here be mentioned; because by the Babylonian captivity, the succession of Davids line, in the royalty of that state might seem to be wholly cut off, without hope of rising, and recovery again. The words of the text may well bear either: and this latter most go with. Howbeit, by *David,* divers, both Jewish, and Christian commenters, understand the Messiah, the seed promised to Abraham, and David; and that was to be *of the seed of David,* Act. 13.23. Rom. 1.3. Now, as of Christ it is said in the Gospel, that God would give him, *the Throne of his Father David;* and he should *reign over the house of Jacob forever:* so is he frequently mentioned and styled by the name of *David,* in the writings of the prophets, Ezek. 34.23,34. & 37.24,25. Hos. 3.5. And this the rather I incline unto, albeit, Solomon spoke it in the other sense; because not of David himself, but of the Messiah, a second David, (as John Baptist, another Elias, Mat. 11.14.) the very next words, ver. 4. (which of necessity must have relation to this clause) are by all sound interpreters understood. As for that learned man, that would turn off, both this, and other pregnant Prophecies of the Messiah, from Christ to Jeremy, he is herein not worth the regard: The meaning then is, *the mercies of the* Messiah, *the David,* not past, but to come: the mercies before promised, and to be exhibited in, and by him; in whom the Covenant is made with Gods people, chap. 49.8. in whom *all Gods promises* are *yea,* and *amen,* 2 Cor. 1.20. but whether way we take it, the apostle to good purpose alleges it, Act. 13.34. for neither had Gods gracious promises, made to that David, nor concerning this David, taken effect, and been fulfilled, had not Christ been raised up again from the dead.

**V. 4.** *{Behold*} Thus are Prophecies, and promises, concerning the Messiah very commonly ushered in. See chap. 7.14. and 42.1. & 52.13. Jer. 23.5. & 33.15. Zach. 6.12.

*{I have given him for a witness to the people;*} The words of God the Father, concerning the Messiah; of whom the Jewish doctors themselves expound this place.

*{given*} That is, *appointed,* or *ordained;* as Jer. 1.5. Ezek. 3.17. as Christ is said to be *consecrated* by God, Heb. 5.9. howbeit the term of *giving,* may withal have a glance at the freeness of Gods mercy, in the bestowing of Christ on us, chap. 9.6. Joh. 3.16.

*{him*} Whom, but the *David,* mentioned ver. 3. See there.

*{for a witness;*} That is, a witness of the truth of Gods promises, chap. 43.10. 2 Cor. 1.20. Heb. 7.22. and, (that which the Jewish commenters also hold out to us) a teacher and testifier of his will, Joh. 7.16,17. & 12.49,50. & 17.6. & 18.37. Hence, he is called, *Amen, the true and faithful witness,* Rev. 3.14.

*{to the people*} Not to Israel alone: So chap. 49.6. *I have given thee for a light to the Gentiles;*

*{a leader and commander to the people,*} *A leader,* as the word is rendered, 2 Chron. 32.21. or, *a Ruler,* as 1 Chron. 9.20. & 11.2. or, *a Prince,* as Ezek. 28.2. and so is Christ termed in the New Testament *a leader,* Heb. 2.10. & 12.2. *a Ruler;* Mat. 2.6. from Mich. 5.2. *a Prince,* Rev. 1.5.

*{commander*} One, whose commands, under pain of eternal destruction, each one stands bound in all things to obey, Act. 3.22,23. 2 Thess. 1.8. Heb. 5.9.

**V. 5.** *{Behold,*} as above, ver. 4.

*{thou shalt call a nation, that thou knowest not;*} Or, *knewest not,* as Psal. 18.43. whom you did not own, or regard, or look after, or take notice of in times past, Act. 14.16. & 17.30. So is the word of *knowing,* oft taken, Psal. 1.6. Prov. 12.10. Mat. 7.23.

*{and nations that knew not thee, shall run unto thee,*} The Gentiles that never heard of you, nor were acquainted with you, nor had any notice of you before, Rom. 15.20. & 16.25,26. Eph. 2.11,12. & 3.5,6. See chap. 65.1. a defect of the relative, as chap. 54.1.

*{run unto thee,*} They shall with all speed, and readiness, repair unto you, as soon as they hear of you, by the ministry of the gospel, Psal. 18.44. this running intimates, as the alacrity of the persons called; so the efficacy of Christs call, Psal. 119.32. Cant. 1.4.

*{because of the Lord thy God, and for the Holy one of Israel; for he hath glorified thee,*} Or, *for he will glorify thee:* or, *because he hath glorified thee;* or, *when he shall have glorified thee;* as chap. 53.10. after your former state of humiliation, and your passion over-past, that the Lord shall have raised you up from the dead, taken you up into the highest heavens, and placed you at his right hand, Psal. 110.1,3. Chap. 2.2. Joh. 12.32. Act. 2.33,41. and 13.48. then shall the Lord, the *Holy one of Israel,* be the *God of the whole earth,* chap. 54.5. See chap. 60.9. They narrow the text overmuch, that would restrain it to the repairing of foreign nations, to worship God in his Temple at Jerusalem, upon the report of such remarkable works of deliverance, as God should do for the Jewish people, Psal. 68.28,29.

**V. 6.** *{Seek ye the Lord, while he may be found;*} An exhortation of the prophet, directed, as some would have it, to the Gentiles, not yet converted, calling upon them to come in, and make their peace, while he may, while Gods gracious offers, and tenders of grace, yet continue, 2 Cor. 6.1. as others to the Jews, now under heavy pressures, for their defections, and revolts, chap. 2.5. I conceive, by what follows, that it is not to be restrained unto either, but extends unto both.

*{Seek ye the Lord.*} As implying, that they had left him, and estranged themselves from him; yea they had lost him, and were fallen out of favor with him, by their sins; and it stood them upon therefore, if they desired their own safety and welfare, to seek after him, and seek to him, to use all the means that might be, to regain and recover his favor again: the word signifies, in the first place *to inquire,* to make inquiry after somewhat that we are ignorant of, 1 King. 1.2. 2 King. 22.13. chap. 8.19. and so God must be inquired after by us, ere we can come to know, or be acquainted with him, Psal. 14.2. & 24.6. & 119.10. Act. 15.17. & 17.27. but that is not the *seeking* here principally intended: in the second place it signifies, *to make request* for grace and favor, to some person offended, to sue to them, for reconcilement again. So Psal. 34.4. and 77.2. & 78.34. and so here: the next branch shows it.

*{while he may be found;*} So Psal. 32.6. *in a time of acceptance,* chap. 49.8. while he offers himself unto you in the means of grace, in the ministry of his Word, Psal. 27.8. and 95.7,8. 2 Cor. 5.20. & 6.1,2. Heb. 3.7. before the term of time, respited for repentance, be expired, Gen. 6.3. Exod. 9.18. Jon. 3.4. Luk. 19.42,44. Rev. 2.21. before the decree go forth, Zeph. 2.1,2,3. and God grow weary of repenting, Jer. 15.6. having borne so long, that he can no longer forbear, Jer. 44.22. and he take a solemn oath, Psal. 75.11. that he will not be spoken with, he will not be found of you, chap. 1.15. Jer. 7.16. Prov. 1.24–28. Hos. 5.6.

*{call ye upon him, while he is near,*} The same, in effect and substance, with the former, while he comes near unto you, in his ordinances, by his ministers and messengers, chap. 51.5. Eph. 2.17. while he is near yet in mercy, and the means and offers of mercy; not in judgment, and execution of wrath and vengeance, Mal. 3.5.

**V. 7.** *{Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts;*} Prayer and supplication, that it may prevail for grace and favor with God, must be backed, and seconded, with sincere repentance, testified by serious reformation, and amendment, both of heart and life, Prov. 28.13. Dan. 4.27. Mat. 3.8. Mar. 1.15. nor can there be any true turning unto God, until men turn away from their sins, 2 King. 17.13. Jer. 18.11. Lam. 3.40. Act. 13.8. and 3.19. & 20.21. & 26.18,20. they must leave, and lose their sins, before they can find God.

*{his way*} *His own way;* wherein he had gone astray from God and his ways, chap. 53.6. as *thine own ways;* opposed to Gods ways, chap. 58.13. or, *his evil way, his wicked way;* as Jer. 18.11. and 25.5. & 26.3. and so, *his thoughts;* that is, *his* own, or, his *unrighteous thoughts: thoughts of iniquity,* as Prov. 6.18. chap. 59.6. and if we take it the latter way, there is a defect of the adjunct; but to be supplied from the quality of the person whose, *way,* and *thoughts,* they are.

*{way*} For course of *life* and conversation; as Psal. 1.6. and 119.1. Jer. 7.3.

*{the unrighteous man*} Heb. *man of iniquity,* or, *wrong,* or, *vexation* rather. See chap. 10.1. So Prov. 6.12. by the former some would have understood the profane, and ungodly; by this latter, the injurious, or, unjust, in their dealings with men: but the terms seem to be promiscuously used; and our prophets manner is, in divers terms, for variety, and elegancy, to express the same thing.

*{his thoughts*} Or, *imaginations,* or, *devices,* or, *projects,* or *contrivances,* or, *purposes:* (for the word is large, Gen. 6.5. Prov. 15.22. & 19.21. Ezek. 38.11.) such as above. See chap. 59.7. and such thoughts, and purposes, as well as ways, and works, are to be purged out, and repented of, Jer. 4.14. Zach. 8.17. Act. 8.23. Rom. 2.15,16.

*{and let him return unto the Lord*} By entering upon a new course of holy life, conformable to the will, and Word of God, Jer. 4.1. Zach. 1.3. Mat. 3.8. Act. 26.10,20. 1 Thess. 1.9.

*{and he will have mercy upon him*} Deut. 4.27–31. & 30.2–8. 2 Chron. 7.14. Prov. 28.13. Jer. 3.12. Ezek. 18.27,28. and 33.11.

*{and to our God*} Whose nature and disposition, in this kind, we well know, having had good proof, and large experience thereof, Exod. 34.6. Num. 14.18. Psal. 86.5. and 103.8. Jon. 4.2.

*{for he will abundantly pardon*} Heb. *he will multiply to pardon:* as, *multiply to wash,* Psal. 51.2. for, wash thoroughly, over and over: and, *multiply to transgress,* Amos 4.4. for, multiply transgressions. Of Gods proneness to pardon, and his frequent abundant, and plentiful pardoning, see Numb. 14.19,20. Psal. 32.5. and 78.34–40. & 103.8–13. Jer. 3.1–12. Mic. 7.18,19. and a lively resemblance of it, Luk. 15.20–24.

**V. 8.** *{For my thoughts are not your thoughts; neither are your ways my ways——saith the Lord*} These words are by divers interpreters diversely referred, and diversely resolved. Some refer them to the requiry of reformation, both in their *thoughts* and *ways;* as rendering a reason why these are to be reformed, if they desire to be reconciled to God; to wit, because there is a great distance between Gods ways, and theirs, his thoughts, and theirs: his thoughts, and ways, being all holy and heavenly, theirs, wicked, and earthly; set wholly upon the things here below: and such, therefore, as must both be reformed, and raised up, if they would have any either reconcilement to him, or intercourse with him, Mat. 5.8. Col. 3.1–5. Heb. 12.14. Others, refer them to the motive annexed to the requiry, containing a promise of finding favor, and mercy with God; and giving assurance of having the same, upon their return to him, made good: And of those that go this way, some expound it of Gods proneness to pardon, and forwardness to receive into full favor again: that Gods disposition, and his dealings are herein much unlike unto mens; men are commonly of unmerciful, and revengeful minds; and where they have been much wronged, are with much difficulty drawn to admit any motion of reconcilement, on any reasonable terms; seldom so freely, or fully reconciled, but that some inward grudge sticks still in their stomachs, some remembrance of the wrong done them, stays still in their minds: yea, that many times, though from the face, and teeth outwardly, they make show of reconcilement, and profess to be satisfied; yet they nourish hatred, and malice inwardly in the heart; and do but wait, and watch, for an opportunity to do the delinquent some shrewd turn, or other, even to mischief him, if they may. See 2 Sam. 3.27,30. & 13.20,22,26,28. & 20.9,10. Psal. 55.21. Jer. 41.1,2. Dan. 11.27. But with God it is not so, he is of a clean contrary disposition, he is of tender bowels, slow to wrath, loath to take vengeance, Exod. 34.6. chap. 1.24. Lam. 3.33. Ezek. 18.31,32. & 33.11. ready to remit the greatest wrongs, such as no man almost would, or could endure to put up, Jer. 3.1. and to receive the wrong-doers into as great grace and favor again, as ever, not retaining the least memory of aught, formerly done, no more than if the same had never been, either done by them, or known to him, chap. 1.10,15–18. & 43.25. Jer. 31.34. Zach. 10.6.
