Others again, expound it of Gods constancy and immutability in his purposes and proposals: Men are mutable and variable; they promise much, and perform little; what accord, and agreement they are brought unto one day, they repent many times, the same day, and the next day revoke: such they are, both in their carriage towards God, and in their courses and dealings one with another, Psal. 78.34,41,57. Jer. 34.10,14,15,16. But it is not so with God; he is a most true and faithful God; there is no mutability, or shadow of change with him: his promises are not so free, and large, but his performances are as sure, and as full, Num. 23.19. Josh. 23.14. 1 Sam. 15.29. 1 King. 8.23. Mat. 5.18. Mar. 13.31. Rom. 11.29. 1 Cor. 1.8,9. 2 Cor. 1.19,20. Phil. 1.6. 1 Thess. 5.24. 2 Tim. 2.13. Tit. 1.1. Jam. 1.17. 1 Joh. 1.9. Rev. 15.3. and this suits well with that which follows, ver. 10,11. But this, and the former, may well stand together, as being both included, and intended in the disparity, propounded between God and Man: and adding much strength to the motives before-mentioned, to persuade people to come readily in unto God.

*{mine not yours,——neither yours mine*} For, *as,* or, *like yours;* and, *as* or, *like mine;* a defect of the note of similitude. See the like, v. 3.

**V. 9.** *{For as the heavens are higher than the earth; so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.*} There is a vast difference, between my disposition, and dealings, and yours: as there is distance between heaven and earth, my disposition and dealings, both for mercy and goodness, and for firmness and faithfulness, are as far above yours, as the very highest heavens are above the very center of the earth: yea, indeed far higher; for the one is, though unmeasurable, yet, finite; whereas the other, because infinite, is for greatness, and amplitude, and immensity, inconceivable. So Psal. 103.11,12. Jer. 31.37. and God is far above man, in mercy and goodness, in truth and faithfulness, as in immensity of height and greatness, Psal. 36.5,6. & 57.10,11. & 108.4. & 119.89,90. & 145.3,9. and there may well be some emphasis in these words, *your ways,* and *your thoughts,* as if he had said, *yours,* even the very best of you, that either have, or would seem to have, some bowels of compassion, some tender-heartedness, some equanimity, ingenuity, and readiness, to remit a wrong; or some firmness, or faithfulness, in making good what you promise. See the like, Mat. 7.9–11. Luk. 11.5,12.

*{For as*} Or, *but as,* So the particle is rendered, chap. 30.16. and 49.25. and may well be here: They are not as yours; but far higher than they; the note of similitude is not expressed in the text; but is to be supplied, and is in the other particle very frequently included. So chap. 54.9. & 61.5.

*{are higher than the earth*} Heb. *are high from,* or, *in regard of the earth.* So 1 Sam. 10.24. Job 11.8,9. & 35.5. and the like in the next branch.

**V. 10.** *{For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth, and bud;*} As these inferior creatures, through my blessing accompanying them, do not fail of their effect, but attain their intended end, in causing the earth to fructify, for the benefit and behoof of mankind, when to that purpose I am pleased to employ them, Job 37.6,11–13. so shall the gracious promises of mercy, and of delivery, that I make unto you, not fail, or be frustrate, but shall certainly take place, and be assuredly effected. Chapter 14.24–27.

*{from heaven*} From above, for all above us, goes under the name of *heaven,* Gen. 1.1,6–9,14,17,20. from the clouds, that are as Gods *chambers,* Psal. 104.13. or, *store-houses,* Job 38.22.

*{returneth not thither; but watereth the earth,*} Or, *till it have watered,* Heb. *but if it have watered;* or, *unless it have watered* as Gen. 32.26. *I will not let thee go, but if thou bless me:* or, *unless thou bless me;* that is, *until thou have blessed me:* neither snow, nor rain return, until they have done the work that God sends them about; who by them is said, *to water the earth,* Psal. 65.9,10. and 104.13. and 147.8. not that they then go up again, (though as the rivers are said to return again to the sea, whence they had their original, Eccl. 1.7. so the moisture that comes from above, being licked up by the wind, and exhaled by the Sun, does, in process of time, ascend up oft in vapors again, Psal. 135.7. Jer. 10.13.) but the meaning is, that it never fails to effect that, for which God sends it, whether it then go up again, or no: for the term used in these forms oft-times implies no more. See Gen. 28.15. Mat. 1.25. See the like form of speech, 2 Sam. 1.22. Ch. 37.29,34. Jer. 23.20. and 50.9.

*{maketh it bring forth and bud*} Heb. *maketh it child;* as we sometime speak: for the term is properly used of *childing* women; applied to Sion, ch. 66.8. and it is indeed used, not of men and women only, begetting and breeding, but of other creatures also that bring forth young: of the earth, or ground, as here, more both improperly, and unusually: for as for that passage in the place cited, where it is said, *Shall a land be brought forth in one day:* by *land,* is meant, not the *ground,* but a *people.*

*{and bud*} Heb. *and maketh it bud,* or *sprout up,* Job 38.27. Ps. 104.14. & 147.8. the word is rendered, sometime, *to grow,* Gen. 2.5,9. sometime *to spring up,* ch. 44.4. Job 5.6. the text may well be read, *till it have watered the earth, caused it* (to wit, the earth) *to bring forth, and make it sprout up: made the earth to spring up,* that is, made grass, and corn, and plants to spring, or sprout out from the earth; as it is, Gen. 2.9. Ps. 85.11. but the same form of speech is also found, Ps. 147.8.

*{that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater:*} Unto bread-corn, especially, has this passage respect, because of greatest moment for the support of mans life, chap. 3.1. ver. 2. and because there is a twofold necessary use of such grain, for food, and for seed; the prophet points at either. See Gen. 47.17,19. Heb. *and gives,* or *hath given:* but the copulative is oft so used, and so rendered, ch. 53.2. Mal. 1.9. Howbeit, this is not to be referred to the earth, but to the *rain,* or *snow;* as by the gender of the terms used in the original, appears: they *give,* because they cause the earth to give, what without them, it could not: For when the heaven is as brass, the earth is as iron, Deut. 28.23. and God himself, by them, moistening the ground, Psal. 104.23,24. unto whom the apostle therefore applies this passage, 2 Cor. 9.10.

**Ver. 11.** *{So shall the word be that goeth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void; but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing, whereunto I sent it*} So Ezek. 12.25.

*{the word*} That is, my promise concerning reconcilement to my people, upon their return to me, and deliverance of them out of captivity: verse 12. So Psal. 119.38,41,42,49.

*{return void*} As ambassadors, or messengers, failing of that they were sent about; or missing that they went for, Genesis 32.3,6. 2 King. 18.14,17,37. Chap. 30.4,5. and 33.7. Jer. 14.3.

**Ver. 12.** *{For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace:*} From Babylon the place of your captivity, a type of mans spiritual thraldom under sin and Satan; as Chapter 52.11.

*{with joy*} Ch. 35.10. & 51.11.

*{let forth*} Or, *led along:* So the word rather imports, Psal. 46.14,15. where it is used of conveying, and conducting, in state: and it seems to have relation to the conduct of Gods people, by the pillar of cloud from Egypt to Canaan, Exodus 13.21,22.

*{with peace*} Or, *in peace;* that is, quietly and peaceably. See ch. 52.12. Exod. 11.7. or, *in safety* (so is the word, *peace,* oft used. See ch. 54.13.) safely, under Gods protection, ch. 52.12. & 58.8. Exod. 14.19,20. Ps. 78.53.

*{the mountains, and the hills shall break forth before you into singing*} So great shall your joy be, and the expressions of it, by singing and shouting, so loud and so plentiful, that the very senseless creatures shall seem to be sensible of it, and affected with it, when the mountains and hills, on every side sounding therewith, return echoes of it, as if they rejoiced jointly with you, and praised God together with you, for it. For thereunto do these, and the like forms seem to allude, Psal. 98.7,8. Ch. 35.1. & 44.23. and 49.13.

*{and all the trees of the forest shall clap their hands*} Heb. *applaud with the hand,* as Ezek. 25.6. or, *with the palm* of the hand; as the word properly signifies, used both here, and Ps. 96.12. where the same gesture is attributed to the floods: the trees of the forest being gently shaken with the wind that you shall have to refresh you by the way, shall by making a pleasant noise, and intertwining their twigs and branches, as their hands and arms, one with another seem to applaud you, and your joy, as you go. See Psal. 76.11,12.

**V. 13.** *{Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir-tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle-tree*} That this passage has, in the first place, a reference to the Jews return from the Babylonian captivity, as well as those, ver. 12. to me seems undeniable, and the best interpreters acknowledge it. Some understand it, of the accommodation of them in their way homeward, when they were to pass through waste wildernesses: and so it should be the same with that, Chap. 41.19. Others, rather conceive it meant of their land and country, that they were to return unto. For whereas assurance was given them, of a quiet dismission from the place of their captivity, and a safe conduct unto their own country again, ver. 12. their minds might be troubled, when they began to think, what there would be to entertain them with at their arrival there; considering that they should find their land, most of it having lain waste, and enjoyed, not a seventh years, but a seventy years, sabbath, Lev. 26.34,35,43. overgrown with bushes, and thorns and briers, and brambles, Chap. 7.24. and the prophet therefore, from God, tells them, that instead of such trash as the face of their land was then overspread with, it should, upon their return, be furnished with such plants and trees, as should be, not useful only, but beautiful, and delightful also; and so the passage is parallel to that, Chap. 4.2. and that Chap. 35.1,2. So the meaning is, that the face and state, of their land and state, should be strangely altered for better. See the like in, another notion, Chap. 60.17. Now this is commonly expounded of, and applied unto, that gracious and blessed change, that should be wrought upon, and appear in, those persons and people, that should, by the ministry of the Word, be converted unto God; being now so strangely altered, and changed, 2 Cor. 5.17. that as they are elsewhere said, to be thereby transformed, out of serpents and wild beasts, into mild and tame creatures, ch. 11.6,8. so here out of such thorny, and prickly shrubs and bushes, as wicked men for their harmful, and mischievous minds and courses, are in Scripture commonly compared unto, 2 Sam. 23.6. Mic. 7.4. into such plants and trees, as are both pleasant and useful, chap. 61.3. or, as others, that those vices and corruptions, that their hearts and minds were formerly overgrown with, as with brambles and briers, Heb. 6.8. should be stubbed up, and rooted out, Jer. 4.4. and the graces of Gods Spirit there implanted in the room of them. But the soundest, and most judicious interpreters, deem it overcurious to descend unto, and restrain the passage to these particulars: they conceive the flourishing estate of the church of God, in general, hereby to be intimated, as abounding in spiritual graces and comforts; those at some times also accompanied and dignified with remarkable deliverances, prosperous successes, countenance of Potentates, peace, plenty, and the like temporal blessings, Acts 9.31.

*{thorn*} See of this, ch. 7.19.

*{brier*} The word *sirpad,* here used, is nowhere else found; the Jewish critics leave us here in the briers; one while telling us, it is a kind of *thorn;* another while, that it is a kind of *base shrub,* and no more: The ancient Greek renders it, *coniza;* an herb described by Dioscorides, l. 3. c. 127. & Pliny, l. 21. c. 10. and is supposed by some, to be a kind of *mullein;* the old Latin, *a Nettle.* Some of our critics would have it signify not any shrub, or herb, one or other, but a thorny ground; a place overgrown with thorns, as compounded of *sir,* that signifies *a thorn;* and the verb *rapad,* or *raphad,* that signifies, *to strew,* or *pave,* (whereof see on Chap. 54.11.) but the opposition of plant to plant, here; not of ground to ground, as Chap. 35.2. shows it rather to denote some particular bush or shrub: and the name of a thorn found in it, seems to imply one of a thorny kind: To which purpose, some late interpreters, conceiving the word rather to be made up of *sir, a thorn;* and *pid,* that signifies *harm,* or *mischief,* Job 31.29. Prov. 24.22. as you would say, *an harmful,* or *mischievous thorn,* do render it, *paliurus,* a shrub, of note, for sharp and thorny prickles: Of which, Dioscorides, l. 1. c. 106. and Virgil, *ecloge,* 5. our version gives it a *brier,* but another word, is by that term elsewhere usually rendered, Chap. 5.6. & 7.23,25. Mic. 7.4.

*{and it shall be to the Lord for a name*} Or, as some render it; *and this shall be to the Lord for a name.* This deliverance of his people and restitution of his church, and the state thereof, shall be a means of bringing much glory to God, Chap. 44.11. & 60.21. & 61.3. for they seem to swerve from the genuine sense of the words, that would have it understood of the acknowledgment of God, for their Sovereign Lord, by bearing his name, as children do of their parents, servants of their masters, wives of their husbands; Genesis 48.16. Chapter 4.1. and 63.19. *name,* for, name, renown and honor, Gen. 11.4. Num. 16.2. Chap. 63.11. See Chapter 56.5.

*{for an everlasting sign*} An everlasting monument, and memorial of Gods gracious goodness to his people. *a sign of perpetuity,* or *eternity,* that is, *a sign,* to endure *forever;* as Exod. 31.17. as *a name of eternity,* for *an everlasting name,* ch. 63.12. That which some suppose to have an eye unto such stones, or pillars, as men use to erect for boundaries, or landmarks, with their names thereon engraven, in lands especially, either newly purchased, or recovered from some adversary that had before held, and withheld them. But I should rather conceive it to allude to such trophies, as are wont to be erected, in memory of some great victory, or extraordinary achievement, such as that monument erected by Moses, upon the discomfiture of Ameleck, and Gods speech thereupon, with those words (as some think) engraven on it, *Jehovah nissi,* Exod. 17.15,16. for what Popish writers here prate of the sign of the cross, is ridiculous.

*{that shall never be cut off*} Or, *that it may never be cut off,* that is, applied to the memorial, and the matter thereby to be remembered, that shall never be forgotten, Jer. 50.5. or that it may never be forgotten, but abide still in mens minds and mouths. See Jer. 7.28. But the text may as well be rendered, *that it shall not be cut off:* and so relating to that which is by the sign obsigned, the meaning will be, that this act of God, in delivering and restoring his church, shall be, as an everlasting honor to God; so for *a sign* to his church, that it shall never be forsaken by God, no more than that act of his forgotten by his people. It shall stand firm and fast forever, under Gods powerful support and protection, never to be cut off, or cast off, again, ch. 48.19. & 54.9,10. Jer. 31.32–37. & 32.40. & 33.25,26. a defect either of the pronoun relative, as ver. 5. or of the finitive particle, as ch. 41.7.

### CHAPTER 56

**Ver. 1.** *{Thus saith the Lord*} This whole Chapter, (the four last verses only excepted) seems to belong to the foregoing sermon, and to be the conclusion of it: wherein God admonishes his people to do that, whereby they may obtain a part in the favors and mercies before-mentioned, Ch. 55. and retain it, when they have them: withal comforting the religious eunuch against want of issue, and the proselytes of other people, (the number of whom he promises to increase) with promise of an equal interest with his ancient people, in all the privileges of his house, the church.

*{keep ye judgment, and do justice*} Or, as some render it, *Observe equity,* (as the word *judgment* is oft used for *moderation,* opposed to strictness, and rigor of justice, Ps. 25.9. & 112.5. Jer. 10.24. & 46.28. Mat. 23.23.) *and deal justly,* so *to do justice,* is ordinary used for to carry a mans self uprightly, and faithfully, in his dealings with others, Psal. 15.2. chap. 64.5. 1 John 3.7,10. *Judgment,* and *Justice,* are frequently joined together; which when they are attributed to public persons, seem to design, the one, the due and equal hearing, and deciding of causes, that come before them; the other, the causing of justice to be executed, for the righting of the wronged, and punishing of the wrong-doer, 2 Sam. 8.15. 1 Chr. 18.14. Psal. 99.4. Jer. 33.15. when to private men, the one seems to import equitable carriage, free from rigor, and extremity, mixed with mercy and moderation, in exacting their own from others; the other, a just and faithful dealing, in, and about those things that they owe unto others, or are employed about, or entrusted with, by others, Ge. 18.19. Ps. 106.3. Ezek. 18.5. the exercise of these offices, God requires here of them, as fruits of true faith, and sincere repentance. So ch. 1.16. Dan. 4.27. Mic. 6.8. Zach. 8.16,17. Mat. 3.8. Act. 26.20. Gal. 5.6. Tit. 3.8.

*{for my salvation is near to come*} Which none must look to partake in, unless they be thus qualified. So Ps. 85.9. ch. 46.13. & 51.5. Mat. 3.2. Mar. 1.15. 1 Cor. 6.9,10. Eph. 5.5.

*{my righteousness to be revealed*} My righteousness, which I shall manifest, as by my faithful performance of my promises to my people; so by just vengeance inflicted upon their oppressors, ch. 1.27. & 51.5.

**Ver. 2.** *{Blessed is the man that doth this*} So Psal. 106.3. *Blessed* are they that *observe judgment,* and each one, *that doth Justice.*

*{and the Son of man that layeth hold on it*} Or, *that holdeth it fast.* So ver. 4. Jer. 8.5. that keeps close to it, that practices it constantly; not by fits and starts, but *at all times,* Psal. 106.3. *Son of man,* the same with *man* before; as Job 25.6. and a defect of the relative in either branch, as ch. 55.5,13.

*{that keepeth the Sabbath from polluting it*} *That so observeth the Sabbath* (Exod. 31.13,14,16.) *that he pollute it not:* for that is the meaning of that phrase. See the like, Psal. 69.23. Chap. 33.15. Hos. 4.6. So ver. 4. The observation of the Sabbath, put here for the whole exercise of religion and piety, as Lev. 19.3. Jer. 17.21,22. to be joined unto, and go along with the practice of those other duties, before required, ver. 1. Amos 5.24. and that here the rather put for the rest; because that might be observed in foreign parts, during the time of their captivity, whereas many other parts of Gods religious worship, being confined to the Temple at Jerusalem, could not, Deut. 12.11–14.

*{pollute it*} Or, *profane it:* by spending it, or any part of it, save in case of necessity, in any profane employment, Exod. 31.14. Neh. 13.17,18. Jer. 17.21,22,24.

*{and keep his hand from doing any evil*} Or, *that it do not any evil,* to wit, *to his neighbor,* as it is more fully expressed, Psal. 15.3. So Zach. 8.17. Heb. *all,* for *any,* as Ezek. 18.13. that is as well careful to walk uprightly among men, as to carry himself religiously toward God, Act. 10.35. Jam. 1.27. and to abstain as well from wronging his Neighbor, as from profaning Gods Sabbath. See ch. 1.13,15. & 58.2–5,13. Amos 5.21,24.

**V. 3.** *{Neither let the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the Lord, speak, saying, The Lord hath utterly separated me from his people*} Let no man think himself excluded from partaking in the gracious promises of God, before propounded Chap. 55.1,2,12,13. in regard of his birth and generation, because he is of another nation, and no native Jew, Gal. 2.15. for Gods offers of grace, are propounded to all, without distinction of nation; be they Jews, or Gentiles, that shall sincerely come in unto God, and embrace his service, Act. 10.34,35. Rom. 2.10,11. & 3.29,30. & 10.12. 1 Cor. 12.13. Gal. 3.28. Col. 3.11.

*{the son of the stranger*} That is, *the stranger born,* or by descent. See ver. 6. But he speaks the rather, in regard of that law, whereby the issue of some people, were for divers descents secluded from admission into the congregation of Israel, Deut. 23.3,7,8. whereunto the Jewish commenters further add, that he makes mention of *the strangers son,* because he had no inheritance in the land; of the eunuch, because though he were a Jew, yet he had no issue to inherit: But God here intimates, that those laws that made such distinction between the native Jew, and the stranger, should under the Messiah be repealed; the partition wall being then removed, that severed Jew, and Gentile, the one from the other, as the veil was from the top to the bottom rent in twain, at his death, Mat. 27.51. Eph. 2.11–16. and in the prophecy of Ezekiel, provision is made for the stranger, also, and his issue, that had joined himself unto Gods people, to inherit also among them, Ezek. 47.22,23. a type of their joint portion in the heavenly inheritance, Ephesians 3.6.

*{that hath joined himself*} Heb. *that is joined,* as it is rendered, Chapter 14.1. where the same thing is mentioned; but these passives have oft a reciprocal notion. See Chapter 5.8. and so Jeremiah 50.5. *let us join ourselves to the Lord.* See further, v. 6.

*{utterly separated*} Heb. *separating separated.*

*{neither let the Eunuch say, I am a dry tree*} Barren, and without possibility of issue: which might peradventure run in the minds of such, as if therefore they should seem to be without the verge of Gods benediction, because fecundity was promised, and esteemed, as a blessing, Exod. 23.26. Deuteronomy 28.4,11. Ps. 128.1,3.

*{Eunuch*} Of the term, see on ch. 39.7.

*{a dry tree*} Or, *a sear tree,* Luk. 23.31.

**V. 4.** *{For thus saith the Lord unto the Eunuchs, that keep my Sabbaths, and choose the things that please me, and take hold of my covenant*} That are careful, as well in other things, generally to please me, and approve themselves unto me: and to keep covenants with me, as in the observation of my day, 1 King. 8.23. Psal. 132.12. Col. 1.10.

*{thus saith the Lord*} This rather does the prophet here prefix, *thus saith the Lord;* because it might seem to cross the Law given by Moses, before-mentioned. So the apostle, 1 Cor. 7.10. *not I, but the Lord.*

*{unto the Eunuchs*} Or, *concerning* them as the particle is rendered, ch. 23.5. for Gods speech here related, is not directed to them, but delivered as concerning them.

*{choose*} Not take them up upon some sudden motion, or from example barely, or tradition, or for some base respects, and sinister ends; as Est. 8.17. but after serious and mature deliberation, upon due consideration, out of judgment rightly informed, and affection thereon grounded, do by a free election, betake themselves to them. See v. 6. so David, *I have chosen the way of truth,* Psal. 119.30. a term very significant.

*{those things that please me*} So ch. 38.3. Joh. 8.29. 1 Thess. 4.1. Heb. 13.16. 1 Joh. 3.22.

*{take hold of my covenant*} Or, *hold fast my covenant;* as v. 2. Ps. 103.18.

**V. 5.** *{Even, unto them will I give in mine house, and within my walls, a place*} By the Law of Moses, none, so maimed, and dismembered, might be admitted into the priestly function, so as to execute any service within the veil of the Tabernacle, or the walls of the Temple, Levit. 21.20,23. Deut. 23.1. but no such bodily maim, or defect, should hinder any true believer, any sincere and faithful soul, from having a part in the spiritual priesthood, 1 Pet. 2.9. Rev. 1.6. and 20.6. and a place in Gods house, the church, 1 Timothy 3.15.

*{Even*} Heb. *And.* as ch. 1.6. & 40.30.

*{within my walls*} The walls of Jerusalem, as some, Psal. 122.7. a type of the church: but I suppose rather, of the Temple; of which, verse 7. and from which, some were excluded though not shut out of the city. See Lev. 21.22,23. Lam. [1].10. Act. 21.28.

*{a place*} Heb. *hand:* as Chap. 57.8. Deut. 23.12.

*{and a name better than that of sons, and daughters*} Mens names are said to be continued in their issue male especially, and to fail consequently in such as wanted issue, Numbers 27.4. 2 Sam. 18.18. and a numerous issue is deemed no small honor, Psal. 127.4,5. & 128.3. Prov. 17.6. God therefore promises here, to supply and make good the want of issue, and of whatsoever, either honor here, or memorial hereafter, might from it, have accrued unto them, by bestowing upon them, matter of far greater honor, and more durable; even such as should continue unto all eternity: that which should abundantly recompense, and much more than countervail that defect.

*{a name*} What this name should be, many debate much, and some would have it to be the name of *Gods people,* Hos. 2.23. some of *Gods servants,* Chap. 44.1,2. some, of *Gods Priests and Ministers,* chap. 61.6. some of *Gods sons, and heirs,* Joh. 1.12. Rom. 8.16,17. 2 Cor. 6.18. Eph. 3.6. 1 Joh. 3.1. But this is not unlike the dispute about the name said to be given unto Christ, Phil. 2.9. but as *name* there, does not import any one particular title, but is put for power and authority; as Act. 3.16. & 4.2. so by *name,* is not any such particular style here meant, but such honor and dignity, as should far surpass that, which issue was able to afford, both for eminency and for continuance. See Chapter 55.15. and 66.15. Howbeit, what Popish writers hence gather for the merit of single life, above the married state, expounding the place of voluntary eunuchs; from Matthew 19.12,13. is groundless, and frivolous.

*{better than that of sons, and daughters*} Heb. *good from,* or *before, sons and daughters:* as Prov. 22.1. Eccl. 7.1. that is, *better than the name of sons, and daughters:* the word *name* supplied from that before-going, as Dan. 4.33.

*{I will give them an everlasting name*} Heb. *I will give him* (that is, each one of them, as ch. 26.19.) *a name of eternity,* as Chapter 63.12.

*{that shall not be cut off*} As that by issue continued, (it failing oft) is, 1 King. 14.10. 2 King. 10.11. Psal. 21.10. & 109.13. See ch. 48.18. & 55.13. Rev. 3.12.

**Ver. 6.** *{Also the sons of the stranger that joineth himself to the Lord to serve him*} Heb. *And the sons of the stranger, that shall be joined to the Lord, to serve him.* Which some render, *And as for the strangers,* because the nominative case seems to be put absolutely.

*{the sons of the stranger*} That is, such as are strangers by descent. See ch. 2.6.

*{joineth himself*} Heb. *are joined;* as it should be rendered, *that join themselves.* See v. 4.

*{to serve the Lord*} The end of this joining himself to him more fully, than before, ver. 4. here expressed; so it is said of the prodigal, that he joined himself to one, that kept a farm, not as a partner with him, but as a servant to him, Luk. 15.15. and so the words here following are. Howbeit, the term here used, would rather be rendered, *to minister unto him,* it being ordinarily applied to the priestly function, Deut. 10.6,8. and it is said here, not as of the Levites, *to minister unto Aaron,* Num. 18.2,4. but as of the priests, *to minister unto the Lord,* Deut. 21.5. thereby intimating, that they should be admitted, unto the sacred administration, to minister, not as Levites only, but as priests. See ch. 61.6. whereas all strangers, all, that were out of that one tribe, whether Israelites, or foreigners, were before excluded from either, Numb. 3.38. and 18.4.

*{to love the name of the Lord, to be his servants*} That is, out of love to the Lord, to be his servants. So Deut. 10.12. *to love him, and to serve him;* that is, out of love to serve him: that was before closely intimated in the term of *choosing,* ver. 4. See the like syntax, v. 10.

*{the name of the Lord*} For, *the Lord himself:* as Psal. 116.4,17. Prov. 18.10.

*{every one that keepeth the Sabbath from polluting it, and taketh hold of my covenant*} See on ver. 2. *every* stranger, that so does; for of them still he here speaks: and he mentions the observation of the Sabbath more specially as the Jewish doctors, some of them, would have it, because that was appointed by God, in more special manner, to be a solemn sign between God and his people, to signify, and obsign his sanctifying of them, Exod. 31.16,17. Ezek. 20.20. and being in Covenant with them, Exo. 31.16,17. Eze. 20.20. some other to distinguish between stranger and stranger, and to show what manner of stranger it was, that he here intended: for among the Jews, say they, there were two sorts of *strangers;* one sort, that observed the commandments given unto Adam, and Noah, but went no farther: another, that were circumcised also, and observed the rites delivered by Moses; among which, the Sabbath, Exodus 16.23. and of these, say they, it appears, that he speaks, by mention made of the Sabbath. But this distinction, we find no ground for, in Scripture; and places are much wronged, to wring this conceit out of them; the Sabbath being the time set apart for Gods constant solemn service, Lev. 23.3. is put for the whole service of God, performed ordinarily on that day. So Levit. 26.3.

**V. 7.** *{Even, them will I bring unto my holy mountain*} Heb. *And I will bring them* (but, *Even them,* as ver. 5. or, *Them, I say:* as Ch. 49.6.) *unto my mountain of holiness;* as Ps. 15.1. to Mount Sion, on which the Temple was situate, a type of the church, ch. 2.2. & 11.9. Ezek. 20.40.

*{and will make them joyful in mine house of prayer*} I will cause them to serve me there, with alacrity, and cheerfulness of spirit, Deut. 16.14,15. for the manifold blessings, wherewith I have blessed them, and for the spiritual comforts, that by their communion with me, in my sacred ordinances, I shall there impart unto them, Ps. 36.8. & 42.4. & 43.3,4. & 63.5. & 84.4,10.

*{house of prayer*} The Temple, in which, and towards which, as Gods palace, and peculiar place of his residence, they were wont to pray, being at Gods command, built, sanctified, and set apart for that purpose, 2 Sam. 7.13. 1 King. 8.19,28–30,33,35. & 9.3.

*{their burnt offerings and their sacrifices, shall be accepted upon mine altar*} Heb. *shall be to acceptance upon mine altar.* So Exod. 28.38. Levit. 22.21. Psal. 19.14. and so the contrary, Levit. 20.21. Jer. 6.20. Howbeit, there seems to be here, a defective form of speech, thus to be supplied, *their burnt offerings,* (of which word, see on Ch. 1.11.) shall *unto acceptance,* or *with acceptance,* go *up upon mine altar:* or they shall *be accepted,* being offered *upon mine altar:* as it is more fully, ch. 60.7. See of the like, chap. 38.17,21. A type of those their spiritual sacrifices, of themselves, or their service, their prayers, their praises, their beneficence, Psal. 50.23. & 69.30,31. & 141.2. Romans 12.1. 2 Cor. 8.5. Phil. 2.17. & 4.18. that should be accepted, Psal. 51.17,19. Mal. 1.11. & 3.4. Rom. 15.16. Heb. 13.16. being offered upon the true altar; that sanctifies every oblation, on it offered, the Lord Jesus, Mat. 23.19. Heb. 13.10,15. Rev. 8.3,4. Jer. 33.18.

*{for mine house shall be called the house of prayer*} Mat. 21.13. Mar. 11.17. Luk. 19.46. *shall be called,* that is, *shall so be;* and be so accounted: as ch. 54.5. Mat. 5.9.

*{for all people*} Heb. *all peoples:* as Psal. 117.1. so rendered also Rom. 15.11. not for Jews only, but for other nations also, without exception, or exclusion of any, Rom. 10.12,13. See 1 Kings 8.41–43.

**V. 8.** *{The Lord God which gathereth the outcasts of Israel, saith*} Heb. *The Saying* (as ch. 1.24.) *of the Lord God that gathereth together: the outcasts of Israel:* as it is well rendered, Ps. 147.2. See Ch. 11.12.

*{Yet will I gather others to him, besides those that are gathered together*} Heb. *Yet,* or *Furthermore,* (as ch. 8.5.) or, (dividing it) *I will further gather together more upon him,* (as alluding to an heap, which to raise higher, materials are laid one upon another) or, *to him,* (so is the particle used, Psal. 16.2. & 23.2. chap. 22.15. & 53.1.) *unto,* or *above* (as Job 23.2. *my stroke is above my groaning*) *his gathered together;* that is, over and above, or besides those, that I shall at first gather together. This, a learned writer of great note, would have meant of the second gathering of some by Nehemy, after the first by Ezra, Ezr. 2.1,2. Neh. 7.7. but we read not of any remarkable number gathered together by Nehemy, who was not that way employed, but about repairing the city, and reforming, and settling of the state, with those, whom he found there. The course of the context rather carries to those foreigners, and strangers, before spoken of, ver. 6,7. who were also to be gathered, and brought in to Gods people, and added unto his fold, the church, Joh. 10.16. & 11.32. Act. 1.41,47. & 11.24. And so not ours alone, but the Jewish commenters also, expound it; only one tells us of an exposition of his fathers, which yet he does not express any allowance of, that this verse, should be understood of Gog, and Magog, of whom, Ezek. 29.16,17. unto whom, he would also apply the passage ensuing, v. 9. reading the text, *I will gather together against him,* &c. But the former passages control this exposition; and the ensuing words seem to be part of another prophecy.

**V. 9.** *{All ye beasts of the field, come to devour, yea all ye beasts in the forest*} Divers expositors annex the ensuing part of this Chapter, to the former; making, some of them, this the coherence, That the prophet, from the consolation of the godly party, in the former part, does in this latter part, proceed unto the reprehension of the wicked, and ungodly party among them. Other of them, that this is subjoined unto the promises before-going, to show that yet before they should be fulfilled, very fearful and sad matters should befall the Jewish state: which by the Romans they conceive to have been done, in the destruction of Jerusalem, Dan. 9.26,27. Matthew 23.38. and 24.15–22. Luke 19.43,44. and 21.20–24. But the most, and best, herein agree, that at these words begins a new sermon, or prophecy: and that the four last verses of this Chapter should go jointly, in one, with the next.

*{All ye beasts of the field*} Heb. *Every beast:* and so in the next branch: but taken collectively; as Chap. 43.20. Ezek. 31.6,13. and 34.5,8. The prophet makes entrance into the ensuing prophecy, with a solemn proclamation, wherein ravenous beasts of all sorts: are called upon to come in to devour, and make havoc of Gods own flock, of his own people; and by such kind of creatures are here designed, as some would have it, the Romans, but, as most rather, the Chaldeans, together with the Syrians, Assyrians, Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, and other people, that joined with the Babylonians, and served under the King of Babylon, in his expedition against the Jews, 2 King. 24.2. Psal. 137.7. Jer. 1.15,16. See the like, Jer. 12.9.

*{come to devour*} Heb. *to eat:* as also, Jer. 12.9. The adversaries of Gods people so described, as also, Psal. 80.13. are incited to do with them, as such creatures are wont to do, with such as they prey upon. Howbeit, some conceive, that the beasts themselves are called to devour their slain, as intimating what havoc would be made of them, and what should become of their corpses, (that which, in likelihood, also, befell many of them after they were dead, Psal. 79.2. Jer. 7.33. & 34.20. See the like, Ezek. 39.17–20. where the ravenous birds, and beasts are invited, as to a feast, to eat, unto their fill, at Gods table, on the carcasses of horse, and men; as also, Rev. 19.17,18. and I suppose there may well, in this passage, be some allusion thereunto: but take the former to be the genuine sense of the place; the rather, for the reason of this call, and invitement, rendered, ver. 9,10. to wit, the defect, and neglect, blindness, and sleepiness of their shepherds, that which is wont to give opportunity to wolves, and wild beasts, not to prey upon dead carcasses, but to break in upon, and worry the flock. See Ezek. 34.2–8.

*{all ye beasts of the forest*} *Beasts in the forest,* for *beasts of the forest:* the usual receptacle, and harbor of such ravenous creatures, Ps. 50.10. & 80.13. 2 King. 2.24. Jer. 5.6. So *mountains in Gilboa,* for *mountains of Gilboa,* 2 Sam. 1.12. and, *the Prince in thy people,* for *the Prince of thy people,* Act. 23.5.

**V. 10.** *{His watchmen are blind; they are all ignorant*} Or, *Their watchmen are blind* (because he speaks of his people; as ch. 5.25.) *they have no knowledge any of them.* Heb. *they know not.* So Ps. 14.4. & 82.5. Chap. 1.3. & 44.18. Their priests, and pretended prophets, or their Rulers, as well Civil, as Ecclesiastical, (for under the name of *watchmen,* both may well go, though these especially seem here intended) that should watch, and look out, to discover any evil, or enemy, approaching, to give warning of it, both to people and state, Chap. 62.6. Jer. 6.17. & 33.2,7. are stark blind, utterly void of any sound knowledge, or ability to discern, Chap. 42.19. Hos. 4.6. and any enemy therefore may safely and easily break in upon, either, without any notice taken of their approaches, or opposition made against them. Some understand this of the Scribes, and Pharisees, in our Savior Christs time, taxed by him, in his preachings under the name of *blind guides,* Mat. 15.14. & 23.15,16,24. & unto them it may be well applied; but seems to be of a far larger extent, and to intend other times.

*{they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark*} That which is principally required of a *watchman,* is to see, and look about him: that which of a dog, set to keep the house, or the flock, is to give warning, by barking, of the reproach of the thief, or any stranger unto the one, of the wolf, or any ravenous beast to the other, Job 30.1. watchfulness is required in either: and in those consequently here resembled by either, Matthew 24.41–45. Mark 13.33–37. Luke 12.36–42. whereas they were blind, dumb, drowsy, and drunk, for so the words ensuing intimate. So the Princes are reveling, when Babylon is taken, Ch. 21.5. Dan. 5.1–4,30. and the shepherds are slumbering, when Niniveh is surprised, Nah. 3.18.

*{bark*} By reproving the people for their sins, Chapter 58.1. and forewarning them of such evils, as would befall them for the same, unless prevented by repentance, Ezekiel 18.19. and it is not unusual in Scripture, to say, that men *cannot* do those things, which they have no mind, or will, to do. So ver. 11. Gen. 44.22,26. Jerem. 13.23.

*{sleeping*} So the most: Yet some, *dreaming:* some, *talking in their sleep:* some, *snorting:* some, *doting,* from an Arabic term, that by change of a letter so signifies: the old Latin, *seeing vain things:* which some impute to a mistake of *hozim,* for *chozim,* or *hhozim,* that signifies *seeing.* A late interpreter of special note, *serving the time,* but of that his version, so discrepant from the rest, no ground is, by him, given; nor am I able to conceive what it should be.

*{lying down, loving to slumber*} That is, lying down of purpose to take their ease, and repose themselves, as the only thing, that they desired, took delight in, and had never enough of, Prov. 6.9,10. & 24.33. Amos 6.4. See the like form of speech, v. 6. So Nah. 3.18. *Thy shepherds slumber.*

**V. 11.** *{Yea, they are greedy dogs, which can never have enough*} To their sluggishness, and love of their ease, is added their greediness, and their insatiable covetousness, an usual concomitant of the former, with the most, requiring means to maintain them, in an idle and loose course of life.

*{yea, they are greedy dogs*} Or, *And these dogs,* or *These dogs also are very greedy.* Heb. *strong of soul,* or, *of appetite,* as *a man,* or *owner of soul;* that is, of *appetite,* for one of greedy appetite, Prov. 23.2.

*{which can never have enough*} Or, *they can never have enough.* Heb. *they know not to be satisfied:* Our margin renders it, as if it were a verb of the infinitive mood; which some of the Jewish Masters also, but doubtingly, deliver. Or, rather, *they know not satiety:* for the word seems to be a noun, in that notion frequently found, Ruth 2.18. ch. 23.18. & 55.2. Ezek. 16.28. & 39.19. Hag. 1.6. as Ch. 59.8. *they know not the way of peace:* that is, they know not how to walk, or carry themselves peaceably: they cannot do it, because they have no mind thereunto. See verse 6. of some such like dogs, David, Psal. 59.6,14,15. the greediness here spoken of, is not of meat, or drink, (though in following their voluptuous courses of riot and excess, they were that way also insatiable, ver. 12.) but of moneys, and means, to maintain that withal, Eccl. 5.10. and 10.19.

*{and they are shepherds that cannot understand*} Or, *and such shepherds* they are, *as have no understanding;* a defect of the relative, as ver. 2. Heb. *know not to understand;* as Jer. 6.15. & 8.12. *they know not to blush,* and *they know not to do right;* Amos 3.10. though some render it; *they know not to teach,* as if it were to *make to understand,* to instruct: and so the word is used, Dan. 10.14. See also chap. 28.19. but is more frequently taken in the former sense, 1 King. 3.9. Prov. 1.2,6. & 14.8. Some would here distinguish between the *dogs,* and the *shepherds,* as if the one were the inferior officers; the other, the superior governors: But the same parties seem to be, in either appellation, intended; as before, ver. 10. they have no understanding to foresee, and conceive, what the issue of things will be, Jer. 6.14. so the Jewish commenters. Or, they have no skill to order the flock aright: a matter of much moment, and in special manner, required in a shepherd, Jer. 3.15.

*{they all look to their own way, every one to his gain, from his quarter*} This clause shows more plainly, what greediness was meant before; to wit, greediness of gain, Prov. 15.27. and 31.15,16.

*{look to their own way*} See Chap. 53.6. they are all for themselves, without any regard to, or care of, the flock, and its welfare, Jer. 22.17. Ezek. 34.2,3. Phil. 2.21. Some make this passage parallel to that, Chap. 53.6. *We have turned every one to his own way.* Others, to that, Judg. 17.6. *every man did that which was right in his own eyes.* Both understand them, as implying not a general concurrence only, in running out into evil; but a diversity of those courses, that they severally took, some abandoning themselves to the giving of satisfaction to one inordinate lust, and some to another: whence, also, some conceive a distribution of them here, into two ranks, some addicted to covetousness, and some to riot and excess. But I suppose the meaning of the words to be simply such as was before hinted: nor do the places pointed to, seem altogether parallel, the pronoun being in them singular, as importing a distribution; whereas here it is plural. Besides, that the same parties seem charged with the same vices, not some of them with the one only, and some with the other. See the like, Amos 4.1. and 6.3,4.

*{his gain*} As Prov. 1.19. & 15.27. It is rendered, *covetousness,* ch. 57.17. Jer. 6.13. Ezek. 33.31. but the word signifies properly, *lucre,* or *gain.*

*{from his quarter*} Heb. *from his end;* which interpreters diversely expound. Some, from the one end of them to the other; that is *from the highest to the lowest,* as Jer. 6.13. all sorts of them; and so the old Latin renders it. Others, from the one end of their way to the other: from the first to the last, they mind and follow nothing but this: it is the whole tenor of their life, to look after their gain. Others, from the one end of the city to the other, as if out of all parts of it, they did rap and rend what they could; no place was free from their pillage: and according to these expositions, the speech should be defective, as wanting the latter term more fully expressed elsewhere; as Exod. 26.28. & 36.33. Others, and so some of the Jewish commenters, from the place of his abode, and they parallel it with that, Gen. 19.4. where the word is not amiss rendered, *quarter,* as it is also according to this sense, which seems the plainest here. Howbeit, some conceiving it further to intimate their insatiable thirst, and pursuit after gain, render it, *without end,* and in that notion is the noun oft used, as Chap. 2.7. and the particle also prefixed before it, is sometime used in the like sense: and so, *from end,* should be here, as much, as *without end;* as *from vision, without vision,* Mic. 3.6. But the pronoun, *his,* affixed, seems to make the construction, in that sense, here, the harsher, and to carry it rather the other way. I shall subjoin only an annotation of a late learned writer: He conceives that the word here used, though commonly signifying, *coast,* or *end,* or *extremity,* does oft-times also denote, *eminent,* or *honorable persons.* So he deems it to be taken, Gen. 19.4. & 47.2. Judg. 18.2. Chap. 26.15. Ezek. 33.2. and so he would have it taken here: and the meaning to be, either referring it to the priests, *they look after, their gain, the very chief of them;* not the meaner sort only: or referring it to the people whom they made a prey of; *they follow their gain, from the principal,* (that is, the richest sort) *of them,* to wit, of that people, whose watchmen they are said to be, ver. 10. But the places produced, are all questionable; nor does it seem to go smoothly either way here: yea, this Author himself elsewhere seems confident, that this phrase signifies, *on every side,* both here, and Jer. 50.26. & 51.31. and in most of the places here alleged by him to other purpose. But howsoever it may be with other places, the pronoun affixed will not permit it to be taken so here.

**V. 12.** *{Come ye*} The speech of these wicked priests, and pretended prophets, either inciting one another, to join together, in the practice of riot and excess; or inviting some of the people to partake therein with them; and so impiously encouraging them unto such vile courses, as their duty was to have reproved in them, and to have by all means endeavored to withdraw them from. Thus they applied themselves to the humor of the people, Mic. 2.11. and strengthened the hands of the wicked, that they might not leave their sins, Ezek. 23.19,22.

*{say they*} These words are supplied, being not in the text, as chap. 22.13. & 45.14. Neh. 13.15. Act. 7.32.

*{I will fetch wine, and we will fill ourselves with strong drink*} Heb. *I will take wine* (but it is well rendered here *fetch,* as also, Gen. 18.7. & 27.9. for it includes two notions, *to take,* and *to bring:* as *to receive:* and *to bestow,* Ps. 68.18. compared with Eph. 4.8.) *and we will be drunk* (as it is well rendered, Mic. 1.10.) *with strong drink:* we will want no good liquor of any kind. Of the word, joined also with *wine* there, see on ch. 5.11. a defect of the particle *with,* as ch. 28.1. Jer. 13.12.

*{and tomorrow shall be as this day, and much more abundant*} Some conceive it to be spoken in derision of Gods prophets, as scoffing at their denunciation of destruction, shortly and suddenly to befall them; we do well enough today, and we will do better tomorrow. See Chap. 22.13. But it seems rather a profession of a wicked and wretched resolution, to proceed in the continued practice of their present excess, day after day, without abating an ace of it, but improving it rather. See somewhat the like resolution of the drunkard, Prov. 23.35.

*{and much more abundant*} Heb. *great;* (that is, *greater* than this: the positive, for the comparative, as Gen. 10.21.) yea *of much more excellency,* or *abundance,* as Gen. 49.3.

### CHAPTER 57

**V. 1.** *{The righteous perisheth;*} Amidst the reproofs of the wickedness and profaneness of the times, and the dreadful denunciations of wrath and judgment, against the main body of the state for the same the prophet here, by the way, inserts somewhat for the comfort of the sincere-hearted, that living in those times, should either by the cruelty of oppression, have their lives shortened, or be taken away otherwise: yet not without a secret nip, unto those other ungodly ones, that regarded it not, nor took notice of God's mercy toward them, in translating them hence, before the judgments denounced came to be put in execution; or, of the warning thereof given by the subtraction of such.

*{The righteous*} This some restrain to Josias, commended for his justice, Jer. 22.15,16. as well as for his piety, 2 Chron. 34.3. and taken away by an untimely end, 2 Chron. 35.23,24. But the word seems more general; being taken collectively, as Psal. 11.5. & 34.19.

*{perisheth*} Is taken away by death: the decease of many such, a forerunning sign of some general judgment approaching. See Chap. 3.2. & 6.13. and see the like complaints of a defection of such, Psal. 12.1. Mic. 7.1,2. Howbeit it is not so to be understood, as if such utterly perished, and were lost; for it is not so; they live even in death, Joh. 11.25,26. But by *perishing,* is understood only decease, and departure hence, as, *ready to perish;* that is, to die, Chap. 27.13. And the prophet the rather uses this term, because to the carnal eye, it seemed so to fare with them; which yet he controls, ver. 2.

*{and no man layeth it to heart:*} Heb. *there is no man,* or, *not any,* (as Chap. 36.6. & 40.26.) *laying it on heart;* as Chap. 47.7. So ver. 11. where a defect also of the pronoun demonstrative is, as here: *heart,* for *his heart.* See the like defect of the possessive, Chap. 27.9. & 53.10. none of them, of those debauched ones, Chap. 56.12. do any whit regard it, or take notice of God's hand, and end, in it. See Chap. 5.16,17. Amos 6.5,6.

*{and merciful men are taken away;*} Or, *pious, godly;* or, *kind, pitiful;* for the word is used for either: for the former, Psal. 16.10. & 32.6. & 86.2. for the latter, Psal. 103.4. & 109.18. Jer. 2.2. & 3.12. Heb. *men of piety,* or *pity:* or, *men of benignity,* or *kindness;* as Prov. 11.17. *a man of benignity,* or *kindness,* opposed there to a *cruel* man: the word is used in the adjective, Psal. 12.1. Mic. 7.2. The Jewish critics thus distinguish these two; the *just,* or *righteous;* and the *kind,* or *bountiful* man: the former, say they, is one that gives precisely to God, or man, in matter of tithes, or alms, and the like, what the strict letter of the Law exacts of him, and no more: the latter, one that affords it with some overplus: For example, the firstfruits of their corn, wine, and oil, was without any certain set proportion, or stint, required of them by the Mosaical Law, Deut. 18.2. howbeit, their doctors had so defined it, that a sixtieth part, at least, was to be given. This they gathered from Ezek. 45.11. where for their oblation, the *sixth* part of an *Epha,* is required out of an *Homer,* which contained ten *Ephaes.* Hence, they made three degrees of offerers, one that brought but a *sixtieth* part, whom they call *a man of a strict eye:* Another that brought the *fiftieth* part, whom they term the *middle* man: A third, that brought the *fortieth* part, whom they call *a man of a good eye.* So Eccles. 35.9. And this third, is the *kind,* or *bountiful* man. Again, from Esaus words to Jacob, Gen. 33.9. they coin four sorts of men: The first, he that says, *Mine to thee, and thine to me;* or, *Mine thine, and thine mine.* And this is the man of the world, that deals strictly in mutual commerce. The second, that says, *Mine to me, and thine to thee;* or, *Mine mine, and thine thine.* And this is the way of Sodom, that would part with nothing to the poor, Ezekiel 16.49. or, the *middle* man, between the *wicked,* and the *kind.* A third, that says, *Mine to myself, and thine too to me;* or, *Mine mine own, and thine mine,* and that is *a wicked* man. A fourth, that says, *Mine to thee, and thine to thyself;* or, *Mine thine, and thine thine own;* that gives freely, looking for nothing again, Psal. 37.21. Luk. 6.35. And this is the *kind,* or *bountiful* man. See Chap. 22.5. True it is, that the word has a notion of *bounty,* and *benignity* in it; but so is the word of *righteousness* also oftentimes used. See on Chap. 54.17. and so Matth. 1.19. nor seems it the purpose of the Holy Ghost, here to distinguish between *righteous* men, and *men of piety,* or *kindness;* but to describe the same persons by words, as they are largely taken, (though in strict notion distinct) of equal extent. So *righteous,* and *good,* Rom. 5.7.

*{taken away*} Heb. *gathered;* as Gen. 25.8. Psal. 27.10. a metaphor taken from the gathering of fruit, or corn, Levit. 23.39. Chap. 17.5.

*{no man considering*} Or, *while none considereth.* Heb. *in there being none understanding,* or *considering:* as, *when no deeps were,* Prov. 8.24. & 29.18. *where no vision is,* or, *without any understanding,* or *consideration:* as, *without instruction,* Prov. 5.23. that is, for want of it: and, *without a wall,* Ezek. 38.11.

*{that the righteous*} The same word comprehending here, the persons spoken of in the two former branches, as being not divers persons, but the same diversely described.

*{is taken away from the evil to come*} Heb. *from before,* or, *from the face of the evil,* (as Jer. 42.17.) *is the righteous gathered:* a resemblance taken from the fruit, that is plucked, and carried into the house; or corn, that is cut, and brought into the barn, when a storm is perceived coming, to prevent such hurt, or damage, as thereby it might have received: So here, they are beforehand taken away, that they may not see the ruin of the state, and the captivity of their people. See instances of the like, in Jeroboams son taken away, that he might not see the downfall of his father's whole family, and the utter extirpation of his stock, 1 Kin. 14.12,13. of Josias gathered up, that he might not see the same with these, had they survived, 2 Kin. 22.20.

**V. 2.** *{He shall enter into peace*} Or, *He shall go in peace:* the particle wanting; as Chap. 41.3. or, as some render it, *Peace shall come,* to wit, to them; it shall befall them; for the word signifies, as well *to come,* as *to go,* Chap. 27.13. & 35.10. and some also supplying the particle of continuation, (which is oft suppressed: as 1 Sam. 18.20. Ch. 2.2. & 10.20. & 11.11.) carry on the sentence, as further relating what it was, that these wicked wretches, who deemed the godly, so taken away, to be wretched, and unhappy persons, did not understand, or consider, to wit, *That he goeth to peace;* or, *That he goeth in peace,* or, *That peace cometh to him.* That they are taken away while outward peace yet continues, 2 Kin. 22.20. and quietly with inward peace in their souls, Luk. 2.29. or, That they depart hence unto rest, and peace, Rev. 14.3. to a place of eternal joy and bliss, Mat. 25.21–23. Luk. 16.25. Joh. 16.22. and this is that which worldly men consider not; because to the eye of flesh it appears not, Col. 3.3. 1 Joh. 5.2. but they seem rather to have perished, ver. 1. 1 Cor. 15.18.

*{they shall rest in their beds*} As their souls pass to a place of rest, and bliss; so their bodies are laid down to rest in the grave, as in a bed, or bedchamber, there to sleep quietly, until the general resurrection, what time they shall awake, and be raised up again, Job 7.21. and 14.12. Eccles. 12.7. 2 Cor. 5.8. Phil. 1.23. and 3.21. 1 Thess. 4.14,17. because the verb here is plural, whereas the former was singular. Some would have it rendered his bones *shall rest in their beds;* but that is not needful: the word was collective before; and *their beds* intimates as much here: and the passage from number to number is not unusual. See Psal. 127.5. & 140.9.

*{each one walking in his uprightness*} Or, *that walketh uprightly,* straight forward, without swerving to the one hand, or the other. Prov. 4.25–27. or, *before him;* that is, before God: as Judg. 18.6. Prov. 5.21. that walks sincerely and circumspectly, as in his sight, Gen. 17.1. Psal. 18.23. & 119.168. chap. 38.3. Jer. 17.16. *before him,* for, *before God:* as, *he said,* for, *God said,* Gen. 15.13. the pronoun, for the noun; *each one,* is inserted; because a distribution is implied oft in such conjunctions of the singular noun, with the verb plural. See on Chap. 26.19. Some of those that rendered the foregoing branch, *Peace shall come* to them; repeat from thence, the word *peace,* here, and render it; *Peace shall go before him,* or *them:* because the word was collective, as Psal. 85.13. *righteousness shall go before him;* and, *their works go along with them,* or, *accompany them,* Rev. 14.13. as if peace were said to conduct them, and convey them unto the place of their rest. But the former reading seems the clearer.

**V. 3.** *{But draw near hither*} After the former passage inserted and premised, for the comfort of the faithful, that should live in those times hereafter ensuing, and preceding that general ruin, and dissolution of the state, and deportation of the people, pronouncing them blessed, that should be taken away; though by the hands of cruel wretches, (as under Manasses, and some of Josias his wicked sons, and successors, it is not unlikely, but that many such were, 2 Kin. 21.16. Jer. 22.17.) because they should not live to see, what should befall the land when they were gone; the like whereunto, see Rev. 14.13. he now addresses himself unto the surviving wicked ones, that were of a far other mind concerning those pious ones, so made away, as deeming them miserable creatures, and themselves happy men, as living still to enjoy the land, and their places, and possessions in it, together with what they had bereaved them of: and first, in lively colors, he lays out their most impious, and abominable courses; then foretells, from God, what judgments should unavoidably befall them, from which none of their complices should be able to deliver them; and lastly, concludes with gracious promises of mercy, deliverance, and restitution, (wherein yet the obstinate wicked ones should have no share) to the pious and repentant.

*{But draw near hither ye sons of the sorceress*} The words run somewhat more emphatically in the original, thus: *And* (for, *But:* as Chap. 53.5.) *ye,* or, *as for you,* (as Chap. 61.6.) *draw near hither, sons of the sorceress;* as if he had said, But as for you, come you hither a while; I have another manner of errand to deliver unto you, some sorceress's brats, an adulterous brood: it is like that of Achijah to the Israelitish queen, *Come in Jeroboams wife, I have heavy tidings to tell thee,* 1 King. 14.6.

*{sons of the sorceress*} Heb. *of a sorceress,* or *witch;* not of Abraham, as you pretend to be, Chap. 41.8. Mat. 3.9. Joh. 8.33. or, of Sarah, Chap. 51.2. but of some *sorceress,* or *witch,* rather: their children are men, in Scripture, said to be, whom in affection, and disposition, they resemble, and whom, in practice, they imitate, Ezek. 16.3. Mat. 3.7. & 12.34. & 23.33. Joh. 8.37,39,40,44. 1 Joh. 3.8,10. the word *sorceress,* does not so fitly answer the term here used; for the word *sorcerer,* or *sorceress,* signifies properly, one that deals with *lots,* and by them divines; coming from a Latin word, that signifies a *lot:* the word *witch,* being more general, may seem to suit better with it; and the rather, because it is here a feminine, in which form, it is nowhere else found: and some would have it to denote such an one, as *bewitcheth* with her eyes; as among the heathen, anciently, some were deemed to do. But of the notion, and notation of the word, see on Chap. 2.6. where the masculine is rendered, a *soothsayer.* By which place, also, it is apparent, that these kind of practices were very rife among that people: whereof, see 2 King. 21.6. and well therefore are they here termed, *witches' children;* because to such practices addicted.

*{the seed of the adulterer, and the whore*} A bastardly brood, begotten by some adulterer, upon an *hore;* (for so I suppose our English word should be written, coming from the word *hire;* as the Latin, *meretrix.* See Deut. 18.18. Ezek. 16.33. Mic. 1.7.) and belong therefore no more to God's family, than such issue, as some adulteress, or common strumpet, has by some adulterer, whom, forsaking her husband, or dealing disloyally with him, she has joined herself unto, Prov. 2.17. & 30.20. See Hos. 1.2. & 2.2. & 3.1. Mat. 12.39. & 16.4. Joh. 8.41,42,44,47. Heb. *a seed* (that is, *issue,* or *race;* as Chap. 1.4.) *of an adulterant,* or *adulterer;* (as Jer. 9.2. & 23.10. Hos. 7.4. by which places it appears, how this sin abounded with them; though of spiritual adultery God principally here speaks) *and* of one, or of *her that playeth the harlot;* for the word here is a verb: as also, Levit. 19.29. Judg. 19.2. Jer. 3.6,8. where it is so rendered: the defect of the relative is very rife, as has been before observed, Chap. 55.13. & 56.2,11. Howbeit, some render it, *a seed committing adultery,* (as also they would have the term used, Mat. 12.39. & 16.4. to be taken;) *that playest the harlot;* (the copulative, for the relative: as Chap. 17.2. & 28.1.) or *thou,* I say, (as Chap. 49.6. & 55.1.) *that hast played the harlot,* Jer. 3.1. Ezek. 16. & 23. or, *a seed that hath committed adultery, and will play the harlot still;* as noting the unsatiableness in their spiritual pollutions, and their pertinacious persisting therein, Jer. 2.25. Ezek. 16.28. But these all offer force to the text; for the verb here is feminine, as in the places also forecited; whereas the word *seed,* and the participle annexed to it, (yet not necessarily in conjunction with it) are both masculine; and neither of them therefore can couple well with this verb. The former sense is fit, and fair, and to me seems to be genuine.

**V. 4.** *{Against whom do ye sport yourselves*} The prophet having to the life limned them, and set before them, an exact picture, and portraiture, of themselves; proceeds now to debate the matter with them, concerning their practices: and he begins first, with their carriage toward God's messengers, whom, when they reproved them for their enormities, Chap. 58.1. and denounced God's judgments against them for the same, Chap. 56.9. they entertained with nothing but mocks and scoffs, and made sport with them, and their messages, 2 Chr. 36.16. Chap. 5.19. & 22.13. & 28.14,22. Jer. 5.12,13. & 23.33. Ezek. 11.3. The prophet therefore advises them seriously to consider, who it was, that they thus derided, and made themselves so merry with: not some sorry silly mortals, as they seemed to make account; but the immortal, and almighty God, whose ministers and messengers they were, and whom therefore they wronged and abused, in them, Exod. 16.8. Num. 16.11. Luk. 10.16. 1 Thess. 4.8. for that it is, that he intends, though he name not the Lord: and the concealment of the party, makes the speech the more emphatical; as if he had said, it concerns you nearly, to consider who it is, though I name him not to you; and it is very like that expostulation, or debate of God, with Sennacherib, Chap. 37.23. They warp too much from the prophet's drift, that would have this branch expounded, of their abandoning themselves to wantonness; as that, 1 Tim. 5.6. which they make parallel to this: or, of their voluptuous feastings at their idols' tables, Chap. 65.11. the like whereunto, 2 Pet. 2.13,14. Jud. 12. but the words ensuing, clear sufficiently the prophet's intent.

*{Against whom do ye sport yourselves*} Or, *with whom do ye make yourselves merry?* The word is most commonly taken in the better sense, for *to delight one's self* in aught; as Psal. 37.4,11. Job 22.26. & 27.10. Chap. 58.15. & 66.11. but yet sometime also, in the worse, in a notion of extreme *delicacy,* Deut. 28.56. Jer. 6.2. See Chap. 47.1. here to make themselves merry and frolic, with jesting, and gibing at God's prophets. See the like, Psal. 35.15,16. Lam. 3.14.

*{against whom*} Or, *at whom.*

*{make ye a wide mouth, and draw out the tongue?*} Heb. *do ye widen the mouth, and lengthen the tongue?* gestures, and expressions of derision, and mockage, Job 16.10. Psal. 22.7. & 35.21. Lam. 2.16.

*{are ye not children of transgression, a seed of falsehood?*} Persons addicted to disobedience, and rebellion; (as *children of wickedness,* Hos. 10.9.) and a race of liars, and counterfeits: as Chap. 30.9. that dissemble with God, professing themselves to be his, when they are indeed nothing less, Chap. 48.1,2. or that by their disobedience to him, discard him, and cast him off, as none of their father, and carry themselves towards him, as none of his children, Deut. 32.5. And this censure of them, is propounded by way of interrogation; which adds much vehemency to it; as also, ver. 6. as if he had said, Deny it if you can. See the like, Amos 2.11.

**V. 5.** *{Inflaming yourselves with idols, under every green tree*} Or, *Ye that are inflamed.* For howsoever these passive forms have sometime a reciprocal notion; whereof, see on Chap. 55.3. Yet here there is no necessity of it. *Inflamed,* or (carrying on the sentence, as the particle prefixed shows that it should be) *ye that are inflamed;* to wit, with filthy spiritual lust, here principally implied; and with corporal also, which went commonly along with it, and was usually practiced by them, at their meetings, and in the meeting places, for the service of their idols, Num. 25.1,2. 2 Chr. 23.6,7. Hos. 4.10–14. Amos 2.8. See the use of the word, Gen. 30.38. Psal. 51.5. Hos. 7.4,6. The old Latin renders it, *solacing themselves;* and the word that signifies, sometime, *to repent;* sometime, *to be comforted,* ver. 7. Jer. 8.6. does in the form, wherein this is here used, come very near to it; but the roots are divers, the formation different, and the former vowel-point not the same.

*{with idols*} Or, *among the oaks:* for the word sometime, signifies *gods,* or *potentates;* great and mighty ones, as Chap. 44.10. Exod. 15.11,15. Psal. 89.6. Job 41.25. sometime *rams,* that domineer, as strong ones, among the sheep, Chap. 1.11. & 34.6. Ezek. 34.17,18,21. whence the ambiguity, and diversity of readings, Psal. 29.1. sometime *oaks,* or more generally, strong and tall trees, of more eminency, than the ordinary sort, and rank of them: And it is therefore rendered more generally, in some places, *trees,* Chap. 61.3. Ezek. 31.14. as the word, in Greek (whereof some think the *Druides,* or pagan priests, and prophets, among the Galles, the *Dryades, wood-nymphs,* or inferior goddesses, among the Greeks questionless, had their names) signifying properly an *oak,* yet is oft taken more largely, for the common sort of forest trees. But of the word itself, see more, on Chap. 1.30. & 6.13. Here those that take it for such trees, some of them render it, *a grove,* or *tuft,* of such like *timber-trees,* dedicated to idolatrous services, Chap. 1.29.

*{under every green tree:*} After the manner of the Gentiles, that, in such places, used to sacrifice to their idols, and perform their superstitious services, being sheltered from the heat of the sun, by their shade. So Deut. 12.2. 2 King. 16.4. & 17.10. 2 Chr. 28.4. Jer. 2.20. & 3.6. Ezek. 6.13. Hos. 6.13. See Chap. 27.9.

*{slaying the children*} Heb. *slayers of the children;* that *slay your children:* for their own they were, whom they so slaughtered and sacrificed, 2 King. 16.3. & 21.6. & 23.10. Psal. 106.38. (a defect of the pronoun, as Job 19.2. Chap. 46.4.) that are wont to murder your children in the service of your idols. A savage practice, which they learned from the heathen that used so to do, Deut. 12.31. Psal. 106.35–38. See Lev. 18.21. & 20.2. Jer. 7.31. & 19.5. Ezek. 16.20. & 20.26. & 23.37,39. 2 Chr. 28.3. & 33.6.

*{in the valleys*} Or, *besides the brooks;* as the particle is used, Neh. 3.15,25. 1 King. 15.13. the word signifies, sometime, *a valley;* so called, because it shoots along as an *hollow pipe,* or *gutter,* between two hills. So Chap. 7.19. such a valley was that of *Elah;* 1 Sam. 17.2,3. and such a valley seems that of *Hinnom,* to have been, where such inhumane services were commonly practiced, Jer. 7.31. sometime, *a brook,* Lev. 11.9,10. Hence, *the brook Kishon,* Judg. 5.21. and, *the brook Kidron,* 2 Sam. 15.23. 1 King. 2.37. 2 Chr. 30.14. whence the vale, lying near about it, is called, *the fields of Kidron,* 2 King. 23.4. and, *the valley of Kidron;* as seems to be intended, 2 Chr. 29.16. this brook is deemed also to have run, among other lower grounds, through the valley of Hinnom: and brooks are so termed; because they run commonly along the valleys, with those waters, that shoot down from the hills, Psal. 104.10.

*{under the cliffs of the rocks.*} Heb. properly, *branches.* See on Chap. 2.21. such overhangings of them, or cliffs branching out from them, as towards the root, or foot, of rocky, or chalky hills oft times, are seen, made by the water undermining them; and afford shade, as well as the branches of thick trees do, Chap. 32.2. Some such caves also might be made, and cut out of purpose, as for habitation and sepulture sometime, Chap. 22.16. so for exercise of idolatrous services, for which they made use, sometime of groves and woods, sometime of dales; sometime of rocky caves; sometime of hills. See Chap. 17.8.

**V. 6.** *{Among the smooth stones of the stream is thy portion*} The prophet here begins to alter the frame of his discourse; not speaking, now, as before, to the people, as children of the state, as a stock, or stem; or, as the issue of some adulterous couple; but directing his speech to the state itself, as to a lewd woman, or common strumpet: and the tenor of his charge therefore now runs in a singular feminine form. So Jer. 2.2. & Ezek. 1.6. & 23.

*{Among the smooth stones of the stream*} Heb. *in the parts,* or *smooths, of the valley,* or *brook.* The former word; (but without such a point, as the middle letter here has) does most usually signify *parts,* and *portions,* as Josh. 18.5,6,9. Ezek. 45.7. & 48.8,21. and it is regularly the plural of the word, here rendered *portion:* whence some therefore render it, *parts,* or *distributions.* And so the old Latin has it. Now of these, some expound it, of the parts adjacent to the *brooks*: for the word is the same, with that before, ver. 5. only singular here, but in a collective sense; as Job 21.33. & 28.4. & 40.22. Others, of the *divisions of the brooks*, parting themselves into divers branches, or streams: amid which, say they, in the islands, were their altars sometime erected; especially, about the fountain-heads, from which they descended. Others, again, of the rocky parts at the hill-foot that were as part of the *vale*, ver. 5. But the Jewish commenters, because of the point commonly called *dagesh*, in the belly of the second radical, understand by it *smooth stones*, directing us to that place, 1 Sam. 17.40. where the same word, so *dageshed*, another voweling point only substituted, is found in the same notion, it being said of David, that he picked *five smooth of stones* (so the words are) *out of the brook*, or *valley* rather; that is, five smooth stones out of those that lay in the vale of Elah; which vale lay between the two armies, and in which the combat was fought between him, and Goliah, 1 Sam. 17.2,3. for of any brook that ran between them, we read not: so, *the smooth of the brook*, or *valley* (for the Hebrew has no more) is here put for the smooth stones (as it is more fully in that other place expressed) *of the valley*, or the *brook*, and there is a defect of the subject, or substantive; as *full*, for *a full cup*, Psal. 73.10. *strong*, for *a strong hand*, chap. 40.10. And by such stones, some understand the smooth pebbles, whereof there was great store in the brooks, or about them in the valleys; in which their altars were erected, ver. 5. Jer. 2.23. Others, those slick and smooth stones, curiously cut out, and polished, Psal. 144.12. whereof their altars were made, contrary to God's command, Exod. 20.25. and this seems most probable; for what the Jewish doctors relate, that their manner was to pick up some fair stone, and adore it, is but a groundless conceit. Nor does that of a learned writer take much with me, (I shall leave it to be weighed and deemed of by others) who referring the word both here, and there, in the story of David, to the former root, would have it rendered, as before, *divisions of the brook* here, as Ps. 1.3. (adding withal, that by Paynims, brooks were adored, as having some kind of deity) so, *divisions of stones* there; that is, not whole stones, but pieces of them; not smooth ones, but rough and broken, as in that regard, much better, and fitter for his use: But whether ragged ones were so fit to sling with, I doubt.

*{is thy portion*} Your altars, and your idol-service, is that which you delight in, and trust unto; as worldly men, in their wealth, Psal. 17.14. Prov. 18.11. that you esteem your inheritance, your lot, and your portion: your idols are to you, so, as God is to the godly, Ps. 16.4,5,6. & 119.57. Prov. 18.10. Jer. 10.16. Lam. 3.24. though some would have it spoken in a menacing way, as foretelling what should betide them, when they should be in captivity, and sit mourning in waste places, beside the brooks' sides at Babylon, Ps. 137.1,2. But this suits not so well with the sequel of the context. However there is an elegant paronomasy, and *antanaclasis*, in the Hebrew, between the words rendered, *smooth*, and *portion*; which our English cannot express.

*{they are thy lot*} Some would have the pronoun, to be put here for the verb substantive, as oft it is. See ch. 43.13. and then should not the word, *are*: be expressed, by any different character. But the gemination of the word (which is here very emphatical, as the like, ch. 43.25.) to me seems to carry it another way; the emphasis being rather in the pronoun, than in the verb: the sentence is the same, in effect, with the former: and a trope in either, taken from the parting, and dividing an inheritance, so as to assign each of the coheirs, or parceners, his, or her portion, by lot; as Num. 26.55. and 34.13. Josh. 14.2. so Psal. 16.5. Chap. 34.17. Howbeit, I cannot concur with those, that would have it to be so understood, as if hereby were intimated, that these their idolatrous practices, were hereditary to them, that they were left unto them, as a legacy, an inheritance, or a portion, from their parents, 1 Pet. 1.18.

*{even, to them, hast thou poured a drink offering, thou hast offered a meat offering*} Heb. *also unto them*; to wit, your idols, ver. 5. or, *upon them*, to wit, your altar stones, or altars in those places erected, ver. 6. for so also does the particle here used sometime signify; as Psal. 9.4. *upon the throne*. chap. 3.26. *upon the ground*.

*{a drink-offering*} By the law of God, unto every sacrifice of any beast, was to be added, a certain quantity of meal, or flour, mixed with oil, which was termed *minchah*, as we render it, *a meat offering*: and a certain quantity of wine, that was termed *nesec*, rendered usually, *a drink offering*, Num. 15.4,5. neither was the sacrifice deemed complete, until this latter, the last rite, used about the body of the beast, was poured upon it. Hence, those speeches of the apostle, *I am ready to be poured out*, 2 Tim. 4.6. and *if I be poured out upon the sacrifice and service* (as Rom. 12.1. & 15.16.) *of your faith*, Phil. 2.17. where he compares the Philippians' faith, and his ministry about them, to a sacrifice; his blood, by martyrdom shed, to obsign and seal up, in way of confirmation, and consummation thereof, the same, to such an offering as this. Howbeit, the word *nesec*, signifying an *effusion*, or something poured out, may seem to be more general, and to comprehend any liquid oblation, were it of *oil*, or of *wine*: For we read of *effusions*, or *pourings*, in the religious performances of the ancient patriarchs, before Moses, as well of *oil*, as of *wine*, Gen. 28.18. & 35.14. and upon some of their *bread-corn offerings*, to wit, their *flour* oblations, was by the latter law, *oil* to be poured, Lev. 2.1. For others of this latter sort, were to be only molded, and made up, or anointed therewith, Lev. 2.4,5. But another term is used in those places, for the pouring out of oil, than that, from which the word *nesec* descends, which may therefore well be deemed to import, specially that of wine, of the pouring out of these to their false gods, wherein they partook also themselves with them. See Jer. 7.18. & 19.13. & 44.17–19,25. Ezek. 20.28. Amos 2.8.

*{a meat-offering*} Or, as some, *a wheat offering*: but as the one is too large; for the flesh-oblations also are called, Lev. 3.6. *God's meat*, Mal. 1.12. and were some of them *meat* for the priests, Lev. 6.26,29. Ezek. 44.29. so the latter is too narrow: for there were some oblations of *barley*, as well as of *wheat*, Lev. 2.14,16. & 23.10,17. Num. 5.15. nor does the word, *meal-offering*, come exactly home to it; because some were of the *ears of corn*, or *corn* yet *in the ear*: the nearest to it seems to be, the *corn*, or the *bread-corn offering*; which will comprehend all the *minchaes* in Moses: for what Caines was of *the fruits of the earth*, being, in terms, so general, and large related, is uncertain. But of this kind of oblation, two sorts of it, the notion, and the notation of the term, See before on chap. 1.13. of these offered to their idols, (for of this kind were their cakes tendered to the host of heaven) see Jer. 7.18. & 44.19. Ezek. 20.28. Amos 4.4,5. The word is here, as the former also: though in a singular form, yet in a plural notion.

*{should I receive comfort in these*} What joy, or comfort, can I have (for this form has oft such a potential notion, as Jer. 2.23.) in such people as these? Chap. 9.17. though they should withal perform other services to me, Chap. 66.3. Jer. 7.9,10. Ezek. 20.39. or, as some, should I *have compassion* on such wicked wretches as these? as also, chap. 9.17. so Jer. 5.7. *how should I spare thee for this?* thus the word may seem to signify, Deut. 32.36. Psal. 90.13. Others, how should I *repent* of the evil, that for these things I intend to bring upon them. So is the word taken, Exod. 32.12. Jer. 18.8. See Jer. 15.6. Psalm 90.13. Others, how should I rid myself of that grief, and shake off that sorrow, that my soul is possessed of, and my Spirit vexed with, by such practices as these, Ezek. 6.9. so the word seems taken, Gen. 24.67. 2 Sam. 13.39. Others, can I be at any rest, or have any joy of aught, until I have taken vengeance for such practices as these? See Jer. 5.9. The old Latin, after the ancient Greeks, read the words in the negative, *Should I not be wroth, or have indignation for these things?* and in these interrogative forms (which run usually with much quickness, and vehemency, as ver. 4.) the negative particle is oft omitted.
