So 1 Sam. 2.27,28. *Did I*, and *Did I?* for, *Did not I?* Job 20.4. *Knowest thou not this of old?* Ezek. 20.30. *Are ye not polluted? Do ye not commit whoredom?* See Jer. 31.19. This therefore here also admitted, I should thus render the words; *Should I not ease myself of such?* To wit, by taking vengeance upon them; as Jer. 5.9. *Should I not visit for these things? Should not my soul be avenged on such a nation as this?* For the use of the word, in this notion, see Chap. 1.24. and the prophet may seem the rather to have made choice of this word, here, to conclude this verse, with a word of the like sound, though not sense, to that wherewith he began the verse foregoing.

**V. 7.** *{upon a lofty, and high mountain, hast thou set thy bed;*} After that passionate parenthesis, wherewith the foregoing discourse was shut up, he returns to relate their shameful, or shameless, rather, pollutions of themselves with their idols. You have not in vales, and caves only, below by the brook-sides, erected your altars, but aloft on the highest hills, in your high places. Such also they made use of as temples for the service of their idols, after the manner of the Heathen, whom God cast out before them, Deut. 12.2. 1 King. 12.31. & 14.23. 2 King. 17.9,29. & 21.3. Jer. 17.2,3. Ezek. 6.13. & 16.16,32. & 20.28,29. He compares the Jewish state to a shameless strumpet, that entertains her companions, not in private chambers, and closets, as having yet some shame of what she did, Ezek. 8.8,12. but without all shame, as glorying rather in her shame, committing fornication, and practicing uncleanness in open view, as Absolom with his tent spread upon the house-top, 2 Sam. 16.22. so with her bed, made, and set in some conspicuous place; lying open, and exposed to the eyes of all. See 2 King. 23.5,12. Jer. 32.29. Ezek. 16.24,25. & 23.41.

*{high and lofty*} Words of the same notion multiplied, to make it more emphatical, and to express the eminency of the place. So Chap. 2.13,14. & 30.25. & 52.13.

*{thy bed*} Ver. 8. Ezek. 23.17,41.

*{even thither wentest thou up to offer sacrifice;*} Heb. *thither also*; as ver. 6. *wentest thou up*; not to do service and sacrifice unto me, (as though in an irregular way your people sometime did, 1 King. 3.2. 2 Chron. 33.17.) but to defile yourself there, (See ver. 8.) by offering sacrifice to those your idols, on your altars, to the honor and service of them there erected, ver. 5,6. for I suppose them to be wide, that conceive the prophet to allude here to the manner of those, who lodged in the temples of their idols, expecting direction from them, by dreams.

**V. 8.** *{Behind the doors also, and the posts, hast thou set up thy remembrance:*} There is no place, either abroad, or within doors, free from some sign, or mark, some memorial, and monument, or other, of your idols, your affection to them, and filthiness with them, Ezek. 17.31.

*{Behind also*} Heb. *And behind*, as Chap. 34.13.

*{the doors and the posts*} Where God commanded his precepts to be set, that they might be ever in their eyes, Deut. 6.9. & 11.20. & 27.2,3. Heb. *the door, and the post*: which some therefore understand, as spoken of the door of God's house, the temple, Ezek. 8.3,5,7,14,17. & 43.8. but the words seem to be taken collectively, as our version renders them; as also the word *valley*, and *mountain*, ver. 6,7. or, if it be taken in a singular notion, because the speech runs of the whole state, as of one strumpet, it may be conceived, as spoken of the door of her own brothel-house, Prov. 5.8. as before of her bed, v. 7. Prov. 7.16,17. Some would have an allusion in it, to the arms, and ensigns of nobility, set over great men's doors: it might rather be, to the titles, and inscriptions wont to be set anciently over common strumpets' cells. But the words here, are, *behind the door*; not so much to invite them to her (of which before, and afterward, ver. 7,9.) as to mind herself of them, Ezek. 8.10. & 23.14. Others, to the *Lares*, or, *family-tutelar-gods*; whose images, say they, they used to have about their doors, to secure their goings out, and comings in: but of that they bring no proof. Others understand it, of the incense that they burnt unto their idols; because the incense seems to be termed, *a memorial*, Lev. 2.2. but that seems not to suit so well with *door*, and *post*.

*{for thou hast discovered thyself to another, than me, and hast gone up*} Heb. *for*, or, *yea*, (as Chap. 15.9. & 16.8.) *from me*, or, *from with me, thou hast discovered, and hast gone up*; that is, yea, more than so; departing from me, or refraining company, and society, with me, of which manner of defective, or comprehensive form of speech, (See on Chap. 1.4.) *thou hast discovered thy* shame, or nakedness, or *prostituted thyself*, (that is the meaning of the phrase, as appears, Ezek. 23.18. Levit. 20.17,18. a defect of the pronoun; as Lev. 18.6.) *when* (so is the copulative used, Gen. 14.14. Chap. 37.9,36. & 53.2.) *thou wentest up*; to wit, unto your bed, set aloft, in open view, ver. 7. there to defile yourself. See the like form of speech, in the like notion with the same quick, and concise manner of delivery, implying much indignation against, and detestation of, the fact mentioned, Gen. 49.4. They swerve from the resemblance used here by the prophet, that understand this passage, of withdrawing herself from God's protection, and abiding under his wing: as also those of the Jewish doctors, who suppose all this, together with the former passage, ver. 6,7. to respect that injunction, Exod. 21.24,25. that whereas God had commanded them, if they built him any altar, to make it, either of earth, or of rude rag, and to place it in some hidden place, (though that be not in the text) and to set it on the plain ground there; she had built altars of hewn stone, to set them aloft, in high places, and gone up to them by degrees: as also those, both of them, and ours, seem to narrow it too much, who expound it, as if it were said, that rising from God's side, or his bed; that is, his temple, she had immediately gone up to her idols' bed, in her high places: for howsoever, some such charge is entered against her, Ezek. 23.38,39. to wit, that the same day that she had committed idolatry with her idols, she had presumed to repair to God's house: Yet the meaning of the text here seems more general, that falling off from God, she had joined herself unto idols, and not in private only, retained monuments of them, but in public view also, committed acts of spiritual uncleanness with them. See Ezek. 14.6. & 23.17,41. Nor can their interpretation be admitted, who render it, following the old Latin, *thou hast beside me*, or *at my side*; that is, say they, in my temple, in my sight, prostituted yourself; as respecting what Ahaz and Manasses did, 2 King. 16.11,15. and 21.4,5,7. because the words of the text will not bear it; nor does that seem probable, which some others tender, concerning the last word, which, to fit the Latin, they render in an active sense, *thou hast caused them to ascend*; expounding it, by the same term used, Gen. 31.10,12. for though the verb admit either notion, yet the use of it before, in the sense commonly received, here carries it the other way. See ver. 7. no more than that, which the Greek gives, *thou hast there offered thy sacrifices*: as Josh. 8.31. though that agree better with what the former place, ver. 7. has. But the prophet is in another resemblance here.

*{thou hast enlarged thy bed*} You have increased your idolatry more and more, by the multitude of your altars; or by enlarging the temples, and places built, for the exercise thereof: as 1 King. 11.7. & 21.3. like a strumpet, that makes her bed, or room larger: or makes many beds, and rooms, to receive, and entertain the more company, 2 Chron. 28.24,25. Jer. 2.28. & 11.13. Ezek. 16.15,16,24,25,51. and 23.14. See ver. 7. So, *enlarge*, or *widen, the place of thy tent*, to receive the more inhabitants, Chapter 54.2.

*{and made a covenant with them*} So the old Latin, and some of the Jewish. You have engaged yourself to their idols, by entering into covenant with them, Deut. 7.2–4. 2 King. 16.10. Heb. *and cut thee out*, or *cut thee down from them*, or *more than they*. Now howsoever it be true, that the word of *cutting out*, be applied unto *covenanting*; the reason whereof, see on, Chap. 28.15. from Jer. 34.8,18. Yet because neither the word is found so used, but where the word *covenant*, is expressed, nor are persons said, to *cut covenant from* one, but to *cut covenant with* him, as in the place before pointed to, and elsewhere; some other sense of the words is to be sought out: where, to pass by those, who, seeming to wander far from the sense of the words here, read it, *thou hast cut thee some of them*, made eunuchs of them: as Chap. 39.7. though of such, the word be sometime used, Levit. 22.24. & Deut. 23.1. Some others render it, *and thou hast cut it thee out* (to wit, your bed, before spoken of) *larger than theirs*; (of which form of speech, see on Chap. 2.6. & 55.1.) that is, felled trees, in your groves, (Chap. 14.8. & 37.24. to make room for your altars, or, temples, built for the service of your idols; and herein striven to outstrip in your idolatries, either your idolatrous ancestors, Jer. 16.11,12. as some; or other idolatrous Heathen, Ezek. 5.6. as others: this latter seems more probable, than the former; because of ancestors, there seems no hint, at all, either before, or after; of strangers, there does. Howbeit, some refer, both the foregoing branch, and this, with somewhat that follows, to a particular act of Ahaz, who seeing at Damascus, an altar erected to the honor of some, either Syrian, or Assyrian, idol, far greater than that of the true God, at Jerusalem, sent a pattern of it to Uriah, the high priest, to have such another made for him, 2 King. 16.10,15. 2 Chron. 28.23. and they render the text, *thou hast enlarged thy bed, and hast cut it out for thyself; taking a pattern from them*: and some such thing may be hinted; but the text seems much more large.

*{thou lovest their bed where thou sawest it*} This some also refer to the altar, that Ahaz saw at Damascus, and was so much taken with it, 2 King. 16.10. of whom, some also render the words, *thou hast cut out for thyself from them, whom thou lovest, their bed, in the place, which thou hast provided for it*: and the defects, both of the relative, as ver. 3. and of the pronoun *it*, as Chap. 46.11. are very frequent: but the pauses will hardly admit this construction; Heb. *thou lovest their bed, in the place thou sawest*; that is, the company of them, as Num. 31.17. Judg. 21.12. See Jer. 2.25. wherever you saw them: and some of the Jewish doctors observe it, as a transgression of that inhibition, Deut. 12.13. but that here, is far beneath the guilt of the crime: it rather, so read, imports their proneness to this spiritual inordinate lust, wherewith, upon any the least occasion, in any place, at any time given, she was as a common strumpet delighting in such filthiness, presently inflamed, Ezek. 23.14,16. a defect of the particle, *in*, as Chap. 44.12. & 48.4. and of the relative, as before; Or, *thou lovest their bed; thou preparedst*, or, *providedst, room*; to wit, for them, to entertain them in: for the verb signifies, not *to see* only, but *to prepare*, or, *provide*, also; as Exod. 18.21. and so the word also parallel to it, Gen. 22.8. and the noun is frequently used for *room*, or *place*: as Deut. 23.12. Chap. 56.6. and in the plural masculine, for *spaces*, or *ranges*, 2 Chr. 23.15. Chap. 22.18. & 33.21. and this I conceive to be the genuine sense of the word: for that which some say here, of *a monument*; as if the word were so taken, 2 Sam. 18.18. to omit, that it may there also be rendered, as our version also has it, as well *Absoloms place*, as *Absoloms monument*, that notion seems not to suit so well here. Howbeit, because the word properly signifies *an hand*; and the old Latin renders it, *with an open hand*; as if the latter word were not a verb, but a noun, some Popish writers would have it to mean, *with an open hand*; that is, not covertly, but openly; without shame, or *with the hand* beckoning to, and inviting company, and customers to her: as Chap. 13.2. and 65.2. Prov. 1.24. or, *with open hand*, liberally, hiring such, and sparing no cost to satisfy her filthy lust, ver. 9. Ezek. 23.31–34. but one of their own coat, does ingenuously acknowledge, that no such noun, as they here dream of, is at all found in Scripture: who would therefore, expound it of the workman's *hand*; put, as he supposes, for his work or workmanship; as we say *a man's hand*, for, his handwriting; the efficient, for the effect: drawing in hither, that of *Absoloms pillar*, and applying it to *Ahaz his altar*; of both which before. Others, of the adulterer's *hand*, in an obscene notion, not fit to be expressed. But thus men out of a preposterous affection, perversely employ and strain their wits, to support and bear out a vicious version.

**V. 9.** *{And thou wentest to the King with ointment, and didst increase thy perfumes*} Another crime charged upon this state is, the sending ambassadors to foreign nations with presents, and in most base manner, submitting and bowing down, to them, 2 King. 16.7,8. Chap. 10.4. either to crave aid and assistance from them, 2 King. 16.8,9. Chap. 30.1,6. & 31.1. Jer. 2.18,36. Ezek. 17.15. Hos. 5.13. & 12.1. or to curry grace, and find favor with them, 2 King. 18.14,15. Chap. 10.4. and 33.7. or to communicate with them, in their idolatries. 2 King. 16.7,8. Ezek. 16.26,28,33,33. and 23.16,40.

*{And thou wentest*} Or, *Thou hast gone also* v. 8. *gone*, either in person yourself, as Ahaz, 1 King. 16.10. or, by your messengers, as the Centurion is said *to have come unto Christ*, Mat. 8.5. compared with Luk. 7.3,4,6. Christ himself to the old world, 1 Pet. 3.19. with 2 Pet. 2.5. and to Ephesus, Eph. 2.17. so the word is supposed to be used, Cant. 4.8. or, *hast respected*, or *observed*, as our margin renders it: and so one of the Jewish commenters, *thou hast sending beheld*. So it should be a defective, or complexive form of speech, as some of ours make it, reading the text thus; *Thou lookest about to the King*, that is, *thou lookest about for aid*, (as Psal. 142.4.) and *sendest to the King*; and such forms are usual. See Chap. 38.17,21. but here seems no need thereof here. The word indeed signifies, most usually, *to view*, or *behold*, Job 20.9. & 33.14, 27. & 35.5,13. but sometime also, *to present*, or *to tender a present*; as appears by the noun thence deduced, used for *a present*, 1 Sam. 9.7. that which I conceive to be the genuine sense of it in this place, *thou hast presented the King with ointment*. The old Latin renders it, *thou hast decked thyself for the King, with ointments, and perfumes*; as harlots use to do, when they are to entertain their companions, Ezek. 23.40. Prov. 7.17. but for this use of this word, I find no ground.

*{to the King*} For, *Molech*, Lev. 20.2. say some; because the word has the notion of a king in it: whence the variety of reading, Jer. 49.1. Zeph. 1.5. Others, by the *King*, understand here, the King of Assyria, to whom Ahaz, both sent, and went, 2 King. 16.8–10. Others, the King of Egypt, whom, divers of them, at divers times, had craved help from, against the Assyrian, and Chaldean, 2 King. 17.4. Chap. 30.1. & 31.1. Jer. 37.5,7. Ezek. 29.16. and others again, of the Babylonians, or Chaldeans, Jer. 51.59. but the word seems to be taken collectively; not of any one particular, either king, or kingdom; but of seeking indefinitely, sometime to one, sometime to another, Jer. 2.36. Hos. 7.11.

*{with ointment*} Heb. *with oil*, as Psal. 133.2. & 141.5. Eccl. 7.1. Amos 6.6. of precious ointment wherewith that land seemed to be stored, see Chap. 39.2. among which, their balsam, peculiar to that country, seems to have been a principal. See Gen. 43.11. Jer. 8.22. & 46.11. Ezek. 27.17. and of this, especially, many understand it here.

*{and didst increase thy perfumes*} Or, *hast multiplied thy confections*; for the word is more general, and comprehends as well *ointments*, as *perfumes*, Exod. 30.25,35. whence the word that signifies, *a confectioner*; so rendered, 1 Sam. 8.13. See also, Eccl. 10.1. Job 41.31. that is, either you have used abundance of them, to prepare, and fit yourself for them; (so, *to multiply washing*, for, to wash abundantly, Ps. 51.2. & *to multiply soap*, for, to use abundance of soap, Jer. 2.22.) or sent abundance thereof to them, to woo, and win them to you. Which latter seems the more likely. See Jer. 2.33. and 4.30. Hosh. 12.1.

*{and didst debase thyself, even unto hell*} Heb. *make low*, or *lay low*: but used here, in a reciprocal, though not form, yet notion; as Psal. 113.6. Jer. 13.18. you have laid yourself low, or debased yourself, as one that bows himself down to the ground, or to the lowest ground, as if you would go even into the ground, or the grave. See chap. 51.21. an allusion, as some think to such vile and base strumpets, who, among the Greeks, had their name, from prostituting themselves on the ground; yea, under the ground, in cellars, and vaults, and in tombs, and monuments, sometimes. I conceive rather, from such, as in a most submiss, and servile manner, cast themselves at the feet of those; whom they sue, and seek to, for aught; as if they would creep into the very ground. See Chap. 10.4. for I suppose they swerve from the prophet's intent, who conceive the meaning to be, that they had, by these their abominable courses, brought themselves to a very low condition, by such like forms of speech sometime expressed, Psal. 7.5. & 63.9. & 88.3,4,6. Chap. 25.12. & 26.5,6. and 47.1. that which yet is true, Chap. 29.4. and she was forewarned of, Jer. 2.25. But this seems to look another way.

**V. 10.** *{Thou art wearied in the greatness of thy ways*} You have even tired yourself out, with the length of your journeys, sending to and fro, so far, abroad. See Jer. 2.38. Ezek. 33.40. Howbeit, some take it, as spoken in reference to their insatiable idolatrous desires; as therein resembling the way, and courses of base harlots, Prov. 30.19. But that place does not parallel so fitly with this.

*{yet saidst thou not There is not hope*} Though you saw that all your toiling, and tiring out yourself was in vain, it was all but lost labor; yet you would not give over, but go on still desperately, in that toilsome and chargeable course. Heb. *it is desperate*. See Jer. 2.25. & 18.12. the discretive is not unfitly supplied; as Chap. 41.11. & 49.4.

*{thou hast found the life of thine hand*} You still imagine, that by these courses you shall find at length, or have already found, and attained that, which so much you desired, sufficient means, and aids to support you, and to strengthen your hand. See Hos. 12.8. the *life of the hand*, for, the *strength* of it, say some; others, the *life of the hand*, for, life, and means of life, and support, by the industry of the hand acquired: and either of these will suit well with the sense above delivered: for they seem to rove too far out of the way, that would have the meaning to be, that either their pains and toil, in seeking abroad so, or their idol-worship, were as pleasant and delightful to them, as their *life*; (of which kind of expression, see Psal. 30.5. & 63.3.) or, than food, or meat, whereby, life is sustained. Of which form, see, Job 23.12. Joh. 4.34. & those yet further, who expound it, *thou gettest thy living by thine hand*, that is, you maintain yourself (as common harlots use to do, thereof in Latin so termed) by your filthy earnings; for neither does the prophet seem to be in that argument here: and the contrary rather is implied, both in the foregoing branch; as also Ezek. 16.31–34. Howbeit, because the word here rendered *life*, as it properly signifies, and is most commonly used, does also signify *a troop*, or *company*, consisting of living creatures, men, or beasts, 2 Sam. 23.11. Job 30.39. Psal. 68.30. some late writers here render it, *thou hast found a troop of thine hand*; that is, say they, forces that will be ready at hand to assist you upon all occasions. Nor might this interpretation seem altogether improbable, (see ver. 13.) but that it is by some questioned, whether that word do in any place at all so signify; and I go rather, therefore, with what was before propounded.

*{therefore thou wast not grieved*} Therefore your pains seemed no pains, but a pleasure, rather, to you; because by such means you did hope, and made full account to accomplish your ends, and what you desired, (as Gen. 29.20. with 31.40.) and seemed sometime so to do, 2 King. 16.7,8,9. though it proved otherwise afterward, in the end, 2 Chron. 28.20,21. Chap. 7.17. & 8.7,8. or, as some render it, *thou wast not wearied*, or *tired*; as the other word before in the front of the verse; as if he had said, though you have toiled, and tired yourself, yet you would not be weary, would not give over: the word properly signifies *sick*, or *weakened*; as Chap. 33.24. it may well be rendered, either thus, or the former way, as sometime also it is, Prov. 23.35. Jer. 5.3. The old Latin renders it, *therefore thou hast not prayed*; that is, say they that follow it, you have not sought by prayer to me, because you thought that you had no need of my help, you had aid sufficient from others; but the verb is never found so to signify in the form here used.

**V. 11.** *{And of whom hast thou been afraid, or feared,*} Some suppose these words to be taken, as an aggravation of her sin, by her impudency in it, that she neither feared, or regarded God, or man, stood in no awe, nor had any shame of either; as Luk. 18.4. See ver. 11. Others, as a preoccupation, & meeting with such pretended excuses, for her seeking to foreign forces for assistance; to wit, out of the fear that she conceived of such powerful adversaries, as were combined together against her, Chap. 7.2: implying, that no such fear of man ought to have prevailed so much with her, as to make her to break with, and to forget God, who could, and would, have secured her against all such fears, had she relied upon, and continued loyal to him, Chap. 7.7,9. This may seem not improbable. Howbeit, I conceive the purpose of the prophet, in these words, to be somewhat other, to wit, to tax her for want of the fear of God simply, as the main ground of her secure, and pertinacious obstinacy, both in this, and other her sinful courses; that which in the close of the verse, is in plain terms expressed.

*{of whom hast thou been afraid, or feared*} The former word signifies *a careful*, or *solicitous fear*, 1 Sam. 9.5. & 10.2. Jer. 17.8. and 38.19. the latter, any fear in general: the copulative is here used, and may be retained; as Chap. 8.12,13. and then it aggravates: but if taken for the discretive, as oft it is (See Chap. 44.10. & 45.10.) then it diminishes: the words may be rendered according to the latter; *Whom didst thou dread, or fear?* that is, whom had you any dread, or fear, at all, of? Or, which I conceive to be the fitter; *whom shouldest thou have dreaded, and feared?* Whom ought you to have been afraid of, as one that would certainly be avenged on you, for your wicked and cross carriages, according to what he had long before threatened? Lev. 26.14–23,24. this form is oft used in such a notion of duty; as chap. 26.9. Jer. 2.8. and elsewhere.

*{that thou hast lied,*} Or, rather, *when*, (as Gen. 4.12. Psal. 75.2.) *thou liest*, that is, deal disloyally, or unfaithfully, with me: as Josh. 7.11. Psal. 89.44,45. Chap. 59.13. whose wrath, and indignation should you have feared, when you dealt so wickedly and unfaithfully with me? Mal. 3.5.

*{and hast not remembered me*} Or, *but* (as ver. 3.) *thou didst not think upon me*; to carry yourself towards me, according to your duty, Eccl. 12.1. Ps. 106.7. for they seem to go aside from the drift of the text, who expound it of flattering the King of Assyria, 2 King. 16.7.

*{nor laid it to thine heart:*} Heb. *thou didst not lay*, or *put it upon thine heart*; as ver. 1. you did not consider, what the issue of these things would be, Chap. 47.7. A learned late writer would have it run thus; *whom wast thou afraid of, or didst thou fear, that thou shouldst lie?* to wit, in denying your sins, when charged with them by my prophets: sure it is not out of fear of me; for *thou dost not think of me, or mind me at all*. But this I shall refer to the judgment of others.

*{have not I held my peace even of old, and thou fearest me not?*} Or, *is it not*, because *I have held my peace*, or *been silent*, and that for a long time, (Heb. *from antiquity*, as Chap. 42.14.) *that* (as Chap. 46.5.) *thou fearest me not?* See the like syntax, Jer. 7.19. My lenity and forbearance of you hitherto, for a long time together, makes you, not to stand in awe of me, but to proceed obstinately in your wicked courses, and go on from evil to worse, Eccl. 8.11. Psal. 36.1,2. and 50.21,22. and 55.19. Chap. 26.10. Jer. 48.11.

**V. 12.** *{I will declare thy righteousness, and thy works;*} I will hold my peace or forbear no longer (Jer. 44.16.) I will declare and lay open, your lewd and wicked courses, and convince you of them; not by a verbal reproof, but by a real rebuke, by taking vengeance on you for them. So Psal. 5.21. Chap. 42.14.

*{thy righteousness*} Spoken, either according to their own estimation, who deemed their own ways & courses, to be all right and just, Prov. 16.2. & 21.2. & 30.12. Or, would still have them, at least, reputed such, Jer. 2.26. Prov. 30.20. Or, it is spoken, rather, ironically, *thy righteousness*, that is, your wickedness, your naughtiness. See the like manner of speech, Gen. 3.22. and the words *righteous*, and *righteousness*, used; where in the parties spoken of, nothing less, is presumed, or intended, Chap. 64.6. Mic. 7.4.

*{for they shall not profit thee.*} Heb. *and they shall not profit thee*; which need not be altered. Your courses, that you trust to, shall do you no good, shall stand you in no stead, but shall rather do you mischief, and prove your bane, in the end. So Prov. 10.2. with 21.6,7. & 11.3,4,5,6. See 2 Chr. 28.20. ch. 28.15,17,18. & 30.2,3,5. & 31.2,3. & 36.6. Ezek. 29.6,7. The forementioned writer reads the words, by way of interrogation, *should I declare thy righteousness, and lay open thy works*, your wicked ways? it would be to no end, *they would do thee no good*: it would not prevail with you, or avail aught for the bettering of you: But this seems not so natural.

**V. 13.** *{When thou criest, let thy companies deliver thee*} When you cry unto me for help, amid your distresses, I will return you no answer, afford you no help; but turn you over to those, and send you to them, whom, forsaking me, you have relied upon, and trusted unto; *thy troops*, (Heb. *thy gathered ones*; as Ezek. 22.20.) either, of strangers, ver. 9,10. or, of strange gods, Chap. 65.11. See Deut. 32.37,38. Judg. 10.13,14. Jer. 2.28. and 11.12.

*{but the wind shall carry them all away*} Heb. *and*, as ver. 3. a puff of wind shall blow them all away, Chap. 40.24. & 64.6. Dan. 2.35. Hos. 4.19.

*{vanity shall take them*} Or, *shall take them away*; as Hos. 11.13. the same, in effect, with the former: they shall all come to nought, Chap. 31.3. a defect of the pronoun to be supplied from the former branch; as, Chap. 13.8,15.

*{But he that putteth his trust in me, shall possess the land, and shall inherit mine holy mountain.*} A word of consolation, subjoined for the stay and support of the faithful, to assure them yet of protection and deliverance, in these calamitous times, Jer. 15.19,21. & 39.17,18. & 45.5. Ezek. 11.16. and of return to possess their land again, and to enjoy God's ordinances in his temple, Chap. 10.21. and 30.18,19.

*{putteth his trust in me*} Makes me his refuge, or place of retreat, (for so the word properly signifies, Psal. 104.19. Chap. 4.6. & 25.4.) and looks not after other vain shelters and succors, Psal. 2.12. & 40.4. & 46.1. See Chap. 28.15,16,17.

*{possess the land*} Psal. 37.3,11. or, *inherit the land*; returning again to their former inheritances, Jer. 3.18. & 12.15. there is in the word, an allusion to the first distribution of the land, by lot, Num. 34.2,13.

*{inherit mine holy mountain*} Heb. *possess my mountain of holiness*; as Psal. 15.1. Chap. 11.9. enjoy my sacred ordinances there. See Chap. 56.5,7.

**V. 14.** *{And he shall say*} Or, *And it shall be said*: for the verb is used here indefinitely; as Chap. 59.19. Mal. 1.4. Proclamation shall be made, to remove all impediments that might hinder God's people, in their passage, from the places of their captivity unto their own country. See Chap. 40.3.

*{Cast ye up, cast ye up;*} Or, *Make causeys*: for their safer and more convenient passage. See Chap. 35.8. & 62.10. Prov. 15.19.

*{prepare the way*} Make plain the surface of it, by sweeping away, and removing out of it, whatsoever might make it uneasy, or unsafe. So Mal. 3.1. See the use of the word, Gen. 24.31. Lev. 14.36. Psal. 80.9. compared with Chap. 5.2.

*{take up the stumbling-block out of the way of my people.*} Heb. *lift up*, or *take off*, or *take away*; as the word is used, Lev. 6.10,15. Dan. 8.11. the *stumbling*, either block, or stone; as Chap. 8.15. and this here more properly: the word is general, and imports anything, that man, or child, may trip, or stumble at, and be endangered thereby to fall. See Lev. 19.14. Psal. 91.11,12.

**V. 15.** *{For thus saith the high, and the lofty God,*} Exceeding high; as Chap. 52.13. whom heaven, even the highest heaven is not able to hold, 1 King. 8.27. but is infinitely higher, than the highest of any creature, Psal. 83.18. & 113.4. Eccl. 5.8. far higher than the highest created heavens, Psal. 113.4. Eph. 4.10. and is said, therefore *to stoop*, in taking notice of the things, as well *in heaven*, as *on earth*, Psal. 113.5,6.

*{that inhabiteth eternity,*} As 1 Tim. 6.16. *who alone hath immortality*, who alone is truly eternal, without beginning, or ending, Psal. 90.2. not immortal only, but immutable, Mal. 3.6. Jam. 1.17. or as some, *that inhabiteth*, or *abideth for ever*: but the former seems more emphatical; and they seem to disjoint the text, who not regarding the points of distinction, render the words; *Thus saith the high one, who the lofty place inhabiteth perpetually*.

*{whose name is holy;*} Heb. *and holy is his name*; as Luk. 1.49. the pronoun demonstrative, with the conjunction copulative, put for the relative: So Judg. 13.2. Ruth 2.1. *his name*, for himself, Psal. 99.3,9. who is not *holy* only, but *alone holy*; as *alone wise*, 1 Tim. 1.17. and *alone good*, Mat. 19.17. *so holy, as none*, but he, 1 Sam. 2.2. so, that those, who are in part holy, by participation from him, are not at all holy, if they come once in comparison with him, Job 9.2. & 15.14,15. Some join this, and the former together, thus reading the words, *inhabiting eternity, and holy is his name*; or, *whose name is inhabitant of eternity, and holy*: so it should be only the demonstrative for the relative; as Chap. 55.15. And true it is, that divers attributes are sometimes joined together, to make up one complexed name; as ch. 9.6. But of that here, there is no necessity; and the text so read, runs nothing so smoothly, as it does the other way.

*{I dwell in the high and holy place;*} In heaven, Chap. 32.15. & 66.1. Psal. 11.4. & 113.5. & 115.3. where is nothing but holiness, 2 Pet. 3.13. Rev. 21.27. whereof also the Holy of Holies in the temple, his palace on earth was a type, Exod. 26.34. Psal. 78.69. Heb. 9.8,12,24. Heb. *I will*, or, *shall inhabit high and holy*: the future, for the present; as Chap. 53.1,7. the word, the same that before, save that the participle there, the verb here: a defect of the subject, or substantive; as Chap. 26.5. & 33.5. nor see I any good ground, why some late interpreters, of special note, should rent this branch off from God's speech, and annex it to his style, rendering the words, *who dwell in the high and holy*; omitting the pronoun, which is here emphatical, and expressed therefore in the text: as also ver. 12. Chap. 43.12. & 45.7,12,13. Howbeit, had they thus rendered it, as a part of God's speech; *I that inhabit*, or *dwell in an high and holy place*, do *dwell also with him*, &c. I should not dissent from them; the suppression of the relative being very frequent. (See v. 3.8.) the supply from the former branch nothing unusual; as Gen. 1.16. and God's dwelling, in, or with the persons here described, in this speech of his, being principally intended.

*{with him also,*} To wit, do I dwell: or, *him also*, do I inhabit: for it may be as well the bare sign of a noun under regiment, as the particle of concomitancy. I dwell, or inhabit both with him, and in him, Joh. 14.17,23. Rom. 8.10,11. 2 Cor. 6.16. & 13.5. Eph. 3.17. Heb. *and him*, or *with him*; as ver. 8.

*{that is, of a contrite and humble spirit*} Heb. *a contrite, and low of spirit*; or, any one of *a contrite, and lowly spirit*. See Ch. 66.15.

*{contrite*} So, *the Lord is near unto all the broken of heart, he will save the contrite of spirit*, Psal. 34.18. that is such as be of a broken heart, and of a contrite spirit; and, *the sacrifices of God are a broken heart; a broken and contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise*, Psal. 51.17. See of the word, on Chap. 53.5,10. By it here, is expressed an inward contrition of heart, and breaking of spirit, softened and humbled by apprehension of wrath, joined with a deep sense of godly grief, sincere repentance, and serious remorse for sin, as sin, as offensive, displeasing, and grievous to God, 2 King. 22.19. 2 Chron. 32.26. & 33.12. Ezek. 6.9. Act. 2.37,38. 2 Cor. 7.10.

*{humble spirit*} One demiss, submiss, low, lowly of spirit. So, Prov. 16.19. and 29.23. In the soul of such an one, God will take up his lodging, in such he desires, and delights to dwell; as in the highest heavens, so in the lowest hearts: the metaphor is taken from the plain country, or the vale, that lies lower than the hills, Josh. 10.40. & 11.2,16. Jer. 17.26. & 32.44. & 33.13.

*{to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones*} Heb. *to quicken*, or *make to live, the spirit of humble ones, and the heart of contrite ones*: *to quicken*, or *make to live*, for *to keep in life*, (as Exod. 1.17. Psal. 22.29. Chap. 38.16.) when ready to faint, and go away, Chap. 40.29. or, to comfort, relieve, refresh, and restore, Psal. 71.20. & 80.18. & 85.6. and 119.25,40,50,88,93,107,159. Mat. 11.28. *heart*, and *spirit*, all one, as before.

**V. 16.** *{For I will not contend for ever, neither will I be always wroth:*} This resolution with God, not to contend for ever, but to give over striving with man, is sometime in wrath; when God, after exercise of his patience, and forbearance, for some space of time, having made trial of divers courses, to reclaim sinners; and finding that nothing will prevail, resolves now to strive no longer with them, but to give them over, and leave them to themselves, as persons incorrigible, and desperately obdurate: as the physician does the patient, that will not be ruled by him, or, whose disease he deems incurable. So Gen. 6.3. Ch. 1.5. sometime, in mercy, when seeing his people, now brought very low, and brought down on their knees; yea, though sometime, not so sincerely, or not so thoroughly, especially where the heart is yet upright, he stays his hand, and either restrains, and refrains his wrath, and further prosecution of any harsh and rigorous course, for the present, or is wholly reconciled again to them. See 1 King. 21.27,29. 2 King. 14.26,27. Psal. 78.34–38. & 85.3. So here: and so Psal. 103.9. *He will not always chide, nor retain wrath for ever*. See also Lam. 3.31,32.

*{for the spirit should fail before me, and the souls which I have made.*} The verb here used signifies sometime, *to cover*, or, *to be covered*, Psal. 65.13. & 73.6. sometime, (especially where applied, as here, to the soul, or spirit) *to be overwhelmed*, or, *to faint*; as one that is muffled and stifled, Psal. 61.2. & 77.3. and 102. title, & 107.5. & 142.3. & 143.4. Lam. 2.11,12,19. Jon. 2.7. Man's spirit would faint, being overspread, or wrapped up in, and overwhelmed with terror and trouble, and the souls, that I made, would fail. The consideration of man's infirmity and weakness, unable to hold out, when God proceeds in wrath against him, does many times move him, in way of commiseration, to stay his hand, and restrain his wrath, Psal. 78.38,39. especially, in dealing with his people, his weak and tenderhearted ones; whom he has a special care of, Chap. 40.11. ver. 15. that they may not wholly be destroyed, or utterly disheartened and discouraged, Job 37.23. Psal. 103.10–14. Chap. 27.8. & 42.3. and 48.9,10. and the saints plead it themselves unto him, Psal. 39.10,11. & 89.47,48. Heb. *spirit*, or *wind*; and *breaths*, or *blasts*; (not amiss rendered *souls*) Gen. 7.15. Psal. 150.6. Prov. 20.27. (words used the rather to express the vanity, and imbecility, of man's constitution and condition. See Chap. 2.22.) are here, one, and the same; as also, Job 27.3. Chap. 42.5. there is in the latter branch a defect of the relative; as ver. 3.8. and of the verb to be supplied from the former branch; as ver. 15. *the souls* would faint away, *which I have made*, Gen. 2.7. Eccl. 12.7. Chap. 42.5. and have a regard to, as mine own work, in mine own people, especially, Psal. 138.8. 1 Pet. 4.19. And this I conceive to be the genuine sense of the place: howsoever divers interpreters run other ways; some rendering, *A spirit*, or *breath, shall go forth from before me, and I will make blasts*, or *gales*. So the old Latin, which many follow, expounding it, some, as of a gentle breath, or blast, that should revive and refresh them, as Psal. 104.30. others as of a prosperous gale of wind at sea, that should carry them to their own country again: applying that unto it, Psal. 143.10. others, *A spirit from my face* (that, is proceeding from me) shall *insinuate itself into you; and I will cause you to breathe*: as he said before, to revive, and refresh them, Ezek. 37.9,10,14. Others, again, *My spirit shall slacken*, or *allay; and the blasts that I made* before. And some again, (taking it a clean contrary way) *My spirit shall overwhelm, and destroy the breathing souls that I made*; as Gen. 6.7,17. But these all strain the text overmuch: Some of them force it against its own sense and drift. A late learned writer would have it rendered from the use of the verb, in the Syriack and Arabick tongues, *The spirit would return from before me*: but how that should fitly suit here, neither he shows, nor do I see.

**V. 17.** *{For the iniquity of his covetousness I was wroth.*} Or, *For his iniquity of gain*; that is, for his unjust lucre and gain, by injurious and wrongful courses, acquired, Mic. 6.9. Luk. 16.9,11. For they seem to be overcurious, who suppose the words, thus conceived, to imply, that it is not the outward act of fraud, oppression, or the like, either, so much or alone, that God regards, as the inward affection, and disposition of the heart: as also those, that would have the word rendered, *covetousness*, to be put here, for all manner of *evil concupiscence*, in general, Rom. 7.8. Col. 3.5. because it is said to be *the root of all evil*, 1 Tim. 6.10. though it be not unlikely, that this vice be the rather mentioned, because many other spring from it, Prov. 1.16–19. Now some conceive it to be spoken, with relation to those watchmen, spoken of, Chap. 56.11. and this vice there taxed in them. But this evil seems to have been more general rife in all sorts among them, Jer. 6.13. & 8.11. and even those also, to have been overmuch tainted with it, who yet were not abandoned to those gross practices of idolatry, nor did run a madding after idols, as those described before, ver. 3–10.

*{and smote him*} See Chap. 1.10. & 60.10.

*{I hid me and was wroth*} Or, *being wroth, I hid me*; or *in my wrath I hid me*; as *in my wrath I smote thee*, Chap. 60.10. for he is wroth first, and then smites, and hides; though in open view, yet hidingly, because by the hand of another, Chap. 10.5. Jer. 1.14,15. he smites, and then hides himself; as one, that in displeasure, having left one to the evil, and harsh usage of some other, withdraws himself out of the way, and having shut himself up in his closet, will not be seen, or spoken with. 2 Sam. 14.24,32. Psal. 10.1. 27.7,9. Heb. *hiding, I hid*, as it is more fully expressed, Deut. 31.18. See of such defective forms, on Chap. 59.13. *I hid myself*, or *my face*; a defect of the noun, and affix, *my face*, so oft expressed, Deut. 31.18. & 32.20. Psal. 13.1. & 22.24. and 51.9. Chap. 8.18. & 54.8. & 59.2. & 64.7. Ezek. 39.23,24,29. or, *myself*; the active form put for the reciprocal, Chap. 45.15. as the passive form is frequently used, 1 Sam. 20.19. 1 King. 17.3. Psal. 55.13. Chap. 28.15. Jer. 36.19.

*{and he went on frowardly, in the way of his own heart*} Or, *yet* (as Chap. 53.4,10.) *he went on*, or, *walked on, perversely*, (Heb. *turning away*: as Jer. 3.14,22.) *in the way of his heart*. See Chap. 53.6. Jer. 18.14. & 23.17. though I manifested my displeasure, by giving them up to their enemies, Chap. 47.6. and withdrawing myself, for some space of time, from them, Lam. 3.43,44. yet they walked on crossly in their own crooked courses, and would not be reclaimed, Jer. 5.3. & 8.5,6. or, it may be read, as rendering a reason, why God did so both smite them, and having smitten them, withdraw himself also from them, to wit, *because* (so the particle is not seldom used, Chap. 52.15. & 53.2. & 64.4,5.) they persisted in their own cross, and rebellious courses, refusing to repent, and return from them. See Levit. 26.23,24. Zach. 7.11,12. and this I conceive to be the proper sense of the place.

**V. 18.** *{I have seen his ways, and will heal him*} That is, say some of the Jewish commenters, I see his repentance, and I will therefore restore him. But the word, *ways*, seems rather to have reference, to the *way of his own heart*, or *mind*, mentioned before, ver. 17. and that way most go; and so the text would be rendered, *I see his ways, but* as Ch. 51.23. *I will heal him*; or, *Though I see his ways, yet I will heal him*. A defect of the former particle, as Ch. 30.20. the latter in the same notion, as chap. 53.10. Though I see what his ways and courses are, how untowardly and obstinately, they have carried themselves: yet for mine own name's sake, I will not wholly withdraw, or for ever withhold my mercy from them, but will restore them again, Ch. 43.22,25. & 48.8–11. Ezek. 36.17–23,32. So is the word of *healing*, commonly used. See chap. 19.22. & 30.26. & 58.8. Jer. 3.22. & 17.14. & 30.17. & 33.6. Lam. 2.13. Hos. 5.13. & 6.1. & 7.1. & 11.3. & 14.5. Psal. 60.2.

*{I will lead him also*} Heb. *and I will lead him*. I will conduct him in safety to his own country, Chap. 52.12. & 58.11. See Chap. 14.1,2. & 40.11. & 52.12. Jer. 3.14. & 32.37. Some of the Rabbines expound it, *I will give rest to him*, or *cause him to rest*; as Chap. 14.3. & 63.14. but the roots are divers.

*{and restore comforts unto him, and to his mourners*} I will restore abundance of comfort to them, in lieu of those manifold sorrows, and discomforts, that they had during their captivity, endured. See Chap. 14.1. & 66.13. *comforts*, for, abundance of comforts: as Chap. 66.11.

*{to his mourners*} The persons, whom God principally respects, and has a more special eye unto, in the favors and mercies here promised, the residue partaking therein only with them, and for them; those *that mourn in Sion*, Chap. 61.2,3. or, *for Sion*, Chap. 66.10. that mourn for the desolations of her, for God's judgments upon her, and for, both their own sins, and the sins of others, as the procuring causes thereof, Ezr. 9.6. Ezek. 6.9. & 7.16. & 9.4. Zach. 12.10. Mat. 5.4.

**V. 19.** *{I create the fruit of the lips; peace, peace, to him that is afar off, and to him that is near, saith the Lord:*} Some carry on these words all in one tenor, *I create*, or, *make the fruit of the lips, to be peace, peace*, &c. expounding the text, either of God's own lips, that is, his word, which he turns into act, by giving his the peace formerly promised them, Psal. 85.8. Chap. 55.9. or, of the lips of his ministers, and messengers, that bring the glad tidings of peace, and reconcilement with God to his people: God making their words to be, not matter of peace only, but means of peace, between them, and him, Chap. 40.1. & 52.7. Rom. 5.1. 1 Cor. 5.19,20. Eph. 2.14,17. or, of the people of God themselves, who, whereas formerly, they had nothing, but to talk of war, in their mouths, should now have occasion given them, to speak of nothing but peace. A learned writer of good note, supposes, that it may be read, and rendered, *I create as the fruit of the banks, peace, peace*; that is, peace in great plenty, like the fruits of such plants, as grow near the river's side: and true it is, the banks of rivers are sometime called their lips: (See on Chap. 19.7.) and that the note of similitude is oft omitted; as Chap. 33.4,11. But to let pass the needless straining of the text, the pauses in the original, expressed also in our version, require the members to be taken asunder, and read apart.

*{I create the fruit of the lips*} Or, as some render it, *I will create*. Heb. *creating*; as Chap. 65.17,18. Of the use of the word, see Chap. 4.5. By *the fruit of the lips*, (to pass by those, who understand *comfort*, and *consolation*, ver. 18.) I conceive, with many other, to be understood the *voice of praise, and thanksgiving*; as we find it to our hands expounded, Hos. 14.2. Heb. 13.15. that, which God promises to give abundant occasion of, by the restitution of them, Chap. 60.18. & 61.3,11. Jer. 30.19.

*{peace, peace*} True, firm, sure, constant, abundant, peace; a large measure of tranquility, plenty, prosperity; for the name of *peace* includes all these, Chap. 48.18. and the gemination of the word imports a large extent of it, 1 Chr. 12.18. See Chap. 26.3. the verb substantive is to be supplied; as Psal. 119.165. *peace, peace*, shall be; or, there shall be *peace, peace*.

*{to him, that is afar off, and to him, that is near*} Heb. *to the far, and to the near one*. The speech runs along in the singular forms, but in a collective sense; because spoken of the main body of a people; to those far and near. As well to him that is abroad in captivity, as to him that abides still at home; or, to those abroad, as well in places more remote, as in places nearer at hand, Deut. 30.3,4. See Chap. 11.11,12. or, *afar off*, and *near*; that is, as well Gentile, as Jew: the one being a people, in time past, near unto God, Psal. 148.14. the other, afar off from him, until called in, by Christ, Act. 2.38,39. Eph. 2.12,13,17. Col. 1.21. See Chap. 56.3. for this, with all the former, though in the first place, relating to the state of that people, and in part fulfilled in them, yet does typically foreshadow the restoration, and enlargement of the church, under the Messiah in the gospel, where the fuller complement of them is found.

*{and I will heal him*} As ver. 8. so the Hebrew, word for word. Howbeit, some render it, *that I may heal them*: as Chap. 41.22. but that seems not so fit here; *peace*, as health; being rather, an effect of healing, than a means of cure: if any change be thought of, I should rather choose to render it, *when I shall heal*, or, *shall have healed him*; as ver. 8. which may well seem to have reference also to a spiritual healing; and may receive strength from what follows, of the exclusion of those from the peace before promised, who are not so healed, ver. 20,21.

**V. 20.** *{But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt*} This, some understand of the wicked enemies of God's people, who envying their peace and welfare, should be restless in seeking, and striving, by all the means that they could, to disturb, and impeach it. See Ezr. 4. & 5.3. Neh. 4. & 6. But the most rather, of the profane, and obstinate wicked ones, among God's people, opposed to the humble and penitent mourners, among them, ver. 15,19. implying, that they should not have any share, either in that inward tranquility, and settlement of mind, nor in that outward peace and prosperity that those other should enjoy; not, that none such at all should be set free from captivity, or return to, and be seated in their own country again; but that little benefit, or comfort, should thereby accrue unto them, their minds being so unsettled, Jam. 1.6. and their consciences so unquiet, Job 15.20. that they should never be able to rest, Job 20.20. or to enjoy any sound, and settled peace, ver. 21. See Chap. 65.20.

*{But*} Heb. *And*: as ver. 3.13.

*{are like*} Or, shall be like. See Chap. 65.13,14.

*{troubled*} Or, *driven*; to wit, with winds, Jam. 3.4. but the word signifies properly, *to drive away*, or, *expel*, Exod. 34.11. it is used in the next branch, for, *to cast out*, or, *cast up*.

*{when it cannot rest*} Or, *because it cannot rest*, Jon. 1.11,13. and no more can they, Job 15.21–24.

*{whose waters cast up mire and dirt*} Heb. *and the waters thereof*, as ver. 15.

*{cast up*} To the shore, when it works.

*{mire*} Or *mud*. The word is nowhere else read; the verb only, Prov. 25.26.

*{and dirt*} This, some expound of the issue of wicked men's practices against God's people; as producing nothing beneficial to themselves, but sorry trash, such as the sea is wont to cast up. Others, of the effect of God's judgments upon them, whereby he would work them to repentance; but causes them only to discover their own filth, wherewith their hearts are full fraught. See Jud. 13. Rev. 16.8–11. But these things seem overcurious, and beside the scope of the place.

**V. 21.** *{There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked.*} Or, *There shall be no peace* to such. See Chap. 48.22.

### CHAPTER 58

**Vers. 1.** *{Cry aloud, spare not;*} This chapter and the next, some join together. In either of them, according to an injunction given him, by God, the prophet lays forth the wicked courses of his people; in this, their hypocrisy especially, pretending much devotion, and assiduity, in holy exercises, chiefly in fasting, and prayer; and charging God with neglect of them, notwithstanding their diligence in these duties; whereby the prophet takes occasion to inform them of the defects in their fasts, and other their devotions, and to instruct them, what manner of service, God requires of them, and expects from them, subjoining many gracious promises of sundry blessings from God, upon their services so, performed.

*{Cry aloud*} Heb. *Cry with the throat*: the throat being an instrument of voice and sound, Psal. 69.3. & 115.7. Or, *Cry with full throat*: as Jer. 12.6. *they cry with full* throat *after thee*: a defect of the adjunct here; as of the subject there. Of which forms of speech, see on Chap. 5.4. thus we use to say, and it might well be so rendered here; *Set up thy throat*. God's speech to the prophet.

*{spare not*} Or, *refrain not*. Howsoever it may be deemed matter of commendation, ordinarily for a man to refrain his tongue, and to be sparing of his speech, Prov. 10.19. & 17.27. yet not when man's duty to God requires it, Psal. 40.9,10. or, when God himself shall enjoin it. Jer. 1.17. & 19.2. & 26.2. Amos 3.8. Act. 4.19–21. & 5.19–21,29. & 20.27. or, *cry as loud as thou canst*. Though intention of voice, or clamor, and loudness of speech, be in some kind, and some cases, neither needful, nor decent, Cha. 42.2. Pro. 7.11. Eccl. 7.8. & 9.17. Eph. 4.31. yet where the matter is serious and weighty, and men willfully deaf, and unwilling to hear, loud crying is necessary, and by God himself here required. So Prov. 8.1–3. & 9.3. Joh. 7.28,37. & 12.44.

*{lift up thy voice like a trumpet*} Make use of your throat instead of a trumpet, not as some fondly, alluding to the manner of managing a trumpet, which a man holds with his hand, and sounds with his mouth; but to make a loud noise, as a trumpet does, and to give people warning of evils approaching, which is one special use of the watchman's trumpet, Jer. 6.1. Ezek. 2.17–21. & 33.2–9. Amos 3.6,8.

*{and show my people their transgressions, and the house of Jacob their sins.*} *My people; and the house of Jacob*; such as one would think should have least need of any, to be so loud cried unto, or so roundly dealt with, yet their wicked courses, and their averseness, requiring it; and though such untoward wretches, owned still by God, as his people. See Chap. 2.5,6. Mich. 6.2,3,5.

**V. 2.** *{Yet they seek me daily, and delight to know my ways;*} As wicked as they are in their practices, yet they make a great show of much devotion, and of sedulity, assiduity, and diligence, in my service. See the like, Chap. 1.12–15. & 29.13. & 48.1,2.

*{seek me daily*} By repairing to my sanctuary, Chap. 1.12. Jer. 7.9. or, to other places, where my people assemble to serve me. Heb. *day day*, that is, day by day; or, day after day: as *morning morning*, Chap. 28.19. So Prov. 8.30,34.

*{delight to know my ways*} Make show as if they so did; contrary to the open, and unveiled impiety of those, who profess, *not to desire the knowledge of his ways*, Job 21.14. as, *they stay themselves upon God*; that is, profess so to do, Chap. 48.2. so here, *they delight to know his ways*; make as though they took great pleasure in hearing aught of them, Ezek. 33.30,31.

*{as a nation that did righteousness*} That walked uprightly, that practiced nothing but what was just, and right, Chap. 56.1. Mic. 6.8. 1 Joh. 3.7,10.

*{and forsook not the ordinance of their God*} Heb. *forsook not the judgment* (that is, the *law*; as Jer. 5.4.) *of their God*: whose people they profess themselves to be; and whose name yet they will bear, Chap. 48.1,2. Jer. 8.7.

*{they ask of me the ordinances of justice*} They come to inquire of me, by my ministers, priests, and prophets, what courses they should take, and what I require of them: as if it were of ignorance only, and for want of information, if they did aught amiss, Jer. 42.2–21. & 43.2–4. & Ezek. 14.1,2. Mal. 2.8.

*{and take delight in approaching to God*} Seem to do so; as before. Howbeit, some turn all these passages another way; expounding the words according to those, ver. 3. of their continual muttering, and murmuring against God, as if it were said, *they demand of me daily*, and desire, *to know what my mind and meaning is*, as if they were a people, that had given me no just cause of offense; *they require more just, and equal courses of me*, (as if I dealt not justly, and equally with them, Ezek. 18.24.) and *desire to approach to God*; not in a kind and familiar manner, or dutiful way, to be better acquainted with me, or to do me, some service; but to debate, and argue the case with me, as one that deals unequally, and injuriously with them, Job 23.3–8. the word is used sometime of an hostile, and malicious *approach*, Psal. 27.2. and 119.150. sometime, of a *judicial approach*, for trial, or hearing, and debating of a cause, Exod. 22.8. Josh. 7.14. Chap. 41.1,5. Mal. 3.5. But I conceive that this exposition, and that use of the word fits not so well with this place.

**V. 3.** *{Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not?*} They complain that they had fasted again, and again, and worn themselves out, by frequent practices of humiliation, and yet God did not regard, or take notice of it, in regard thereof, to relieve them, and free them from such troubles and afflictions, as they were still annoyed and encumbered withal; or, And it is as if he had said, they will expostulate with God, when after some hypocritical performances, and external humiliations, they be not by and by heard, and answered, according to their mind; as if in the most serious, and sincere manner, they had sought him, and served him. See Jer. 3.4,5. Mic. 6.6.

*{have we fasted*} Or, *do we fast*: that which some understand of the yearly set, and solemn fast, on the day of propitiation, Lev. 23.27,29. and this seems to be backed, by that of the Sabbath, ver. 13. For that day was a day of strict rest, Lev. 23.28,30,31. as if their formal fasting on that day, were sufficient to expiate and satisfy for all the sins of the whole year with them. But others rather expound it, of other more frequent, voluntary, and occasional fasts, such as those, upon some exigencies, undertaken before the captivity, Chap. 22.12. Jer. 14.12. & 36.6,9. Or held, and continued by them, during the time of the captivity, Zach. 7.3,5. & 8.19. either public, or private, Dan. 9.3. Zach. 12.12–14.

*{say they,*} A necessary supply; as Chap. 22.13. and 56.12.

*{seest not*} Or, *seest it not*; that is, *regardest it not*; as Psal. 10.11,13,14. a defect of the pronoun *it*, here, as there.

*{wherefore have we afflicted ourselves,*} Or, *do we afflict our souls*, that is, *ourselves*; as Psal. 44.25. & 123.4. to wit, by fasting, Lev. 23.27,29.

*{and thou takest no knowledge?*} Heb. *thou knowest not*: as Jer. 3.13. you take no notice of it, of what we do; a defect of the pronoun, as before.

*{Behold,*} Take notice of the reason, why these your performances are not accepted: You are faulty, and failing much otherwise in such things, as God requires, and regards, as much as, yea, much more, than these formalities, as Chap. 1.15–17. Jer. 14.12.

*{in the day of your fasts ye find pleasure*} According to this version it might be supposed, that upon their fast days they took their pleasure, and solaced themselves as those revelers, Ch. 22.12,13. But there is nothing less here intended, and the contrary appears; both by their profession, ver. 3. and God's concession, ver. 5. Some of those therefore that follow this translation, expound the words, thus rendered, as if it were said; on these very fast days of yours, on which you would seem to be most devout; yea, on that very day of solemn humiliation that you abstain from food, yet you abstain not from evil practices; you follow those courses that you are most taken withal, and are as delightful, as any the daintiest dish to you, 1 Kin. 21.12. Prov. 2.14. & 4.16,17. Jer. 9.3. Ezek. 23.38,39. Mat. 23.14,23. Luk. 18.12. But the words would rather be read, *In the day that ye fast, ye find your own desire*, *pleasure*, or *will*. Heb. *In the day that ye fast*, or *of your fasting*: as, *in the day that ye eat*, or *of your eating*, Gen. 2.17. that is, *when*, or *what time ye fast*; and *ye eat*: so Ruth 4.5. *in the day that thou buyest*, that is, *whensoever*, or, *at what time thou buyest*: nor need the word, *day*, be restrained to that very day, on which they held their fast; but may be taken more largely, as Chap. 3.18. & 22.12. & 26.1. & 27.2. much less to the solemn day of humiliation: For the actions hereafter mentioned, were such, as were not practiced, nor in likelihood would be permitted, or could be executed on that day, being no day for matter of judicature; and for that of Naboth, 1 Kin. 21.9,10. it seems not to have been either enjoined to be done, or put in execution, on the very fast day: but a fast being proclaimed, as if some wrath were feared, and some evil expected, a course was enjoined withal to make some previous inquiry, for the finding out of such delinquents and delinquencies, for which judgment might be feared, that justice being done on those that were found guilty of such crimes, the fast might prove the more effectual. The meaning then I conceive to be, that at those times, whether of that general and solemn annual fast, or other occasional ones, they did not at all break off their sinful *wills, desires, minds, pleasures*, or *purposes*, (for so the word here used, does at large signify, 1 Sam. 18.25. Eccl. 3.1,17. & 8.6. Chap. 53.10.) but persist, and proceed still in a resolution and purpose, to pursue them, howsoever they might not be employed publicly, in the acting of them, on that particular day, on which the fast was held; but suspended the practice of them for the present: not unlike those, of whom another prophet, Amos 8.4,5,8. *find*, for *follow*; because *finding* the end of *following*; as *seeking*, for, *getting*, Eccl. 3.6. and for *finding*, as some, Chap. 65.1. because this the end of that: and a defect of the pronoun; as, *word* for *thine own word*, ver. 13. So, *desire*, for, *your own desire*; as it is more fully there expressed: and *their own will*, for, *the desires of the flesh*: and, *the wills of the flesh, and thoughts*, or, *minds*: that is, their fleshly desires, and carnal minds and wills, Eph. 2.3. Some conceive this place to be parallel to that, Zach. 7.5,6. *when ye fasted, in fasting fasted ye*, or, *fasted ye at all to me; to me*, I say? and *when ye did eat and drink, did not ye eat and drink*, not to me, but for yourselves: (the former branch shows, that the latter must be so conceived and supplied) as if he had said, You had no more regard to me, in your fasting, than you had in your eating or feasting: you did both for your own ends. And so here, in your fastings, you intend nothing, nor regard aught, save the compassing of your own ends, and satisfying of your own desires: Then you follow, and find even then when you fast. See somewhat the like also, Hos. 10.1. *Israel is an empty vine: he bringeth forth fruit for himself*.

*{and exact all your labors*} By *labors*, some of the Jewish doctors, whom some of ours also follow, understand, their *wealth* their *gettings*, their *gains*: so called, because by labor and travail usually achieved, Eccl. 4.8. & 5.16–18. alleging for this interpretation, that place, Prov. 5.10. where the word is so used: and accordingly, Psal. 128.2. though another word be there used, *The labor of thine hand thou shalt eat*: and Eccl. 5.19. *to rejoice in one's labor*: that is, that wealth and store, which, by labor, has accrued unto either: And they draw hither the greediness of gain, taxed in them, Chap. 56.11. they might better that, Chap. 57.17. for the former is special; the latter more general. But others, rather, take the word more largely, and understand by it, their *debts*, or *dues*, whether of moneys, or services, so termed, not from the labor and pains taken, in the getting and compassing; but from the *grief* and *pain*, those are put unto, from whom, by rigor, they are *exacted*: Of which term, see on Chap. 53.7. for the word (as also another of the [like] notion, Job 5.6,7. and both the Greek and Latin, answering to either, and our English *labor* too, as when we say; *a woman is in labor*) signifies, as well *pain* and *dolor*, as *labor* and *pains*; whereof Jabetz had his name, 1 Chron. 4.9. Thus the meaning should be, You exact of your servants, servile labor & pains, with extremity, contrary to God's command, Lev. 25.39,40,43,45,53. Or, detain them in servitude, beyond that extent of time, by God prescribed, for an hired servant three years, Deut. 15.18. (See Chap. 16.14.) for one sold outright six years, Exod. 21.2. Deut. 15.12. (See Jer. 34.8–11,14–16.) or to the year of Jubilee, whether came first, Lev. 25.40. as also your debts you require with rigor and cruelty, either where the party is not of ability, or where God requires them to be remitted, Lev. 25.28. Deut. 15.2. See 2 Kin. 4.1. Neh. 5.2–13. And this some the rather suppose to be charged upon them, as a fault more frequent, at their fast time, than at others; because about that time of the year, to wit, at the beginning of the seventh month, called *Tisri*, of the *new wine* then made, their fruits being all gathered in, Lev. 23.24,39. Deut. 16.13. the old year, for civil affairs and accounts, ended, & the new began that month; for such matters, though being reckoned the first, and the new year beginning with it, Exod. 34.22. Now on the tenth day of that month, being the solemn fast, the trumpet of remission and release was to be blown, Lev. 25.9. Some read the words, *That ye may exact all your labors*: And so the particle is oft used; as Chap. 13.2. & 41.22. But it seems here not so seasonable. Others, rather, *While ye exact all your labors*; as 1 Kin. 11.25. *While he reigned over Syria*, (for so it would be there rendered) and, *While Mordecai sat in the King's gate*, Esth. 2.21. See Chap. 36.9. Howsoever we take the words, by their failings in these offices of mercy and charity, and their practices contrary unto either, he shows all their pretended devotion and piety, to be unsound, and unsincere. So Chap. 1.17,18. Mat. 23.23. Jam. 1.27. 1 Joh. 3.17. & 4.20,21. And God seems to argue the matter with them, as if he should say, Do you think to obtain any mercy from me, when you show none to your brethren? that I should set you free from evils, when you refuse to let your brethren go free? That I should remit all to you, when you remit nothing to them? See Jer. 34.17. Mat. 5.7. & 6.14,15. & 18.24–35. Jam. 2.13.

**V. 4.** *{Behold,*} As before, v. 3. which some therefore conjoin with this; but repeated, to add the more vigor and vehemency to it; as if he should say, Do you wonder, if God regard not your fasting, when you fast in this manner? ver. 5.

*{ye fast for strife and debate*} Or, *unto strife and debate*. These words are by interpreters variously expounded. Some would have the meaning to be, that this was the end of their fasting, to expiate their former sinful and injurious courses, that they might return the more freely to them again; as the Papists, in some places, are reported to have a common saying in their mouths; *We must sin, that we may be shriven; and be shriven, that we may sin*. Others, that on the solemn fast day, when they met together, they fell to quarreling one with another, about their debts and mortgages; as if the fast day had, for no other end, been instituted, but to quarrel and contend upon: Or, that on that day, they had much brawling and brabbling with their servants, whom, by the law, they were then to dismiss, and used them with much cruelty. Others, that the fast days, being kept as Sabbaths, or days of rest, from other servile labors, and employments abroad, they were willing to have fast days, that they might have the more leisure to cast up their accounts, and survey their debt books, to prepare matter for actions to be commenced, and pursued against their debtors. Others, that the words here imply not, that they fasted at all, but that about the time thereunto designed, they did practice such things, because at that time there was more special occasion of them, than at other. And so indeed is the word, *the fast*, taken, without special relation to any action of that kind then performed, Act. 27.9. But both the verb here used, not the noun, as there, and the whole drift and current of the context, shows, that the rite of fasting, performed by them, is here specially intended. I conceive, therefore, (supposing that most of the works before recited, could not that day be done, save by minding of them, or occasionally speaking of them, if they observed the solemn fast) that the words would be read, not as our version has them; *Ye fast for strife and debate*, as importing the end for which they fasted; but, *Ye fast unto strife and debate*: as implying the issue and consequent of their fasting. Of which manner of speech, see Chap. 3.8. your fastings end in, and are seconded with, vexatious suits and brawls.

*{and to smite with the fist of wickedness.*} Or, *with a wicked fist*; as, *with wicked hands*, Act. 2.23. the word is used also, Exod. 21.18. and nowhere else in Scripture: Some apply it to the misusing of their servants, Exod. 21.20,21,26,27. Others to the harsh usage of their debtors, not able to pay them, or the laying of violent hands upon them, Mat. 18.28. it may well comprehend either.

*{Ye shall not fast as ye do this day, to make your voice to be heard on high.*} This some understand, as if it were said, alluding to their branglings and brawlings, and clamorous outcries, used in prosecution of persons obnoxious to them, whether servants, or strangers: You are not to fast as you use to do, so quarreling and chiding upon your fast days, that your voice may be heard to the very hills, that they ring again with them: Or, that the cry of your violences goes up unto heaven. See Gen. 18.20,21. Exod. 22.23,27. 2 Chr. 28.9. Chap. 5.7. & 22.1,5. Jon. 1.2. Jam. 5.4. Others, as alluding to their loud cries, that they used commonly in their fasts, and days of humiliation; by some, out of fervor, and intention of spirit, 2 Chr. 14.11. & 32.20. Joel 1.13. Jon. 3.8. But by these here, either for popular applause, to let others know that they fasted, and hear how devoutly and earnestly they did it; as the Pharisees did also with their alms, and their prayers, Mat. 6.2,5,16. Or, as if by their loud cries, they made account to be heard of, and prevail with God; as Baals priests with their idol, 1 Kin. 18.27,28. But the most, and best, understand it, as informing them, that the way they now took, fasting in such manner, as was before related, was not the way to cause God to hear, and grant those things, which, by humble suit and supplication, joined, of course, with their fasts, as being the main end of their fasting, 1 Sam. 7.5,7. 2 Sam. 12.16. 2 Chr. 20.3,6. Ezra 8.21. Mat. 17.21. Act. 13.3. they desire at God's hand to obtain. See ver. 3. As if he had said, Never look to have your fastings accepted, or your suits *heard on high* (that is, in heaven, as Chap. 57.15.) 1 Kin. 8.23. so long as you continue these courses of vexation and oppression. See Chap. 1.15. Prov. 28.13. and this to be the genuine notion of the place, the opposite part, ver. 6. shows. Heb. *Ye shall not fast, as today*, or, *as this day*, &c. which some render, *Ye fast not as these times* are, or, *according to the manner of this time*; to wit, *to cause your voice to be heard on high*. But this reading seems somewhat harsh: and our version is plain and smooth enough, whether we supply aught, or no.

**V. 5.** *{Is it such a fast that I have chosen?*} Or, *As I have chosen*: the relative wanting; as Chap. 57.8,16. Or the demonstrative put for the relative; as Chap. 51.15. the same in effect; but *as* fitter than *that*, because *such* went before; such as I approve, affect, desire, and delight in; as Zach. 7.5. so Psal. 119.30. Chap. 56.4.

*{a day for a man to afflict his soul?*} Or, *for a man to afflict his soul for a day*; as ver. 3. not that God did not require such humiliation on the solemn fast days, Lev. 16.19,21. & 23.27,32. but that it was a fond and frivolous thing to imagine, that it was enough for them, to use such external exercises for a day only, and there an end of all, 1 Tim. 4.8.

*{Is it to bow down the head as a bulrush,*} *To bow down*; as Mic. 6.6. *his head as a bulrush*, that being bruised, does with the weight of itself hang down. See Chap. 19.14. Or, *as a cord*, made of bulrush, Job 41.2.

*{and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him?*} As the manner of those times was, in solemn mournings, usual, 1 Kings 21.27. Esther 4.3. Job 2.8. & 42.6. Chap. 61.3. Jer. 6.26. Matth. 11.21.

*{wilt thou call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the Lord?*} That is, such a fast as God accepts of, as before; *a fast, and a day acceptable*, for, *an acceptable fast day*. See the like, on Chap. 4.5,6. Heb. *a day of goodwill*, or, *well-liking*; as Chap. 49.8. & 61.2.

**V. 6.** *{Is not this the fast, that I have chosen, to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?*} Having showed them what manner of fasts, God did not approve, nor would accept, ver. 4,5. he proceeds now to show what manner of ones they were, that he required, and would accept; to wit, such as were joined with reformation, and amendment of their former injurious and vexatious courses, such as were seconded with a practice of the contrary duties of compassion and mercy: Not that the fast consisted, to speak properly, in them: but that it was to be always accompanied with them, as was Cornelius his, Act. 10.2,4. See the like speech, Jam. 1.27.

*{that I have chosen*} That I like, and am pleased with; as ver. 5. So is the word used, Job 29.25. *If I chose their way*, that is, *If I liked*, or *was pleased*, to come among them, or join with them: And so it may well be rendered, Psal. 25.12. *Who is the man that feareth the Lord? he will instruct him in the way, that he* (to wit, God himself) *liketh*, or, *approveth of*. Heb. *I shall choose it*, or, *like, approve, accept it*, the demonstrative for the relative; as before, verse 5.

*{to loose*} Heb. properly, *to open*. See Chap. 51.14.

*{the bands of wickedness*} Or, *wicked bands*; as, *the fist of wickedness*, ver. 4. The word is found only here, and Ps. 73.4. and it is by some deemed, to consist of a term, that signifies, *to cut*, whence also the *threshing sled*, called by the Latin *tribula*, and from it, our English *tribulation*; and of another, that signifies, *to vex*, or, *grieve*: Of which, see on, ver. 3. so joined in one, because *constrictions*, as some render it, or *straight bands* do both. By it, some understand the combination of those that are in places of judicature, by unjust sentence, and extreme rigor of law, hired to vex and oppress. See Mic. 7.3. Others, the bands, which they held their poor brethren enwrapped in, by unequal, injurious, and usurious contracts, Exod. 22.25. Lev. 25.35,37. Neh. 5.25. See *the bond of iniquity*, in a divers sense, Act. 8.23.

*{to undo the heavy burdens,*} Heb. *burdens of declination*. So the Chaldee renders it: and not unfitly, because it comes of a word that signifies, *to decline, stoop, bow down*, Lev. 25.35. Prov. 25.26. such *bunches*, *bundles*, or *fardels*, (so it is used of lesser ones, Exod. 12.22. of greater, the elements lying as globes, or bundles, are upon, or over another, Amos 9.6. of a troop of men, as made up in a bundle together, 2 Sam. 2.25.) lying so heavy upon a man, that they bend him down, and make him to stoop. See Jer. 1.14. for this latter word also signifies, *a yoke*, so called, because it *presses down, pulls down*, and *holds down*, Jer. 27.2. & 28.10,13. See more afterward. And this may well have reference to the heavy bondage they kept their brethren in. Whereof, see before, on ver. 3.4.

*{and to let the oppressed go free,*} Some restrain this, to such as they kept in prison, and in bonds, for debt; but it seems more large: And the word includes all such, as are made like a bruised, or broken reed, or cane, chap. 36.6. & 42.3. much weakened, crushed, and broken, (as we use to say) in their states and persons, by vexation and oppression. See Deut. 28.33. Hos. 5.11. Amos 4.1. this branch is found inserted with that passage, chap. 61.1. in the Evangelist's recital of it, Luk. 4.18.

*{and that ye break every yoke*} Heb. *and every yoke ye shall break*: a defect of the particle *that*, as Chap. 41.7. and a redundancy of the pronoun *it*: as chap. 8.13. & 45.9. *to break every yoke*, for, to give ease of, or set free from, any grievous course, of vexation, and oppression; as Chap. 9.4. the term here used, is taken sometime; for *a yoke*, as was before hinted. Howbeit, it is deemed primarily, and properly, to signify the *staff*, or *bar*, that runs through the two ends of its bow, to hold them fast, the one to the other: the word being used of the *staves*, shot through the rings, by which the ark was borne on the Levites' shoulders, 1 Ch. 15.15. as also of that, on which the two spies carried the great bunch, or clusters of grapes, between them, for bruising, Num. 13.23. or, as some think, the *bands*, or *cords*, wherewith, either those staves are fastened to the rest of the yoke, or the yoke itself to the neck of the beast. So it is rendered, Ezek. 34.24. *When I have broken the bands of their yoke, and delivered them out of the hands of those, that served themselves on them*: and yet more fully, to suit with the form above mentioned, and the explication thereof, Lev. 26.13. *I brought you out of Egypt, that you might not be*, or, *abide, their bondmen; and brake the bands of your yoke, that ye might go upright*. Now when either the *staff*, or the *bands* of the yoke are broken, the yoke falls off, and the beast is at liberty.

**V. 7.** *{Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, & that thou bring the poor, that are cast out, to thine house? when thou seest the poor, that thou cover him, and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?*} Instead of injurious, and vexatious courses formerly taken, to practice offices of mercy and charity; a sound argument of serious and sincere repentance, Dan. 4.27. Luk. 19.8.

*{to deal*} Heb. *break*, or *divide*; as Jer. 16.7. for their loaves were such as might be ordinarily broken, Mat. 26.36. Luk. 24.31,35. See Ezek. 18.7. Lam. 4.4.

*{and that thou bring to thine house*} Heb. *and thou shalt bring home*, or, *unto thine house*: a defect of the particle *that*, as ver. 6. and of the pronoun; as chap. 37.4,23.

*{the poor cast out*} The latter word seldom found; in this place, in this form, alone. Some render, *attenuated*, or *brought to extreme poverty*; as parallel, to another used, chap. [unclear].2. & 11.4. the Greek renders it, *harborless*: the old Latin, *wandering*. Some of the Jewish critics, after the Chaldee, *cast out*; or, *tossed to and fro*, as the word, they use, signifies, and one from the same root, Chap. 22.17. and to make up the notation of it, because the verb, the root of this, commonly signifies, *to rebel*, and the active participle, or verbal, *a rebel*, Dan. 9.5. Ezek. 20.38. therefore some render this passive participle, or verbal, *cast out, and driven to and fro, as rebels*: but in the Arabick, the word is said to signify, *going to and fro*, or *traveling*; and such as so wander, we also call *travelers*, or they themselves, rather: the harboring of the harborless, is both commanded, and commended, Mat. 25.36. Rom. 12.13. Heb. 13.2. precedents of it, see Gen. 18.3–8. & 19.2,3. Job 31.32. Judg. 19.20,21.

*{that thou cover him*} Heb. *and thou shalt cover him*: as chap. 53.2. See Job 31.19,20. Mat. 26.36.

*{hide not thyself*} By turning your face from him: as refusing to see, or own, or take notice of him, Ps. 39.11. & 142.4. Luk. 10.31,32. See on chap. 53.3. & 57.17.

*{from thy flesh*} Your poor brother, who is the same flesh with you, Judg. 9.2. 2 Sam. 5.1. Neh. 5.5. Prov. 28.27.

**V. 8.** *{Then*} A promise follows, of many favors, and abundance of blessings, that should hereupon ensue: when your fasts, and other the like performances, are in this manner qualified, they shall find gracious acceptance with God, as by the fruits thereof following the same, here related, shall appear.

*{shall thy light break forth as the morning*} Your adversity shall then be dispelled, and removed, as the night, or as the foggy mist, and prosperity shall then succeed, as broad daylight, or bright sunshine, breaking out, in the room of it, Est. 8.16. Psal. 37.6. and 97.11. & 112.4. Prov. 4.18. chap. 9.1,2. & 60.1.
