*{and thine health shall spring forth speedily*} Your calamitous condition shall soon be altered, and your former damages, and detriments, suddenly repaired: all recovery out of, or delivery from, any foregoing evils, is in Scripture termed, by a metaphor, taken from the state of man's body, *an healing*, or *a restoring of health*. See chap. 6.10. & 57.18. Jer. 3.22. & 30.17. & [unclear].5.

*{and thy righteousness shall go before thee*} That is, as some, Christ your righteousness, Jer. 23.6. & 33.16. 1 Cor. 1.30. shall conduct you and be your guide, Luk. 1.79. & 2.32. Heb. 12.2. Rev. 14.4. Others, the fruit, and testimony of your uprightness, shall show itself forth and appear conspicuously, in the eyes both of God and man, Psal. 37.6. or the fruit and reward of it, from God, in God's gracious conduct of you, thereby procured, shall go before you, as a light to direct you, or as an harbinger, to fit your way for you; both to remove out of your way, what might impeach your passage, and to discover unto you, what way you should go, to cause all things to proceed and go on, prosperously with you, Psal. 5.8. Prov. 6.22. Act. 10.4. See Psal. 85.13. Ch. 52.12. v. 11.

*{the glory of the Lord shall be thy rearward*} By *glory of the Lord*, some understand here; a very glorious estate: *glory of God*, for, *great glory*; as, *hills of God*, and, *trees of the Lord*, Psal. 36.6. and 104.16. Other, the glory that God shall then confer upon you, Psal. 149.4. Or, rather, *the glory of God*, manifesting itself, as Chap. 40.5. that is, the *God of Glory*, Act. 8.2. or, *the glorious Lord*, Chap. 33.21. shall by his power, providence, and glorious presence, both conduct, and protect; both guide, and grace you, go before you to prevent you, with his blessings; and to come after you, to follow you, with further favors, and to secure you from any, that may come on your back, to assault you unawares. See Psal. 21.3. & 33.6. It is an allusion to God's manner of carrying on his people, through the wilderness. Exod. 13.21. & 14.19. Of the phrase here used, see Ch. 52.12.

**V. 9.** *{Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am.*} You shall have no cause then to complain, as formerly, ver. 3. that God regards you not, nor your suits, and requests; he will be most ready to hear, and to help, to grant you readily, what you require, Psal. 34.15,17. & 37.4. Chap. 30.19. & 65.24.

*{Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer*} Or, *Then when thou callest the Lord will* (as after, *he will say*) *answer*; as Chap. 44.14. & 53.2. *answer*; that is, grant your request; return you, not a verbal, but a real answer; do what you desired, Psal. 99.6. & 118.5.

*{thou shalt cry, &c.*} Or, as before, *when thou criest*, (being in danger, or distress, Psal. 121.1.) *he will say, Here I am*. Heb. *Lo I*. See Chap. 6.8. & 65.1. I am ready at hand to help, relieve, and deliver you, Psal. 46.1.

*{If thou take away from the midst of thee, the yoke*} If you put from among you, those grievous oppressions, before mentioned, and whatsoever either looks that way, or tends thereunto.

*{from the midst of thee*} *from within thee*, as some; as intending the reformation, as well of the heart within, as the alteration of the act without, Psal. 51.6. Chap. 55.7. Jer. 4.14. Jam. 4.8. Or *from thee*, simply, as Chap. 4.4. or, rather, *from among you*; (because he speaks of the people, or state, as of a body, or a family, consisting of a multitude, though in the singular number, yet collectively, ver. 1,2.) as Chap. 37.12. & 40.6.

*{the yoke*} As before, ver. 6.

*{The putting forth of the finger*} Heb. *to put forth the finger*: as after, *to speak*; the verb infinitive, for the noun. Hereby some understand the pointing with the finger, in way of scorn, and derision, at godly persons, and God's prophets. Whither also they draw that, Prov. 6.13. But that suits not so well here. Others would have it, to be a note of refusal, or, a gesture, (intimating a denial) of putting off, or putting by, one, that seeks, and sues to them for mercy, or remission, and release of aught. Others, the violent fastening, and laying hold of one, to maim, or to mischief him; as somewhat the like is frequent, in another term not far from it, 1 Sam. 22.17. & 26.11. Job 1.11. which place comes nearest to this notion. So they bring this home, to the *fist*, before mentioned, ver. 4. and they suppose it a gesture of one in rage, if not attempting, yet threatening, with his finger, to dig out a man's eyes, against whom, he is so enraged. Others, lastly, whom I concur with, conceive it to be a gesture, simply, of menacing; not by words so much, or in harsh terms; as by the hand, or finger, thrust out only: as if he had said, if you put away, and forbear, not acts of violence, or threatening terms only, Eph. 6.9. but even all expressions of that kind whatsoever.

*{and speaking vanity*} As Chap. 59.4. that is, *falsehood*, say some; as Jer. 9.4. (though the words there are other) whence this used for *an idol*, Chap. 66.3. *iniquity*, say others: but there is another word, very near unto this, that does properly so signify: and albeit, this also be almost generally so rendered, in that form of speech, so frequent, *workers of iniquity*; or, *wrongdoers*, Job 34.5,22. Psal. 5.5. & 6.8. yet the word does properly, and most commonly, signify *affliction*, or *vexation*. See Chap. 1.13. & 10.1. Job 4.8. & 5.6. Psal. 73.5. & 92.10. and *iniquity*, or *wrong*, only, as it procures afflictions, and produces vexation, and grievance to those, that are wronged; for which the Chaldee therefore has *violence*, here. I should render the words, *and speaking* (Heb. *to speak*; as before, *to put out*) *vexation*, or *grievance*, or words of *vexation*, or *grievance*: as, *thoughts of affliction*, or *vexation*, Chap. 59.7. that is either harsh language, such as may vex, and afflict others; such as Nabals words were, 1 Sam. 25.10,11. Prov. 18.23. Jam. 5.3. or discourse of such kind of matter, talk concerning the wringing and wronging of others; as Chap. 59.13. Psal. 36.3. & 73.8. that which God would not have so much as once talked of, or once named, unless with detestation, and disgrace, among his people, Eph. 5.3–5.

**V. 10.** *{And if thou draw out thy soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul:*} The prophet returns here again, to the works of mercy and charity, before required, ver. 7.

*{And if*} The conditional supplied from the former verse; as Job 22.23. compared with Job 8.6. Job 31.9,26. Howbeit, it seems not so needful here, as there; because the copulative may carry it well enough on without; *If thou take away the yoke, and draw out thy soul*, &c.

*{draw out thy soul*} Or, as most, after the old Latin, render it, *pour out thy soul*: a phrase sometime used (though with another word) of prayer, 1 Sam. 1.15. Psal. 42.4. and it may seem to have a twofold notion in it, of *drawing out*, and of *pouring forth*: as it is said, 1 Sam. 7.6. *they drew water, and poured it out*; and in the term of *drawing out*, is liberality and bounty intimated; for the word implies plenty, Psal. 144.13. in the term, *soul*, an inward affection, and disposition, going along with, and accompanying the outward action of beneficence, as proceeding from benevolence, put, the one therefore, which the Jewish doctors well observe, for the other, as Prov. 18.22. So that it is, as if he had said; If you relieve your poor brother, freely, liberally, cheerfully, cordially, compassionately, so as that your heart go along with your gift; Deut. 15.7–11. Psal. 37.21,26. & 112.5. 2 Cor. 8.5,12. & 9.5,7.

*{and satisfy the afflicted soul:*} Not relieve him in some scant and niggardly manner, with such a poor pittance, as will scarce afford him any relief, and may rather enhance, than allay, his hunger; make him more sensible of his want, rather than satisfy and supply it; but afford that unto him, that may supply his necessity, and may satiate his soul: *the afflicted soul*, for, *the afflicted person*: but the word *soul*, makes the speech the more affectionate, and emphatical. So Psal. 107.5,9. Jer. 31.14.

*{then shall thy light rise in obscurity, and thy darkness be as the noonday*} Heb. *then shall thy light arise* (that is, light shall rise to you) *in darkness*, or *in the dark*, (as Psal. 112.4.) *and thy mist shall be as the noonday*. See Chap. 59.9. Your adversity shall be turned into prosperity; and that in a very eminent degree, Job 11.17. Psal. 37.6. See before, ver. 8.

**V. 11.** *{And the Lord shall guide thee continually*} Or, *lead*, or *conduct thee*: as Psal. 5.8. & 23.3. & 25.5. & 143.10. chap. 57.18. See ver. 8. Yet some render it, after the old Latin, *the Lord will make thee to rest*; as Chap. 14.3. & 63.14. but the roots are divers.

*{and satisfy thy soul in drought*} *he will satisfy thy soul*, Psal. 103.5. as you did satisfy the poor man's soul; that is, his desire, by supplying his want, the cause of it, ver. 10. See Prov. 11.25. *in drought*, Heb. *in droughts*; that is, in extremity of drought: for the plural usually implies eminency, or extremity of aught, good or evil. So, *wisdoms*, Prov. 1.20. & 8.1. *understandings*, Psal. 78.72. Prov. 11.2. Chap. 40.14. *deaths*, Chap. 53.9. *dearths*, or, *restraints*; the same in effect with *droughts* here, Jer. 14.1. He will afford you a competency, and supply you with a sufficiency, in times of the greatest dearth, and famine, Job 5.20. Psal. 33.19. & 34.9,10. & 37.19. a metaphor taken from plants, that are carefully watered, when rain fails, by man's industry. See Chap. 17.11. & 27.3. Howbeit, because the word here used, comes from a root, that signifies as well *pure, clear*, and *bright*; as *dryness*, and *drought*, Cant. 5.10. Chap. 18.4. Lam. 4.7. in regard that the one does usually accompany, and proceed from the other. Hence it is, that the old Latin renders the words, *he will fill thy soul with brightnesses*; but that notion suits not here.

*{and make fat thy bones;*} That is, according to this version, as some, he will fill your bones with marrow, Job 21.24. Prov. 3.8. or, as others, *make thy body fat*, and in good plight, Prov. 11.25. & 28.25. *bones*, for, *body*, say they, consisting of them; as Psal. 35.16. & 141.7. but *bones*, more especially: because in beasts thoroughly fatted, there is much fat, not in the belly only, but about the bones too: and in this notion, do ours most commonly take it; as also does the ancient Greek render it. Howbeit, the old Latin renders it, *he will deliver*, or, *set free, thy bones*: as alluding to the loosening of men's joints, and their bodies, consequently, out of bands, and fetters: and some of our latest interpreters, *he will make thy bones expedite*, that is, nimble and active: the word most generally signifies *to loose*, or, *to set at liberty*, Prov. 11.8,9. sometime, *to draw out*, Lam. 4.3. sometime, *to pull off* shoes, or the like. Chap. 20.2. sometime, *to put on* armor, or harness, and make ready, and fit for fight, Numb. 32.17,20,32. The Jewish critics themselves are much puzzled about it. Some go the same way that ours do, taking the word, in a notion of *fatting*: all the ground they give for it is, because they find that phrase, Prov. 15.30. *a good hearing fatteth the bones*; but there is no affinity between the term there used, and this, either in letters and sound, or use, elsewhere; and they add therefore, that this word has in that notion no fellow. Yet some others of them conceive, that they have found a fellow for it: to which purpose, they would draw in a place of Job 36.15. where they suppose the word to be found in the same notion, in those words, as they render them, *he fatteth the afflicted in his affliction*: but neither is the verb in the same form there, nor seems it there to carry that sense. The most give the words otherwise, as at first sight, they sound, *he delivereth the afflicted in his affliction*. Others of them produce a saying, out of their rituals, wherein it should so signify; but of the sense of that saying, they seem to speak somewhat doubtfully. Some say it is here in a notion of *rest*: as if it were said, *he will make thy bones rest*: contrary to that, *there is no rest in my bones*, Psal. 38.3. but of this use, they produce no precedent at all. Others, lastly, render it, *he will arm thy bones*, or, *strengthen thy bones*; according to that notion of fitting men for fight: so keep, and confirm them, *that they shall not be broken*, Psal. 34.20. the bones being, say they, as the foundation of the bulk of man's body. I should most willingly go with the first, were there any good ground for that use of the word; because it best suits with the metaphors, both before, and after: but that failing, I concur with this last, as most probable: because it comes nearest of any to some, not unusual, notion of the word, of addressing, and fitting men for military employments: or, if that seem somewhat too far-fetched, with that of the old Latin, concerning *loosing*, or *setting free*; as answering to their loosing of bands and yokes, and letting their bounden ones go free, ver. 6. as if he had said, God will set you free, if you set these poor souls, your brethren free.

*{and thou shalt be like a watered garden*} Or, *a well-watered garden*: for there is in the word, a notion of abundance, Psal. 23.5. Chap. 34.7. an emblem of a flourishing and prosperous estate, Num. 24.6. alluding to the garden of Eden, Gen. 3.8–10. & 13.10. Ezek. 31.3–9. Cant. 4.12–15. See Jer. 17.8.

*{like a spring of water, whose waters fail not*} Heb. *do not lie*, or *deceive*; as Hab. 3.17. that runs constantly all the year long; and is not dried up, as some small brooks, or winter floods, in heat of summer, or droughts of any continuance, are, what time there is most need of them, 1 King. 17.7. Job 6.15,20. an emblem, not of flourishing for a time; but of constant prosperity. See Chap. 33.16. Joh. 4.14.

**V. 12.** *{And they that shall be of thee, shall build the old waste places:*} Heb. *the wastes of antiquity*: as Chap. 61.4. those that come of you, shall re-edify the ruinous places of Jerusalem, and other cities of Judah, that have lain long waste, Chap. 49.8. and 51.3. See Neh. 3. Yet some would have it meant of people, replenishing the cities with inhabitants, which are as flesh and blood to them, being but as skeletons, or dry bones without them: but the former is more familiar.

*{thou shalt raise the foundations of many generations*} Heb. *raise*, or *settle*, (as 2 Sam. 7.25.) *the foundations of age, and age*, either build upon those foundations, that have lain divers ages desolate; or lay the foundation of such buildings, as for many ages shall endure. See Chap. 44.26. & 61.4.

*{and thou shalt be called*} That is, you shall be; as Chap. 61.6. Heb. *it shall be called to thee*: as Chap. 48.8. & 62.2.

*{the repairer of the breach,*} Or, *the maker up of the breach*, that God had made in the wall, or fence, of their city, and state, for their sins, Chap. 5.5. See Psal. 106.23,29. Ezek. 22.30.

*{the restorer of paths to dwell in*} That is, the clearer of those ways, by which men may return to those places, where they are to inhabit, whereas they were formerly neglected, and disused, and consequently overgrown, either through want of people to travel, or of safety to travelers, Judg. 5.6,7. Lam. 1.4. or, the *returner* of those places, that were made paths of before, by the enemy passing to and fro over them, having ruined the buildings, and flatted the foundations of them, to be places for men to inhabit again. For they seem to stoop too low, that understand them of fencing their vineyards, and clearing the way to them: and they to shoot as wide, that render the words, *The restorer of paths to the Sabbath*: for though the words be in sound somewhat like; yet they differ both in roots, point, and form.

**V. 13.** *{If thou turn away thy foot from the Sabbath.*} This some understand of the yearly Sabbath, or day of strictest rest, in the solemn convention for humiliation and propitiation, Lev. 16.31. and 23.27,31. whereof, see on ver. 3,4. Others, more largely, of the weekly Sabbath: one special commandment, as a principal, put for the rest of those, that concerned the religious worship, and service of God; as Chap. 56.2,4,6. Jer. 17.21. and the words of the text are applicable to either.

*{turn away thy foot*} The Jewish doctors expound it, of walking abroad: but ours rather, of forbearing, and withdrawing their minds and affections, from such studies and employments upon that day, whereby the same might be polluted or profaned, Ezek. 22.26.

*{from doing thy pleasure on mine holy day;*} Heb. *to do*, or *doing thy pleasure*, or *will*, or *business* (See on ver. 3.) *on my day of holiness*: the preposition supplied from the foregoing branch; (See the like defect, Exod. 19.12.) and expressed again afterward: and, *day of holiness*, for, *holy day*; as *hill of holiness*, for, *holy hill*, Chap. 57.13.

*{and call the Sabbath a delight*} That is, account it such, or make it such: or, as some, not amiss render it, *thy delight*: the pronoun supplied; as ver. 7.13. by taking delight in the offices and holy duties of the day. See ver. 12. for the form of speech; for the word, ver. 14. So did the servants of God, in former times, count the services of God, in his house, on those days, their chiefest delight, and the very life of their souls; lamenting and bemoaning themselves, as even dead on the nest, when they were debarred from, or deprived of, them; desiring nothing more earnestly, than free access again to them, when they were restrained from them; and rejoicing in nothing, more affectionately, than in the enjoyment of them, when they had liberty so to do. See Psal. 27.4. & 36.8. & 42.1,2,4. & 45.2–4. & 65.1–5. & 84. & 122.1,2. And that is the genuine meaning of the place, for whether Sabbath of the twain we take it. For it is but frivolous, that the Jewish doctors expound it, of eating dainty and delightful meats; which, though on some festivals, was seasonable, Neh. 8.10. yet was not suitable to the afflicting Sabbath: and of as little worth is it, that in the word, *call*, here, some reference should be to the solemn convocation, because that word comes from this of *calling*, Lev. 23.3,27. Chap. 4.13.

*{the holy of the Lord, honorable;*} Or *and the Lord's holy day honorable*: so call, and account it, as well honorable, as delightful: For the word is to be understood in this clause also; as the like, ver. 12. Heb. *the Lord's holiness*, for *his day of holiness*; *his holy day*; as before: a defect of the noun regent; as Chap. 17.5. to be supplied from the words foregoing.

*{and shalt honor him*} Or, *it*: To wit, his day: for the word will bear either: And we may be said, as well, *to honor God*, or, *to honor his day*; as, *to sanctify him*, Chap. 8.13. and, *to sanctify his day*, Exod. 20.8. But here again our Jewish masters run their carnal way, telling us, that the Sabbath is to be honored, by wearing good clothes, and having better diet upon that day: that which too many incline to them in, more regarding such matters, than those things, that do indeed concern the right honor of the day, contrary to that Apostolical rule, Rom. 13.14. Besides that on the Sabbatical fast here also intended, such suits of apparel, as well as good cheer, would be very unseasonable, Exod. 33.4,5.

*{not doing thine own ways,*} Heb. *from doing*; that is, abstaining, or restraining yourself, as before, *from doing thine own ways*; that is, following your own wicked works and courses, as Chap. 56.7.

*{nor finding thine own pleasure,*} Of this branch, see before, ver. 3.

*{nor speaking thine own words.*} Heb. *and* (for, *or*; as Chap. 48.5.) *to speak*, or *speaking a word*, or *aught*; as Jer. 36.2. *thine own* is supplied from the former branches, as, *first*, 1 Tim. 2.13,14. *Adam was not* first *deceived*. Howsoever, by your *word*, or *words*, are meant, such words, or things, as were before mentioned, ver. 9. and they were there forbidden, as too usual with them, even at such times: For this place does apparently answer to that; and the Chaldee therefore renders it, *words of wrong, and oppression*; as the Jewish doctors also expound the term there used, though roving another way themselves. For as for those two late learned annotators; the one whereof would have it rendered, *a proud, insolent*, or *lofty word*, as he supposes two other terms, that signify a *word* to be taken, Job 15.13. & 20.29. And this the rather, because the root it comes of, has sometime such a notion: Whereof, see on, Chap. 17.6,9. & 61.6. The other, would have the copulative taken, in an adversative notion, rendering the text, *but speaking the word*, to wit, of God, I suppose that either of them goes, therein, a way by himself, and that solitary, without company, for want of probability.

**V. 14.** *{Then shalt thou delight thyself in the Lord,*} This is sometime required as a duty, Psal. 37.4. sometime promised, as a reward. So Job 22.26. and so here. And it is, as if he had said; If you keep the Lord's day, forbearing your wonted evil thoughts, and mindings, on it, and shall diligently apply yourself unto the duties of the day, therein employing yourself, not as of necessity, and by constraint: but cheerfully, and with delight; you shall find in the Lord, not sufficient only, but abundant matter of such delights, as shall minister a fullness of satisfaction unto your soul, Psal. 36.8. & 37.11. Chap. 55.2. & 66.11. such delights as the ungodly man shall never enjoy, Job 27.10. Prov. 14.10.

*{and I will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth,*} To dwell aloft in places of security and safety, and to ride to and fro, there, at pleasure. See Chap. 33.16,17. The words seem to be taken from Moses his song, Deut. 32.13. and to have some glance at the land of Judea, being much of it mountainous, Psal. 87.1. Chap. 14.25. & 37.24. A passage from person to person, as Chap. 57.10–12.

*{and feed thee with the heritage of Jacob, thy father:*} With the good things of the land of Canaan, given for an inheritance unto him, for his posterity, Gen. 28.13,14. Psal. 135.11,12. a type of the heavenly inheritance. The Jewish doctors here move a question; why the prophet should rather say, *Jacob thy father*, than *Abraham thy father*: And divers answers they give; as that Abraham kept no Sabbath, but Jacob did: and that Abraham had an Ismael, as well as an Isaac, and Isaac an Esau, as well as a Jacob; and they descant upon the promises made severally to them, Gen. 13.15. & 26.3. & 28.13,14. But these are, the first unsound, and in part untrue; the last of them, curious and frivolous. Somewhat may be in the second, whereof, see before on Chap. 43.1.

*{for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it.*} See Chap. 1.20. and 40.5.

### CHAPTER 59

**Vers. 1.** *{Behold*} This chapter, whether a continued discourse with the former, as some; or, an entire sermon distinct, and divers from the former; yet consists of two principal parts, as that also did: The former, a relation of the grievous enormities of that people, as the main cause of those calamities that lay heavy upon them, ver. 1–15. the latter, a prediction, and promise of deliverance to God's faithful afflicted ones, both from oppressions at home, and invasions from abroad, verse, 16–19. together with the continuance of spiritual favors unto them, by the Messiah, here also foretold, and hereafter to be exhibited; wherewith the prophet usually concludes his discourses, as the complement of all outward mercies, and temporal deliverances, as tending thereunto, and being thereof types to them, ver. 20,21.

*{Behold*} See Chap. 42.1. & 58.3,4.

*{the Lord's hand is not shortened that he cannot save*} This may either have reference to the former part of the foregoing chapter, when they complained of God, for not hearing, and regarding their fastings and prayers, Ch. 58.3. as if he had said, You complain of God, that he does not hear and help you, as he had wont to do others of his in times past, Psal. 22.4,5. & 44.1,22. Ch. 51.10. that deliverance is not wrought, and effected for you, v. 9,10. the fault is not in God, (who is still the same, not subject to any defect, or default, Num. 11.23. Mal. 3.6.) but in yourselves, and in your sins, Jer. 5.25. Lam. 3.42,44. Or, it may back the latter part, and confirm the close of it, as giving them assurance of the undoubted making good unto them, of all those large and liberal blessings, there propounded upon their repentance, seemed they never so improbable, or incredible, in regard of their present low, and forlorn condition, Chap. 58.11,12,14. for that God was no less, either able, or willing, to hear, or help, than in former times he had been, did not their obstinacy in sin, restrain him from the doing of either, Chap. 50.1,2.

*{hand*} His power; as Psal. 136.12.

*{is not shortened*} Or, *abridged*, or, *straitened*; as Mich. 2.7.

*{that it cannot save*} Heb. *from saving*; as Chap. 50.2. and so after, *from hearing*. See on Chap. 23.1. & 58.13.

*{neither his ear heavy*} That is, *deaf*, or thick of hearing, as we use to say: so is the word used, being applied to the ears, Ch. 6.10. Zach. 7.11. as it signifies, *dim*, when applied to the eyes, Gen. 48.10. *dull*, or *hard*, when to the heart, Exod. 9.35. & 10.1.

*{that it cannot hear.*} Heb. *from hearing*, as before, *from saving*. See ver. 2.

**V. 2.** *{But your iniquities have severed between you, and your God:*} Heb. *Have been*, or, *severing between you, to between your God*: a redundancy of speech, somewhat like whereunto is found, Gen. 1.4. *between the light, and between the dark*: and nearer to this, Gen. 1.6. *between waters to waters*: and Deut. 17.8. *between blood to blood, between suit to suit*; or, *strife to strife, and between stripe to stripe*: But this is yet more redundant than either of those forms, used, not improbably, to imply the great distance, that sin makes between man, and God: not in position of place; (for God is everywhere present, as well, with bad, as good, Psal. 139.7–12. Prov. 15.3. Jer. 23.25. Amos 9.2,3. Act. 17.28.) but in disposition of mind, and affection of heart, Psal. 138.6. Prov. 15.29. Chap. 29.13. Jer. 12.2.

*{and your sins have hid his face from you*} That is, have caused him, in anger to withdraw his gracious presence, and assistance from you, as refusing to be seen of you, or to be spoken with, by you. See Deut. 31.17. Psal. 10.1. Chap. 54.8. & 57.17. a defect of the pronoun; as Chap. 53.3.

*{that he will not hear;*} Or, *not hear you*; a defect of the pronoun, as Chap. 1.15. Heb. *from hearing*; as ver. 1. Or, *from hearing you*. See Zach. 7.11,12. God serves you, as you serve him: You refuse to hear him; and he refuses to hear you, Prov. 1.24,28. & 28.9. Lam. 3.42,44.

**V. 3.** *{For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with iniquity.*} The prophet that he may not be deemed to charge them, without good ground, and just cause; and the better to clear God's justice, in thus estranging himself from them, does at large relate, and in lively colors lay forth, their general injurious, merciless, and mischievous carriages. Of this first branch, see Chap. 1.15. Lam. 4.14. 2 Chron. 21.6. *hands* and *fingers*, are here the same, as *lips* and *tongue*, in the next branch: only the one is added unto the other, to make the speech the more emphatical.

*{your lips have spoken lies, your tongue hath muttered perverseness*} Or, *your lips speak lies, and your tongue meditateth*, or *talketh of perverseness*, or, *unrighteousness*, as it is rendered, Deut. 25.16. or, *iniquity*; as Mic. 3.10. where it is joined with *blood*. Your common practice, is, by false suggestions, and suborned depositions, to strip men of their states, and to bereave them of their lives, Psal. 52.2–8. Prov. 14.5. & 25.18. Jer. 9.3. See Chap. 58.9.

*{muttered*} So the word seems sometime to signify. See on c. 8.19. but most commonly *to meditate*: and so some here render it. Howbeit, because *meditation* is not the proper work of the tongue, some conceive it to be a complexive form of speech; *Your tongue uttereth premeditated iniquity*; and so it should be like that, Psal. 52.2. *Thy tongue deviseth mischiefs*; that is, utters mischievous plots, devised by you. But the word here used, signifies as well, *to talk*, as *meditate*, and *to utter*, as *to mutter*. So, *My tongue shall speak*, or *talk of thy righteousness, and thy praise*, Psal. 35.28. & 71.24. and, *they speak not through the throat*, Psal. 115.7. it may well therefore be rendered; *Your tongue talketh of iniquity*: lips and tongue; as Psal. 12.3,4. & 120.2.

**V. 4.** *{None calleth for justice; nor any pleadeth for truth:*} All sorts of people are given to vexation and oppression; and no man endeavors to relieve and right the wronged, or to redress and remedy aught that is done amiss: No man stands up for right or truth, against falsehood and wrong; ver. 16. Eccl. 4.1. Jer. 9.3. These general terms, are not to be understood, exactly and absolutely, but of the greatest part, of the most: the better part being so geason, and so drowned in the generality, that they were not to be seen, they seemed as none. So Psal. 12.1. & 14.1,3. Chap. 56.10. & 64.6,7. Jer. 5.1. & 6.28. Mic. 7.2,4.

*{pleadeth for truth:*} Heb. *is judged*; that is, *pleadeth in judgment*; as Chap. 66.16. Jer. 2.35. & 25.31. Or, *is judged*, *is tried* (has sentence passed in his cause, Psal. 109.7. 1 Cor. 6.1.) *in truth*, that is, truly, faithfully, uprightly, as 2 Chron. 31.12,15. & 34.12. no man can have his cause justly decided.

*{they trust in vanity,*} Heb. *trusting in vanity*, or, *emptiness*. Of the phrase, see on ver. 13. Of the term rendered *vanity*, see on Chap. 24.10. & 40.17,23. it is here used for deceit, fraud, and lies: because, they are things void, and empty of being, of soundness and subsistence, and so will prove in the end, unto all those that trust to them. See Chap. 28.15,17,18.

*{and speak lies*} Heb. *and speaking* (as before, *trusting*,) *vanity*; that is, *lies*; as Psal. 41.6. & 144.8,11. the same in effect with the former. See Psal. 36.3.

*{they conceive mischief, and bring forth iniquity.*} Heb. *conceiving*, or, *going great with grievance, and bringing forth affliction*, or *vexation*: they are continually contriving of some injurious and vexatious plot, or other, and never at rest, as a woman going with child, until by putting it in practice and execution, they be, at length, delivered of it. See the very like phrases, Job 15.35. Psal. 7.14. and of the practice Psal. 36.4. Prov. 4.16. Mic. 2.1.

*{they conceive*} Heb. *conceiving*, or *going great with*, rather. See on Chap. 7.14. they are as much straitened with it, as a woman near her time: like Boaz, that could not be at rest, until he had finished the business that his heart was set upon, Ruth 3.18. and the manner of speech is emphatical; for it is both deficient, and redundant: *conceiving*, for *conceiving they conceive*; or, *going great*, for *going great they go great with*, as also, Job 15.35. and hereafter, ver. 13. and, *bringing forth*, for, *bringing forth they bring forth*: and so before, *trusting they trust*; and, *speaking they speak*; that is all they trust to, and that is their whole continual talk: for these forms of reduplication whether expressed, or implied, have much emphasis in them; and it is, as if it were said; such courses as these, are their minds, tongues, and hands, continually taken up with; they are the constant employment of them. See further, on v. 13.

*{mischief, and iniquity*} Of these two terms, see on Ch. 10.1.

**V. 5.** *{They hatch cockatrice eggs*} Or, as some, *adders*. See of the word, on Chap. 11.8. They contrive, and bring forth mischievous plots. Nothing proceeds from them, or is produced by them, but what is poisonous, and pernicious, Deut. 32.32,33. Rom. 3.13–16.

*{and weave the spider's web:*} They contrive such plots, as may entangle others, as the spider's web does the fly, to their damage, and detriment, or to their utter undoing, and destruction, Ps. 10.9. Mic. 7.2. Howbeit, some expound it of the vanity of their wicked plots and projects, that in fine, they shall prove uneffectual, and unuseful, no more helpful to them, or able to stead them, than a company of cobwebs. So Job 8.14,15. and hereafter, ver. 6. and so it should have reference to their confidence before mentioned, v. 4. which makes that notion here, not improbable. And yet can I not assent unto a late learned writer, who therefore would have the former branch to be rendered, not *they hatch*, but *they break* such eggs: as alluding not to eggs that fowls, or serpents, first lay, then sit on, or brood, & so hatch, by cleaving of the shell, (which the word properly signifies) to bring forth their young, but to the usual manner of those, that having gathered fowls, or tortoises' eggs, ch. 10.14. do break them to feed on: as if the prophet should say, of those that maintain themselves by rapine, and spoil, or fraud, and deceit, that they clothe themselves with spiders' cobwebs, and feed themselves with vipers', or adders' eggs: the one frivolous stuff, that will do them no good: the other, matter pernicious, that will do them much mischief, but both the use of the word elsewhere, Chap. 34.15. sides with the former exposition: and this latter to me seems somewhat too far-fetched.

*{he that eateth of their eggs dieth*} Not he that eats of cockatrice, or adders' eggs, but he that eats of their eggs, compared to such, whom the prophet here speaks of: yet not such eggs, as they feed on, but such eggs, as they hatch, wherewith to do others mischief. Whosoever eats of their eggs, that is, has any commerce, or dealing with them: it proves dangerous, yea, deadly to him. See ver. 7. So I rather understand it, than with some other, of such, as partake with them, in their mischievous designs, Pro. 29.24. Chap. 1.23. the poison of serpents is pernicious unto others, not to themselves: though it be true, that wicked men drink both first, and most, of their own venom, their malice: and it will prove their own bane in the end, Psal. 34.21. But that seems not the drift of the prophet in this place.

*{and that which is crushed, breaketh out into a viper*} That is, say some, if any descry and disclose their plots and purposes, they fly out upon him, as a viper, or some other suchlike serpent, furnished with deadly poison, to work his destruction: or if one will be tampering with them, to make some trial of them, induced by the fair outside of some specious and friendly pretenses, he shall meet with such matter, as in the end he shall rue it: as if a man taking a serpent's egg, for the egg of some fowl, that men usually eat of, should, upon the breaking of it, light on that, which he least of all looked for: or as others, if a man fall into dealing with them unawares, it shall be with him as by one that treads, by chance, on the egg of some serpent, which being crushed, a young one springs out of it in his face. The meaning seems to be, which way soever we take it, that there is no safe dealing any way with them. Nor is it improbable, that some would have, who in these words, suppose a reason to be rendered of the former branch, thus rendering the words *for that which is crushed*, or broken, to feed on, *breaks out into a viper*: where a man made account to find some wholesome and toothsome meat, when he has broken the shell, he is entertained with a viper: the copulative for the causal, we had oft before, Ch. 40.26. & 52.15. & 53.2. Less to me probable seems to be what some others of no small note exhibit; one reading the words, *if any disperse them, a viper breaketh out*: another, *it is with him, that is but sprinkled with them, as if a viper had sprung out* and fastened upon him, as on Paul, Act. 28.3. as if it were said the least aspersion of them, or drop from them, is not perilous only, but even pernicious. This variety of versions hence arises, for that in Hebrew, verbs, though of divers forms, yet in letters much alike, are oft, in use and notion, confounded the one with the other. I incline most to the last of the first, because I find the very same word that here is used for *compression*, or *crushing*, Chap. 1.6. and again, for *crushing*, or *breaking* of eggs, by treading on them with the foot, Job 39.15. Which yet I suppose him to have roved far, from the true meaning of, who so rendering the text, expounds the words; as if it were said, he that can crush their plots in the egg, or the shell, is safe enough; for the snake, or serpent, will then be gone: so it should be somewhat like that, Psal. 137.9. as also that other learned man, who by alteration of a vowel, making it an active participle, reads the words, *if one scatter* them; that is, refusing to eat of them, cast them away, and so break them: for the like use of the participle pointing us to Psal. 141.7. 1 Sam. 2.13. 2 Sam. 14.10. & 19.8. 2 Kin. 7.2. The text seems to look a far other way, than either of them drives to.

*{a viper*} Thus the most. Yet the ancient Greek, and the old Latin, render it, *a Basilisk*, the one; and a *regulus*, the other: by a name answerable to the former, which we commonly call, *a cockatrice*: the former, they style an *asp*. The Jewish doctors tell us only, that it is a kind of hurtful serpent: and some of them would have this, and the forementioned, to be one and the same; but of that, there seems no probability: it seems to be a serpent, that was rife in the southerly wastes, bordering upon them, Chap. 30.6. and such an one as had a venomous tongue, Job 20.16. yet not like to be *a viper*; because albeit Pliny, l. 10. c. 62. rank the viper among those that lay eggs; Yet Aristotle (with whom the most, and best writers accord, and whose words Pliny seems to have mistaken,) avows more than once, that of all serpents, the viper alone, lays no egg, but brings forth young ones; as also the dolphin, or porpoise, seal, whale, and some other fish, do. (See his *history of living wights*, l. 1. c. 6. l. 3. c. 1. l. 5. c. 34.) whence also in Latin it is deemed to have its name, *vipera*, as *vivipera*; not, as some fable, from a forcible delivery. Some other serpent therefore it must be, to which the prophet here alludes.

**V. 6.** *{Their webs shall not become garments, neither shall they cover themselves with their works:*} Their devices, plots, and practices, though they may hurt and mischief others, yet they shall not help, or avail themselves; all the good, or gain they get, and gather by them, shall stand them in no stead, they shall not be able to shelter them against God's wrath, no more than a coat of cobweb is able to shelter him, that wears it, against a fierce shower of hail, or a thick volley of hail-shot. See Chap. 28.15,18,20. & 30.12,14. they shall all prove, in conclusion, as cobwebs to themselves, for any succor, or benefit, that they shall receive from them, or reap by them. See Job 8.14. Prov. 10.2. & 11.4.

*{their works are works of iniquity, and the act of violence is in their hands.*} Or, *their works are works of vexation*, (and grievance: as ver. 3.) *and the practice of violence is in their hands*; that is, their whole employment is no other than a continued practice of vexation, and oppression. See ver. 3,4. for they strain the text unreasonably, who by *work*, or *act*, would understand here, *the work of punishment* inflicted upon themselves, for their wrongful, and violent dealing; as *violence* for the just reward of it, Ps. 7.16.

**V. 7.** *{Their feet run unto evil, and they make haste to shed innocent blood*} So Prov. 1.16. Jer. 22.17. Rom. 3.15.

*{their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity*} Or, *vexation*; as, *works of vexation*, ver. 6. vexatious thoughts, and vexatious works; such contrivances, and courses, as tend wholly to the vexation, and wrong, and ruin of others. See Chap. 55.7.

*{wasting and destruction are in their paths*} Or, *devastation and destruction*, (Chap. 60.19. Heb. *breaking*; as Chap. 1.28.) *are in their causeys*, Chap. 7.3. & 33.8. See Rom. 3.16.

**V. 8.** *{The way of peace they know not*} They are strangers unto, and utterly unacquainted, with any quiet, or peaceable carriage; or nothing of that nature pleases them, or is entertained by them, that tends to the prosperity and welfare of others. See Rom. 3.17.

*{and there is no judgment in their goings*} Or, *tracts*: (for it signifies properly the tract, that a cartwheel makes, 1 Sam. 17.20.) no regard of equity, or right, in their courses: *judgment*, for, *right*: as Chap. 56.1.

*{they have made them crooked paths*} Heb. *they pervert their paths to them*. So Prov. 10.9. & 28.18. opposed there to such as walk uprightly: and an elegant redundancy in that form, *to them*; like that, Jer. 23.12. *their way shall be to them*.

*{whosoever goeth therein, shall not know peace*} He that treads their tracks, shall never attain to any true prosperity, or welfare, to any sound peace, Chap. 48.22. & 57.21. *shall not know it*; that is, *not have it*: as 2 Cor. 5.21. *to know*, for, to attain, possess, enjoy: as, *to see good*, is, to enjoy it, Psal. 34.12. *to see life*, to live, Joh. 3.36. and, so, *to know good and evil*; whence the tree, inhibited, had its name, Gen. 3.16,17. to know either experimentally; to have experience, as well of the one, as of the other, in oneself: and, *to know Christ, and the power of his resurrection, and the communion of his sufferings*, Phil. 3.10. that is, to have, and enjoy him, together with the fruit, and efficacy of either: but it is a phrase very emphatical, they shall not so much as once know it, not so much as once know what it means, Rev. 2.17. See the like, Joh. 3.3,5. 1 Joh. 3.4.

**V. 9.** *{Therefore is judgment far from us, neither doth justice overtake us*} The prophet having, at large, described the general, and horrible depravation of the people of God, in those times, does here begin to apply, what he had hitherto related, concerning the same, to the stopping of the mouths of those hypocritical murmurers, who had before complained, that notwithstanding their frequent fasts and suits, and solemn seekings unto God, yet their prayers had not prevailed with him, for the delivery of them out of their present difficulties, and distresses. For this cause, says he, that is, for these your vile, and detestable courses is it, that God stands aloof off from you, and neither executes judgment for you, upon your enemies, nor protects you, against their wrongs; he stands by, and permits them to deal with you, as you deal yourselves one with another, Hab. 1.13–17. *judgment*, put, as frequently, for *vengeance*, or righting persons wronged, by justice done upon the wrongdoer, Numbers 33.4. Chap. 1.27. Ezek. 14.21. & 16.38,41.

*{we wait for light, but behold obscurity; for brightness, but we walk in darkness*} We expect deliverance out of our troubles, but they rather increase with us. Of the use of the words, *light*, and *darkness*, see Esther 8.17. Psal. 112.4. Chap. 58.8,10. Of expectations, in the like manner frustrated, Jeremiah 8.15. & 14.19.

*{but behold obscurity*} Heb. *and* (as Chap. 57.20.) *behold* (see how cross, and contrary to our expectation, things fall out; as Gen. 29.25.) *darkness*, as Chap. 5.20. & 8.22.

*{for brightness*} Heb. *brightnesses*; that is, brightness in abundance: (See on Chap. 58.11.) we look for, (to be supplied from the former branch: as Jer. 8.15.) and the more is expected, the more grievous is its failing.

*{we walk in darkness*} Heb. *in mists*, for, in an extreme thick mist, or fog; correspondent to the *brightness* that they expected, and hoped to have had: darkness, like that in Egypt, called, *a darkness of mist*, for, *a misty darkness*: or, *a thick mist*, Exod. 10.22. or, *a mist of God*, for a most extreme thick mist, Jer. 2.31. Their present condition is resembled, by a man walking, or wandering, rather, in some place full of dangers, environed on either side with an extreme thick mist, able from no part to descry any the least glimpse of light; and being at his wits' end therefore, as not knowing which way to take. See Chap. 8.21,22. & 50.10. & 58.10. Jer. 13.16. 1 Joh. 2.11.

**V. 10.** *{We grope for the wall like the blind; and we grope, as if we had no eyes:*} Or, *We grope*, I say; as Chap. 49.6. & 55.1. ver. 17. For the latter is, in effect, and meaning, the very same with the former. We are as blind men, who wanting eyes, use their hands instead of their eyes, Act. 17.27. We are wholly destitute of counsel, and can find no issue, out of our calamitous condition. So Deut. 28.29. Job 5.14. & 12.25. Lam. 4.14. Zeph. 1.17.

*{we stumble at noonday, as in the night*} Heb. *evening* or *twilight*, Prov. 7.9. put for the *night*, Chap. 5.11. for, *darkness*, Jer. 13.16. noonday is no other with us, than as midnight. See Amos 8.9. a proverbial speech it is, both with Greeks, and Latins, *to stumble at noonday*; used here of people, nowhere safe; but ready to miscarry, and fall into mischief, even where least danger might be, either expected, or suspected, Joh. 11.9,10.

*{we are in desolate places, as dead men.*} The word here used is nowhere else read; that is one cause that makes it the more ambiguous. A second, because question is, whether the first, or the last letter of it, be radical. A third, because of the confusion of forms, that in sound of letters, seem near the same. The most render it, *desolate*. They that so do, deduce it from a word, that primarily, and most commonly, has a notion of *guilt* in it; Yet sometime of *desolation*; as Ezek. 6.6. Hos. 13.16. Joel 1.18. because it comes near in sound to one that, properly so signifies. Howbeit, those that thus render it, do not all understand it alike: For, some of them take it simply, as it sounds, that their lands were laid waste and desolate, by hostile invasions and incursions, Chap. 1.7. Others, as an emblem only of a sad and rueful condition; like people abandoned, unto such places of abode, Psal. 44.19. & 68.6. Jer. 17.6. Others, conceive meant by it, *graves*, or *sepulchers*; so the Chaldee, and divers of the Jewish doctors, because the grave, say they, is a place of desolation: Though some go further, conceiving that not graves, or sepulchers, barely, or simply, are hereby meant, such as are newly delved, or built; but such as have been deserted and abandoned; so that the bodies laid in them, are now putrefied and dissolved. And to add strength to this conceit, some have recourse to the ordinary signification of the root, and render it, *places condemnable*, or *abominable*; fetching hither that of our Savior, Mat. 23.27. And these expound the words, as if it were said, we are even like dead men, laid up in our graves, and there in a manner clean dissolved, or dried up. And so indeed is depth of calamity and misery, joined with despair especially, in Scripture oft described, Psal. 22.15. & 88.4,6. Chap. 26.19. Ezek. 37.11,12. and the style of dead men seems to intimate somewhat the like here. And yet we need not strain the other word so far: It is enough, that he resembles them to dead corpses cast out, and lying unburied on some waste, as those, Ezek. 37.1,2. But others render the word, *dark*, or *misty places*: So the old Latin, and some of the Jewish writers before. And of dark places, we had mention before, ver. 9. See Psal. 74.20. & 88.6. But these show us not, how the word should come so to signify. No more do those, who on the other hand would have it to signify *the daylight*, that it may answer to *noonday*, before mentioned; as if it were said, *like men dead in the day*, that have no use, or joy at all, of the daylight, as the living have, Eccl. 11.7. because no benefit at all thereby. Which, howsoever they might either of them fit well with the tenor of the prophet's speech; yet until it may be showed, what grounds there is, of giving the word such a notion, we have little reason to admit. Others, fetch it from a root, that signifies *fatness*: and these again run two various ways; the one partly (so some of the Rabbines) understand it of persons: *We are as dead men*, say they, *amongst the fat*; that is, those that are alive, in good health and plight: meaning the Gentiles, among whom, in captivity, they lived but a kind of lifeless life, Lev. 26.38,39. Deut. 28.65–67. Ezek. 36.11. The other party, (and so some of ours) expounding it, of places, or estates: These render it, *in fatnesses*; (and a word very near it, is used for *fatnesses*, Gen. 27.28,29. and for *fat places*, Dan. 11.24.) as if he had said, amid abundance of plenty, and outward means, yet we are as men dead on the nest; we have no joy or comfort, of aught that we have, by reason of calamities otherwise, Job 20.22. Chap. 24.9. See Eccl. 5.17. & 6.2,3. The first, or second; and of those two, the latter, to me, seems most probable of any.

**V. 11.** *{We roar all like bears, and mourn sore like doves:*} All that we can do, is but to lament and bemoan our calamitous condition, either in an higher strain, by roaring like beasts, or, in a lower tone, by mourning as doves. See Psal. 22.1. & 32.3. & 38.8. Hos. 7.14.

*{roar*} The word is used of dogs, Psal. 59.6,14. and one very near it, if not the same, of lions, Prov. 28.15. Chap. 5.29. and of men also vexed within themselves, and by outward lamentation, expressing their inward indignation, and heart's grief, Prov. 5.11.

*{mourn sore*} Heb. *moaning moan*. Of the word, see Chap. 38.14.

*{like doves*} That make a mournful sound, Chap. 35.14. Ezek. 7.16.

*{we look for judgment, but there is none; for salvation, but it is far off from us.*} See before, on ver. 9. Jer. 8.15.

**V. 12.** *{For our transgressions are multiplied before thee,*} In your sight, provoking you to wrath and indignation against us, Psal. 51.4. & 90.8. Ezra 9.14. the reason, why God, and his aid, are so far from us, ver. 2.

*{and our sins testify against us,*} Heb. *answer*, each of them, *against us*; (for the verb is singular, the noun plural, as Chap. 26.19.) as witnesses produced, one by one, and examined upon interrogatories, do answer, and give in evidence, against the party, called in question. So Exod. 20.16. See Chap. 3.9. Jer. 14.7.

*{for our transgressions are with us;*} We cannot possibly, either shun or, shift them off, they stick so close to us, Gen. 4.7. Psal. 32.3,4. & 38.4. & 51.3. Jer. 2.22,23.

*{and as for our iniquities we know them.*} Heb. *and our iniquities we know them*: a very usual redundancy of speech, in that language. See the like, Job 3.8. ch. 8.13. & 45.9. & 48.6. Mat. 21.41. we acknowledge them; we cannot but confess them, Psal. 51.3. Jer. 3.13. It is either a serious and severe profession of the notoriousness of them, as being such as could not be concealed; as Ch. 64.6. or an humble confession and acknowledgment of them, as in the person of the church: as Jer. 14.20. the prophet not exempting himself from that politic body, whereof, with the rest, he was a member; but including himself among the rest, though not as guilty of their sins, yet taking them to heart, as well as his own: and being affected with them, as if they had been his own. So Moses, Exod. 34.9. and Daniel, Dan. 9.5,6,13.

**V. 13.** *{In transgressing, and lying against the Lord, and departing away from our God:*} The prophet passes on to a more particular and distinct enumeration, of those sinful courses, that he had pointed at in the lump, ver. 12. The words run all along in an infinitive form; but they are to be expressed in the indicative: Otherwise, the tenor of the prophet's discourse will not run even: And there is in the phrase, or form of speech, a deficiency, thus to be supplied. *We rebelling rebel; and dealing disloyally, deal disloyally with the Lord, and departing depart away from our God*: that is, *we do exceedingly rebel, and deal exceeding unfaithfully with the Lord, and depart exceedingly from our God*. See the like, (where the tenor being interrupted, does more fully confirm it) Dan. 9.5. *We have sinned, and done unjustly, and dealt wickedly and, rebelled, and departing departed from thy precepts*. And again, ver. 11. *Yea, all Israel have transgressed thy law, and turning aside have turned aside, that they might not hearken to thy voice*. The like syntax we had before, ver. 4. And hereafter again, in the latter part of this verse. I am not ignorant that some interpreters, of prime note, whom ours seems to follow, retaining the verb infinitive only, carry the text on in a continued frame, from the foregoing verse, thus; *we acknowledge our sins*; to wit, *that we trespass and lie*, &c. And this, in Latin, indeed, runs very smooth: But the former is more consonant to the Hebrew idiom. See also the like, Eccl. 9.11. Chap. 43.8. Jer. 6.11. & 14.5. Ezek. 1.14.

*{trespassing*} Or, *rebelling*; as Chap. 1.3.

*{lying*} Or, *dealing disloyally*; as Chap. 57.11. & 63.8.

*{departing away*} Or, *removing ourselves*; as Deut. 27.17. Hos. 5.10. or, *turning backward*, as ver. 14.

*{from our God*} Heb. *from after*; that is, *from walking after him*; or, *following him*; as Psal. 78.71. Hos. 1.2. Amos 7.15. Zeph. 1.6. So, *to come after*, for *to follow*, Mat. 16.24. *the Lord*, and *our God*; as Chap. 56.7.

*{speaking oppression, and revolt:*} Or, *talking, we talk of oppression and apostasy*. See Chap. 59.9. ver. 4. Deut. 13.5. Jer. 29.32. these things are the main matter of most men's talk; apostasy from God, and oppression to their brethren.

*{conceiving, and uttering from the heart words of falsehood*} We do nothing but *conceive*, or, *contrive in our hearts*, (for that is the forge wherein all mischievous matter is framed, and from whence it is produced, chap. 10.12. & 32.6. Mat. 15.19. & 12.34,35.) and *utter*, or *bring forth from our hearts* (for in such things alone are we cordial) *words* or *matters* (as Jer. 7.4,8,22.) *of falsehood*, things fraudulent and deceitful. See on ver. 3,4. There is an elegancy in the words, which our English cannot express.

**V. 14.** *{And judgment is turned away backward, and justice standeth afar off:*} There is no regard had of right, or wrong, in places of judicature: causes are carried the contrary way; and justice is exiled from court and bench, Eccl. 3.16. and no marvel then if God deny it unto us, who have no regard to practice it ourselves, ver. 9.11.

*{for*} Or, *because*; as Chap. 48.8. Jer. 3.21.

*{truth is fallen in the street,*} Truth for want of support, or being overborne with falsehood, falls to the ground, and miscarries in the public, where causes are heard and tried, Job 29.7. Psal. 55.11.

*{and equity cannot enter.*} As Chap. 23.1. & 24.10. or, *cannot go or pass*, as Gen. 10.19,30. it cannot find entrance, being shut out by violence, and not suffered to come in: Or, if it be, for fashion's sake, admitted to some hearing, yet it is not able to pass, or obtain any good issue: the same in substance with the former. See Hab. 1.4.

**V. 15.** *{Yea, truth faileth:*} Heb. *And*; as Chap. 55.1. All regard of truth, either in public, or private, is gone, Hos. 4.1.

*{and he that departeth from evil maketh himself a prey,*} He that will not do as others, makes himself a prey to others: He cannot be safe, that will not be wicked: a man gains nothing, by living harmlessly, but to be made a prey and spoil to wicked ones, Psal. 38.20. Hab. 1.13. 1 Joh. 3.12. So is the word used, Psal. 76.5. Some of the Jewish critics, whom also some of our great ones follow, render it, *is accounted a madman*, or, *causeth himself to be counted a madman*: as was Elishaes minister, 2 King. 9.11. and as the wicked are said to have deemed the devout, Wisdom 5.4. but they produce no clear place, where the word is so used; for that, Job 12.17. is another word; and that Mic. 1.8. as the other also there, of another notion. Nor is it needful here to fly to any uncouth phrase, in that language; as to say, *a man despoiled*, to wit, of his wits; for, *a madman*, (though in Latin the form be not unusual; but with them, then full) when the text will well admit the word in its ordinary notion.

*{And the Lord saw it and it displeased him, that there was no judgment.*} Or, *And this*, or these things, *the Lord seeth; and it is displeasing to him* (Heb. *it was*, or, *is evil in his eyes*; as 2 Sam. 11.27.) *that there is no judgment*: This it is, that incenses God's wrath so against us, Psal. 10.14. Lam. 3.36.

**V. 16.** *{And he saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no intercessor:*} Or, *Interposer*; as Job 36.32. none that would stand up, and endeavor to set things in better order, by speaking, and bestirring himself, in the behalf of truth and right, ver. 4. Chap. 63.5. So rather, than, as some other, following the Chaldee, none to intercede with God, in behalf of his people, Chap. 64.7. Ezek. 13.5. & 22.30. Some supply here from the former verse, *It displeased him, to see that there was no man*; that is, *no helper*, as Chap. 63.5. Or, *no interposer*, as afterward, which *he wondered to behold*.

*{wondered*} Not that God wonders (to speak properly) at aught: but it is spoken in an human strain, to show the strangeness of the thing; that so great, grievous, and general a corruption, should be found among those that were God's own peculiar people having had, from time to time, such constant courses taken with them, for the better information, and institution of them; which other nations abroad had not, Deut. 4.7,8. Psal. 147.19,20. And hence therefore the apostle concludes the universal depravation of mankind, in his natural condition: because it was found so extreme, and in such extremity, so common also, even amongst those, that had the best means, to make them better, Rom. 3.9–19. And some read the words, in a continued tract, either in the present, or the future, *Since that God therefore seeth*, or, *When God shall see that there is none* (that will stir hand, or tongue, to help) *and he wondereth*, or *shall wonder, that none interposeth, his arm shall save for him, and his righteousness it shall sustain him*; as foretelling, what God, at length, will do, for the relief, and deliverance, of his people, when all human helps fail them. The like manner of syntax, see Chap. 30.20. and 35.4. and 37.9,36. & 44.14. & 53.2. and the reading is very probable.

*{therefore his arm brought salvation unto him;*} Heb. *and his arm saved him*, or, *shall save him*, or *save for him*. Either his own power did sustain, and save his people, Chap. 51.5. the pious, that were a prey to the rest, ver. 15. or, he did the work alone himself, without the assistance of any other, or use of other means. See Chap. 63.1,3,5. *arm*, for, *power*; as Chap. 53.1. and, *to save*, for, *to bring salvation to one*; or, *to work salvation*, that is, deliverance, *for one*, Jer. 11.12. Ezek. 44.22. and Psal. 98.1. *his right hand, and his holy arm, hath saved him*, or, *saved for him*; (and the like form is, Judg. 7.2. Psal. 44.3.) which our version there renders, *hath gotten him the victory*: but it may well be here rendered; and so Chap. 63.5. *his arm avenged him*, or *took vengeance for him*; or, *it shall avenge him*, or, *take vengeance for him*; according to that, ver. 18. for it is aright rendered, 1 Sam. 25.26,33. *from saving for thyself*; that is, *from avenging thyself*, (as our version has it) or, *from taking vengeance for thyself, with thine own hand*. For as for that which a learned man observes, that the word of *saving*, in this syntax, signifies *to help*; alleging to that purpose, Deut. 22.27. & Prov. 20.22. it is not general; some of those places pointed to, if not those two also seem to go further. But let it be considered, whether this *for him*, or, *to him*, be not here a mere elegant redundancy; as the like also, Ch. 40.10. *his arm brought him salvation*, that is, *his arm brought salvation*. See the like, Chap. 31.8. *he shall flee him*, for, *he shall flee*, as also Hosh. 8.9. Amos 2.13.

*{and his righteousness it sustained him.*} By *righteousness*, some understand his mercy, and goodness, to his poor oppressed ones, Chap. 54.14. & 56.1. But I conceive rather, that by it, is understood the justice, that he will do for them, upon their oppressors; because what is here termed *his righteousness*, is the same called, *his wrath*, Ch. 63.5. All this, some expound of spiritual deliverance by Christ. Others, whom I rather concur with, of temporal, from ver. 16–19. of spiritual, ver. 20,21.

**V. 17.** *{For he put on righteousness, as a breastplate, and an helmet of salvation upon his head.*} The prophet here describes God, as a man of arms, putting on his armor, and fitting himself for the performance of some notable exploit. The meaning is, that God will so conspicuously show his almighty power, justice, regard of his own glory, and tender affection to the welfare of his people, in the deliverance of them, and in the destruction of their enemies, that they should as evidently appear, and be seen in them, as goodly raiment, or glistering armor, is on the back of one that wears it, Psal. 93.1. & 94.1. & 98.2.

*{For*} Heb. *And*: and so Chap. 52.15. & 53.2. yet it may well enough stand in his native sense here.

*{he put on*} Or, *he will put on*.

*{righteousness as a breastplate*} So Eph. 6.14. Yet see here, ver. 16.

*{an helmet of salvation*} Eph. 6.17. 1 Thess. 5.8. though these are to be understood far otherwise of God, than of us; yet unto these terms the apostle seems to allude there.

*{and he put on the garments of vengeance for a clothing, and was clad with zeal as a cloak*} Or, *he will*, I say (as Chap. 58.10. v. 10.) *will put on*; and, *will clothe himself*. See before. Of the word here rendered, *cloak*, see on Chap. 61.10.

**V. 18.** *{According to their deeds, accordingly he will repay fury to his adversaries, recompense to his enemies*} Heb. *According to retributions, according to them, will he repay wrath to his adversaries*, &c. *retributions*, for, *deeds*, or *deserts*: as Judg. 9.16. 2 Chr. 32.25. and a defect of the pronoun; as Chap. 52.8. He will take vengeance upon the enemies of his people, for all the wrongs that they have done unto them. See chap. 34.8. & 63.6. The like trajection to this here, is observed, Chap. 52.6. Howbeit, the word may be taken in its proper sense, and the text thus rendered, *As in retributions*, (or, in way of large *retribution*, see of such plurals, on ver. 9. Chap. 58.11.) *as in such*, I say, (the repetition makes the sentence more vigorous, as Chap. 8.13. & 48.6.) *he will repay*, &c. the like use of the particle, see Psal. 119.14. Or, as the Jewish doctors expound it, and the points seem to favor it: *As in retributions* (he has done formerly) *he hath repaid*, (to wit, unto Pharaoh, and others the enemies of his people) *so in retribution he will* now again *repay*; repay, I say, *he will wrath to his adversaries, retribution to his enemies, retribution to the islands*: or, reserving the latter verb, as in the text it lies, to the last, *wrath to his adversaries, retribution to his enemies; retribution to the islands he will repay*. Somewhat is supplied in the first member from the second, in the second from the first; as Psalm 1.6. Chap. 13.13. & 30.17. & 60.13,19. and this seems to be the genuine both sense and syntax of the place.

*{to the islands he will repay recompense*} To those of them, that live in divers countries, either maritime parts, or beyond the seas. See Chap. 41. & 49.1. & 66.6.

**V. 19.** *{So shall they fear the name of the Lord, from the west, and his glory from the rising of the sun*} Heb. *And* (as Chap. 41.7.) or, *Then* (as Chap. 36.3.) *shall they fear the name of the Lord*, that is, *the name of the Lord shall be feared*; as Chap. 57.14. *from the evening coast*: as Chap. 45.6. God's name, and his glory, by occasion of this his marvelous work, in the deliverance of his people, and in executing of vengeance upon their oppressors, shall make him renowned throughout the whole world. See the like expressions, Psal. 113.3. Mal. 1.11.

*{when the enemy shall come in like a flood, the Spirit of the Lord shall lift up a standard against him*} This passage is exceedingly vexed and tortured, by variety of enforced strains: the most whereof therefore forbearing to mention, I shall pitch upon those only, that the text may, with some good probability, admit. Some understand the words of a violent irruption made by the enemies, or adversaries of God's people, in, or upon them, together with God's opposition made against them, and defeating of them. To which purpose makes that, which our version has admitted into the text, and is by many authors approved; *when the enemy*, or *adversary*, (as the word is most commonly rendered, and so was, ver. 18.) *shall come in like a flood*, (as foreign forces are not unusually in Scripture said to do, Chap. 18.2,7. Jer. 46.7,8. Amos 8.8. & 9.5. implying, that the enemy's force and fury should be great, and the danger from them no less grievous. See Chap. 8.7,8. Psal. 124.4. Rev. 12.15.) *the Spirit of the Lord shall lift up a standard against him*; that is, shall raise, or lead forces, against them; as the word seems sometime to import, Psal. 60.5. Chap. 10.18. or, *the Spirit of the Lord shall flee*, or, *run upon*, or *against, him*: as if it were said, they shall come rushing in, as with a strong torrent, Chap. 17.12. but the Spirit of God, as a stiff gale of wind, shall run, or rush, upon them, to cause them to recoil; as alluding to that, Exod. 14.20. or, because doubt is, not without just cause, made, whether the verb of *fleeing*, be ever so used; for the word of *flying*, Chap. 14.11. is of a far diverse notion. Some other therefore, not swerving much in sense from the former, render this latter clause, as our margin also exhibits, *the Spirit of the Lord shall put him to flight*; deeming the particle here (as Exod. 7.20. Chap. 53.12. Lam. 1.17.) superfluous: or, supplying the word, *blowing*, and so giving it, at full; *the Spirit of the Lord shall* by blowing against him, *make him to flee*, or, *put him to flight*; as if he had said, *the Spirit of the Lord shall blow him to flight*. (See of such kind of forms, on Chap. 38.17. & 57.8.) God with a blast of his breath only, shall blow him away, and cause him to flee; not unlike that, Zach. 4.6. and this suits very fitly, both with the story, and terms, used, of Sennacheribs, both irruption into the land of Judah, Chap. 8.7,8. & 17.12,13. & 36.1. and the defeat there given him, Chap. 37.7,36. together with his sudden, and shameful, flight thereupon, Chap. 17.13. & 31.8,9. & 37.37. and albeit, the word of *fleeing*, be in another form used for, *to put to flight*, or, *to cause to flee*, Exod. 9.20. Deut. 32.2. not in this; yet that the word is in this form, regular for that notion, from the root, that signifies to flee, neither is, nor can be, denied: and the same root is in the same notion found used in both forms. But some understand this whole passage, as spoken all of one and the same person: and of these, some would have it, as a description of the violent irruption, only of the adverse party, to this purpose rendering the text, *when he shall come like a violent river*, or, *a forcible stream, which the Spirit of the Lord shall drive*; that is, when the enemy shall break in like a river, that being on either side hemmed in with banks, runs in that regard, more swiftly, or having been straitened, in some place, and getting liberty again, runs down with more fury and rage, than before, especially when it shall be driven forward with a mighty wind; for so may the *Spirit*, or *wind of God*, be taken for a mighty strong, or stiff gale of wind: as, *hills of God*, Psal. 36.6. and, *trees of God*, Psal. 104.16. and, *a sleep of God*, 1 Sam. 26.12. for, *steep hills*; *tall trees*; *deep sleep*: or it may have reference to some act, or instinct of God, putting them on upon the service to their own ruin. See Chap. 8.7. Ezek. 38.4. Mic. 4.12. Others, lastly, expound it wholly of God himself, coming in to the rescue, and deliverance of his people, and to the defeat of the adverse party, thus rendering it; *when he shall come like a strait river, which the wind of God driveth*; that is, when God himself, or, an army raised by him, shall come against his enemies, before mentioned, ver. 18. like a strong torrent driven on with a stiff wind, that which as some expound of Cyrus, and his forces, sent by God, against Babylon, Chap. 13.3,17. & 43.14. & 45.1–6. Jer. 51.42. So some other, in the spiritual application of it, suppose it to have some reference to that gale of wind, that came, rushing in upon the apostles, and filled the whole house, wherein they were, at the feast of Pentecost, Act. 2.2. And to pass by all other, a learned man of special note, understanding it, of God's coming in, and by Christ, to propagate his church, and carry on the gospel, throughout the whole world: as Malach. 1.11. Acts 1.8. thus renders it; *For he shall come like a strait river, the Spirit of the Lord lifting him up, for an ensign*: which he further thus explains; He, that is, *the Lord*, or, *the name of the Lord*, supplied from the words foregoing, shall come with much swiftness, and great force, in a short space of time, running through the whole world, and bearing all down before him, that might hinder his free passage; the Spirit of God, in the ministry of the apostles, and Evangelists therewith inspired, lifting up, and bearing before him, Christ, or the name of Christ, (Acts 9.15. Gal. 3.1.) as an ensign, for the faithful to resort unto, and to follow. So is God, or the name of God said to be, as an ensign to his, Exod. 17.15. Psal. 20.5. & 60.4. If the text be understood of temporal deliverance primarily, (as to me, it seems, with the most) I should go with the first, taking the latter term in a notion of flight: if of spiritual wholly, I should concur with this last.

**V. 20.** *{And the Redeemer shall come to Zion*} This some understand of the angel, sent to free Jerusalem, from the fear of Sennacheribs army, chap. 37.36. Others, of Cyrus, sent to Babylon, to set free Sions citizens, there in captivity detained, chap. 43.14. & 45.13. Yet withal, not denying them to have reference unto Christ: of whom others directly, and in the first place expound them; among whom also, some of the ancienter Jewish doctors, and unto whom the apostle himself applies them, Rom. 11.26. nor is it a thing unusual, with this Evangelical prophet, to slip from temporal deliverances, in a close way, unto spiritual, whereof those were types; and to close up the prophecies of the one, with the promises of the other.

*{the Redeemer.*} *Deliverer*, Rom. 11.26. the word properly signifies such an one, as in regard of propinquity, or nearness of kindred, had a right to redeem a mortgage, or the like engagement of land, or livelihood, Levit. 25.25,26. or to prosecute the law against a murderer, Num. 35.19,24. but is used also more largely, for any deliverer, out of thraldom, or avenger of wrong in general, Prov. 23.11. Jer. 50.34.

*{to Zion*} To the Sionites, the people of God, the citizens of Sion. See chap. 1.27. it is, *out of Zion*, Rom. 11.26. which seems to make some difference: and some think the apostle altered it of purpose, to apply it unto the times of which he was then treating, the prophet speaking of the time, wherein Christ was first exhibited unto that people; and said therefore to come unto them, Acts 3.26. the apostle, of a second visit, that Christ should afford that people, in these latter days, towards the world's end, as coming now out of the new Sion, the church of the Gentiles, to them, Heb. 11.23. Acts 3.20. which things, although they be orthodox, and sound; yet I suppose rather, that the apostle retained the ancient Greek version, commonly received in his time, having nothing material to cross that in aught, for which he alleged it, nor disagreeing from truth. If it be objected, that the Greek copies now have not *ἐκ from*, but *ἕνεκα for*; and that therefore the apostle's text ought so to be read, I answer, That it appears by Jerome, that the Greek version was anciently, as the apostle now relates it, both in this branch, and in the next.

*{and unto them that turn from transgression in Jacob, saith the Lord*} Or, *even unto them*, or *unto them*, I say, as chap. 56.5,7. & 58.10. ver. 10,17. for this is added only by way of explication, to show, who of, or in, Sion alone they are, that shall have share in, and benefit by, this deliverance; to wit, those alone that turn from their sins, Deut. 30.2,3. 2 Chro. 6.37–39. & 7.14. & 15.4. for such indeed are the true citizens of Sion, Eph. 2.19. the right Jacob, Psal. 24.4,6. the sincere Israel, Joh. 1.47. the Israel of God, Gal. 6.16. The apostle reads it: *and he shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob*: whereby it appears that he took the Greek, as it was commonly then read, both readings holding out undoubted truth: none having interest in him, but those that turn from their sins; nor any turning from their sins, but by his help. See Acts 3.26.

**V. 21.** *{As for me, This is my covenant with them, saith the Lord.*} *As for me*, Heb. *And I*; as 1 Chr. 28.2. Chap. 66.18. *This is*, or shall be, *my covenant with them*: the words which the apostle adds, *when I shall take away their sins*, Rom. 11.27. seem to be taken, either, as some, from Jer. 31.34. where the same covenant is, in effect and substance also, related; or, as others, from another place of this prophecy, chap. 27.9. or chap. 4.4. in either of which places, the effect of them is found. What covenant should be here intended, is questioned. Some would have it, to be the former promise of the deliverer to be sent unto them. Others, concerning the word, and Spirit, to be continued in Sion: and to this latter, I suppose the words do more specially relate: because the mention of the covenant renewed comes in still, elsewhere, after the redemption, and return, Jer. 31.21,22,31,32. & 32.37–42. & 50.4,5. Ezek. 36.24–27.

*{My Spirit that is upon thee, and my words which I have put in thy mouth, shall not depart out of thy mouth, nor out of the mouth of thy seed, nor out of the mouth of thy seed's seed, saith the Lord, from henceforth and for ever:*} These words, some would have to be a speech of the Father unto Christ; as promising him the continuance of his word, and Spirit, of which, chap. 61.1. for ever, with that seed of his, of which, chap. 53.10. Others, to the church, promising a perpetual succession of the Spirit of prophecy in the church. Others, to Esay, either as a promise, that that Spirit of prophecy, wherewith he was at present endued, should not fail in his followers, or disciples, called his children, chap. 8.16,18. or, that, what God had by him promised, should so be fulfilled, that the memory of it should continue unto all posterity, Psal. 111.4. Or, as some other would have it, in way of a charge, enjoining the prophet to take order, that these spiritual documents (so is the *Spirit* taken 1 John 4.1.) concerning salvation by the Messiah; and that to none, but those alone, that turn away from their sins, should be perpetually in the minds and mouths of his people, after his departure. So Deut. 31.19,27. 2 Pet. 1.12. But passing by these, and other the like interpretations; that which the best, and soundest interpreters give, is this, That God's Spirit and word, should continue with his church, (whom he now turns his speech unto) to direct and instruct it, and the children of it, in all necessaries, throughout all ages successively, even unto the world's end, chap. 30.20,21. & 54.13. Jer. 31.34. Mat. 28.20. John 14.16,17. Eph. 4.11–13. 1 Joh. 2.20,27. 2 John 2.

*{Spirit and words*} Because the word is unavailable without the Spirit concomitant, and cooperating with it, John 6.63. Acts 10.44. 2 Cor. 2.16. & 3.6. & 4.13. See a lively resemblance hereof, Ezek. 37.9,10. Nor does the Spirit of God ever cross or contradict the word, or give directions beside it; and the one therefore is to be tried by the other, Deut. 13.1–4. Chap. 8.20. Joh. 5.39. Acts 17.11. & 26.22. Gal. 1.8,9. 1 John 4.1.

*{thy seed*} The faithful, the seed according to the promise, Deut. 30.6. Rom. 9.6–8. Gal. 3.16,29.

*{thy seed's seed for ever.*} This some would have to contain a more special promise, of the constant continuance of the main body of the Jewish people, in the faith of the Messiah, after their return, that shall be, without any apostasy, or revolt again from him, to the world's end. To which purpose they apply also that, Jer. 32.40. But it may seem to be more large, as above.

### CHAPTER 60

**Vers. 1.** *{Arise, shine:*} In this chapter is the glorious estate of the church of God, under the Messiah, in a most rhetorical manner described, (the restitution of Jerusalem, and the re-edification of the temple there, being underlaid as a type of it) by the multitude of proselytes, and those of chief note and place, that should be joined to it; and with all their best endowments, become serviceable thereunto; and the abundance of spiritual graces and comforts, that should therein be exhibited and enjoyed, and that as in a more eminent manner and measure, than in former times here, so in a fullness of perfection, without any the least interruption, or impeachment, everlastingly hereafter.

*{arise*} Jerusalem presumed to be in a very low and dejected condition at present, being considered (for so the type runs) as in thraldom, at Babylon, is called upon now to *arise*; (as on the contrary, Babylon was commanded *to come down*, chap. 47.1.) and to rouse up herself to an hopeful expectation of her deliverance, restitution, and advancement, now approaching. So chap. 52.1.

*{shine*} Heb. *be enlightened*, or *be light*; some render it, *awake*. I should rather, *look up*; as we use to say, *shore up your eyelids*. So is the word used, 1 Sam. 14.27,29. where it is said of Jonathan, upon the tasting of the honey that *his eyes were enlightened*, whereas, through faintness, he was not able to look up or to look out with them before.

*{for thy light is come;*} Your night of affliction is over, and the day of your prosperity approaches: the day is dawning with you; the morning is arising upon you; and it is high time therefore for you to rouse yourself, and look up, chap. 58.8. & 62.1. Matth. 4.16. Luke 1.78,79. John 8.12. Rom. 13.11,12. Eph. 5.14.

*{and the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee.*} God is beginning to show himself glorious, in your deliverance and restoration; his glory shall be seen upon you, as it sometime appeared on Mount Sinai, Exod. 24.15,16. and upon the tabernacle, Exod. 40.32,33. and in the temple, 1 King. 8.11. But the metaphor, in the verb itself, is taken from the sun rising, and by his bright and lightsome luster, dispelling and chasing away the dolesome darkness of the forepassed night, Cant. 2.17. & 4.6. Mal. 4.2. See vers. 2,3.

**V. 2.** *{For behold,*} Take notice with admiration of a strange change. So chap. 51.22,23.

*{the darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the people:*} There shall be a strange alteration in states: for whereas formerly other people enjoyed much peace and prosperity, while God's people continued in captivity and thraldom, Zach. 1.11,12.
