But I rather, by *righteousness*, understand here, God's beneficence and bounty, with the fruits of it conferred upon his church, his spouse, in a just, that is, in a full, ample, large, and liberal manner and measure, Luk. 6.38. See on ver. 3,11. So seems the word *righteousness*, to be taken, Psal. 112.3,4,9. compared with 2 Cor. 9.9,10. as also, chap. 48.18. & 51.6,8. & 54.17. Dan. 9.7,9,16.

*{as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments,*} Or, that *maketh*, or *useth, priestly*, or *princely attire*, or *bravery*; a defect of the relative; as ver. 9. the verb signifies properly *to exercise*, and *execute, the office of Priest*, or, *Prince*; for the word signifies either. See on ver. 6. and in the next place, *to use priestly*, or *princely carriage*, or *habit*; or *to demean himself as a Priest*, or *Prince*: so here, for apparel; and some conceive it to have reference to the high priest's goodly rich robes, Exod. 28.2,3,40,41. or it may as well allude to some great prince's stately attire, at the time of some solemn festival, Ezek. 23.15. the noun notes *attire*, or *bravery*. See on ver. 3. *like a bridegroom*, who on his marriage day, though but a mean man, yet strives to make himself as brave as he can, as if he were a person of some eminent place, a priest, or a prince; or, as some, as a bridegroom, that (on his wedding day) *ministereth* unto, and attends upon his bride among others, but in a suit or raiment, distinct from, and more eminent, than others: and so also there should be an allusion to the priests' ministerial apparel.

*{and as a bride adorneth herself with jewels.*} Or, *as a Bride, that* (the relative supplied, as before) *decketh herself with her implements*: for the word here used, is of a very large extent, comprehending any utensil, vessel, or instrument, used about house, or husbandry, or persons themselves whatsoever. See on chap. 22.24. & 32.7. as a bride, that is wont to be most curious, in dressing and decking up of herself, and will be sure not to forget, or omit any the least implement, that may be deemed requisite to make her completely set out. See chap. 48.19. Jer. 2.32. There is a sweet elegancy, of like sound, in the original, between the words of *bride*, and *implement*; as in the former branch, the like between *bridegroom*, and *priest*, or *prince*: neither of which can in our English be expressed. Of these rich ornaments of the church, Christ's spouse, and of Christ her bridegroom, see Psalm 45.8,9,13,14.

**V. 11.** *{For as the earth bringeth forth her bud, and as the garden causeth the things, that are sown in it, to spring forth; so the Lord will cause righteousness, and praise, to spring forth, before all the nations.*} God will cause his gracious goodness, which shall produce abundant matter of praise, and fill all places among you, therewith, in so large and plentiful a manner, to extend itself unto you, and to manifest itself among you, that your whole land shall seem to be covered over with it, and it may seem to have shot suddenly up out of the ground; and the people that live about you, shall be enforced to take notice of it, as before, ver. 9. unto that which was there spoken, does this speech of God's people here relate, as acknowledging that now fulfilled and accomplished, that was there promised and foretold. See the like expressions, Psal. 72.3. and 85.11,12. chap. 45.8.

*{the earth,*} Or, *the ground*, being tilled, manured, and husbanded, chap. 5.2. Mark 4.28. Heb. 6.7.

*{bringeth forth her bud*} Or, *sendeth out her buds*, or *sprigs*; for the term, though singular, is here collective; as Psal. 65.10. See of the word, chap. 4.2. of the generality of it, Gen. 19.25. and of the use of it, by way of resemblance, Ezek. 16.7.

*{as the garden causeth the things that are sown in it, to spring forth;*} A garden, a place wont to be more carefully and curiously kept and tended, than others ordinarily are, chap. 1.29. as such a place especially being well watered, chap. 58.11. makes the seeds sown in it, to spring up, soon, and thick, and to thrive exceedingly, chap. 44.4.

*{the Lord will cause righteousness, and praise, to spring forth.*} He will make these things to be as rife among you, as if your whole land were but one garden, sown all over with such seed. See the like similitude, Jer. 31.27.

*{righteousness and praise*} The fruits of his goodness, and beneficence; which shall minister matter of, and produce abundance of praise from his people, in the cheerful and comfortable enjoyment thereof. See ver. 10.

### CHAPTER 62

**Ver. 1.** *{For Zion's sake will I not hold my peace, &c.*} In this chapter the prophet professes his serious purpose of constant and unwearied solicitation of God, for the complete performance of his church's restitution, before promised, chap. 60. & 61. exhorts, and incites other his fellow ministers, to the like practice, ver. 6,7. and relates again, in God's name, with new illustrations, the former promises, confirmed with a solemn oath.

*{For Zion's sake will I not hold my peace, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not rest;*} Some would have these words to be spoken, as in the person of God himself, professing, that he will not let the world, and the kingdoms of the world, be at rest, until he have, by Cyrus, restored his people to liberty, and settled them in their own land again. So some, both of the Jewish and Christian commenters, who add, withal, that God is said to sit as quiet and silent, while he suffers men to tyrannize over his people, Psal. 35.22,23. & 83.1. chap. 42.14. & 65.6. Others, in the person of Israel, the main body of the people, incessantly soliciting God in the time of their captivity, for reparation and restitution, Lam. 2.18,19. so likewise, some of either sort. But others again, with whom I concur, conceive them to be spoken by the prophet, in his own person, imposing on himself, a continued task, to be incessantly employed, either in the preaching and publishing of these gracious promises, and glad tidings, concerning the deliverance and restitution of God's people, or in dealing with God, by intercession and prayer for the speedy performance of it. See the like in the people, Psal. 137.5,6. in Daniel, Dan. 9.2,3. & 10.2,3.

*{Zion, and Jerusalem*} Are here, one and the same; as chap. 2.3. a type of the Christian church: the same thing in divers terms reiterated, to express his earnest desire of the welfare of God's people.

*{until the righteousness thereof go forth as brightness, and the salvation thereof as a lamp that burneth*} Until God's people be fully righted against their adversaries, and their deliverance entirely accomplished.

*{until*} Not that the prophet either was sure, or did make account that he should survive, either until the dissolution of the Babylonian deportation (for he deceased long before it began) and much less until the incarnation and appearance of the Messiah, under whom these predictions were to have their full complement: but that for his time, so long as he should continue, he would never give over preaching of, and praying for these things; as the Psalmist of himself, Psal. 104.33. and others after him successively, he hoped would do the like, ver. 7. and that if he were to live and survive, until either, he would never intermit, or surcease that employment: it is like the apostle's speech of himself, 1 Thess. 4.17. *We that are then alive, and remain*, to wit, at Christ's coming, that is, I, and you, if we be found surviving; or like his charge to Timothy, 1 Tim. 6.14. *to keep the things enjoined him, until Christ's appearance*; which yet he was not to live unto; but he for his time, and others, after him, successively, and respectively, for theirs. So Mat. 28.20.

*{the righteousness thereof go forth as brightness*} Until God clear their cause, by executing justice on their adversaries, chap. 51.22,23. & 59.16,17. See the like expressions, Psal. 37.6. Mic. 7.9.

*{as brightness*} Or, *according to brightness*, that is, *brightly, clearly*; (as, *according to purity*, that is, *purely, exactly*, chap. 1.25.) Or, because the article is here included, *according to the brightness*, not the light alone, to wit, of the day, Prov. 4.18.

*{and the salvation thereof, as a lamp that burneth*} Till her deliverance and restitution, be in a conspicuous and eminent manner effected, chap. 60.1,2.

*{a lamp that burneth*} That burns clearly, John 5.35. and being set aloft, may be seen afar off, Mat. 5.14. a defect of the relative, as chap. 61.9.

**V. 2.** *{And the Gentiles shall see thy righteousness, and all Kings thy glory*} Or, *That* (the copulative for the finitive; as chap. 53.2.) *nations may see thy righteousness, and all their Kings* (a defect of the pronoun; as chap. 61.7.) *thy glory*. Or, *Then shall Nations see thy righteousness, &c.* as chap. 49.21. the end is intimated in the one; the event, or consequent, in the other. The prophet turns his speech to Sion, to the church: a change of the person, as chap. 24.19. & 61.7. That foreign people may see, and take notice of what God has done for you, how he had both righted and honored you; or, Then they shall so do. See chap. 60.3. & 61.6,7,11.

*{all Kings*} That not the meaner sort of people only, but kings also, who are wont to set light by, what inferior ones have in high esteem, may admire your excellency; and not some of their petty princes only, but all, even the greatest, and stateliest of them. See chap. 52.15. & 60.10.

*{and thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name*} That is, as some, your fame, and renown, shall be far greater than ever it was; God so disposing of you; *name*, for *note*, or *renown*, as Gen. 6.4. & 11.4. or, as others, you shall be set in a new estate, such as you were never in before, whereof God shall be the author, Rev. 2.17. & 3.12. or, you shall have a new name assigned you by God, whereby you shall be commonly known, and called, implying a strange alteration of your state, from what formerly it was. See ver. 4. chap. 65.15. Some render this also, in a continued tenor, *That thou mayest be called by a new name, &c.* as before.

*{a new name*} That is, *a pleasant name*, say some; as, *a new song*; that is, a *pleasant song*, Psal. 96.1. & 98.1. and, *new wine*, for, *pleasant wine*, Mat. 26.29. but neither does the word seem so to signify in the places produced, nor need it here be so rendered, rather, as *new wine*, in the one place, is another kind of wine, than that our Savior then drank with them: (for it is not the same word with that used, for *wine new*, in regard of age, opposed to *old*, Matth. 9.17. Luke 5.38,39.) so a *new name*, here, may be put for *another name* (so is it expressly said, chap. 65.15.) than she had been formerly called by: as for *new tongues*, Mar. 16.17. is said *other tongues*, Acts 2.4. but to alter the ordinary version is no need. What this new name is, see expressed ver. 4.

*{which the mouth of the Lord hath named*} Heb. *hath named it*: a redundant form, in that language very frequent. So Psalm 1.4. & 144.8. which God himself has, as by word of mouth imposed on you, answerable to that state, that he has raised you unto: *hath named*; that is, *hath expressed*, say the Jewish critics, referring us to the places, where it is said, *expressed by name*, Num. 1.16. 1 Chron. 12.31. & 16.41. Some of ours, *set, assigned*, or *appointed*, you; as Gen. 30.28. *appoint*, or, *set me out, thy wages*, so rather, than as some, *which the Lord's mouth hath engraven*: as alluding to the manner of engraving men's names, to perpetuate the memorial of them, in marble, or brass; for neither does the metaphor of *engraving*, suit well with the word, *mouth*; nor is the word anywhere found used, for *to engrave*; though *to pierce*, or *bore through*, is it sometime used, 2 King. 12.10. chap. 36.6.

**V. 3.** *{Thou shalt also be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a royal diadem in the hand of thy God.*} Heb. *And thou shalt be, &c. And*, for, *Also*: as chap. 60.17,21. Or, *That thou mayest be, &c.* carrying on the sentence still, as before, ver. 2.

*{a crown of glory*} Or, *as a crown of glory*; the note of similitude is oft wanting. See Psal. 11.1. & 119.119. and hereafter, ver. 5. *a crown of glory*, that is, *a glorious crown*. So Prov. 4.9. Jer. 13.18.

*{in the hand of the Lord*} Here some interpreters make much ado; and having tied a needless knot, devise many ways how to untie it again: a crown, say they, is no ornament of the hand, it is wont to be borne on the head, not to be carried in, or worn on, the hand: and how is Sion then said to be *a crown*, or *as a crown in God's hand*? To this some answer, and so one of the Jewish critics, that there are some places, where they wear their crowns on their hands. So indeed the Christian soldier, in Tertullian's time, carried his laurel wreath, or garland in his hand; because he made scruple of putting it on his head: but in what country they used to wear crowns on their hands, I suppose that grand master could not readily have told. Others therefore suppose, that the word *crown* may signify any rich, or costly jewel in general, as rings, bracelets, and the like. Whereof *rings* may the rather be so termed; because the word that this comes of, signifies *to environ*, or *encompass*, Psalm 5.12. & 103.4. 1 Sam. 23.26. and the ring, as an hoop, encompasses the finger round about: and here again is drawn in that of *engraving*, ver. 2. as well suiting with this notion; because the manner was to carry about them, the names or pictures of their special friends, engraven on their rings, to have them always in their eye. See chap. 49.16. but of that before. Some place would be produced, where the word here found, is so liberally used; for that of 1 Maccab. 4.57. of the *golden crowns*, wherewith the forepart of the Temple was adorned, at the feast of Dedication, mentioned, John 10.22. will not prove it. Others therefore say, that *in*, or *on, the hand of the Lord*, is no more than, *in*, or, *on, the Lord*: and that it may be as well, *on his head*, as, *on his hand*. So, *by the hand of thy servants hast thou reproached the Lord*, chap. 37.24. that is, simply, *by thy servants*; who also did it with their mouths, or tongues, not with their hands: but these two phrases, as they render the particle here, are not matches: and yet the one helps, and leads us unto the genuine notion of the other, being rendered as it ought. The Jewish commenters some of them expound it, *in the hand*; that is, *in the power* and *protection of God*: the hand being mentioned, not as wearing the crown, but as holding and keeping the crown fast on the head of his people, from falling from it; as Lam. 5.16. or being forced off it: as Rev. 3.11. & 12.4. whereunto also some of ours add, that hereby is implied, that this crown is, not to be set on God's head, but to be put into his hand; that is, committed to his care and charge: and *hand*, for *power* or *protection*, is indeed frequent in Scripture. See chap. 49.2. Psal. 31.15. John 10.28,29. as also, for *care*, and *charge*, Psal. 31.5. chap. 3.6. But this seems not to suit so well with this place: for it is not a crown set on the heads of God's people, that is here spoken of; but God's people are said rather to be *a crown*, or, *as a crown*, in some sort, unto him. I conceive therefore, that the words should be rendered; *that thou mayest be as a glorious crown, or diadem, by*, or, *through the hand of the Lord*; that is by means of that work, which the Lord shall effect for you, in your deliverance, and advancement; the particle is very commonly used in that notion, to import the efficient cause or means, whereby aught is effected. So, *thou that savest by thy right hand*, Psal. 17.7. & 136.12. *by*, or, *with a strong hand and an arm stretched out*: and, *by thee, and by my God we shall do valiantly*; and the like, Psa. 18.29. & 44.5. & 60.12. and *hand*, for, *work*; or, if you so please, *power working*, is no less frequent; *that it may be known that it is thy hand, and that thou hast done it*, Psal. 109.27. and, *his hand is still stretched out*; that is, he is working still, chap. 5.25. & 9.12,17,21. as also *finger*, is found used in the same notion, Exod. 8.19. Luke 11.20. See also, Ezra 7.28. & 8.22. Nehem. 2.8. & 5.8. and that the word *Crown* is commonly taken for aught that is a grace, and an ornament, that is, matter of honor, and eminency, in, or, unto, any, it is no less apparent; for so is *wisdom* said to be a crown to him that has it, Prov. 4.9. and *a virtuous woman* a crown to him that has her, Prov. 12.4. and *children's children a crown* to their parents, Prov. 17.6. and, *the hoary head, a crown* to the righteous aged, Prov. 16.31. and, *wealth, a crown* to the wise, that know how to use it, as they should, Prov. 14.24. the meaning then is, not so much as some, that God's people should be as dear, and as precious unto God, as his crown is to a king, the like whereunto, is of his signet implied, Jer. 22.24. as that they should become exceeding glorious and eminent, above other people, as the crown is an ensign of the highest state, and honor, and should in regard thereof, become very conspicuous, of great renown, far, and near, (the crown worn on the head, being more in sight, than any ornament, on any other part of the body) by God's good hand upon them, and for them, by his works already wrought, and to be further wrought for them, and by his constant residence among them, and gracious abode with them, ready, upon all occasions, to engage himself and his power for them, chap. 4.2,5. & 11.10. & 60.1,2,7,9,15,19,20. & 61.9–11. and consequently, that they should become as a crown unto him, the subject matter of his glory, a glory unto him, by whose hand they had thus been advanced, chap. 44.23. & 49.3. & 60.21. & 61.3. for I conceive that to come far short of the prophet's intendment, which some have, that the meaning is, that they should be a kingdom again: they had come nearer home to it, had they said, that they should all of them be kings, or they should be a kingdom consisting of none but kings. See ver. 6.

*{and a royal diadem in the hand of thy God*} The same thing repeated in divers terms; but of the same notion in general.

*{a royal diadem*} Or, *as a royal crown*; the note of similitude supplied, as before. Heb. *crown of Kingdom*; or, *a Kingdom*, as Est. 6.8. the word, *a diadem*, would better fit the former term: both signify *a crown*; but with some difference, in regard of the native notion of either: for the former comes (as has been shown) from a word that signifies, *to environ*, or *encompass*; and so takes in *crowns*, or *wreaths*, of all sorts: so termed, because they do all encircle the head: and thence also has the *diadem* its name in Greek; because it was bound about the head, and was sometime no other, than *a fillet*: as appears by the story of Mithridates his queen, who therewith endeavored to strangle herself: but this latter word has its rising from a root that signifies, not *to encircle*, but *to enwrap*. See cap. 22.18. and does therefore properly denote such an one, as we call *a close crown*; wherewith the head is not environed, and encircled only, but enwrapped, and enclosed in it: whereas *open crowns*, as well as *close*, are in the former word included; the former [whereof], is but as *a wreath*; this as *a wrapper*. Now because these enwrapping tires, I mean solemn, and honorable ones, were of two sorts, the Priestly one, rendered *a miter*, Zach. 3.5. and the Princely one, rendered *a diadem*, as here, so Job 29.14. though not so fitly, as has been shown; therefore as well for distinction, as for further amplification, the crown here alluded unto, is said to be, *the crown of a Kingdom*: not such as the high priest wore; though that also was rich, Exod. 28.36,37. nor such as might beseem some petty prince to wear: but *a crown royal*, such as the King of Ammon's was, 2 Sam. 12.30. such as was Solomon's, Cant. 3.11. such as King Ahasuerus his, Est. 6.8.

*{in the hand of thy God*} Or, *by the hand*. Heb. *palm*; for the *palm* of the hand does the word properly signify. See chap. 1.6. & 49.16.

**V. 4.** *{Thou shalt no more be termed, Forsaken; nor shall thy land any more be termed, Desolate.*} Or, *That thou mayest be no more termed, Forsaken; nor thy land any more termed, Desolate.* Heb. *It shall not be said any more to thee, Forsaken; nor to thy land shall it any longer be said Desolate.* Of which form of speech, see on chap. 61.6.

*{Thou shalt no more be termed, Forsaken*} You shall no longer continue in contempt, and disgrace, as you have done all the time of your captivity; during which, she was not only forsaken of her people, chap. 60.12. but seemed also forsaken, and forgotten, by God himself, chap. 49.14. like a woman cast off by her husband, chap. 49.21. & 54.6,7. & 61.7. Jer. 30.17. Hos. 1.10. 1 Peter 2.10.

*{nor shall thy land be any more termed, Desolate*} Or, *Desolation*: as chap. 1.7. & 17.9. & 64.10. It shall lie no longer desolate, but be peopled, and husbanded, and become fertile, and fruitful again, chap. 4.2. & 61.4,5.

*{but thou shalt be called Hephzibah; and thy land Beulah:*} Or, *But that thou mayest be called, &c. but it shall be said to thee——and to thy land, &c.* as before.

*{Hephzibah*} Or, *Chephtsi-bah*; that is, *my delight is in her*: the name of Ezekiah's queen, Manasses' mother, and it was, it seems, a name, in those times, not unusual, 2 King. 21.1. it implies the delight that God would take in his people reclaimed now, and refined, Psal. 132.13,14. & 147.10,11. & 149.4. So the Saints are David's *Chephtsi-bam*, Psal. 16.2.

*{Beulah*} That is, *Married*; as Gen. 20.3. Deut. 22.22. chap. 54.1. It shall be with you, and with your land, as with a woman that has got a good match; whereby her state is much improved, and advanced, ch. 54.5. Jer. 3.14. Hos. 2.19,20. or, with one, who having been left, by her husband, upon some breach between them, for a time, is now reconciled again to him; and lives now, the breach being wholly made up, in as entire and inward a conjugal conjunction to him, and communion with him; as ever, Hos. 2.7. 1 Cor. 7.11. For they much diminish the force of the term, that render it, with the old Latin, following the Greek, and the Chaldee likewise, *inhabited*; or, as some other, *possessed*: albeit, that be true, which the Jewish commenter here has, that a land inhabited, seems to be as a married wife; a land dispeopled, to sit as a lone woman, or a widow, Lam. 1.1. but they express not the elegancy of the resemblance, here used.

*{for the Lord delighteth in thee*} Or, *because the Lord delighteth in thee*; the reason why she might well be so termed, when the Lord, by restoring of her in that manner, and advancing her to that height of honor, should abundantly show what affection he bore unto her, Psal. 147.11.

*{and thy land shall be married.*} So is the word used, Prov. 30.23. It is as if he had said, Whereas your land has been without inhabitants, having been dispeopled; and so like a lone woman, without children it shall now, as if it were a married wife, enjoying the company of an husband, in a comfortable and honorable way, be replenished with people; as with children, through God's blessing upon it, chap. 54.3,5. Jer. 31.27.

**V. 5.** *{For as a young man marrieth a virgin; so shall thy sons marry thee:*} Or, *when* (as Psal. 75.2.) *as* (the note of similitude supplied; as chap. 47.3,8.) *a young man marrieth a virgin; so* (supplied, as Pro. 26.11.) *thy sons shall have married thee*; carrying on the discourse in a continued context, from the beginning of the Chapter, unto the end of this verse.

*{as a young man marrieth a virgin;*} He does not say, as one of the Jewish doctors well observes, as when an old man marries a young maid, nor, as when a young man marries a widow, whose prime, and flower, another has, before him, enjoyed: but as when a young man, yea, *a choice one*, (for so the word here used, properly signifies: See Ch. 40.30.) marries a *virgin*: implying such an exact correspondency of condition on either side, as might give full contentment, and mutual delight, unto either: a fit resemblance, whereby to decipher the most comfortable and flourishing condition of a Kingdom, or State, so unanimously compacted, and co-united together, that all parts and parties, in it, have abundance of mutual contentment, one in another, Psal. 122.3. Act. 2.40–47. & 4.32–34. for they seem to shoot short, that would have it, an intimation only of peaceable times; for that in times of peace, young men have opportunity of contracting marriage, and enjoying their matches, while they stay at home; whereas in times of hostility, they are sent out to war.

*{so shall thy sons marry thee:*} Concerning this clause, there is much debate among interpreters; and there seems to be in it some difficulty: For how the children of Sion should be said to marry her, their mother, may some doubt well be moved. This difficulty will be utterly taken away, if we admit either the ancient Greek, or the old Latin versions, which render the text, *A young man dwelleth with a virgin; and thy sons shall dwell with thee*; that is, say they, that receive and retain this reading, Your people shall dwell together within your walls, as lovingly, and contentedly, as such a couple are wont to live together. And so the question might soon be at an end, if the Hebrew term here used, and in our version rightly expressed, did not necessarily enforce to some further consideration. Some, therefore, by *Sion's children*, here, understand such of them, as were Teachers, and Pastors, which God promises to raise up from among them, and to furnish his people with, Chap. 60.19,21. Jer. 3.14,15. said here to *marry* her, yet not to themselves, but unto God and Christ, of whom, in the next branch, as makers of the match, between him and her. So Paul of himself, 2 Cor. 11.2. But I find not where this word of *marrying*, in Hebrew, is used, for the making up of a match between two parties; though we so use the word, sometime in our language: but for to take a wife to one's self, and to *own*, and *possess* her, as his wife, as the word originally imports. Others by her *sons*, conceive to be meant her rulers, governors, and the meaning to be, that she should no longer continue in subjection to strangers: but should have rulers and governors of her own natives, Jer. 30.21. as God had, at first, appointed that it should be, Deut. 17.15. For the king, or Ruler, seems to be as an husband to the State, and the state as a wife to him: And she is therefore said to be as a widow, when she is deprived of her king, her Head, chap. 47.8,9. Lam. 1.1. Others, again, by her *Sons*, would have meant her people in general, who being of the same faith and religion, with her, should be joined first, as in a conjugal bond unto her, that is, unto the church, and being so united unto her, should then, together with her, be joined in marriage unto Christ. And true it is, that God's church, and his people, in such tropical speeches, do many times admit notions of divers relations, upon divers considerations, which being taken in propriety of speech, would be inconsistent one with another. So the *new Jerusalem*, is said to be *the Lamb's bride*, Rev. 21.2,9. and they are pronounced *blessed*, that are *as guests invited* unto their *wedding feast*, Rev. 19.9. Now, though in propriety of speech, and the truth of the thing so taken, the *bride*, and the *guests*, cannot be one, and the same: yet certain it is, that this new Jerusalem can be no other than the church; nor the guests at this feast, any other, than the faithful, of whom this selfsame church consists, called the Saints, Rev. 19.8. Again, here children are said to marry her; whom yet she is said to put on as her wedding apparel, or ornaments, elsewhere, chap. 49.18. Howbeit, because the accommodation hereof to the present passage, seems not to come off so smoothly; there are some other ways of solving this doubt, and salving this seeming incongruity exhibited by others. These hitherto have followed the reading, which our English versions, three of them retain. But our ancientest version, commonly extant, renders it, *God shall marry himself unto thy sons*: But besides that, the verb is plural, which unless we will refer to *Elohim*, which is a plural form, and has sometime both verbs, and nouns, plural, joined with it; as Gen. 20.13. Josh. 24.29. and in this very argument, chap. 54.5. will not suit well here, and it may seem overfar to fetch it in hither, from ver. 3. this version leaves out the word, *thee*, affixed to the verb of *marrying*, which may not be omitted. One therefore, of good note renders it; *as a young man joineth in marriage* unto him *a virgin*; so will *he* (to wit, the Lord) *join in marriage* to himself *thee*, and *thy sons*; but he renders no reason of this reddition: And besides the insertion of the copulative, which yet is frequently omitted, (though whether in the conjunction of a pronoun affixed with a noun loose may be doubted) the number of the verb gives a further just ground of demur. Others, lastly, of prime reckoning, render it on this wise; *As, when a young man taketh a virgin, when thy sons take thee wives*: not meaning that they take wives for her, but for themselves: So the word *thee*, should be but an expletive elegantly used; as in those forms, *go thee*, Gen. 12.1. compared with Act. 7.3. *sit ye*, Gen. 24.5. *depart thee*, 2 Sam. 2.22. the like whereunto, is in other languages also very rife; and the reddition of the similitude should be all in the latter part of the verse. But this seems somewhat harsh also, as well as the former. Nor does that run any more smoothly, which another has, and I comprise under this, because it swerves not much from it, who would not have any similitude here implied, but a collation rather of things foretold, to wit, that there shall be again marrying of young men, and maidens with them, and keeping of nuptial festivals, with joy and mirth, an argument, of times of peace and tranquility: for in times of trouble and distress, such things cease, and so did with them, for some time, Jer. 7.34. & 16.9. & 25.10. & 33.11. but that the joy and delight shall be far greater, than any joy of that kind, either among them, or elsewhere, that God and his church, shall mutually enjoy either in other. And this sense to bear, the words must be rendered, *A young man shall wed a virgin*; but *thy sons*, much more delightfully, *shall wed with thee*; that is, in your land; *and the bridegroom shall have much joy of* his *bride*: but *God shall rejoice* much more *over thee*; *and*, for *much more*, says he, as Prov. 6.16,17. & 30.19,31. but nor are those places so pregnant for it; nor is *and*, here, in the text, where he would have it, though it be in the vulgar Latin. In this great variety I shall make bold to deliver my own conjecture, with the grounds of it, and so leave it to the learned. An hint whereof, I have from one of the Jewish doctors, who taking his rise from the Chaldee before mentioned, says the meaning is, that her people should *possess her*; that is, their land, and not be dispossessed of it again, as formerly they had been: and that seems somewhat indeed of it, but not all. The verb *Baal*, therefore does, in the first place signify, *to possess*, or *be possessed* (as we use to speak) *of*, aught, in general, as Lord, or owner of it, 1 Chon. 4.22. after that, more specially, so *to take*, and *be possessed of* a wife, Mal. 2.11. *Judah hath married*, or, *holdeth in marriage the daughter of a strange god*. And indeed, this latter is the more peculiar notion of the word. So Deut. 24.1. *when a man hath taken a woman* (to wit, *to wife*, as chap. 21.11.) *and is possessed of her*, that is, does keep, or hold her, converse and live with her, as a wife: so rather than *married* her, for that was mentioned; implied, at least, in the taking of her before. Hence the noun *baal*, signifies first, in a large extent, *a Lord, Master*, or, *Owner* of aught in general. See on Chap. 41.15. So *the owner of the house*, Exod. 22.7. and, *the owner of the pit*, Exod. 21.34. more specially, *an husband*, as *Lord*, Gen. 18.12. or, *owner* of his wife, Exod. 21.3,32. and the participle active, *boel*, a man *possessing*, or *possessed of*, a wife, being *an husband*, ch. 54.5. and the passive *beulah*, a woman *possessed* by an husband, *a wife*. So it is fully expressed, Deut. 22.22. *a woman held*, or *possessed*, to wit, *of* or *by a man*, as a wife by an husband. This laid, as a ground, I conceive the word rendered *marry*, to be here used in a sylleptical, or metaleptical notion; call it whether you please: and it may be; the former way in the one branch; the latter, in the other: and that the text without much straining, may be thus read; *When, as a young man, that shall have married*, or, *is in marriage possessed of a virgin: so, thy sons shall, as in marriage, possess thee*, or, *keep with thee*, that is shall possess you, hold and enjoy you, as surely as if they were joined in marriage unto you; or, they shall keep, and dwell, and live, together with you (for that is the consequent of marrying) in as cheerful, and comfortable manner, with as much contentment and delight, as a young man is wont to keep, and live with, some young beautiful damsel, whom he has taken unto wife. There is, besides the supplies in the received reading, no more than that of the relative, so rife, as nothing more. See Chap. 60.8. & 61.9. ver. 1. nor is aught here wrung from the text; but what, being fairly dealt with, it freely affords.

*{and as the bridegroom rejoiceth over the bride; so shall thy God rejoice over thee.*} Heb. *with the joy*, or, as *with the joy of a bridegroom, over a bride, shall thy God rejoice over thee*. God will take as much delight and pleasure in you, as such are wont to take the one, in the other: the reason why she should be termed *Chephtsi-bah*, ver. 4. See Chap. 65.19. Zeph. 3.17. and the like form, Chap. 9.3. & 22.17,18. & 24.17. they detract overmuch from the force and fitness of the resemblance, that render the terms here, *a father in law*, and *a daughter in law*; though the words sometime so signify.

*{thy God*} As ver. 3. Christ; God, and Man; and as man of your seed, chap. 7.14. Rom. 1.3. & 9.5. who shall join himself as an husband to you, chap. 54.5. Hos. 2.19,20. 2 Cor. 11.2. Eph. 5.23.

**V. 6.** *{I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem*} That these are the words of God himself, that is, delivered as spoken in his person, is generally agreed. But some read them, as our version renders them in the time past, or present, as spoken of some that God had already set apart, and designed unto the office here mentioned, that which some of them conceive to have reference to God's former speech, as they take it, ver. 1. that he would not rest, until he had restored Jerusalem, and had set some therefore to be continually minding him of it; as one of the Persian kings, sometime, appointed one to call every day upon him, that he might not forget it, to be avenged on the Greeks. Others suppose it to be an answer, much to the same purpose, with the prophet's foregoing speech, carried on from the first verse hitherto. Others read them, in the time to come, *I will set Watchmen upon thy walls*: and these expound them, of the course that God would take for the safeguard of the church, after the restitution of it, for the continuance of its quiet, and flourishing condition, against all perils, or evils, whereby they might be either openly assaulted by day, or secretly surprised by night, chap. 21.6,8.

*{I have set*} Or, *I will appoint*: It is God that sets and assigns men to this office, Jer. 6.27. Ezek. 3.17. & 33.7. 1 Cor. 12.28.

*{watchmen*} Heb. *keepers*, or *watchers*, Judg. 1.24. & 7.19. the Angels, say some of the Jewish doctors, nor do some of ours exclude them; and they seem to be termed *watchers*, Dan. 4.13,23. and are undoubtedly employed, as watchmen, for the safety of God's people, Gen. 32.1,2. 2 Kings 6.17. Psal. 34.7. & 91.11. Mat. 18.10. Heb. 1.14. but they seem not to be so much here intended; the most therefore by *watchmen*, here understand prophets, and Pastors, that are set to watch over God's people, for the safety and welfare of their souls, Jer. 6.17. & 31.6. Ezek. 3.17. & 33.7. Heb. 13.17. Yet some extend the term here unto Rulers, in general, as well Civil, as Ecclesiastical. See chap. 56.9.

*{upon thy walls*} The usual place, where watchmen are placed, as standing in sentinel, to see the further, and discover the approach of any enemy, or other matter remarkable that may concern the public, 2 Sam. 13.34. & 18.24. Yet some would have it rendered, *for thy walls*, expounding it, for the safety of you and them: and true it is, that the particle indeed sometime so signifies; as 1 Chro. 6.49. chap. 31.4. as also, that this is the end of such watching, to keep all in safety, Psal. 127.1. and in this regard, are the *watchmen* termed *keepers of the walls*, Cant. 5.7. But there is no need to alter here the received reading, and most proper use of the particle, chap. 36.11.

*{O Jerusalem*} The same with Sion, ver. 1. a type of the church.

*{which shall never hold their peace*} Heb. *shall not be silent continually*. Which shall never cease, either calling upon God's people, by informing and instructing them, or calling upon God in their behalf, for his mercy toward them, and blessings upon them. For these two are their special employments, as they are *watchers*, Acts 6.4. and some suppose it to allude to the usual practice of watchmen, whose manner is, say they, to pass the time, by night especially, in chatting, or chanting, to keep one another awake: but others conceive, that to *be still*, or *silent* here, imports not so much ceasing to speak, as surceasing, and intermitting their watch, the prosecution of their employment, and their attendance thereunto. So the word is used, Judg. 18.9. 1 King. 22.3.

*{day and night*} Heb. *all the day, and all the night*, as Exod. 10.13. 1 Sam. 28.20. Hence would some gather, that a guard of Angels is here implied; as also, Rev. 4.8. because men must of necessity have times of rest, and intermission: and one of the Jewish commenters observes therefore a difference between these watchers, and worldly ones: for those, when they watch by night, they sleep in the day; whereas these watch day and night: and some run out into allegories, of watching as well in times of prosperity, designed by the day, as in times of adversity, resembled by the night; because dangers are alike in either, Prov. 30.8,9. but neither is any such absolute incessancy, as they imagine, here intimated; nor are any watches in garrison towns ordinarily intermitted, though not by some individual parties continually maintained, but by a constant intercourse of other successively supplied: nor need we have recourse to enigmatical speculations, where the notion is plain and familiar; it is nothing but a promise of a sufficient supply of able persons, that should constantly look to their charge, and diligently perform their duty imposed on them by God, and required of them, for the safety and welfare of his people, described by the employment of Watchers, and Warders, that are set by day, to descry any open approach of an adversary; by night, to discover any more secret access. See the like expression of a constant watch, chap. 21.8. and a pattern of it in Paul, Acts 20.31. 1 Thess. 3.10.

*{Ye that make mention of the Lord, keep not silence:*} The prophet here turns his speech again, from God, to some other, whom he called upon, for the diligent, and constant performance of some offices with God, that might help to further, and hasten the consummation of his church's glorious estate. And the verses therefore seem not to have been so exactly distinguished, either here, or in some other places of this prophet; as chap. 53.9,10. & 58.9. & 59.15. no more than the chapters oft fitly divided. See chap. 4.1. & 26.20. & 52.13,14,15. & 64.1. See 2 Chron. 30.18,19.

*{Ye that make mention of the Lord,*} Whom the prophet here directs his speech unto, (for I cannot accord with those, who make them the watchmen's words, and insert the word *saying*) is not agreed upon, among interpreters. Some, both of the Jewish, and ours, expound it, in general, of all the pious, and religious ones, among the people of God, that should live in those sad times, wherein the church of God should be in that low estate, and despicable condition, before intimated, ver. 4. & chap. 61.1–3,7. of whose *remembrance* of God, in those calamitous times, mention is made, chap. 26.8. and who are called upon, to solicit him, in the behalf of his church, Lam. 2.18,19. and these read the words, *Ye that remember the Lord*: and so the word seems to be used, in this form, Gen. 41.9. Or, *Ye that mind the Lord*, to wit, of his church, whereof more hereafter. But others rather conceive, that some special persons are here intended, set apart unto this peculiar office; to wit, such watchmen, as were before mentioned: and these, though agreeing concerning the persons, yet differ about the notion of the style, or term, here given them: some rendering it, *Ye that mention the Lord*, either by praising of him, as chap. 12.4. & 63.7. or, by praying to him, as chap. 26.13. Others, *Ye that mind men of the Lord*; that put men in mind of God: a special work, and duty, required of God's ministers, to mind them of him, of his bounty and mercy to them, and their duty, in regard thereof, unto him, Psal. 145.5,6,7. 2 Tim. 4.1,2. 2 Pet. 1.13. Others, which I take to be the genuine notion of the term, *Ye that are the Lord's remembrancers*, whose office it is, to be constantly minding God, and soliciting him, in the behalf of his church, as being in special manner called, and set apart, to that employment. See ver. 1. Eph. 1.16. & 3.14,16. Phil. 1.3,4. Col. 1.3,9. 1 Thess. 1.2,3. & 3.10. and it is a term borrowed from certain officers, that are about kings, and Princes, for such purpose, to mind them of those matters that concern the public weal, and welfare. See on chap. 36.3. not that God is subject to forgetfulness, as man is, who had need therefore of such minders, to help his frail memory; or, that he can forget his church, and those things that concern the good and welfare of it, chap. 49.15,16. but that he has in his holy wisdom, so disposed the passages of his Providence, for his own greater glory, and man's more abundant good, that he will be sought to, and solicited for the performance of his gracious promises, as by all his people, in general, so more specially by those, whom to this office he has designed, Ezek. 36.37. Thus is the word used, whence this term comes, in the title of Psal. 38. & 70. *A Psalm to mind*, or, *to bring to remembrance*; to mind God of the present sad condition of the Psalmist himself, in the one; and of the people of God, generally in the other; and to crave relief, and deliverance, for either: contrary to the mind of those, who expound it, *to celebrate God's mercy*, in their delivery; the subject matter of either Psalm, directly crossing that conceit. This notion of the term here, the words ensuing confirm. And that in this office also, the Angels have some interest, may appear by Zach. 1.12.

*{Keep not silence*} Heb. *let not silence be unto you*; or, *let not rest be unto you*. So Psalm 83.1. *let not silence*, or *rest, be unto thee, O God*. See hereof on the former part of the verse, and Psal. 22.2.

**V. 7.** *{And give him no rest*} *him*, to wit, the Lord, whom you are to mind of the condition of his people, ver. 6. *no rest*, or *silence*: the same word that was before, ver. 6. Suffer not the Lord to rest, but call instantly, and constantly, upon him, be importunate with him, to hasten the deliverance of his people, and the restitution of his church. See of such importunity, and wrestlings, to God very grateful, Gen. 32.25,26,28. Hos. 12.3,4. Luke 11.8–10. & 18.1–8. Rom. 15.30. for that which some of prime note here have, who render it, *suffer not silence to be concerning him*; that is, say they, concerning Christ: though the particle be sometime so used; as chap. 56.4. yet seems not to suit so well in this place.

*{till he establish, and till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth*} Until by establishing his church, he make it; or until he so establish and settle his church, that he make it (see of the phrase, chap. 61.5.) *praise*; that is, the subject matter of praise, (as chap. 60.18.) either for which the whole world may praise him, Psalm 67.3,4. & 102.21,22. or, for which, it may become famous throughout the whole world, Psal. 89.3. Chap. 60.9. & 61.9,11. ver. 1,2. *praise*, for, matter of praise; as, *joy*, for matter of joy, chap. 65.18.

**V. 8.** *{The Lord hath sworn,*} The better to confirm, and strengthen the hearts of his people, in an hopeful expectation of the forementioned mercies and favors, he tells them, that God had taken a solemn oath, both for the performance of them, in their due time, and for their continuance also with them. So chap. 54.9,10. Heb. 6.17,18.

*{by his right hand, and by the arm of his power*} Or, rather, *his arm of power*, or *might*; that is, *his powerful*, or *mighty arm*; as, *his arm of glory*, or *bravery*, for, his *brave*, or *glorious arm*, chap. 63.12. God is said to swear, sometime *by himself*, Gen. 22.16. chap. 45.23. Heb. 6.13. sometime, *by his soul*, the same with *himself*, Amos 6.8. sometime, *by his holiness*, Amos 4.2. sometime, *by Israel's excellency*; which he himself alone is, Amos 8.7. here, *by his right hand, and his arm*; which are no other, than his might, and power, manifested in the exercise thereof, Psal. 136.12. chap. 26.11. & 30.30. engaging his almighty power therein; because it was to be employed, and discovered in this great, and glorious design, concerning his people. See ver. 3. It is, as if he had said, Let me not be deemed almighty; let it be said, that I wanted ability to effect it, if I make not this good. See Num. 14.15,16.

*{Surely I will no more give*} Heb. *If I shall any longer give*. Of which form of an oath, see on chap. 5.9. & 22.14. the word *saying* is here wanting; and to be supplied, as Psal. 110.4. & 132.11. expressed Psalm 105.11. Heb. 6.14.

*{I will no more give thy corn to be meat for thine adversaries; and the sons of the stranger shall not drink thy wine, for which thou hast labored:*} Strange people, your enemies, shall not enjoy the fruit of your labors; as formerly they have done, chap. 1.7. See chap. 65.22.

*{I will no more give thy corn to be meat for thine enemies;*} Or, *I will no longer make thy corn meat for thine enemies*; for so the word of *giving* does very commonly signify. See on chap. 61.8. So Psal. 79.2. *they have given the corpses of thy pious ones meat for the beasts*. And God is said to have done it; because by his just judgment on them, for their sins, and excesses; as it was formerly threatened, Lev. 26.18. Deut. 28.30,33,52. so it had been effected, and inflicted on them, Jer. 5.15,17. Amos 5.11. See Judg. 6.3.

*{the sons of the stranger*} Heb. *a stranger's sons*; that is, *strangers*; as Psal. 144.7. See chap. 2.6. & 56.3. & 61.5.

*{thy corn, and thy wine*} *corn* and *wine*, put for all manner of provisions; because two of the principal. So Gen. 27.28,37. Deut. 32.14. Psal. 4.7. Zach. 9.17. in which last place the word rendered *new wine*, is here used for *wine* in general. See Chap. 49.26.

**V. 9.** *{But they that have gathered it, shall eat it, and praise the Lord; and they that have brought it together, shall drink it in the courts of my Holiness*} Your people shall enjoy the fruit of their labors, blessing God for them; and imparting of them unto those, that have been serviceable unto them, in the getting of them in; and to the ministers of God, that were therein to partake with them, Psalm 128.2. chap. 65.21. a note of a quiet and peaceable time and state, chap. 37.13. Jer. 29.23. Amos 9.14.

*{they that have gathered it*} Heb. *the gatherers of it*; to wit, of your corn, ver. 8. they taking part of it, with you, that had their pains used, to get it in for you: for of them, equity required, that a special regard should be had, among other of meaner rank than themselves. Deut. 15.13,14. & 16.11,14. & 24.14,15. & 26.12–14. the contrary practice is condemned, as an accursed course, and a crying sin, Jer. 22.13. Jam. 5.4.

*{praise the Lord*} Themselves blessing the Lord for his blessing upon their labors, and serving him the more cheerfully, in regard of his goodness therein towards them, Deut. 8.10. & 16.10–15. & 26.1–11. & 28.47. and those that partook of it with them, blessing God both together with them, and for them, Ruth 2.4. Job 31.16–20. 2 Cor. 9.12,13.

*{they that have brought it together*} Heb. *the gatherers of it*; to wit, of the wine, ver. 8. or, the grapes of which it was made: this word and the former, are both of one notion; and do here include all the pains taken, as well about the tilling of their grounds, and dressing of their vines; as about the cutting down, and bringing in, of their corn; and the cutting of their grapes, and making their wine; being put for the rest, because the end, and upshot of them, Jam. 5.7.

*{shall drink it in the courts of mine holiness*} Either, *in my courts of holiness*; that is, *mine holy courts*: as, *mine hill of holiness*, for, *mine holy hill*, chap. 11.9. & 56.7,13. or, *in the courts of my sanctuary*; as the word is found used, Exod. 31.11. Lev. 10.18. See chap. 65.18. that is, in the buildings, and places near about the Temple, in which the holy things were to be eaten, Lev. 6.16. for the prophet alludes here unto those solemn anniversary feasts, that were held by them, at Jerusalem, unto which the Levites among other, were invited, Deut. 12.17–19,26,27. & 14.22–29. & 16.11,14. and more specially unto that part of their increase, that was in a more peculiar manner appropriated unto the priests, and was not to be eaten by any, but by them, and theirs, and that within the precincts of the sanctuary, taken at large, for the whole fabric of buildings, within the utmost verge, or wall, of it, Lev. 6.16,18,20,26,29. & 22.10–13. as implying, that they should be as priests. See chap. 56.5. & 61.6. For I cannot assent unto that reverend writer, who supposes a trajection to be in the words of the text, and would have them thus read, *The gatherers thereof shall eat it, and the inners thereof shall drink it; and shall praise the Lord in the courts of my sanctuary*: as if the courts of God's house, were the place here designed, not to the eating of it, but the praising of God for it; which way soever we take it, there is a passage from person to person, as chap. 61.7.

**V. 10.** *{Go through, go through the gates*} The prophet, as in spiritual raptures is usual, does oft wind and turn, in his discourse, from one matter to another, from one party to another; though all concerning the main argument principally intended, the restitution of God's people. In regard whereof, the context of his speech, both here, and elsewhere, is very abrupt, and by reason thereof, sometime also, somewhat obscure. He had before introduced the Lord, promising to furnish his people with a constant supply of faithful watchmen, for their better security, ver. 6. he had then called upon those, whom that office belonged unto, for the diligent performance of some duties, for the furtherance of their weal, ver. 7. he had then brought in again God by a solemn oath, assuring them of a constant course of tranquility, ver. 8,9. he now directs his speech to the people themselves; and from them instantly diverts it, again, to others, that were to be helpful, and useful, in their return from captivity, ver. 10. then returns again to God, and a proclamation in his name published, ver. 11,12.

*{Go through, go through the gates*} Heb. *pass, pass by*, or, *through the gates*; so is the particle taken, Jer. 7.2. & 17.20. now because this admits a divers construction: for it may be understood as well of coming in, as of going out. Hence arises much variety in the interpretation of the place; for some suppose it to be an intimation of the great multitudes of those, that, upon return from captivity, should come thronging into the City, chap. 60.11. or an invitation of people to come flocking into the church, whereof the City was a type, chap. 26.2. Others, an adhortation unto those, that being returned, were now seated in the city, to repair to the Temple, there to perform holy duties, in way of thankfulness to God; as Psal. 118.19,20. ver. 9. And whereas the words, next ensuing, of fitting the way for them, may seem to imply, that the place is not meant of persons, now returned, and at their journey's end; but of persons preparing for, and about to travel: This to salve, some would have it understood of those already there seated and settled; as called upon to go forth at the gates to meet, and make way for others that were coming, and on the way toward them; which they apply unto the faithful Jews, at first, called to Christ, as incited to prepare for, and receive the Gentiles, that were to come in to them. But in all the parallel places of this prophet, the mention of preparing and fitting the way, is constantly for the people returning from Babylon, and that by others, for them: not by them, for any other; whom they should go out to meet: though it is not denied, that their return was typical; and a type resembling the delivery of people from the thraldom of sin, and Satan, and the conversion of them, unto Christ, Acts 26.18. Those therefore that conceive this passage to concern those that were now upon return, understand them; Some, as directed to the persons themselves, as calling upon them, to pass by the gates, and come forth out of Babylon, or other cities, where they made their abode, having by Cyrus his Proclamation, liberty now so to do, alluded unto, ver. 11. and so it is in effect the same with those places, chap. 48.20. & 52.11. where they are in like manner called upon, so to do: and this I take to be the genuine sense of the place; though if any shall suppose, that in these words, other people are called upon, to go out of their gates, that is, out of their several cities, or places of abode, (as Deut. 12.17. & 14.27.) to help to make the ways fit for God's people to pass by, I should rather thereunto incline; than to that which some other, as well of the Jewish, as of ours, have, that it should be a command given to officers, *to pass unto the gates*, that is, *from gate to gate*, as Exod. 32.27. or from city to city, to proclaim the liberty for return granted to God's people, Ezra 1.1. or, to that of our ancientest English, that renders it, *Depart, go asunder, ye that stand in the gate*; as if it were a command given to people, to quit, and clear the gates, for the freer passage of God's people. Howsoever it be taken, the word is doubled, to add the more emphasis to it: as the like is, in the words ensuing.

*{prepare ye the way of the people*} Or, *prepare way for the people*. Make the people way; or, prepare and fit the way, for God's people to pass. See chap. 41.3. & 57.14.

*{cast up, cast up, the highway;*} Or, as some render it, *tread down, tread down, the causeway*; because the verb is so deemed to signify, Jer. 50.26. & Lam. 1.15. and causeways are first cast up for the raising of them, then trodden, or rolled, to make them even and plain: but of the sense of the former place there is some doubt; and the word in the latter place is divers from this, and seems to be of another house; the received reading is safe and sure. See chap. 57.14. and of the noun, chap. 35.8.

*{gather out the stones;*} The verb here used, signifies in general, *to stone*; but more specially, sometime, *to pick stones out*, as chap. 5.2. sometime, *to cast stones in*, or *at*, one: as 2 Sam. 16.6,13. Hence arises a divers exposition of this place. Some rendering the word, *stone it*; that is, *pitch*, or *pave*, it, *with stone*: as the particle is used, Cant. 1.1. & 3.9. to make it the more firm, and plain; as ways well paved, or pitched, are wont to be. Others, whom our version follows; *stone it*, that is, *by stoning*: as Chap. 5.2. clear it, or, free it, *from stone*; that is, *from stones*: the word being taken collectively, as Hab. 2.11. that there may no stones, or, stone, be left lying in the way for God's people to trip, or stumble, at, Psal. 91.12. as Hos. 9.12. *I will bereave them from a man*; that is, so that there shall not be a man of them left: pick the stones out of the way, to make it the more easy, and the less troublesome, or offensive: and this the rather I embrace, because in that place parallel to this, Chap. 57.14. the words are, *take away the stumbling*, (whether stone, or block) *out of the way of my people*.

*{lift up a standard for the people*} Or, as others, *to the people*; (as chap. 53.1.) or, *peoples*, rather, as chap. 56.7. for the word is plural. Heb. *over the peoples*; so high, that being over them, or above them, it may be seen of them. Because the Jews in their captivity, were dispersed into many places, and were now sojourning among sundry people, there is an ensign said to be set up aloft; either, for those people among whom they should then be found resiant, to cause them to bring the Jews home from among them, Chap. 49.22. & 66.20. or, as others, to those people, for the Jews abiding with them; that resorting to it, and having gathered themselves together, they might travel in troops, Chap. 60.8. with more conveniency, by mutual society, and safety. See Chap. 11.11,12.

**V. 11.** *{Behold the Lord hath proclaimed unto the end of the world,*} Heb. *The Lord hath made to hear* (that is, *published*, or, *caused this to be heard*; as chap. 45.21. 2 King. 7.6.) *unto the end of the earth*: so far as any of them might, be dispersed, Deut. 30.4. chap. 48.20. The words have reference to the Proclamation sent abroad, through God's appointment and procurement, into all parts, by Cyrus, 2 Chron. 36.21–23. Ezra 1.1,2.

*{Say ye unto the daughter of Zion;*} Let this be published, and made known, unto those that belong unto Sion, to my people in all parts; so chap. 48.20. Zach. 9.9. Mat. 21.5. *of the daughter Sion*. See on Chap. 1.8.

*{Behold, thy Salvation cometh,*} Or, *is come*; your deliverance is at hand: or the time of it is come, Psal. 102.13. chap. 51.6. & 56.1. & 60.1. or, *thy salvation*, for the Author of *thy salvation*; your *Savior*, as Luk. 2.30. your King, that saves you, chap. 33.22. is come to you, to save, and deliver you, Psal. 74.12. Zach. 9.9. Joh. 12.15. and that it is thus to be here taken, the clause ensuing shows, See chap. 59.20.

*{Behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him.*} Of this passage, see before, on chap. 40.10. For I suppose that learned man to be out of the way, who conceives the meaning of the latter to be, that God, for his work, or service, done him by Cyrus, had given him his reward beforehand, chap. 45.1–4. As for some other, he rewarded Nebuchadnezzar afterward, Ezek. 29.18–20. The prediction of God's coming in this manner, is ushered in with a threefold *Behold*; as to note the certainty of it, as a thing in present sight; so to intimate the state and magnificence of it, as being a matter of much admiration and wonderment, See chap. 63.1. and the like threefold *Behold*, but in another argument, Jer. 23.30,31,32.

**V. 12.** *{And they shall call them, The holy people;*} Or, *and men shall call them*, (to wit Sion's sons, or those that belong to her; and shall now again people her, ver. 5.) or, *they shall be called* (as the like, Mal. 1.4.) *an holy people*. Heb. *a people of holiness*; as, *a seed of holiness*, for, *an holy seed*, Chap. 6.13. See Chap. 4.3. and 60.21.

*{the redeemed of the Lord*} Such as God, by rescuing, and delivering them out of the hands of so powerful adversaries, in so strange a manner, has shown, that he owns for his, chap. 35.9. & 51.10. & 63.4. See the term also, Psal. 107.2.

*{and thou shalt be called, Sought out;*} *thou*, O Sion, ver. 11. (a passage from person to person: as ver. 2.) *shall be called*. Heb. *it shall be called thee*. See ver. 4.

*{Sought out*} Or, *Sought unto*, or, *Sought after*: as one had in high estimation, and regard: whom out of respect, and regard, men repair, and resort unto. See Psal. 111.2. contrary to that, which was formerly said of you, in the time of your low, and dejected estate, *This is Sion that none seeketh after*, Jer. 30.17.

*{a city not forsaken*} As she seemed to be formerly, in the time of her captivity. See ver. 4.

### CHAPTER 63

**Ver. 1.** *{Who is this, that cometh from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah;*} Whether this passage has any connection with that foregoing, or no, is questionable. Some suppose that it has. And that to confirm God's people, in the assurance both of their deliverance, and of their continuance in a settled estate after their return, therein promised, God is brought in, returning, as in triumph, from the conquest, and slaughter of those, that were the chief enemies of his people: partly thereby to make way for the one; and partly to give, security unto them, for the other: as Chap. 37.29–36. & 38.6. and it may seem indeed to have reference unto those words; *Behold, thy Savior cometh*, Chap. 62.11. Whether it have or no, (and it is probable that it has) certain it is, that the prophet's words run, as if in a vision he saw the party here spoken of, appearing as some great Commander, in goodly rich robes, the more goodly, because besprinkled with the blood of his enemies, returning in triumph from the slaughter, and conquest of those, whom he had vanquished in fight. See somewhat the like passages, in that triumphant Psalm, 68. ver. 7,8,12–14,17,18,21–23,33. as also, Rev. 19.11–16.

*{Who is this,*} It is a question, who it is, that moves this question. It is the Angels, say some of the ancients. It is Israel, say some of the Rabbins. It is the church, say some of ours. It is the prophet Esay, say others, of either: to whom the sight, or apparition was offered in a vision, or ecstasy; with whom I concur. So one of the Elders to John, but as inviting him to ask, what they were, *Who are these?* Rev. 7.13,14. And it seems spoken by way of admiration; as the like, Cant. 3.6. & 8.5. And it is a second question, who the party should be, that thus appeared to the prophet. Some say, God, that gave order for the Proclamation before mentioned, Chap. 62.11. So some, both of the Jewish writers, and other. Some say, Christ, the Messiah; so many of ours, both Old, and New. Some say, Michael, one of the chief Angels; that had been fighting with the Persian, Dan. 10.13. so some of the Jewish masters. Some, Judas the Maccabee, of whose victories, against the Edomites, Joseph the Jew, lib. 12. ch. 11,12. & 1 Mac. 5.3. so a learned late writer. I shall accord with the first, because this place seems parallel to that other, Ch. 59.16–18. the very same terms, some of them, being used also in either.

*{that cometh from Edom,—from Bozrah;*} I join these two together, for the more expedite explication of either; concerning which to let pass the Rabbins' ridiculous conceit, taking Edom, still for Rome, where in these Prophecies, they meet with it; because in Hebrew the letters of either are much alike: and their state was by the Roman Empire, utterly ruined: as also the groundless opinion of some Christian writers, that would have Edom here to be Antichrist; though I doubt not, much less deny, but that by these victories achieved by God, for his people, against their adversaries, and oppressors, are typified Christ's proceedings against the enemies of his church, and so against Antichrist, among the rest, Rev. 19.19–21. & 20.7–10. But by *Edom*, in the first place, is here meant *Idumea*, the country inhabited by the posterity of Esau. Of which see Chap. 11.14. By *Bozrah*, what is meant, is by some made more questionable. For whereas there were two *Bozrahs*, at least, one, in the land of Moab, Jer. 48.24. another in Idumea, Gen. 36.31,33. Jer. 49.13,22. and was the royal city of that Realm, Amos 1.12. Some would have that of Moab to be here meant; because they find Edom, and Moab to be joined sometime together, as the joint adversaries of God's people; as Ch. 11.14. But I suppose rather that *Bozrah* to be here meant, that was held by the Edomites (from whose country this Conqueror is said to come) and was their head city: as also, I find them both joined together, Chap. 34.6. a place parallel to this. But it is demanded why this gallant Commander should be said to come from the overthrow of the Edomites, and from Bozrah; and not rather, from the conquest of the Chaldeans, and from Babylon; these being the principal oppressors of God's people, whose state therefore for the deliverance of them, was to be destroyed, Chap. 14.1. & 44.14. Whereunto the answer is, that the Edomites are put for the enemies of God's people in general, in regard of the ancient, intestine, and inbred enmity, and malignity in their first founder, against their progenitor his brother, Gen. 25.22,23. & 27.41. continued, yea, perpetuated in his posterity, Amos 1.11. and that notwithstanding the nearness of kindred between them, Mal. 1.2. and the fair, and friendly carriage of the Israelites towards them, in their passage to Canaan, Deut. 2.4,6. And the Laws made afterward in favor of them, above some other neighboring nations, Deut. 23.7. yet none had demeaned themselves more spitefully and cruelly, than they at the surprisal of Jerusalem, and the sacking of it by the Chaldeans, Psal. 137.7. Obad. 10–14. in regard whereof God's people, as they threaten Babylon, that she should be served with the like sauce, as she had served in to them, Psal. 137.8. so they foretell Edom, that she was to drink drunk of the same cup, that they had drunk so deep of before her, Lam. 4.21. Add hereunto, that Edom is the rather mentioned, in respect of her neighborhood; to assure God's people of their better security, and more constant tranquility, their neighboring adversaries being subdued and quelled, as well as their enemies more remote. See Chap. 60.11,18. & 62.8,9. For as concerning that, which a reverend and learned interpreter has, that neither Edom, nor Bozrah, are here mentioned with any reference at all unto those places, but in allusion only to the names they bore; the one signifying, *red*; (a twofold reason whereof, see Gen. 25.25,30.) whence also the *Edomcan*, or the *red sea* was so termed: and suits well with one, that comes from *shedding of blood*, ver. 3,6. in garments also therewith besmeared, ver. 2. the other having a notion of *vintage* in it; and this Warrior is said also to come from *treading the winepress*, ver. 3. I suppose it to be somewhat overcurious; albeit that to the notations of terms, allusions be oft found. But not to insist on that which might be excepted, that *Bosrah* (whence by change of a vowel, the Punic, *Butsra*, and by transposition of letters, the Greek and Latin *Byrsa*, though Ptolomy, coming near to the Hebrew, retain the name *Bostra*) comes not from the verb *batsar*, as it signifies, *to cut grapes*, Lev. 25.5. Deut. 24.21. but as it signifies, *to fortify*, or *to fence*, Chap. 22.10. & 51.23. the Prophecy here seems principally to have an eye unto the place, and to the disposition of the people thereof possessed, Gen. 26.9,33. Deut. 2.5.

*{with dyed garments*} Or, *with garments tainted*, or *stained*. Heb. *leavened*, as some: because the verb it comes of, signifies, *to leaven*, or *to be leavened* rather, Exod. 12.34,39. Hos. 7.4. But the word, though nowhere found so used in Scripture; yet in the writings of the Rabbins, is used for *to dip*, or *to be dipped*, whether to wash, or to dye. And from words of that notion are the terms that betoken *dyeing, tainting*, and *staining*, both in Greek and Latin derived; hence some render it, *wetted*, or *moistened*: I should rather, *dipped*, or *stained*; and this receives strength from that parallel place, Rev. 19.13. he was clad with a garment dipped in *blood*, see ver. 3. the Hebrew is, word for word, *dipped*, or *stained of clothes*, or *garments*, that is, having his garments stained, as if they had been dipped in somewhat that might stain them. So ch. 36.22. *rent of garments*, for having their garments rent: one of the Rabbins renders it, *red*, or *redded*, that is, *dyed*, or *stained red*. But he seems therein rather to have regarded the subject matter of the relation, than the strict notion of the term.

*{thus that is glorious in his apparel:*} Heb. *this gorgeous one in his apparel*, that is, this gorgeously appareled one, in such a rich coat of arms, as great commanders, and generals, used to go out to war in. See the term applied to apparel, Job 40.10. Psal. 104.1. Prov. 31.22.

*{walking in the greatness of his strength;*} Or, *marching*, or, *stalking*; as intimating a going in state, as a word in Hebrew, next door to it does, Judg. 5.4. Psal. 68.7. It seems properly to signify, *a traveling unto, in*, or *from some foreign Country*, chap. 51.14. Jer. 48.12. in which latter place also it is used, for *to cause*, or enforce others so to do. Whence the Rabbins here, some of them expound it, either of driving the enemies of God's people out of their countries, or of bringing back the Israelites into their own country, from the lands wherein they remained as exiles, ch. 51.14. but it is not here in that form: one of them renders it *girt*: and God indeed is said to be *girt with might*, Psal. 65.6. But he shows not how this word should come so to signify: the old Latin renders it, *gradiens*: some late writers, *incedens*: both terms used of a warlike march, and stately gait: and may seem either well to suit with the notion here intended; which those that render it *traveling*, seem not to reach: For the meaning seems to be, that he passes along, not as one fleeing, or retiring, after some foil received, or discomfited in fight; as chap. 31.8,9. but as one marching leisurely, with a stately gait, and with strength entire, having made a full riddance of his foes, and fearing no enemy behind.

*{in the greatness of his strength.*} Or, *with his greatness of might*; that is, *with his great might*, as Psal. 33.17. *by his greatness of strength*, that is, *by his great strength*: and *his arm of might*, for his *mighty arm*, chap. 62.8. *marching with his*, that is, *his own might* (as, *his soul*, for, *his own soul*, Psal. 22.29.) not, as other commanders, with strength arising from troops of horse, and horsemen, and companies of foot; but with his own might alone, ver. 5.

*{I that speak in righteousness;*} God's answer returned to the prophet's demand; describing himself, by his fidelity in his promises, and his ability to perform them: both which were now manifested by the accomplishment thereof; as by his present garb, and gait might appear.

*{speak in righteousness;*} That is, as some, *that speak of righteousness*; as the particle seems to signify, Deut. 13.12. Jer. 38.24. & 48.27. of God's justice to be executed upon his enemies, and the enemies of his people; which the old Latin swerves not much from, rendering it; *That speak righteousness*, that is, pass a just sentence of condemnation upon them; as *to speak judgments*, is used, Jer. 1.16. & 39.5. But I suppose, with others, that *in righteousness*, here, is *righteously*; as, *in truth, truly*; sincerely, Psal. 145.18. ch. 38.3. So, *in righteousness, righteously, faithfully*, (for *faithfulness* is a branch of *righteousness*, Heb. 6.10. 1 John 1.9.) So *to swear in righteousness*, is, *to swear righteously, uprightly, faithfully*, with a purpose to perform, chap. 48.1. Jer. 4.2. I utter nothing in my promises, but what I intend to make good, and what you may now see accomplished. See Chap. 55.10,11.

*{mighty to save?*} Heb. *much*, or *great*; as Psal. 25.11. some render it *sufficient*: some, *ample*: it implies indeed God's ample power and ability, of itself all-sufficient to save and deliver his, without assistance of any other. See ver. 5.

**V. 2.** *{Why art thou red in thine apparel?*} Or, *Why is thine apparel red*: As before ver. 1. A second question, by the prophet, moved unto this great Warrior, thus appearing. As if he had said, If you be of that might that you speak of, how comes your gorgeous apparel to be all overstained thus, like one that were come out of some winepress, from treading of the grapes?

*{and thy garments like him that treadeth in the wine-fat?*} Or, to make the sentence full and exact to the text, *and why are thy garments, as* the garments of *a treader in the winepress?* See the like defect, and supply, chap. 5.29. Dan. 4.33. Like one that by treading of the grapes in the winepress, comes to be besmeared all over with the blood, (as it is termed, Gen. 49.11. that is, the juice) of them; the liquor crushed out of them. See chap. 16.10.

*{that treadeth*} Heb. *a treader*. One that treads grapes: as before the Noun regent was wanting, so here the Noun under regiment. Of the like whereunto, see on chap. 61.3.

*{in the wine-fat*} Or, *winepress*; as it is rendered, Lam. 2.15. Joel 3.13. But I suppose our translators render it thus here, for variety sake only; because another, of the same notion, is used in the next verse. The term here is, *gath*: in the use whereof, some would find an allusion to the name of *Gath*, a town of the Philistims, where Goliah was born, 1 Sam. 17.23. So called, say they, because winepresses were there first invented, and great use of them in those parts. But to pass by the improbability of the notation, and the ground given for it, there is little reason to imagine that the prophet, in using the common and most usual name of a winepress, and speaking of Idumea, should have any glance at a city in Palestine.

**V. 3.** *{I have trodden the winepress alone;*} God's answer to the prophet's second demand, ver. 2. and that conceived in a metaphorical sort, correspondent to the similitude, made use of in the question. As if he had said, You say that I am arrayed like one that had been employed about the treading of grapes in some winepress: and it is true indeed, that I come from such a like employment: I have been treading in a winepress, but another manner of winepress, than that wherein grapes are wont to be trodden. And here again some conceive Bozrah to be alluded unto: For, because, say they, the country about Bozrah was, much of it planted with vines; it is as much in effect, as if he should say, I come from another manner of vintage, and treading of grapes for the making of wine, than that, at, or about Bozrah, uses to be. But whence they have this concerning the land bordering upon Bozrah; unless it be from the notation of the name, of which see on ver. 1. I know not. I find not the land of Edom, for bearing of vines, or yielding of much wine, anywhere commended in Scripture. This we find, that when through the wrath of God, people endure heavy pressures; especially unto the utter undoing, and destroying of them, they are in Scripture phrase compared unto grapes, that are squeezed, and crushed under men's feet in the winepress, and are said to be trodden in the winepress of God's wrath. See Lam. 1.15. Rev. 14.19,20. The meaning is plain, I have discomfited the enemies of my people, and trodden them down, as grapes in a winepress. So of Christ, Rev. 19.15. in which place, parallel to this, the reason seems rendered, why his garment was said to be *dipped in blood*, ver. 13. *because it is he that treadeth the winepress of God's wrath.*

*{trodden the winepress*} That is, the grapes in the winepress as before, ver. 2. So, *to drink the cup*; for, the wine in the cup, Jer. 49.12. Ezek. 23.32.

*{winepress*} A word divers from the former, ver. 2. but in sense the same. It comes from a word that signifies, *to break*, or *dissolve*; Psal. 74.13. chap. 24.19. and is so called, because the grapes are bruised and broken in it. The word is nowhere found but here, and Hag. 2.16. where this rather than the former might be rendered, *a fat*: for it is there distinguished from the *press*; (which is by a third term there expressed) and seems to be put for the *fat*, or vessel that receives the wine, running into it from the press. And by collation of these two places, it may justly be deemed to comprehend both.

*{alone; and of the people there was none with me*} This is added, as to render a reason why his raiment was so besmeared with blood: because he trod the winepress himself, whereas the owners of vineyards, and great wine masters are wont to do it by others not meddling with that kind of employment themselves: so withal to intimate the great might and valor of this gallant Warrior, that performs all himself, in the slaughter and conquest of his enemies; not needing, or requiring the assistance of any, for the effecting of aught, like worldly Commanders, that of themselves can do nothing without the help of men and ammunition; but able to dispatch, and transact all that he pleases by his own might alone, of himself. See ver. 1. chap. 44.24. Hence divers interpreters are induced to expound this whole discourse wholly of the work of men's redemption, by Christ wrought upon the cross, by the effusion of his blood: the rather, for that there he is said to have spoiled principalities and powers, and to have led them openly in triumph, Col. 2.15. In which action of his, most certain it is that he had no creature his coadjutor. But others, even of the best note and rank, do herein dissent from them, conceiving the current of the context to run rather another way, as respecting rather, in a spiritual sense, Christ's designs, as a powerful Prince and a valiant Warrior, in the behalf of his people, by executing vengeance upon his and their enemies, than the performances of his priesthood. Against which if it be objected; that in the destroying and subduing of such, God ordinarily makes use of men: and it cannot be said therefore, that therein he is alone, and none with him. To this some answer, that the meaning is not, that none assisted him; but that there were none able to maintain fight with him, Chap. 27.5. And the latter branch of this passage may well admit that sense. *Of the people*; that is, of the Edomites, from the slaughter of whom I come, there was none *with me*; that is, none that durst, or was able to stand it out *with me*. For so is the like phrase used, Psal. 55.18. where when David says, *there were many with me*; he means not many fighting for me; but warring *with me*, that is, against me. And the words following, both in this verse and the next, will well agree hereunto; yea, the next branch indeed seems to exact it: for there is nothing to refer the pronoun demonstrative thereunto, in these words, *I trod them*, but the word, *people*, in this. And this may seem to be therefore the genuine sense of the words. But this answer, though it may clear the sense of that passage, and so may take off the edge of the argument, so far forth as it is thence drawn; yet it meets not with the word *alone*, nor with that which comes after, ver. 5.
