Others, therefore answer, that God indeed uses men as instruments, as well bad as good, for the effecting of such things; but so, as that, to speak precisely, they afford no assistance, they add no strength to him: Yea, they receive from him whatsoever strength they have, Chap. 45.1,5. Being no more able to do aught without him, than a rod or staff to strike; an ax, or a saw, to hew or saw, without the hand of the workman, or of him that holds it, chap. 10.5,15. Nor, to add that they many times mind nothing less, than the doing of God's work, or the fulfilling of his Will, chap. 10.6,7. And that God oftentimes, so carries things, when he makes use of them, that by his power alone it appears, that those works were brought about, which he is pleased to effect by them, Psal. 109.27. Chap. 49.26. Thus it is said, Deut. 32.12. *The Lord alone did lead him.* And yet, *he led* them *by the right hand of Moses*; hereafter, ver. 12. and, *by the hand*, that is, Ministry, *of Moses and Aaron*, Psal. 77.20. So, albeit, the Lord made use of human helps; of foreign princes, as Cyrus, Darius, Artaxerxes, of godly governors, as Zerubbabel, and Nehemy, of men and arms, for the restitution of his people and protection of them, and the re-edifying, both of Temple and City; yet by his prophet speaking to them of these things; *Not by might*, or *strength*, says he, to wit, of man, *but by my Spirit, saith the Lord*, Zach. 4.6. And although God make use of men also, for the battering, and *beating down* of Satan's *strongholds*, erected in men's hearts, and the *subduing of all unto the obedience of Christ*; yet the *power*, whereby all this is done, is *from God* alone, 2 Cor. 10.4,5. and the business is so carried, that *the power* may appear to be, *not of man, but of God*, 2 Cor. 4.7.

*{for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury*} Or, *but I trod them down in mine anger, and trampled on them in my rage*. Heb. *and*: but the copulative is sometime used as a discretive, or adversative; as Chap. 60.10. & 61.6. and sometime as a causal; as chap. 53.2. & 64.4,5. Some would have the words read, as our version renders them, not in the time past; because it is a prophecy of a thing to come. But that is no good argument; because the prophets' usual wont is, to speak of matters future, as past, or present. And here there seems a necessity of it; because the party here mentioned is described, not as going out to war, but as returning from fight and from the slaughter of his foes, ver. 1. as did David from the slaughter of the Philistines, 1 Sam. 18.6.

*{for I will tread them*} Or, *for I trod them down*. Which notion of the particle, if we retain, it may be added as a reason, by way of explication, rendered of his first words; *I have trodden the winepress: For I trod them down, and trampled on them*, as the treaders do on the grapes in a winepress. Or, of the word, *alone*; I alone did it; for I myself *trod down* all that I met with. Or, of the branch next beforegoing, in the sense forementioned, none could maintain fight with me: for I trod them all down before me. Or, according to the other sense, reading the particle, *but*; there was *none with me, but I trod them down* myself: *mine own arm* did what was done: ver. 5.

*{tread*} Or, *tread down*; that is, discomfit and destroy, Psal. 44.5. & 60.12. chap. 25.10. and there are two things here implied in the term; the facility of the dispatch, I trod them down, as easily as one treads down clusters of grapes in a winepress, and the havoc made of the enemy; they were utterly spoiled, as grapes are under the treaders' feet, and their blood was spilled on the ground, as the juice or liquor is wholly forced out of them, ver. 6.

*{them*} That is, the Moabites, ver. 1. the people next before spoken of: and so it is expressed, ver. 6. Otherwise we must understand his adversaries, those he fought with: and so then must the pronoun (as sometime it is, See Chap. 30.8.) be put for the noun.

*{trample them*} Or, *trample on*: It is a word somewhat more emphatical, than the former. See chap. 41.25. Dan. 8.7,10. 2 Kin. 9.23.

*{fury*} See chap. 43.25. & 59.18.

*{and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment.*} Or, rather, *their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I stained all my raiment*: For it is a part of the answer to the foregoing demand, by what means his garments came to be so stained, ver. 2. as they then appeared already to be, ver. 1.

*{their blood*} Not his own blood; for he shed none in fight himself, but theirs with whom he fought: and this passage therefore does not belong to Christ's passion. Heb. *their strength*, or *support*; as the word signifies, 1 Sam. 15.29. Lam. 3.18. and *the blood* is so termed, as the Jewish critics agree, because the life, strength, and support, of the living creature therein consists, Gen. 9.4. Lev. 17.11,14. See further, ver. 6.

*{sprinkled upon my garments*} As was Jezabel's upon the wall, 2 Kin. 9.23.

*{stain my raiment*} By this means my garments came to be stained. Heb. *polluted*; or, *defiled*; for blood pollutes, Chap. 59.3. Lam. 4.14.

**V. 4.** *{For the day of vengeance is in mine heart*} Or, *was in mine heart*: For he speaks still, as of a thing past; as if he had said, Do you ask why I was so fierce and furious against them, and shed so much blood with them: the day was come wherein I had resolved, having a long time forborne them, to take vengeance upon them, for all their wrongs and insolencies committed against me and my people, ch. 34.8. and 61.2.

*{in my heart*} That is, as some, the day much desired and longed for, by me; as Psal. 40.8. or rather, the day, or time, in my secret counsel foreappointed, and designed thereunto, chap. 65.6. Act. 17.31.

*{and the year of my redeemed is come.*} Or, *was come*; the time was come, wherein my people were to be rescued out of the hands of their oppressors, and righted upon them. See chap. 34.8. Psal. 103.13. an allusion to the Jubilee, the year of remission of debts, [and restitution] of states; as chap. 61.2.

**V. 5.** *{And I looked, and there was none to help, and I wondered that there was none to uphold:*} Or, *And when I beheld, that there was no helper; and wondered, that there was no upholder; then did mine own arm bring salvation, &c.* The like syntax, See chap. 53.2. & 59.16. a place, parallel to this, whereof see more there: Then God struck in for the relief and deliverance of his people, when all human helps failed, and none appeared that would once offer to put forth his hand toward the helping, or upholding of them. So 2 Chron. 20.12,15–17. Chap. 26.18,19. & 37.3,36.

*{therefore mine own arm brought salvation unto me; and my fury it upheld me.*} Or, *then*: Heb. *and*; as chap. 30.30. & 37.36. God by his own might made a glorious conquest, and did all that was to be done; that which he can do, when means are all missing, and men all fail, in doing their duty, Psal. 98.1. and there needed nothing but his own just indignation, and zeal for his people, either to stir him upon the work, or to make him go thorough stitch with it, chap. 37.36. See ch. 59.16.

**V. 6.** *{And I will tread down the people in mine anger.*} Or, *I trod down*, as before, ver. 3. See there. See also, Chap. 14.25.

*{and make them drunk in my fury;*} Or, *made them drunk in*, or *with my fury*; his *fury*, being here considered, either, as the cause impellent, putting him on it, to deal with them, as he did; as chap. 14.6. Psal. 95.11. ver. 3. or, as the efficient cause unto them, through the direful effects of it upon them, of their dismal condition, Chap. 51.21–23. *I made them drunk*; that is, by the evils inflicted on them; I did so astonish them, that, like persons overcome with drink, they were not able to stand, nor knew which way to turn themselves, See Psal. 60.3. & 75.8. Chap. 19.14. Jer. 25.16,27. or, to keep to the resemblance in which we are, the meaning may well be; I drenched them in their own blood, I gave them their fill of blood, I made them *drunk* with it, as *with wine newly trod*, chap. 49.26. for so the word there used does properly signify. See Rev. 17.6. & 18.24. & 16.4,6.

*{and I will bring down their strength to the earth.*} Or, *I did shed their blood upon the ground*. Heb. *I made their strength*, or *support, to descend* (that is, to go down, or run down) *to the earth*: the word is the same that was before rendered *blood*, ver. 3. and there seems no reason to render it otherwise here, than there. So of Edom, and Bozrah, chap. 34.7. *their land shall be soaked with blood*. Howbeit, some would have the meaning here to be, *I will bring down their strength*, that is, their men of *strength*; the strongest among them; *strength*, for men of *strength*, strong ones, chap. 3.25. as *Justice*, for a man of *Justice*, a just one, ch. 41.2. *Wisdom*, for a man of *Wisdom*, a wise one, Mic. 6.9. and *Might*, for men of *Might*, mighty ones, chap. 3.25. But the course of the context pleads sufficiently for the former.

**V. 7.** *{I will mention the loving kindnesses of the Lord, and the praises of the Lord, according to all that the Lord hath bestowed on us, and the great goodness toward the house of Israel, which he hath bestowed on them according to his mercies, and according to the multitude of his loving kindnesses.*} Here seems to begin a new discourse, if not a new sermon, continued unto the end of the next Chapter. Wherein the prophet having begun with an ample acknowledgment of God's great goodness to his people, complains, in the next place, of their ungracious, and rebellious demeanor toward him; bewails God's estrangement of himself from them, for the same, and the evils, that thereupon had befallen them: and earnestly sues unto God, yet out of his free mercy, to mind them in their present misery, and to be reconciled again unto them. In this verse, is contained his thankful acknowledgment, of the abundant mercies and beneficences of God exhibited to them, which he so dwells upon, as if he could never find words enough, or pregnant enough, to express them. See Daniel dwelling in like manner, in his prayer, on the confession of their sins, Dan. 9.5,6. and the like various expressions of the amplitude of God's grace and goodness in Christ, Eph. 2.5,7.

*{I will mention*} Some would have these to be the words of the people; I see not why they should not be the words of the prophet, as the Chaldee makes them, though attempered and accommodated unto the condition of the people, in the time of their captivity; *I will mention*, as chap. 48.1. or, *I will call to mind*, as Gen. 41.9. or, *I will celebrate*, with praise and thanksgiving acknowledge, as chap. 12.4. But here rather, the first or second; the main drift and scope of the prophet, being hereby to exaggerate their rebellious demeanor towards him who had done so much for them, ver. 10. and expected other manner of behavior from them, ver. 7. See Jer. 2.2.

*{the loving kindnesses of the Lord*} His manifold, great, ample, abundant, loving kindness: and so afterward again, *the multitude*, or *magnitude of his loving kindnesses*. So Psalm 89.1. Lam. 3.22. these are brought to remembrance, partly, yea principally, to aggravate the unworthy carriages of God's people towards him, who had dealt so graciously and bountifully with them; as Deut. 32.7–14. and partly also it may be, to stir up in the hearts of them amidst the calamities of those times, some hopeful expectation of finding the like favor with God again, as Psal. 77.5–11.

*{and the praises*} A defect of the copulative, as chap. 30.33. unless we will supply from the former branch (as Gen. 1.16.) I will mention, or celebrate *his praises*.

*{bestowed*} The word carries usually with it a notion of *retribution*, Psal. 103.10. 1 Sam. 24.18. but sometime again of *a free contribution*, as Psal. 116.7. & 119.17. and so here.

*{the house of Israel*} See chap. 5.7. & 14.2.

*{mercies*} Or, *tender mercies*; as the word is rendered, Psal. 25.6. and that in Greek answering it, Luk. 1.78. See chap. 54.7. abundance of mercy, and tender mercy; *mercy* not *merit*, Deut. 7.7,8. & 9.4,5. So Psal. 6.4. & 25.6,7. Dan. 9.9,18.

**Ver. 8.** *{For he said, Surely they are my people; children that will not lie.*} Heb. *And* (as chap. 53.2.) *he said*: he thought with himself; he made account, he presumed, (as 2 King. 5.11.) what time he brought them out of Egypt, and took them to be his people, that they would carry themselves loyally and dutifully unto him. A speech taken from the affection and disposition of men, who expect respective carriage from them, whom they have shown kindness unto; or of a Father, presuming and hoping the best of a child, whom he has had special care of, and been at much cost with: implying how such favors should have wrought upon them, and how they should have stood affected toward him, who had dealt so kindly and bountifully with them, Psal. 81.8–10. See the like affection ascribed in like manner to God, Zeph. 3.7.

*{they are*} It need not be put in a different character: for the pronoun demonstrative, supplies the place of the verb substantive, as Ezek. 2.7.

*{my people*} Whom I have taken in a more peculiar manner to myself, Exod. 19.5,6. Deut. 7.6. & 26.17,18.

*{that will not lie*} Will not deal disloyally, as chap. 59.13. but see the contrary pronounced of them, chap. 30.9. a defect of the relative, as chap. 62.1.

*{so he was their Savior.*} Heb. *and* (as chap. 59.19.) *he was unto them for a Savior*. Upon these hopes, this expectation, these grounds, and these conditions, he undertook the protection of them, Exod. 19.5,6. Psa. 81.8,9. the like syntax, see 1 Chron. 19.12.

**V. 9.** *{In all their affliction he was afflicted,*} There is a double reading here in the Hebrew, some copies, it seems, anciently, having the word *lo*, written with an *aleph*, and then it is an adverb negative, and signifies *not*, some with a *vau*, and then being a preposition, with a pronoun affixed, it signifies *to him*: the like diversity about the same word, is found also, Exod. 21.8. Job 13.15. Psal. 100.3. chap. 9.3. & 49.5. Lev. 11.21. & 23.30. 1 Sam. 11.3. 2 King. 8.10. 1 Chron. 11.20. Esdr. 4.2. Hence, the words come to be diversely rendered. Some, with whom our version concurs, *In all their affliction he was afflicted*. Heb. *affliction was to him*, as *affliction is to me*; for *I am afflicted*, Psal. 18.6. Lam. 1.20. he took to heart their afflictions; he was himself grieved for them, and with them, Judg. 10.18. a form of speech taken from the manner of men, as the Jewish masters well here observe. See Psal. 106.44,45. Zach. 2.8. Acts 9.5. Others, taking it in the negative, yet reading the words by way of interrogation, (as some also do that Job 13.15. & Psal. 105.26. to reconcile the elder version with the latter) *was not affliction to him?* or *was he not afflicted?* for sense and substance, come home to the former. But others, and some of the Jewish doctors also, read them in the negative, by way of enunciation, *he did not afflict them*; or, *affliction was not to* them *they were not afflicted*, that is, as some, he afflicted them not, (having no will or desire so to do, Lam. 3.33.) but they brought affliction upon themselves, chap. 3.9. Job 36.23. Jer. 2.17. or, though they vexed him, yet he spared them, and did not afflict them, as they deserved that he should, Psal. 78.38. & 103.10. or they were not long in any affliction; (and a little is as nothing) because he speedily delivered them out of it, Psa. 106.44. Or, as some, if not including both, yet admitting the one, and supplying the other; there was *no affliction* to him: he was not afflicted, he was not troubled with their troubles; he seemed for some time not to regard them, that they might have a more effectual work upon them, cha. 8.17. & 30.18. & 45.15. & 57.17. Hos. 5.15. or, because this seems to cross the prophet's drift in this place; Others, there was *no strait* to him, (as Psal. 31.9. & 59.16. & 69.17. *straitness is to me*, that is, I am straitened, I am in straits, in distress) or, he was *not strait*; as chap. 49.20. *the place is too strait to me*, or *for me*: he was not *strait-laced* towards them, as we use to say; or he was not *strait-handed*, chap. 59.1. he was not backward to help them, as they speak, Josh. 10.6. *slacken not thine hand from helping us*: he was forward to help them; or he was not weary of helping; it was no trouble at all to him to help them. Or lastly, as a learned late writer, *He was not an enemy*, or *adversary* to them; (as the word commonly signifies, Lam. 1.5,7,10.) he carried himself toward them, not as a foe, but as a friend. And this, as also the next before, may either of them carry some good probability with them. Howbeit, the first I conceive to be the genuine sense, and the words to have special reference to God's taking to heart, their afflictions in Egypt, Exod. 3.7,9.

*{and the Angel of his presence saved them:*} By *the Angel of his face* (as the Hebrew sounds) or *his presence*: the Jewish doctors here understand, some of them, *Micael*; the tutelary Angel (as they account him) of their nation, Dan. 10.13,21. called *the Angel of his face*, or *presence*, because he stands continually attending in God's presence. See Mat. 18.10. Others, *Metraton*, whom they feign to be God's *harbinger*, or *messenger*, from a Latin word that imports the former: And some of them say, that this Angel is no other than Enoch, since his translation, so employed. Others again, that this is but the title of his office; but his proper name is Micael, and so bring it home to the first: nor want there of ours, who out of some of their writings, wherein they talk much in a wild manner, both of the title (which is indeed no more than a mere deformation of the Latin *metator*, an *harbinger*) and of the party that bears it, would prove that this *Metraton*, can be no other than the Messiah; as many of our divines also conceive *Micael* to be, mentioned Dan. 12.1. Jude 9. Rev. 12.7. Certain it is, that this Angel here spoken of, is that Angel of whom God spoke unto Moses, Exod. 23.21–23. termed both *Jehovah*, Exod. 13.21. & 14.1[unclear],24. and *his face*, or *presence*, Exod. 33.14,15. and *an Angel*, Exod. 33.2. who that he was no other, than the *Messiah*, Jesus Christ, the conductor of them in the wilderness, holy Steven informs us, Act. 7.38. the eternal Son of God, the resplendency of his Father's Majesty, and exact image of his person, Heb. 1.3. in whom therefore his name is said to be, Exod. 23.22. he that appeared unto Moses in the bush, Exod. 3.2. styled *Jehovah* there, ver. 4. and by Jacob, *the Angel, that delivered*, or *rescued him out of all evil*, Gen. 48.24. and by Malachy lastly, *Jehovah, the Angel of the Covenant*, Mal. 3.1. termed *an Angel*, or *Messenger*, in regard of his Mediatorship, Heb. 8.6. *of God's face*; either because he does exactly resemble God his Father, John 14.9,10. Col. 1.15. or, because *he appeareth before the face*, or in the presence of God, for us, Heb. 9.24. See Rom. 8.34. Rev. 8.3. this Angel secured, and safeguarded them all the way through the wilderness, from Egypt to Canaan, Deut. 8.2,4. & 32.10,12.

*{in his love, and in his pity, he redeemed them.*} He rescued them out of the Egyptian bondage, out of mere affection to them, and compassion toward them, Deut. 7.7,8.

*{and he bare them, and carried them, all the days of old.*} Or, *he took them up*, (as chap. 40.15.) *and carried them all the days of old*. Heb. *days of perpetuity*, or *of antiquity*; *days of yore*, as in our old English they had wont to speak: for in the former notion is the word taken, when speech is of times future; in the latter, when of times past, as here. He not led them only, but lifted them; took them up in his arms, as parents, or nurses, are wont to do with young children, and weakly ones, (alluded to Psal. 91.12.) chap. 46.3. and carried them, as the Eagle does her young ones, not fully fledged, or unable yet to fly, on her wings, Exod. 19.4. Deut. 32.11. all the time of that their infancy, and constantly also afterward from time to time, as occasion and their necessities required it, chap. 46.4.

**V. 10.** *{But they rebelled*} They answered not God's expectation, ver. 8. they proved disloyal children, chap. 30.9. and a rebellious race, chap. 48.4,8. See Exod. 16.2,5. Numb. 14.4,11. & 16.3,11,42. Deut. 9.7,24. & 31.17. Psal. 78.56. & 95.9. & 106.7. Ezek. 20.8,13.

*{and vexed his holy Spirit*} Heb. *his Spirit of holiness*, and so ver. 11. as, *his hill of holiness*, for his *holy hill*, chap. 56.7. *his name of holiness*, for, *his holy name*, Ezek. 36.21. *his day of holiness*, for his *holy day*, chap. 58.13. They so carried themselves towards him, as might justly be cause of vexation, and grief of heart to him; a form of speech, borrowed, as the former, ver. 8,9. from the nature of man: though God be not subject to such infirmity and passion, as men are. See the like forms in this kind, Gen. 6.6. chap. 7.13. & 43.24. Psal. 78.40. Ezek. 6.9. Amos 2.14. Acts 7.51. Eph. 4.39.

*{his Spirit*} Which he had set among them, and put upon them, to guide, and govern them, verse 11. and whereby he had striven, and struggled with them, to reclaim and reduce them, Gen. 6.3. Num. 14.11. Psal. 95.10.

*{therefore he was turned to be their enemy,*} Heb. *and*: as chap. 47.8. he was enforced to carry himself, as an enemy towards them, Jer. 30.14. Lam. 2.4,5. So Job 13.24. & 30.21. & 33.10.

*{And he fought against them*} There is a defect of the copulative; as v. 7. but it is supplied with an expression of the pronoun, not so usual, and having therefore an emphasis in it; as if he had said, he that before fought for them, did then fight against them, chap. 29.2,3. he not only forbore to assist them against their enemies; but fought for these against his people: he raised up adversaries against them, and caused them to fall before them, Lev. 26.25. Deut. 28.25. & 32.30. chap. 30.17. Psal. 44.9,10. *the hand of God was against them for evil, whensoever they went out*, Judg. 2.14,15. So he threatened, that if they *walked crossly*, or *thwartly with him*; he would also deal in the like manner with them, Lev. 26.23,24. Psal. 18.26.

**V. 11.** *{Then he remembered the days of old,*} *Then*; as chap. 38.4. or, *Yet*: as chap. 9.1. & 60.10. Heb. *And the days of old*. Heb. *of antiquity*; as Psal. 44.1. See ver. 9. This is spoken, as some conceive, of God himself, calling to mind what he had formerly done for this people, and as loath now to lose all the fruit of his former favors, notwithstanding their present untoward carriages, thereby induced to work new deliverances for them: (the argument, that God's servants press him oft with, in their prayers, Exo. 32.11,12. Deut. 9.16,18,19. Num. 14.13–19. Josh. 7.7,9.) and whether we understand it of a discursive *remembrance*; (after the manner of men, given unto God) as Exod. 32.13. Psalm 78.39. or, an active *remembrance*, in manifesting his mindfulness of them, by what he did for them: as Gen. 8.1. & 30.22. it should have reference to those former deliverances, that God upon this consideration, had in times past afforded this people, notwithstanding their manifold, frequent, great, and grievous delinquencies, after he had brought them out of their troubles and distresses: and this may seem probably to be the genuine sense of the place. Yet others suppose it to be spoken of God's people, (and so the most, as well Jews, as ours) amidst their troubles, better bethinking themselves, and as calling to mind, what God had formerly done for their ancestors. Psal. 22.4,5. & 78.34,35. so complaining that at present he did not the like for them, Judg. 6.13. See Psal. 44.1–14. And this may seem not altogether improbable: one main difficulty is, that the verb is here singular; whereas of the people he spoke before in the plural ver. 10. and so afterward again. Whereunto might be answered, that the word *people*, being, though of a collective notion, yet of a singular form, it is joined oft, with singular both verbs and nouns. See chap. 5.26,27. where the very like syntax is; and as the words are there rendered, *they shall come*; so, this sense admitted, they might here be rendered, *then they remembered*.

*{Moses, and his people*} About these words, there is no small disagreement among interpreters. Some of the Jewish masters conceive *Moses* not to be at all here mentioned, but the word *moshe*, here to be a participle of that verb, from which Moses had his name, Exod. 2.10. and they read the words, *He remembered the days of old, him that drew out his people*; to wit, out of the Egyptian thraldom; or, *that brought him up*, out of the Red Sea; as in the next branch: so David says of himself, *He drew me out of many*, or, *mighty, waters*, 1 Sam. 22.17. Psal. 18.16. where the same word is used, and save in the story of Moses, not elsewhere. Nor want there of ours, that go this way; but as if it were a noun, rendering the words, *the eduction*, or *bringing out, of his people*. But the most, both of theirs, and ours, take Moses to be meant here: and of theirs, some suppose a defect of the preposition, before the word, *people*; the like whereunto they find, 1 King. 3.15. these read the text thus; *him that sent Moses to his people*: but I find one only of ours, that does therein follow them. Others of them, will have rather a defect of the copulative, such as they find Habb. 3.11. and with these most of ours concur, yet not agreeing about either the syntax, or the sense of this clause: for some refer these words both to *days*, *the days of old, of Moses, and of his people*. Others, to *remembered*; *he remembered Moses and his people*; that is, say some, what by the Ministry of Moses, he had done for his people, Exod. 3.10. & 32.1,7. Psalm 77.20. Others, the covenant, that by the mediation of Moses, he made with his people, Exod. 19.3–9. & 24.3–8. Gal. 3.19. Or Moses his vehement and prevalent intercessions at sundry times, in the behalf of his people, Exod. 32.11,32. Num. 14.19,20. & 16.22. & 21.7. Psal. 106.13. Now which of these latter ways we understand the words, is not greatly material; especially, if we consider them, as things in times past remembered, whether by God, or by his people; though the text seems to run more smoothly, if we refer them to his remembrance, rather than to theirs. But if we shall transmit the matter unto future times, and transfer the words to the people, that were to be in the Babylonian captivity, as the Rabbins most of them do; then it must be conceived in the time to come, and read, *They shall remember the days of old*: and the former words should rather run in this tenor: *But they have rebelled and vexed his holy Spirit; and he is therefore become an enemy unto them, he himself hath fought against them: Yet they will remember the days of old* in *Moses* his time, and *his people* that then were; or, *Moses, and his people*: where *his people*, unless we refer it to *Moses*, as if they should call them, *Moses his people*, as God himself also, but in anger, does, when he says to him, *Thy people, whom thou broughtest out of Egypt*, Exod. 32.7. the form will not so well suit with the person of the people. But this rub would be removed, and all defects salved, without any supply, if, with a grave and learned writer, we might thus read the words; *And his people will call to mind the days of Moses* his *age*. But this reading, the points, or stops, in the original, will not admit: for they make a stay at *age*, but none at *Moses*; and in the text, *his people*, comes after *Moses*.

*{saying, Where is he that brought them up out of the sea*} The word *saying*, is not in the text, but is inserted by interpreters; as Psalm 105.15. chap. 26.19. & 45.14. & 56.12. and elsewhere, so here; understanding it as before; some, of God; some, of the people: but some other instead thereof, insert, *But now*: as the like expression is, in a parallel place, Judg. 6.23. deeming the words ensuing, to be the prophet's own, complaining, if not in the person, yet in the behalf of the people; as if God did not mind them, as formerly he had done, notwithstanding their manifold sins and excesses, chap. 49.14. The Chaldee thrusts in, *Lest the Gentiles should say*; and one of the Rabbins, *The Gentiles now will say*: But these seem overbold insertions.

*{Where is he?*} Such kind of speeches, concerning God, are used sometime in derision, as intimating, that God was not able to relieve, or deliver his, in their distresses, as by the enemies of God's people and servants, Deut. 32.37. Psal. 42.3. & 115.2. and so the Chaldee here accounts it: sometime in way of expostulation and complaint, as implying, that God did not manifest his power and providence, in the behalf of his people, as in times past he had done: so Judg. 6.23. and so rather here. There is a third manner of usage of such like forms, to wit, in way of inquisition, as inquiring after God, that had done such things for his people, out of a desire to know him, and to serve him: the neglect of which inquiry is taxed, both in priests, and people, Jer. 2.6,8. and it is not amiss, by some, observed, that it seems here to be intimated, that they who had not regarded to ask after God, in this kind formerly, in the time of their prosperity, should be enforced to complain of the want of him, and his absence from them afterward, in the time of their adversity. So 1 Sam. 2.17. & 7.2. Jer. 22.21. & 2.31,32,37. *Where is he?* says he, or say they, either the people, or the prophet, as in their person; implying, that he was not now to be found; as before he had threatened, Hos. 5.6. because they had neglected to seek him, when he might have been found, Psalm 32.6. cap. 55.6. But some of those of chief note, that conceive these to be God's words, render them somewhat otherwise, than the reading commonly received, thus; *Where should he be?* as if God should thus reason with himself, Where would the glory of God appear, and be manifested, if he should suffer his people to perish? Or where would the fruit of all be that he had done for his people, if dealing with them according to their deserts, he should utterly destroy them? Of this somewhat before. But it seems overharsh here: Nor can I be induced to concur with them, in attributing this part at least of the present discourse unto God; because it is apparent, ver. 14. to be spoken of him, and unto him in part also, by some other, at which place they are enforced, to bring in the people speaking, without any color of reason, cutting that off from the rest.

*{that brought them up out of the sea,*} Heb. *made them to ascend from the sea*: both carried them safe through the sea, the Red Sea, and brought them safe out of it, from the very bottom of it, Exo. 14.29,30. & 15.5,8. ver. 13,14. one of the greatest miracles that God ever wrought for his people, which God himself therefore mentions, as one of his masterpieces, chap. 50.2. and it is by them therefore likewise most frequently commemorated, Nehem. 9.11. Psalm 68.22. & 77.19. & 78.13. & 106.9. & 114.3,5. & 136.13,14. especially in the times of their distresses and extremities; as here, so Psal. 74.13,14. chap. 51.9,10. ver. 12,13.

*{with the shepherd of his flock?*} There seems to have been here also a double reading in the ancient copies, some having the word with a soundless *jod*, and some with an *he* in the end. Whence some of the Jewish critics read it, not *shepherd*, but *shepherds*; which our margin also gives us. Those that read it in the singular number with an *he*, expound it of Moses, of whom, v. 11. and who was the Leader and Governor of God's people; yea, as a king among them, Deut. 33.4,5. and unto such is the name of *shepherd* given, chap. 44.28. Ezek. 34.23,24. Those that read it in the plural, with *jod*, expound it of Moses and Aaron both, according to that in the Psalm 77.20. *Thou leadest thy people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron*: whether of the two we take to, the *flock* is said to be neither the one's, nor both's, but God's, *the Shepherd of Israel*, Psal. 80.1. who led it by them, verse 11. Howbeit, some of the Jewish doctors, following the Chaldee, render the words, *as a shepherd his flock*; that is, supplying the verb from the foregoing participle; *as a shepherd* bringeth forth, or leadeth out *his flock*: for so is that word oftentimes taken at large; as Lev. 11.54. Josh. 24.17. Ezra 4.2. Jer. 50.9. and the manner of shepherds, in those parts, is to lead out their flocks, Joh. 10.3,4. so the particle *with*, should be here a note of similitude, which I suppose is hardly found; and the former exposition being familiar and ready, there is little reason to refuse it.

*{where is he, that put his holy Spirit within him?*} Heb. *his Spirit of holiness* (as ver. 10.) *in the midst of him*; that is, *within him*, or *in him*; as Zach. 12.1. with 1 Cor. 2.11. so the most, both of the Jewish, and ours. But the Jewish restrain it, to the Spirit of Prophecy. Ours extend it, to that spiritual endowment, wherewith Moses was, in a very large measure, furnished, and thereby enabled, both for the instructing and government also of God's people. See Num. 11.17. Deut. 18.15. but other, of either ranks, render it, *in the midst of him*, or *of them*, (because the word *people*, to which they suppose it referred, is a collective) that is, *among them*; as *the Canaanites dwelt amongst the Ephraimites*, Josh. 16.10. and so Neh. 9.20. *thou gavest* them (to be supplied from the words foregoing) *thy good Spirit to instruct them*; for it was given to them, and placed among them; because bestowed upon those with them, and over them, in their behalf, and for their behoof, 1 Cor. 3.22,23. See chap. 59.21. and this is that *Spirit*, which they vexed by rebellious courses, 1 Thess. 4.8. ver. 10.

**V. 12.** *{That led them by the right hand of Moses*} See Psal. 77.20. on ver. 11. Yet it is said, *The Lord alone did lead him*, Deut. 32.12. of which place, see on the word, *alone*, ver. 3. a defect of the pronoun, as Neh. 9.20. chap. 57.13. but supplied here from ver. 13. where it is expressed.

*{by the right hand of Moses*} Heb. *at the right hand of Moses*. So the old Latin renders it; and most interpreters, both Jewish and Christian: In which form of speech, because the *right hand* is used commonly, in a successful and well-boding notion, and the *left*, in the contrary, Mat. 25.30,34,41. Some would have noted the sure and safe passage, and journeying of the people under Moses his conduct: But that seems overcurious; and the term of *right hand* seems to have, after the phrase most frequent in Scripture, not so much a notion of prosperous success, (which among heathen people it usually has, Ezek. 21.21,22.) as of power and ability, the *right hand* being generally accounted the strongest, and the more active than the left. So Psal. 21.9. & 89.26,43. Others therefore read it, *that led* them, being *at Moses* his *right hand*, to help and assist him. So the Psalmist, Psal. 16.8. *he is at my right hand, that I be not moved*; and, *the Lord at thy right hand shall strike through Kings*, Psal. 110.5. and the Jewish doctors, some of them, suppose, that there is an eye had in this term, to the *staff*, that Moses held in his *right hand*, over the Red Sea, at the dividing of it, Exod. 14.16,21. The Greek reads it, *that led Moses by the right hand*; and so is God said, *to hold by the right hand* those, whom he strengthens and supports, Psal. 63.8. & 73.23. ch. 45.1. but neither is any instance produced of the use of the particle here prefixed in that notion: and the form of the substantive shows, that Moses is subjoined to it, as governed by it.

*{with his glorious arm*} Heb. *his arm of bravery*, (as the word is rendered, chap. 3.18.) or *gallantry*, (See ch. 62.3.) for, his *brave*, or *gallant arm*; as, *his arm of might*, for, *his mighty arm*, ch. 62.8. and *a name of gallantry*, for, *a gallant name*, or *fame*, ver. 14. The particle *with*, is not in the text: but the want of it is very usual, as Psal. 17.13,14. & 44.3. chap. 51.19. Now by his *arm*, Some of the Jewish doctors understand the Angel that conducted them, Exod. 14.19. most of ours, God's mighty power assisting Moses, and working by him, whatsoever was done of him, for the safety and protection of the people committed unto him; as the word is, in this argument especially, most frequently taken, Exod. 6.6. & 15.16. Deut. 4.34. & 5.15. & 7.19. & 9.29. & 11.2. & 26.8. Psal. 77.16. & 89.11. & 136.12. And this some suppose the rather added, in regard that the former word seemed to have some glance at the *staff* in Moses his hand, to show that the dividing of the Red Sea, upon holding up of the staff over it, was not effected by any virtue, either in his hand, or in the staff it held; but by the powerful act of God alone. See Exod. 15.21. Howbeit, some, for that according to this reading, there are defects in the text; the one, of the pronoun before mentioned; the other, of the preposition here inserted, suppose that the text, as it is, without any such supplies interjected, may be thus read and rendered; *That made his glorious*, or *gallant arm, to go*, or *walk at Moses* his *right hand*; that is who by his mighty power went along with Moses, and was ever at hand to be assistant unto him, according to his promise, Exod. 3.12. & 33.14. Nor is this reading altogether improbable: the most that I suppose can be objected against it, is, that the word of *making to walk*, or *go*, may seem not to suit so well with the word *arm*; and that it is in the next verse applied to the people.

*{dividing the water before them*} Or, *that divided* (for it runs in the same strain with the former, *that led*) *the water* (to wit, of the Red Sea before mentioned, v. 11.) *before them*: before his people, the Israelites, to make a passage through it for them, Exod. 14.21,22. Josh. 3.16. ch. 43.6. So Neh. 9.11. chap. 43.12. Some would draw away the former clause to this branch, reading the words; *That by his glorious arm divided the Sea before them*: but this reading crosses the stops in the original; which without cause to disturb, or solicit, is not meet.

*{to make himself an everlasting name*} To procure to himself, by a work never before the like heard, an everlasting fame; both in regard of his almighty power therein manifested, and of his providence therein appearing over his people: *name*, for, *fame*, or *renown*; as Gen. 6.4. & 11.4. Jer. 32.20. and, *a name of eternity*, or *perpetuity*, for, *an everlasting name*; as Chap. 56.6. Yet the words are by some deemed to import, not so much the end, as the event; not so much what God aimed at, in the doing of it; as what from the doing of it, accrued and redounded unto him, as Chap. 59.19. Exod. 14.17. of such forms, see on Chap. 3 8.

**V. 13.** *{That led them through the deep, as an horse in the wilderness, that they should not stumble.*} A further amplification of this strange work. The like whereunto, yea, the very same in effect, see Psal. 106.9.

*{led them*} Heb. *made them to go*: the word used before, ver. 12. as also in the Psalm.

*{through the deep*} Heb. *depths*, or *deeps*: and so also is it, Psal. 68.22. & 106.9. implying, that it was not in some shallow or shoaly place, that the people passed that sea, but where it was with the deepest. See Exod. 15.5,8.

*{as an horse*} This is not in the Psalm, but is inserted here, by the prophet, for the further amplification of this act of God, in the conduct of them, enlarged also further, ver. 14. God is said to make Judah *his goodly horse for battle*, Zach. 10.3. and men are very chary of these choice ones, that they keep for such purpose.

*{in the wilderness*} This in the Psalm seems to be referred unto the people, because of an *horse* is no mention there made; and may imply, that they went as safe and as easily through the sea, as they had traveled, either before, or afterward, in the wilderness. But here it is referred unto *the horse*: *he led them through the deepest* of that sea, as safely and inoffensively, as a man could lead *an horse*, or as *an horse goeth in the wilderness*; that is, (says one of the Rabbins, whom some other also herein concur with) *on dry land: the wilderness*, for *dry land*; because wastes, in those parts, are commonly such, chap. 41.18. Jer. 17.6. But I conceive rather that the word rendered *wilderness*, does here signify *a plain*; as also another of the Jewish doctors here suggests: nor is it otherwise to be taken, Jer. 9.10. Lam. 4.19. & 5.9. and that the text would here at least, if not in the Psalm also, be rendered, *as an horse* goeth *in the plain*; that is, as he goes on plain ground, where there is neither clod, nor stone, nor ruck, nor ridge, without stumbling. See ver. 14.

*{that they should not stumble*} Or, so that *they stumbled not*, Jer. 31.9. Heb. *they shall not stumble*, or, *did not stumble*. So Psal. 78.53. *he led them safely*, or, *securely; and they feared not*; that is, *so that they feared not*: they were without fear; but here the particle is omitted, as oft, in the like syntax, chap. 40.24. & 41.7. & 43.17. & 58.6. See the promise, Psal. 90.12.

**V. 14.** *{As a beast goeth down into the valley,*} In the former part of this verse, most interpreters conceive to be a full, and formal similitude, consisting of two parts, a proposition, and a reddition, more largely laying forth, what was more concisely delivered, v. 13. in those words, *as an horse*; the former part whereof, they suppose to be contained in these words; which some therefore thus read, *As a beast, that goeth down into the vale* is led; (supplying the relative, as ver. 8. the verb from the words next ensuing; as Chap. 28.7. & 30.17.) that is, gently, and quietly, as an horse is wont to be led, or beast driven, down an hill, not headlong, as those swine, whom the Devils drove, Mat. 8.32. so rather, if we retain this version, than, as some would have it, *easily*; for this reason, because it is easier going down, than it is going up, an hill: and some would have an eye herein to be had, to the condition of the Jews' own country, which being mountainous, much of it, Psal. 125.2. Luk. 1.39. their manner was to drive their cattle down to graze in the vale. Others would have it to allude to their descent into the channel of the Red Sea; from the land, or the shore, that must of necessity, lie far above it; as before to their ascent, or, coming up again, from the same, on the other side, in the word, *made to ascend*, ver. 11. But I suppose the word rendered, *goeth down*, does here signify no more than as it also does oft elsewhere, *to go on*, or *to go along*: hereof, see instances enough ch. 38.8. and so the Chaldee, whom some of the Jewish commenters follow, seems here to take it: the words therefore, as I conceive, may be thus rendered: *As a beast goeth along in the vale*; or, *As a beast that goeth along in the vale*; that is, freely, easily, without any let, or impediment; as a beast, whether horse, or other, (for the former resemblance is here enlarged) travels in the vale, where the way is usually clear before it: and thus taking them, that which a learned writer suggests, to me seems very probable, who annexing this, unto that in the verse beforegoing, thus reads them together; *That led them through the deeps, as an horse in the plain, without stumbling; as a beast going down*, or, *going along in the vale*: so considered, they make up the former illustration; do not begin any new collation, to be abruptly broken off again, in the very next sentence. The meaning is, that God did not only divide the sea, to make way for them through it; (which albeit he had done, and done no more, they might have been stifled in the mud, and buried in the ooze, or have tumbled down headlong, in the descent, on the one side, or never have been able to get up again on the other) but he so disposed the matter, that as the water stood like solid stone walls, on either side of them, Exod. 15.8,16. so the muddy soil, was as firm ground under their feet, Exod. 14.22. & 15.19. Neh. 9.11. and they had their whole way through the sea so fitted for them, that notwithstanding any such descent, or ascent, or aught else, that might obstruct, or impeach their passage, they made it, as easily, as if they had gone on plain, and even ground all the way: thus did God as their harbinger, level their way for them, Chap. 26.7. and 40.4. & 45.2.

*{the Spirit of the Lord caused him to rest*} How these words come in here, is by many much questioned. Some would have them, to be inserted, as a parenthesis, between the proposition, or the former part, and the reddition, or latter part of that similitude, which they suppose to be in this verse; because, *so*, the note of reddition, comes after it: and that for this cause inserted, to prevent, and meet with, a doubt, that might arise in some men's minds, how it were possible that such miraculous matters should be brought about; which to remove, it is by the way cast in, that it was the *Spirit of God*, that did all this, unto whom nothing is either impossible, or difficult, Job 42.2. Psal. 115.3. & 135.6. Jer. 32.27. Others, among whom, one of the Jewish commenters, would draw this passage within the latter part of the similitude, supposing a trajection in the words, which should thus be disposed, *so thou leadest thy people, and the Spirit of the Lord made them to rest*. But this seems to make overbold with the context. And no less wide seems that to stray from the text, which a reverend writer of ours has on it, who knitting these words to the former part of it, thus renders the context; *As a beast, which the Spirit of God leadeth, goeth in the valley*; to wit, quietly and in safety. For howsoever it be true, that God's providence and protection, reaches even unto beasts, Psal. 36.6. and that God, for man, takes charge of them, and care for them, Gen. 8.1. Num. 20.8. Yet is there no such thing intended, by the prophet, in this place. Nor seems that so suitable which a late learned annotator suggests, who thus renders the words, *As a beast goeth down into the valley, and the wind of God giveth him rest; so didst thou lead thy people*; that is, as the descent of a beast down a steep hill, especially traveling with a burden on his back, is troublesome and toilsome; but the wind, when he is therewith wearied, gives him some rest and refreshing; so led you your people a toilsome journey through the wilderness, to bring them to rest in the land of Canaan: And whereas the affix *him* is masculine, whereas the word *beast* is feminine; that he seeks to salve, by referring it to the word *horse* here intended, v. 13. the like whereunto some suppose to be, Gen. 4.7. & 13.10. 1 Sam. 15.9. But the resemblance seems not to come so handsomely off; and howsoever some of the ancients have so expounded, *The Spirit of God*, that is, *the wind of God*, Gen. 1.2. alleging to that purpose that, Psal. 147.18. *He maketh his wind blow*; yet the version seems harsh, and in neither place convenient. More probable to me seems the conceit of that learned writer before mentioned, who supposing no such formal similitude, consisting of proposition, and reddition, to be contained in this verse; but the former branch to depend upon the verse beforegoing, does make these words an entire axiom, neither having any such special relation to either, nor being any such insertion between either of those two supposed parts of a similitude, as those other authors conceive of them; but an adjection only to what went before, concerning God's settling his people quietly in the land of promise. Of which, more anon.

*{the Spirit of the Lord*} *The Word of the Lord*, says the Chaldee: whereby some conceive to be meant, the second person, the Son, Joh. 1.1,14. *the Angel* that went before them, say others, ver. 9. *the Spirit of the Lord*, whereof, ver. 10,11. the Holy Ghost, the third person, say others: God himself, say the Jewish doctors, and others also of ours: *the Spirit of the Lord*, here, say they, as *his soul*, Chap. 42.1. for himself: and *the Lord himself* is said to have gone before them, Exod. 13.21. Num. 14.14. and to lead them, Neh. 9.12. Psal. 77.20. But howsoever the name of *Spirit*, is given to all the three persons, to the *Father*, Joh. 4.23,24. to the *Son*, 2 Cor. 3.17. to the *Holy Ghost*, 1 Joh. 5.6–8. and the external operations of the deity, are undivided: yet I conceive the distinction of persons to be intimated in such forms as this, and the third person to be more peculiarly here implied.

*{caused him to rest*} Concerning both the notion of the verb here used, and of the person here pointed to, there is some diversity of opinion, as well among the Jewish critics, as among our writers. Some reading the words, as our version, *He caused him to rest*, understanding it, of the people hereafter mentioned: whom, say they, God gave rest to from their adversaries that pursued them, by a safe conveyance through the sea, of the one; and the total subversion in the same sea, of the other, Exod. 14.26–30. Psal. 78.53. & 106.10,11. Others, rendering them, *he led him*. So the Chaldee, some of the Jewish, the ancient Greek, the old Latin, and divers of ours, as well as those that follow it. And among these, some understand it, as the former, of the people; so the Greek, who render it therefore in the plural, *them*; as before, *that led them*, ver. 13. and so the same should be said here, with that in the next branch. Others, of Moses, by whom God led them, Psal. 77.20. the Spirit of God, say they, led Moses, and them, by him. See ver. 13. The reason of the main ambiguity, is, for that the words of *resting*, and *leading*, are both for letters and sound of very near affinity the one with the other; and words of such neighborness, do oft mutually lend to, and borrow, the one from the other; as by many instances might be shown: The analogy of the form, here used, pleads for the former; the tenor of the context seems in the judgment of many learned, to speak for the latter. I conceive it may include a double notion, as some other, taking part from two divers roots, are deemed to do. I will point only at one of them: it is but one word that is rendered, Zach. 10.6. *I will bring them again to place them*: and in like manner, I suppose that this may here be rendered, *The Spirit of the Lord leading him*, or *them*, (to wit, his people) *caused them to rest*, that is, so led them, that they traveled quietly, and had places of rest, by the way: to which purpose it is said, Num. 10.33. that *the Ark went before them*, (the visible sign of God's special presence among them) *to search out rest* (that is, *a resting place*) *for them*. Nor do I mislike what some of the Jewish writers here have, to wit, that the prophet having before spoken of their passage through the sea, ver. 13. and having done with that, does here come to speak of God's conduct of them, after they came out of the sea, all the way through the wilderness, until they came unto Canaan: to which purpose the learned interpreter before alleged, carrying on the *rest* here intended, to their *rest* in that land: whereof see Deut. 13.9. Psal. 95.11. Chap. 14.3. renders the words, *The Spirit of the Lord brought them to rest*; as if it were said, *The Spirit of the Lord led them*, (that is, never left leading of them) until *he brought them unto rest*: and this exposition receives strength from that, Jer. 31.2. where it is said, of those that escaped the sword in the wilderness, that *God went out to make them rest*, that is, to settle them in the land of Canaan, where they were to rest. See the note on the place. I add only what I further conceive, that the words may well be read, by way of interrogation, as all the former along are; *The Spirit of the Lord that brought them to rest?* to wit, *Where is he?* as before, ver. 11. the stop in the original favors it; nor does the defect of the relative, in the text, at all hinder it, being a matter so rife, as before, ver. 8. So it should be the close of the expostulation beforegoing, debated hitherto, whether by the prophet with himself, or the people with themselves; not directed yet to God, unto whom, in the next words, the tenor of the discourse turns.

*{So didst thou lead thy people,*} Or, *Thus didst thou lead thy people*; that it may have reference to the whole former passage, not to any particular branch of it alone. See the like conclusion, where the speech is likewise directed unto God, when as it ran otherwise before, Judg. 5.31.

*{to make thyself a glorious name,*} Heb. *a name of bravery*, or *gallantry*. See ver. 12. Chap. 62.3. and this seems added, as intimating, what honor and renown God might gain to himself, by manifesting his power and providence, in the delivering of them now: though in an humble and modest manner, they do not, as yet, expressly mention it, or directly crave it; yet thereby to induce the Lord to do the like for them, that then he had done; if not for their sakes, who had deserved nothing less at his hands, yet for his own name's sake, and in regard of that glory, that might thereby accrue unto him. See Psal. 106.8. and 116.1. Chap. 43.25. and 48.9,11.

**V. 15.** *{Look down from heaven, and behold from the habitation of thine holiness, and of thy glory.*} Here, they, or the prophet, in their person, begins to fall directly unto prayer, and supplication, for favor and mercy; yet mixed with some passionate, but submissive expostulation, therein differing from the former, that it is directed unto God himself.

*{Look down from heaven,*} Or, *Behold from heaven*. So Deut. 26.15. Psal. 80.14. Lam. 3.50. not that God has not an eye in all places, Pro. 15.3. as well on earth, as in heaven, 2 Chron. 16.9. nor that he is not present, as well here on earth, as in heaven, Jer. 23.25. but because heaven is as his *palace*, in which he does in greater glory and state manifest himself, Psal. 11.4. & 115.3. there his *throne* is, Psal. 11.4. & 103.19. or that is his *throne*, chap. 66.1. from which as being *high and lofty*, Chap. 6.1. (as a king sitting above others, in his chair of estate, 1 King. 10.18,19. looks down upon these, that either stand, or lie prostrate, before, but far beneath him) is God said to *look down upon men* here on earth, Psal. 14.2. & 33.13.

*{and behold*} Or, *see*; as chap. 37.17. *behold, and see*; as Psal. 80.14. as, *see, and behold*, Lam. 1.11. words much of the same notion, used to express their earnest desire, that God would be pleased, not barely to see them, or look on them; for nothing is hid from his sight, Chap. 26.17. Job 34.21,22. Prov. 5.21. & 15.11. Heb. 4.13. but to have respect, and regard to them, to look with tender pity and compassion upon them; and to make it appear, by some gracious effect, and deliverance, wrought for them, that he so did. So Psal. 25.18. & 74.19. & 84.9.

*{the habitation of thine holiness, and of thy glory.*} Or, *thine holy, and glorious*, or *magnificent habitation*: A description of heaven; yet in such terms, as are given also to the Temple, a type of it. Heb. *thine habitation of holiness* (and so Exod. 15.13. Deut. 26.15. Psal. 68.5. & 136.2. Jer. 25.30.) *and of thy gallantry*, or *magnificence*; as ver. 15. See Chap. 60.13,15.

*{where is thy zeal, and thy strength, the sounding of thy bowels, and of thy mercies towards me?*} A new expostulatory complaint, that there seemed now not to appear any such affection in God towards his people, or any such ability with him, to do for them, as he had given evident signs, and conspicuous proof of, in times past: so ver. 11.

*{where is*} What is become of them? Where are they to be seen? So Psal. 89.49.

*{thy zeal*} Such an ardent affection of love, as cannot endure to see the party beloved, to be wronged or molested. See Chap. 9.7. & 26.11. & 37.32.

*{thy strength*} Heb. *powers*, or *valors*: for, *exceeding great power*, and *valor*; as Job 41.12. Psal. 71.16. & 90.10. & 147.10. or, for *valiant acts*, as Deut. 3.24. Psal. 145.12. & 150.2. See Jer. 14.9.

*{the sounding of thy bowels*} Some would have it to be, *the strutting of thy paps*, or *breasts*; as if it were a metaphor taken from women that give suck, whose paps, or breasts, when they are full of milk, pain them, and they cannot be at rest, until they have milked it out, and so given themselves some ease: but the mention of *bowels*, whose place, the belly is, not the breast admits not this trope. Some render it, *the multitude of thy bowels*: and the word here used does sometime signify *a multitude*. See Chap. 13.4. & 17.12. & 33.3. and the word *bowels*, in Greek, is used for a tenderness of affection, arising from pity and commiseration, Luk. 1.78. Phil. 1.8. & 2.1. Col. 3.12. 1 Joh. 3.17. and so the meaning should be, *multitude of tender compassions*; and of *multitude of mercies, and tender mercies*, is found mention in Scripture, Psal. 51.1. & 69.16. see also, ver. 7. But neither does the word, here used, when it is taken for *a multitude*, signify any *multitude* in general; but a *multitude* of men, or persons, gathered together; so called, not in regard of their number so much, as of the noise that they are wont to make: Nor is the Hebrew term of *bowels*, or *entrails*, here found, anywhere simply so used, as the Greek is, with whom, the word also deduced from it, has a notion of *compassion*, and *commiseration* in it, Mat. 9.36. Mar. 1.41. Luk. 7.13. whereas, in Hebrew, from the word that so signifies, there is none such: The word therefore is here to be taken, in reference to its first and native signification, wherein it signifies *a noise*, Amos 5.23. which hereby appears in that the verb of *sounding*, or *making a noise*, from whence the word comes, is in this notion commonly joined with the word *bowels*, Cant. 5.4. Chap. 16.11. in which forms of speech, there is a metaphor taken from those *rumblings* in the *bowels*, that sudden and strong passions of this nature do sometime produce: and it may well be here rendered, *yearnings*; as the like is, 1 King. 3.26. where it is said of the mother of the child, which the king bade should be divided; *her bowels yearned upon her son*: though the words there be divers, but in the same notion with these. It is a resemblance taken from human frailty, to help man's shallow capacity, attributed to God, as here, so Jer. 31.20. Hos. 11.8.

*{and of thy mercies towards me?*} Or, *and thy tender mercies*. See ver. 7. the word, in the singular number, signifies properly *the womb*, Gen. 20.18. Exod. 13.2. and more generally, *the belly*, Chap. 46.3. where both are put as parallel; and *belly*, for *womb*, Psal. 132.11. and so *uterus*, in Latin, used of either sex. Hence, in the plural, it is used for *bowels*; because the *belly* is the place of them. So of Joseph it is said, Gen. 43.30. *his bowels yearned upon his brother*: and of that mother before, the like; in both which places the same word is used: so that this word may well also be here rendered, *bowels* (being of the same notion with the former; as *womb*, and *belly*, are one, and the same, in the place before mentioned) had we like variety of words, fit to express both by: for the sense of either *bowels*, or *entrails* (which in the former member may not do amiss) seems the same.

*{are they restrained?*} This distinction of the text, in our version, is somewhat discrepant from the pointings in the original, wherein the stop, is at the latter word, that signifies *bowels*, and the word rendered *toward me*, is carried on, and joined to this last. This most other, both translators, and expositors, have observed, and therein therefore this our last version seems to go by itself; to reckon up all the various readings, and renderings, would be too tedious. I will point at some few of the principal only; the old Latin gives it us in the enunciative; *they contain*, or, *restrain, themselves upon me*, or, *toward me*: that which a learned late writer controlling, would rather have it read, *they do with violence* (like *a torrent*, Job 6.15. Psal. 126.4. hence so called) *pour themselves forth upon me*: a metaphor from waters, that having been pent up some time, break forth, and run down with more violence, when the floodgates are set open: but this is directly contrary to the main drift of the whole passage; and the Geneva version therefore coming nearer home to the Latin, *they are restrained from me*: wherewith those also do, in sense and substance, concur, who read them interrogatively apart by themselves; and render them, as does the Italian, *Do they restrain themselves towards me?* Nor do they much differ in regard of the sense of the place, who bring this last branch, within compass of the foregoing interrogation; which the lesser stops hinder not; either renewing the interrogation, at the mention of *mercies*; because no conjunction comes between that, and the former: and reading it, (which divers do) *the yearning of thy bowels, and thy mercies, are they restrained?* or, as, others, *should they restrain themselves, towards us?* or, carrying on the whole, in a continued tenor to the end of the verse, as our ancienter English versions, and some other do; *How is it, that thy jealousy, thy strength, the multitude of thy mercy and loving kindness, will not be entreated of us?* But these do not so fitly, and exactly express the notion of the word here used: the word is in a reciprocal form, and signifies properly, *to contain*, or, in a manner, *to enforce one's self*, that is, by force, to refrain, and keep in, from expressing, and manifesting itself, some inward affection, that is hard to conceal, and would be breaking out. So of Joseph it is said, when *his bowels yearned upon his Brother* Benjamin, he made haste to withdraw, and having wept a while in private, (for he could not wholly forbear) he washed his face, and coming out again, *he refrained*, or, *restrained, himself*, Gen. 43.30,31. and again, Gen. 45.1. *Joseph could no longer refrain himself*; it is applied unto God, Chap. 42.14. & 64.12. I concur therefore with those, that adjoin these words to the latter part of the interrogative, reading them, either with a learned late writer, *Where is the yearning of thine entrails, and thy bowels*, (so I conceive it to be most fitly rendered) *which restrain themselves towards me?* (the relative supplied, as ver. 8.) or rather, with the Greek, which instead of the relative, supplies the particle, *that*, (as the like is, ver. 13.) *Where is the yearning of thine entrails, and thy bowels*, (what is become of them?) *that they* (to wit, your entrails, or bowels) *do restrain themselves towards me?* that they keep themselves in, as shut up, under forcible restraint, and do not break out into tender pity, and compassion towards me, in this my present doleful, and distressed condition? it is that which John says, *If a man see his brother in want, and shut*, or *close up, his bowels from him*, 1 Joh. 3.17. or, if any shall deem it better, to sever them from that branch, and take them apart by themselves, I should choose to render them in a potential notion, *can they contain themselves at us?* or, *towards us?* as if they had said, how is it possible, that such compassionate bowels, as you abound with, beyond the reach of man's thought, should be able to contain themselves from yearning upon me, at the sight, and consideration of my present condition? the potential use of these forms is frequent. See Num. 23.8,10,21. Chap. 38.18. the like expostulatory complaint of the suspense, or, restraint, of God's mercies, see Psal. 77.7–9. Chap. 64.12.

**V. 16.** *{Doubtless, thou art our Father;*} To move God the rather to compassion towards them; and to intimate why they expect it from him, and may seem not without some good ground, to complain of the restraint of it, they mind God of the relations between him and them. So Chap. 64.8.

*{Doubtless*} Or, *Certainly*. So is the particle used, Chap. 49.18. & 60.9. Yet it is here by some rendered, *For*; as chap. 29.27. and it may be read, *Since that*, as some render it: or, *Yet*; or, *Howbeit*: as Job 5.7. Chap. 9.1. and 31.4. and 49.25.

*{thou art our Father*} Deut. 32.6. Mal. 2.10. Mat. 6.9. and a father cannot but be compassionately affected towards his children, Psal. 103.13. Mal. 3.17. Mat. 6.26, 32. & 7.9–11. Luk. 11.11. & 15.17,18,20. or, you are he, upon whom alone we depend, as upon our Father, for support and relief. See Mat. 23.9.

*{though Abraham be ignorant of us, and Israel acknowledge us not*} Or, *for* (as Psal. 12.1.) *Abraham knoweth us not; nor doth Israel ken us*: he is alike ignorant of us: for it is but the same notion, in divers terms; as is very frequent with this prophet, and so the latter word is commonly used; as Gen. 27.23. Ruth 3.14. 1 King. 20.41. As for Abraham and Jacob, they were our fathers indeed; but we are now out of their cognizance: and it were in vain for us to expect aught from them, who being departed hence, are strangers to the affairs of this world, and altogether unacquainted (for aught we know) with our present condition. So the Jewish commenters themselves on this place; Abraham, says one, knew us not, when we were afflicted in Egypt: nor did Israel know us, when we wandered in the wilderness; for they were long before taken out of the world. And another of them; fathers of flesh and blood, may know their children, and their children's children, so long as they live; but Abraham, and Israel, were dead many ages ago; but you alone are our living and lasting Father: and you do, through all ages, continue so to be; and we have no father here to seek to, besides you. See Job 14.21. 2 King. 22.20. and this exactly goes with the Hebrew. Yet some would have the meaning to be that they were grown so degenerate, that neither Abraham, nor Israel, were they alive again, would own them. See Joh. 8.39,40. Rom. 9.6,7. And others, that though Abraham, and Israel, should refuse to own them, yet would not God cease to be their Father; as Psal. 27.10.

*{Abraham, and Israel*} These two he mentions, say the Jewish doctors; because the one was the first of the three chief patriarchs, and the covenant was by God, with him plighted, for himself, and his seed, to be God to him, and them, Gen. 17.7. the other, because he was the last of them; and his whole issue taken into the covenant: whereas Isaac's whole seed was not. See chap. 43.1. & 44.1.

*{thou, O Lord, art our Father*} Or, as some, *yet* (supplied, as Chap. 49.4. & 57.10.) *thou art our Father*; or, *but* supplied, as chap. 54.15. *thou art our Father*; you continue so to be; as Dan. 1.21.

*{our Redeemer, thy name is from eternity.*} You are both our Father, and our Redeemer, chap. 44.24. See Deut. 32.6. or, because of the stop, at *our Father*, in the text, as some read it, *our Redeemer is from of old thy name*; you have, through all ages from time to time, been called, and accounted, the righter, and rescuer of us your people, Psal. 90.1. See chap. 47.4.

**V. 17.** *{O Lord, why hast thou made us to err from thy ways, and hardened our heart from thy fear?*} Why have you given us up to a spirit of error, and obstinacy, by denying unto us the conduct and guidance of your good Spirit, vers. 11. and leaving us to be led away by our own corrupt and perverse lusts, Psal. 81.12. Rom. 1.26.28. and so it may seem to have reference unto that dreadful and direful doom, by God, passed upon this people, chap. 6.9,10. or, why should you, by suffering us to lie under such heavy pressures for so long a time together, in the hands of cruel oppressors, give this people occasion to leave your law; and in a desperate obstinacy, casting off your service, to betake themselves to wicked and heathenish ways. See Psal. 125.3. Whether way of the two we take, I suppose it to be by the prophet conceived, not as some would have it, in the person of the profane, and worse sort among them, murmuring against God, and imputing to him, the cause of all their miscarriages; but in the person of the pious, and better party, lamenting, that God had, (though justly) thus given up his people unto error and obstinacy; and as amazed to consider, that God their Father, who had formerly been so gracious to them, and chary of them, should now inflict on them, so heavy a judgment as to withdraw himself from them, and to leave them thus to themselves; and bewailing the horrid effect, and event, that it either already had, or was like to have, with many, who were, or would be, thereby induced to withdraw themselves from God, and betake themselves to heathenish superstitions, and the service of other gods: and this latter, with a learned writer, I incline to, as conceiving it to be the genuine sense of the text.

*{made us to err*} Or, *wander.* So Abraham of himself, *when God caused me to wander*, Gen. 20.13. But I suppose, if we follow the former sense, it would rather here be rendered; *why hast thou permitted*, or *suffered, us*; or, as some, *dost thou permit*, or, *suffer us, to wander from*, or, *out of, thy ways?* for in this notion, not of impulsion, but of permission, is this form frequently used, and sometime rendered. So Prov. 10.3. *The Lord will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish*: and, *Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live*, Exod. 22.18. & Psal. 37.33. *The Lord will not condemn* (that is suffer him to be condemned, but cause him to be cleared, vers. 4. Psal. 109.21.) *when he is judged*; as also, Psalm 119.10. *let me not wander*, or, *suffer me not to stray*, (the very same word that is here used) *from thy commandments*; or, according to the latter reading, *Why shouldest thou cause us to wander from thy ways?* Why should you give this people any occasion, which their wicked hearts are over-prone to take, so to do; as if you had put them thereupon. So it should be, not unlike that speech of David, 1 Sam. 26.19. *by driving me from abode in the Lord’s inheritance, they say, Go serve other gods*: as if they should say, What gain will there, or can there, accrue unto you, by keeping us so long, in this forlorn condition, (as they reason, Psal. 30.9. & 44.12.) especially, by the revolt of many of your people from you, a thing likely thereupon to ensue?

*{and hardened our heart from thy fear*} Or, *why hast thou hardened our hearts*, (for the word *heart*, is here collective, as Psal. 119.70.) *hardened our hearts*; as it is said of Pharao, delivered up by God, unto the hardness of his own obstinate heart, by God’s forbearance, and mercies, yet further obdurated, Exod. 7.3,8,15,19,32. & 9.7,12,34,35. & 10.1,20,27. & 11.10. & 14.48. But so the word here used, is nowhere found, save here, and Job 39.16. where it is said of the ostrich, that *she hardeneth herself against her young ones, as if they were not hers: from thy fear*; *that we should not fear thee*: for that is the constant notion of this form; as Psal. 69.23. *from seeing*, for, *that they may not see: from speaking*, for, *that one may not speak*, 1 Sam. 25.17. *from house, so that no house is left*, Chap. 23.1. *from entrance, so as none can enter*, Chap. 24.15. *thy fear*, for, *the fear of thee*; as Psal. 5.7. and as, *his knowledge*, for, *the knowledge of him*, Chap. 53.11. not as the subject, but as the object of either: or, *why shouldest thou harden our hearts from thy fear?* that is, *from thy service.* So as we should not serve you, but leaving you and your service, go after strange gods; as they, Jer. 44.16,17. for so is the word, *fear*, very frequently used in Scripture, See 2 King. 17.25–28,32,33,35,36,40,41. Chap. 29.13.

*{Return for thy servants’ sake, the tribes of thine inheritance,}* Or, *unto the tribes of thine inheritance*: as Moses at the stay of the ark, *Return, O Lord, unto the many thousands of Israel*; a defect of the particle, as 1 King. 2.15. Chap. 52.4.

*{Return*} Turn from your wrath, and return in mercy, and favor; be reconciled again to your people: as Psalm 80.14. & 90.13.

*{for thy servants’ sake*} For Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob’s sake, unto whom you made your promises, Gen. 22.17,18. & 26.3,24. & 28.13,14. Psal. 105.9,10. in regard whereof, you have yourself professed to have selected us, and to affect us, Deut. 7.6–8. So Moses, Exod. 32.13. for these, though not excluding other their religious, and pious progenitors, as David among the rest, of whom mention is also made in the like kind, Psal. 132.1. chap. 37.35. or, for those few, your faithful ones, that remain yet among us. See chap. 65.8. but here rather, the former.

*{the tribes*} This some by way of apposition, join to the words before going, *thy servants*, expounding it of those, their ancestors, who were, say they, as *rods*, (so the word in its native notion signifies) out of which these people, as sprigs, did sprout. But I conceive it rather to be meant, as before was said, of the people themselves, who were divided into tribes, and according to their tribes had the land of promise divided among them, Num. 34.13–15. Psal. 78.55. of those, not for whom, but unto whom, God is entreated here to return.

*{thine inheritance*} As well the land itself, (which seems here intended, by what follows, vers. 18.) as the people are called God’s *inheritance*; and *the rod of God’s inheritance*; because lands of inheritance, upon distribution, among coparceners, were ofttimes meted out by the rod, Psal. 74.2. & 78.71. & 79.1. & 94.5. cha. 19.25. So rather, than as some, both of the Jews, and others, that render the word here *rods* and expound it, *rulers*: as relating to that, chap. 43.28. and this therefore they plead unto God, as intimating, that it might be deemed a dishonor unto him, not to regard his own inheritance, (whether the men, or the land) but to suffer it so to be trampled on, and such waste to be made of it, Jer. 50.11. Joel 2.17. & 3.2.

**V. 18.** *{The people of thine holiness have possessed it but a little while*} Or, *Thine holy people* (Exod. 19.6. Deut. 7.6. Heb. *thy people of holiness*: as, *thy mountain of holiness*, chap. 56.7. and, *thy cities of holiness*, chap. 64.10.) *have held it but a little while*; the pronoun *it*, is not in the text, but to be supplied; as chap. 46.11. & 57.8. and has reference to *inheritance*, verse 17. that is, the land of promise, as most here take it. Where question is moved, how it should be said, that God’s people had possessed their land but *a little while*, when as they had held it for so many hundred years. Whereunto some answer, that it is said, *a little while*, because a long time seems but little when it is once past, in that estate, and those things especially, that men desire longer to enjoy, Job 9.25,26. Psal. 90.4. Others, *a little while*, in regard of God’s promise, that they should possess it forever, Gen. 17.8. & 26.3. & 28.13. Exod. 32.13. which promise yet had a condition always implied in it, and is expressly mentioned, 2 Chron. 33.8. See Jer. 18.9,10. and these answers are the most probable, the words being thus rendered. For some take in the word, *sanctuary*: So the ancient Greek, joining this branch to the former verse: *Return to the tribes of thine inheritance, that thy people may possess thy sanctuary a little longer.* But this the words will not well bear. Others reading this whole verse, thus; *Thine holy people but a while possessed thy sanctuary, which our enemies trample on*: and here one of the Jewish accountants helps them a little, that go this way, which he seems also somewhat to incline to, observing on the place, that the temple stood but, 420 years: whereas from the promise made of the possession of the land, to their deliverance out of Egypt, was above 430 years, Gen. 15.13. Exod. 12.41. and from their deliverance out of Egypt, or, (as they use to speak) from the lamb, or, the law, to the temple, 480 years, 1 King. 6.1. But one of ours rather would have it so said; because they had slighted it, and made little good use of it; and might well be said therefore but a little while to have possessed it. But this seems to be overmuch strained; besides, that it makes a needless trajection of the terms in the text. Others therefore understand it of the adversaries of God’s people; one reading the words, *They have almost possessed themselves of thy people.* Another, *For a little space of time have they possessed thy people, and trampled upon thy sanctuary*; that is, for three year and a half, under Antiochus, Dan. 12.7,11,12. But the former comes short of the prophet’s purpose; the latter directly crosses his drift: a fond thing to imagine, that the people of God should complain, that their enemies had been but a while possessed of them. The old Latin reads it, *As a thing of nought have they possessed thine holy people*; that is, as those that follow it, they possess, and use your people, as some sorry thing of no account. See verse 19. & Lam. 1.11,17. & 3.45. and the common use of the word may seem to wind it somewhat this way; for it is used sometime for *little*, whereof *Zoar* was so termed, Gen. 19.20,22. sometime, for *the younger*, as in Latin, *the less*: and as *great*, for, *elder*, Gen. 25.23. sometime, for, *a small company*, 2 Chr. 24.24. sometime for *one of small account*, or reckoning, Psa. 119.141. Mic. 5.2. See chap. 60.22. but of time, or shortness of time, I nowhere find it used. And I deem therefore this reading not improbable; the rather, because the particle prefixed, has oftentimes the like use, as Gen. 16.3. when it is said, that Sarah gave Hagar unto Abraham, not *to be his wife*, (as it is amiss rendered) but, *to be as his wife.* And I should much rather incline to it, than to that, which yet some of prime note hold out, *Even unto the least do they* *as by right of inheritance possess thine holy people.* But this I leave to the judgment of others, hinting only mine own dissent.

*{our adversaries have trodden down thy sanctuary*} Or, *tread down*, or, *trample upon, thy sanctuary*; that is, as some, your holy land: whereunto the name of *sanctuary*, is sometime given, Exod. 15.17. Psal. 78.54. Jer. 12.10. See Chap. 43.28. Or, as others, rather, your holy house, your temple, your palace, where you had wont to appear to your people; and where your people had wont to worship you, Chap. 64.11. Psal. 74.3 4. Lam. 1.10.

**V. 19.** *{We are thine; thou never barest rule over them; they were not called by thy name*} That is, We are yet still your people, ver. 18. your servants, your subjects, so called, and so accounted, and such as do call upon you, Chap. 48.1,2. & ver. 8. That which these people, our enemies, ver. 18. never were, never did, Chap. 65.1. Jer. 10.25. or, *we have been* your people *of old.* So the Chaldee, and one of the Jewish doctors, on the place, and some other; We are those, whom you have long since taken to yourself, to be your peculiar people, Ver. 19. Exod. 19.5,6. Deut. 7.6,7. that which they never were, Amos 3.2. But the word, *thine*, is not in the text; and at *we are*, or, *we have been*, there is a stop. The ancient Greek, and the old Latin, therefore, whom divers others, even of ours, follow, read the words, thus; *We have been*, or, *are, as from the beginning, when thou didst not rule over us, nor was thy name called upon us*; that is, before the deliverance out of Egypt, say some, or, (because that seems not so to be.
