See Exod. 3.7. & 4.12.) before Abraham’s time, say others, Josh. 24.2,3. We are no more regarded, nor looked after by you, than before you took us to be your people: the note of similitude is supplied; as Chap. 62.5. the particle of time; as Chap. 48.13,21. Divers of ours, with whom I concur, *We are become*, as those, *whom thou didst never bear rule over, nor were ever called by thy name*: or, as I conceive, more exactly to the terms of the text; *We are*, as if we were those, *whom from of old, thou hadst not ruled over, nor had thy name been called upon.* We are in that despicable condition, so vilely used, & basely dealt with, as if we were none of your people, much less such as have been so long time your subjects, living under your protection, & whom you have been pleased from time to time, to own as yours. See Chap. 26.13. and ver. 18. as if we were those (the like supply, see Job 39.16. *she carrieth herself hardly towards her young ones, as if they were not hers*) *whom from old* (as ver. 16.) *thou hadst not ruled over*, or, *thou hadst never* (as Chap. 64.4.) *ruled over*; (Heb. *ruled over them*; the demonstrative, for the relative: as Chap. 42.1. & 46.4. or, a defect of the relative; as ver. 8. and a redundancy of the demonstrative: as Jer. 1.2.) *nor had thy name been called upon.* So the Hebrew. One’s *name* is, in Scripture, said to be *called upon* those, that bear his name, or are called by his name, as having relation to him, in some kind, or other, as their superior, and one that has special interest in them, and power over them. So children are said to have their father’s name called on them, Gen. 48.14. the wife her husband’s, Chap. 4.1. the subjects, and servants, their sovereign lords, and their masters. So here. See Jer. 14.9. Dan. 9.19. So Deut. 28.10. 2 Chron. 7.14. Chap. 48.1. & 43.7.

### CHAPTER 64

**Vers. 1.** *{O That thou wouldest rent the heavens, that thou wouldest come down;*} That this chapter runs on in one tenor, with the latter part of the former, is not doubted. But here appears plainly, what was formerly observed (see Chap. 58.3. & 62.6.) that the Masorets, or whoever they were, that divided the books of Scripture, into chapter, and verse, did not sometime exactly distinguish either: For these words, together with those, that make up the first verse of this chapter with us, are in the Hebrew copies, cast into the last verse of the chapter foregoing, and so close up that chapter; (see the like 2 Chron. 30.18,19.) and this chapter is made to begin at our second verse, which has a manifest dependence upon this, whereas this has no such coherence with that, which by them it is annexed unto. So that this chapter, according to the division of the Greek & Latin versions, as we have them now divided, and of our English ones likewise, begins in the middle of a verse, according to the distinctions in the Hebrew, and that with better ground, if we regard the course of the context, as any intelligent reader may easily discern. Yet this to salve, the Chaldee thus renders this passage; not, as a learned man relates him; *Didst not thou rent the heavens for us?* but, as if the word were not *lu*, but *lo*; *Thou hast not rent the heavens for them*; to wit, for those, *over whom thou didst not rule, nor were called by thy name*, Chap. 65.19. whereunto one of the Jewish commenters treading in his steps, adds, *As thou didst sometime for us.* But herein the other Jewish masters dissent from him, and agreeing with us, refer us, for the signification of the particle to Psal. 81.13. which writers do now generally accord in: Only some of them render it in the time past, *O that thou hadst rent the heavens, and come down*; when Nebuchadnezzar was about the storming of our city; as you did, when you came to deliver your people from Pharao’s pursuit of them, Exod. 14.24. Psal. 77.16–18. and as you did against Sennacherib’s forces, when they lay before Jerusalem, Chap. 30.30. & 37.36. But the most, as our versions, in the present, or future, for notion, if not for form, *O that thou wouldest* (beholding how basely your holy people are dealt with, and how horribly your glorious courts and palace, are profaned and polluted, and in despite of you, trampled and trodden upon, Chap. 62.19. and taking to heart such insolencies and indignities, offered to your sacred majesty) no longer forbear, but *rent the heavens, and come down*; that is, come down in furious and violent manner; as if you did rent the heavens, and all asunder before you, to destroy your adversaries, and deliver your people. See Psal. 18.8,9–16.

*{that the mountains may flow down at thy presence?}* Or, *that they might run down*, or *melt.* See on ver. 2,3.

**V. 2.** *{as when the melting fire burneth, the fire causeth the waters to boil,}* That these words belong to the former verse, as intimating in what manner the mountains would *melt*, or *run down*, if God in such manner should appear, and are amiss therefore disjoined from them, writers of the best note observe and acknowledge. Some suppose them, to contain two distinct similitudes; the former, taken from the melting of metals, the other, from the boiling of water in a cauldron, or kettle. Others, but one only, and that this latter. To pass by the great variety of improbable versions, and pitch on those only, that carry some probability with them. Some of those that make them two, thus read the words; *As when the fire of burnings melteth*, or, *as when the fire burneth the meltings*; that is, *the things melted*: for the verb is taken sometime actively; as Chap. 50.11. Jer. 17.4. sometime passively; as Deut. 32.22. Jer. 15.14. and so the meaning should be, the mountains should run down with fire, as the metal that runs by the force of the fire that melts it; and, *as the fire* (whether falling into the water, as some, or kindled under it, as others) *doth cause it to boil*, or, *to swell*, and to rise up in *bubbles*: whence those swelling *blains*, or *blisters*, Exod. 9.9,10. have their name. See on Chap. 21.12. & 30.13. as if it were said, that it might be with the mountains, as with water boiling in a pot, which the fire underneath it, makes to work and swell, and rise up in bubbles; as Job 41.31. Of those that conceive but one resemblance alone, some read them; *As when the fire burneth the dry stubble*, or *the spray, the fire* (that is, *it*, the noun for the pronoun; as Chap. 37.14. 2 Tim. 1.18.) *maketh the water to boil*, or *bubble.* Others, *As when a melting fire*, or, *a vehement fire burneth, the fire* (that is, such a fire) *maketh the water to boil.* Which way soever of all these we take it, the meaning will be very near the same; that upon God’s so descending, as is here desired, and in such manner manifesting himself, the mountains may be strangely wrought upon, and made to work, as hard, and as rocky as they are, like water boiling amain over some extreme forcible fire. Some, following the Chaldee paraphrast, would have it an allusion to the fire, that upon Elias his prayer, falling from heaven, consumed not the sacrifice only, but the stones also that the altar was built with, and the water in the trench about it, 1 King. 18.38. but it is by others, deemed rather to have respect only to the force of fire in this kind, upon water in general: Whereunto may be added, that sulfury mines (of which more anon) being kindled underground, near to streams of water, or to the seaside, do sometime make those streams to boil up in strange manner; yea, to make the sea itself, to boil like a cauldron, as not long since, at one of the Western Islands, where the fish died therewith in great abundance; and an island of some good bigness, shot up out of the sea, at a great depth, whereinto afterward it sunk again. The similitude is not amiss, by some deemed to hold, especially, in the large quantity of steam, or vapors, that a pot, so working, is wont to send up: That which may help to back the opinion of those, who suppose the case of Mount Sinai, when God appeared in fire on it, to be here, at least, glanced at, as it is commonly supposed to be intended, ver. 3. at which time it is said of it, that *the smoke of it ascended*, as the smoke of a furnace, Exod. 19.18.

*{As when*} Of the use of the note of similitude, including the particle of time. See on Chap. 17.5.

*{the melting fire*} The word here used, is nowhere else found: whence divers opinions of it; a Jewish critic says it signifies, *dry stubble*: some of ours render it, *spray*, such as is commonly put under pots to make them seethe, Psal. 58.9. Chap. 27.11. Eccl. 7.6. But neither give they any reason why the word should so signify, or any instance of such use of it. A learned writer would have it deduced from a Syriac word, said to have a notion of *boldness*, and to signify, *a vehement fire*: The most take it to be, word for word, *a fire of liquefactions, dissolutions*, or *meltings*; supposing the root from whence it comes, as it has, for letters and sound, near affinity with the word that signifies *to melt*, so to be of the selfsame notion with it; with whom I concur, as conceiving it to suit very well, with what both that learned man, and the Jewish doctors say of it, to wit, that it imports, as he, *a vehement*; as they, *a great*, or *strong fire*: not like that of *stubble*, or *spray*; but of some more solid matter, such as is able to melt and dissolve metals, stones, rocks, or any other materials that it meets with, Job 28.2. Howbeit, a late learned annotator, would have it, from the Arabic, to signify, *a gentle fire*, such as makes no great noise; and the meaning to be, as a gentle or soft fire is enough to make water boil; so your very name made known to your adversaries, will be sufficient to affright them. See Psal. 68.1,2. But this I leave unto the judgment of others.

*{to make thy name known to thine adversaries,}* That your adversaries may see and take notice of your power: *name*, for, *might, power, majesty*, and the like; as 1 King. 8.42,43. Psal. 106.8.

*{that the nations may tremble at thy presence,}* Heb. *the nations will tremble at thy presence*: but there is a defect of the particle *that*; as Chap. 63.13. See Exod. 15.14–16.

**V. 3.** *{When thou didst terrible things which we looked not for;*} Or, *As when*, &c. carrying on the sentence: the note of similitude supplied; as chap. 62.5. See v. 2. Oh that you would do now such dreadful things, as, in times past, you did for our forefathers; and that then, when they little looked for any such matters.

*{thou didst terrible things*} In the behalf of your people, both while they were yet in Egypt, and afterward also in the wilderness, Psal. 78.12,13,43–53. & 105.27–36. & 106.9–11. Neh. 9.9–11.

*{which*} The relative supplied; as Chap. 63.8.

*{we looked not for*} *We*, that is, our forefathers, with whom, we are as one race, as one body. So Jer. 2.6,7. Mic. 6.4. This is the rather inserted, to strengthen their faith, and to encourage them to seek unto God, for the like terrible things now to be done for them; considering, that God had been pleased, in times past, to do such things for those, who then expected them not. See Psal. 65.5.

*{thou camest down*} To deliver your people, and to destroy their oppressors, Exod. 3.8. a metaphor taken from the practice of some great prince or potentate, that should come down, in state, from his palace, to hear the suits of poor suppliants, and to see justice done for them, upon such as had wronged them. So ver. 1.

*{the mountains flowed down at thy presence.*} Or, *so that* (supplied, as ver. 2.) *the mountains melted at thy presence.* These words have, questionless, reference to some particular story of things, formerly past and done. And it is by most interpreters deemed, that there is in them a special respect unto God’s glorious appearance on the top of Mount Sinai, at the giving of the law; at which time, say some of the Rabbines upon this place, the thick cloud wherein God appeared, and out of which he spoke, and from which those fearful thunderclaps, and flashes of lightning, proceeded, Exod. 19.16,18,20. & 18.20,21. did withal pour down such showers of rain, as in such case is wont to be, that the mountains all about, not Sinai alone, but mount Paran, Hab. 3.3. Mount Seir, Deut. 2.5. and others, did run down with streams of water. And we find indeed somewhat the like to have been at the passage of God’s people through the Red Sea, and the submersion of Pharao and his forces, that pursued them, Judg. 5.4. Psal. 68.8,9. & 77.17. but of any such showers that should be at the time of the giving the law, I read not: Nor seems it very probable, if any such were, that they should reach so far, as to Mount-Paran, and to Mount-Seir, much less, so far distant from Sinai. But I suppose the word rendered, *flowed down*, as deemed to come from one commonly used of water, Job 36.28. Psal. 147.18. Jer. 9.18. would, in this place, at least, be rendered, *ran down*, or *melted*, as in the like argument, where that word is questionless used, it is rendered, *The mountains melted at his presence*, Judg. 5.5. And as the psalmist, though using another word there, *The mountains melted like wax, at the presence of the Lord*, Psal. 97.5. Here so the rather, if not in regard of the foregoing resemblance of the melting of metals, ver. 2. because that is by some questioned; and the word is here in somewhat another form, than that in the other place, so rendered: yet for, that it is by a Jewish critic conceived to come from a root, that signifies, as *by melting to waste*, whence *a rioter* is so termed, Deut. 21.20. Prov. 23.21. because by riotous courses, he *melts*, and *wastes away* his means. And though it should not be denied, but that the words might have an eye to that dreadful sight on Sinai; yet rather with reference to the fire, and the flashings of it, than to any water, or floods thereof, that should at that time be seen. And it may well be deemed, that there is withal some allusion, to the usual manner of those burning hills, such as Etna in Sicily, Soma in Italy, Hecla, and Hogla in Iseland, which breaking out, are wont to run down with streams of fire, and sulfury matter, into the seas beside them, and valleys beneath them. Nor is it unlikely, but that, as in those Egyptian tempests, it is said, that *the fire ran along upon the ground*, Exod. 9.13. so in that terrible apparition, the mountain which was all on a flame, Deut. 4.11. did run down with fire, as if it had been melted and dissolved therewith; as it is said, that in the general execution of God’s vengeance upon his enemies, the mountains should be *melted with their blood*; that is, they should run down with such streams of blood, as if they were melted therewith, or dissolved thereinto, Chap. 34.3. Nor is it needful, because mention is made of mountains; that therefore we should have recourse unto those more remote ones. There seems to have been a cluster, or combination of mountains in that place, the two principal and highest whereof being Sinai, and Horeb, and they joining much and near together, the place in the mount, on which God so appeared, is sometime called *Mount-Horeb*, Exod. 3.1. & 33.6. Deut. 4.10,15. & 5.2. sometime *Mount-Sinai*, Exod. 19.11,18,20,23. of *Sion*, and *Moriah*, see somewhat the like, on Chap. 2.2. & 14.13. Howbeit, in regard that that apparition on Mount Sinai was not intended so much for a terror unto God’s enemies, as to strike a reverent awe, and dread of his majesty, into his own people, Exod. 20.19,20. Deut. 5.29. I conceive the words here to have respect, not unto that alone, but unto other God’s majestical manifestations of himself in dreadful manner about those times, for the preservation of his people, and in way of opposition to their adversaries, and unto that more specially before mentioned, when Pharao pursued them, being then near the brink of the Red Sea, having gotten them, as he thought there, in a trap, Exod. 14.3. at *Piharoth*, that is, *at the mouth of the mountains* (so the word signifies) between the jaws whereof they seemed to be shut up, no way left to escape, but by rushing into the sea, wherein they must of necessity perish, Exod. 14.3,9. and the *mountains* here mentioned, may well be those among others, between which they passed neighboring so near upon that place, where that admirable deliverance was wrought for God’s people, with so remarkable a destruction of their insolent adversaries. See Hab. 3.3–15. I shall propound but one conjecture more, which I shall leave to the consideration of the learned. I observe that an interpreter, of special note, carries the latter part of this verse, to the beginning of the first, the words being in either place precisely the same: and renders the words, as there; so here; *Oh that* (I say) *thou wouldst so come down, that the mountains might run down at thy presence*: so the whole tract of the context between the one and the other should be inserted by way of parenthesis; which if it be admitted, I suppose that the former words of this verse might not improbably be deemed to have reference unto that strange, and indeed unexpected (in all likelihood, for the manner of it) defeat given unto Sennacherib’s army before Jerusalem, and the deliverance of the city and state, thereby produced, Chap. 37.36: and then the *mountains* here mentioned, might have some eye also unto *those mountains*, on which God threatened *to tread down the Assyrian*, Chap. 14.25. See the lively description of that defeat, Chap. 30.27,33. Howsoever, they stray from the genuine sense of the text, that would by *mountains* have here understood, mighty men, or great potentates; as Chap. 2.14. drawing hither that, chap. 33.10–12. which is but to sew together things unsuitable.

**V. 4.** *{For from the beginning of the world men have not heard, nor perceived by the ear, neither hath the eye seen, O God, besides thee, what he hath prepared for him, that waiteth for him.*} Or, *Nor have men ever heard*, or *heard of*; *nor hath any eye seen a God besides thee that hath done*, or *can do so for him, that waiteth for him.* These two versions exhibit, though not all the particular, yet the principal differences, about the sense of this passage. It is not without just cause deemed to be here brought in, as in the person of God’s people, to intimate, that they wanted not some good ground to solicit God to do for them, as they here desire, in their present distress; because they knew him to be such a God, as was able to do for those that depended upon him, as no other was ever known to do for his people; or because those wonderful works that he had done, could do, and would do, for those that relied and rested upon him, were such, as no human eye, or ear, had ever either seen, or heard. See Chap. 66.8.

*{For*} Heb. *And*; as Chap. 63.8.

*{from the beginning of the world*} Heb. *from the world*; whence a Rabbine here expounds it, the people *of the world*; as the boar *from the wood*, for, *of the wood*, Psal. 80.13. but I find not where this form is so used: It is rendered sometime, *from everlasting*, (which seems a very improper speech) or, *from eternity*, Pro. 8.23. Psal. 90.2. Chap. 63.16. sometime, *from of old*, Gen. 6.4. Chap. 57.11. or, *in old time*, Josh. 24.2. and *ever of old*, Chap. 25.6. (where the one seems superfluous:) and with the negative, *never*, Chap. 63.19. and may well be so rendered here.

*{men have not heard*} *Men* is not in the text: the Jewish master before mentioned; *they of the world have not heard*; but the verb seems indefinite, *they have not heard*; and the noun, says another of them, is enclosed in the verb; *the hearers*, or *they that hear, have not heard*; as, *they embalmed him*, that is, *the embalmers embalmed him*, Gen. 50.26. or, more plainly, *they have not heard*, that is, *there hath not been heard*; as, *they shall call them*, for *they shall be called*, Mal. 1.4.

*{nor perceived by the ear*} This word, as it is oft joined with the former, Deut. 32.1. Psal. 49.1. Chap. 1.10. & 28.24. & 51.4. so they are much of the same notion the one with the other: yet some here so distinguish them, as if the one implied the hearing of a thing immediately; the other, a receiving it by report from others. So that whereas there are three ordinary means, by which men come to notice of things; either by hearing them immediately themselves, or by hearsay from others, or by eyesight; all three should be here excluded: whereunto the apostle seeming to have an eye to this passage, adds a fourth, 1 Cor. 2.9. the discourse of reason; *nor hath entered into man’s heart*: but that also receives still some ground from sense. Now these two branches, or this branch rather consisting of two sprigs, some of the Jewish commenters seem to refer unto *the terrible* things mentioned, ver. 3. such, as the like before, had never been heard, Chap. 48.6. See Deut. 4.32–34.

*{neither hath the eye seen, O God, besides thee*} That is, as those that go this way, which some also of the Jewish writers do; no human eye, or sense, ever was able to reach, or apprehend, the things that God intended, to do for his, before he did them; or that he intended to do, before they be done, though to God himself they were well known before, Acts 15. 18. to which purpose, the apostle also seems to apply them, 1 Cor. 2. 9, 11. Others read them, *no eye hath ever* (supplied from the former branch) *seen God beside thee*; there was never any such a God heard, (as Deut. 4. 33, 35, 36. & 5. 24.) or heard of, (as 1 King. 8. 42.) or seen (Deut. 4. 36.) that has done or can do, the like things that God, has. See Psal. 66. 8. & 89. 6, 8.

*{what he hath prepared*} Heb. *what he will do*, or *hath done*; for the tenses are oft promiscuously used: yet the word is sometime rendered, *to prepare*, as Ezek. 46. 2. and so our translators here give it, the rather, I suppose, because the apostle uses that term, 1 Cor. 2. 9. though the ancient Greek has it not: and they are mistaken therefore, who say, that the apostle here followed them. Those, that take the word *God*, before in the vocative case, are enforced here to acknowledge a change of the person, *he hath prepared*, or *done*, for, *thou hast prepared*, or *done*; or, *he will do*, for, *thou wilt do*: as, *ye have desired*, for, *they have desired*, chap. 1. 29. and, *thou that teareth himself*, for, *tearest thyself*, Job 18. 4. those that make it an accusative, or a governed case, do not alter the person, but insert the word *so*; *that hath so done*, or *can so do*: the former supply both the antecedent and the relative, included in the word *what*; that is, *that*, or *those things*, *which*, as the like is, vers. 5. & Jer. 2. 8, 11. the latter, the relative only; as before, verse 3. *that*, or *which*, (to wit, God) *hath done*, *will do*, or *can do*; for the indicatives are oft in a potential notion. See on chap. 49. 15. Some of either take the words in the time past; as meant of acts already done: so does the old Latin. Others take them, in the time to come: so does the ancient Greek. And from some of the Jewish commenters, we have a hint given us, that some of their ancienter doctors expounded them, of the times of the Messiah, & matters under him, to be effected. Of which, the apostle is also commonly supposed to understand them (see ch. 52. 16.) as being of the mind, that no prophecies went beyond the Messiah his days. But others of them understood them, as they profess also to do, of the world to come. I agree to them, that hold the text to have an eye to what God had formerly done for his people; such things, as no other God had ever been known, to have done, or was able to do. See chap. 41. 21–29. & 43. 9–13. And this is confirmed by that which follows, running on in the same strain, v. 5. The apostle seems to have made use of the prophet's words, applying them to his present discourse, as he does those other of the Psalmist, Rom. 10. 18. borrowed from Psal. 19. 4.

*{for him that waiteth for him*} For *him*; or, *for them*; (and the apostle has it in the plural) for the word is taken either collectively, for *all those*; or distributively for *any one of them*: the like see vers. 5. & chap. 17. 15. *that waiteth for him*, or *for thee*: if there be such a change of the person, as was before intimated, and the true God be here intended, for those that patiently wait, and depend upon you, chap. 8. 17. & 28. 16. & 30. 18. or, *that waiteth for him*; to wit, on any other god besides you; as Baal's priests did on him, who could not do for them, as the true God did for Elias, 1 King. 18. 26, 29, 36–39. But the other also, according to this exposition, is, though not expressed; yet implied: for when it is said, no other God has ever been known besides you, that has done, or can do so for them, that expect help from them: it is plainly intimated, that God had done, and could do strange things, for those that rely upon him; and that sometime, even beyond their expectation, as it is v. 3. For what is here said, *that wait on him*, the apostle has, *That love him*. And indeed, as none truly wait on him, but those that sincerely love him; so all that truly love him, are content, and willing to wait on him for them. See 2 Tim. 4. 8. with Heb. 9. 28. Jam. 1. 12. Nor do I doubt but the apostle had an eye to this place; howsoever the ancients some of them have not stuck to affirm, that the testimony alleged by him, is not at all found in the books of the Old Testament; and some, both of them, and of later times, would have it taken out of some apocryphal writing, going under the name of *Elias*; as of that of Jude, vers. 14. out of the like of *Enochs*: but such base counterfeits the apostle would scorn to own, or to grace, as these allegations they do.

**V. 5.** *{Thou meetest him that rejoiceth, and worketh righteousness, those that remember thee in thy ways.*} Or, *Thou didst meet him that rejoiced and wrought righteousness*; and, or even, *those that remembered thee in thy ways*: for it seems a continuation of their commemoration of God's dealings, for, and with, his people in times past.

*{Thou meetest*} Or, *didst meet*: hadst wont to meet. The word here used, is diversely taken, sometime, in a notion of kindness, and reconcilement, as the prodigal's father ran to meet him while he was yet afar off, Luke 15. 20. and as we use to say, *I will meet him halfway*; when we are willing, upon equal terms, to come to an accord with one, with whom we have been at variance: so most take the word here. You did in former times, meet our forefathers in mercy and goodness, you did freely of your own accord, show them abundance of kindness, and did prevent them, even unasked, with your favors, Psalm. 21. 2, 3. Or, as most of the Jewish commenters, when you were displeased with your people, yet did you accept of the intercession of those righteous ones, that were among them in their behalf, Exod. 32. 11–14. Numb. 14. 13, 20. Psalm. 99. 6–8. Of this use of the word, see on chap. 47. 3. & 53. 12. & 59. 16. But the former sense seems more natural, this latter more strained, scarce finding any clear instance to back it: that yet more constrained, which they relate from some other of their masters; who because they find this word, of *meeting*, not seldom used, in a contrary notion, as we also use it, when we say of one, whom we intend some shrewd turn to, *I will meet with him*; & signifies, to *run on*, or *fall foul*, (as we use to say) *upon* one, Num. 35. 19, 21. 2 Sam. 1. 15. 1 King. 2. 29. whereof also, see on chap. 47. 3. would have it here so to signify, *Thou didst slay*, or, *take away*, or, *Thou hast slain*, or, *taken away the righteous ones*: understanding it, some of them, of the times past; of Moses and Aaron, whom God took away, when as yet, at their entreaty, he had spared, and destroyed not, the mutinous multitude, Num. 20. 12, 24. Others, of the time present, that God had taken away all the godly ones, that might stand in the gap, to intercede for his people: the complaint of the prophet, that lived in the same times with Esay, Mic. 7. 1. See chap. 59. 16. vers. 7. but neither does the word itself, in the places produced, signify to take away, or to slay, though joined with those, that so signify; nor is the syntax here, the same with that there used; and cannot therefore here have place.

*{him, that rejoiceth, and worketh righteousness*} Or, *him that rejoiced, and wrought righteousness*. This some Jewish writers understand as spoken of Abraham: you were beneficial to Abraham, that rejoiced in your favor, and walked uprightly, Gen. 15. 1. & 17. 1, 17. Others of Moses & Aaron, as was before shown. But the word, though singular, yet does not design any one particular person, or persons; but is indefinite, as the like in the close of vers. 4. The term of *rejoicing*, some refer to the word, before going, and render the words, *Thou didst meet with joy him*, or *them, that wrought righteousness*. But, beside, that they take no notice of the copulative, the word here used, is never a noun; ever, either a verb, as chap. 66. 14. or a participle, as Psalm 119. 162. and so here. Others, therefore generally join it and the next epithet together; but so as they take this former in divers notions; for some understand it of the outward estate of the persons intended: *rejoicing*, that is, being in a cheerful and prosperous condition, as opposed unto the sad estate, wherein themselves were at present; but the most rather conceive it meant of their inward disposition, *that rejoiced, and wrought righteousness*, that is, *that rejoiced to work righteousness*, (see the like, chap. 61. 5.) that served you cheerfully, and delighted in well-doing, Deut. 16. 11, 14, 15. & 28. 47. Psalm 2. 11. & 37. 4. & 68. 3. & 112. 1. chap. 58. 13. of the phrase, *working righteousness*, see on chap. 56. 1.

*{those that remember thee in thy ways*} Some read these words, in the future, *they will remember thee in thy ways*; so the meaning should be, your people, who at present being at liberty, and in prosperity, regard you not, nor look after you; yet when they shall be in distress, and under restraint, will then think upon you, and seek to you for relief, chap. 26. 16. Lev. 26. 39. Jer. 2. 31, 32. & 22. 21. Psal. 78. 32. Dan. 9. 4. Hos. 5. 15. Others in the present, as our version, but most in the time past; yet so, that some distinguish these from the former, rendering the words with a supply of the copulative; *and those that remembered thee in thy ways*, that is, you did deal graciously, not with those alone, that in times of prosperity had walked uprightly before you; but with those also, who when your judgments were upon them, being thereby reclaimed and reformed, did then mind you, and sue to you for mercy, chap. 26. 8, 9. Deut. 30. 1, 2, 3. Psal. 22. 27. 2 Chr. 15. 4. But others rather conceive these to be the same persons with the former, by another character further deciphered; and render the text therefore with the supply of an explicative; *even those that remembered thee in thy ways*: such as were constantly mindful of you, and of their duty to you, according to the divers passages of your providence about them, as well to praise you in prosperity, as to pray unto you in adversity, to serve and to bless you in both, chap. 26. 13. Deut. 8. 1, 19. Job 1. 8, 21. & 2. 3. & 13. 15. & 27. 3–6. Psal. 44. 17, 18. the ways here mentioned, seeming to be rather ways of providence, and disposal, than ways of injunction, and direction; as those, Psa. 119. 1, 2. & 128. 1. whether way we take it, there is in the text a defect both of the antecedent, and relative; such as before, v. 4. as also of the copulative, according to the one, as chap. 63. 7, 10. of the explicative according to the other, as chap. 51. 22. & 57. 2. though there want not here, that supply, some, the causal, reading the words, *because they remembered thee in thy ways*: others, the illative therefore, or, *then, they praised thee for thy ways*: for those your dealings with them, as chap. 57. 17. Of the use of the word, *remember*, see on chap. 12. 4. But I adhere rather to the last of those before mentioned.

*{behold thou art wroth, for we have sinned: in those is continuance, and we shall be saved*} The prophet's concise language seems to have made this place the more obscure. Scarce two interpreters agree all out in the sense of them. The Jewish doctors much to this purpose expound them; *If*, or, *when, thou wast wroth, because we* (to wit, your people) *have sinned, yet by those* (just ones, vers. 4. our peace being made with you) *we were ever*, or *of old saved*; or, *when thou art wroth; because we have sinned; by those*, or, *for those*, (to wit, such righteous ones, were they always among us,) *we also might ever*, or, *as of old, be saved*. Among ours, some, *Behold, thou art wroth; and we sin still, in them* (to wit, our sins,) *have we always been*; or, *against them* (to wit, your ways, your precepts) *have we ever sinned; and yet have we been saved*: as Psal. 106. 6–8. Neh. 9. 26–28. or, as some, *and how should we be saved?* as Ezek. 33. 10. Others, *Behold, thou art wroth; because we have sinned; in those* (your ways) *had we ever been, we also had been saved*: had we continued in your ways, as they did, we had been saved from those miseries, wherein we now are, Deut. 30. 20. Chap. 26. 16. or, had we remembered you, or, been mindful of you, *perpetually, in those* (your ways) *we also had been saved*. Others, referring it to God; *in those* (your ways) *is continuance, that we may be saved*: (*and*, for, *that*; as Chap. 53. 2. and so Psal. 80. 3.) you continue constant in those your courses with us, to work thereby our salvation, Rom. 2. 4. 1 Cor. 11. 32. Others, *but in those* (your ways) *thou art ever, therefore are we saved*; or, *therefore we shall be saved*: (the copulative, in an illative notion; as Chap. 48. 7.) you continue constant in your mercy and goodness; and that is the reason, why we are not yet destroyed: or, it is that that puts us in hope, that you will yet save, and deliver us, out of our present distresses, Lam. 3. 21, 22. Mal. 3. 6. Divers other expositions there are; but these have authors of note, and may seem more than enough. I concur with that latter of the Jewish doctors; the rather, for that it suits best with what follows, ver. 6, 7.

*{behold,*} Or, *if*; as Jer. 1. 10. and, *if*, for, *when*; as Psal. 63. 6. or, *though*: as Job 13. 15.

*{thou art wroth*} A degree above anger: *when thou art*, or, *though thou beest, grievously angry*. So Chap. 47. 6. & 57. 16, 17. ver. 9.

*{for we have sinned*} Heb. *and*: here, *for*; as Psal. 60. 11. & 108. 12. Chap. 53. 2, 11. or, *because*, rather; as Chap. 57. 17. 2 Sam. 24. 1. *because one had moved David*; or, *David had been moved*: where this use of the particle observed, would help much to clear that place; *because we have sinned*; or, *do sin*, (as 1 King. 8. 46.) and provoke you unto wrath, by our sins: though one of the Jewish critics, (to intimate, that sin goes before wrath, and wrath comes after sin,) would have the notion of it here, not *because*, but *after*; as Exod. 14. 21. *and made the sea dry land, and* (that is, *after*) *the waters were divided*: and, Exod. 16. 20. *and it bred worms, and putrefied*; that is, *after it had putrefied*: and so here; *thou art wroth, and we have sinned*; that is, *after we have sinned*; not before: but this seems somewhat nice; and the other is more familiar, and frequent.

*{in those*} Or, *by those*; as Chap. 38. 16. or, *for those*: as Chap. 47. 9. & 57. 17.

*{is continuance*} The Hebrew word here used, is very general; it has in it a notion sometime of *eternity*; sometime, of *antiquity*; sometime, of *perpetuity*; sometime, of *diuturnity, durability, continuance, constancy*: whence it comes to be rendered, sometime, *of old*; sometime, *forever*. So vers. 4. here, whether it be understood of the time past, or present, it may be rendered the former way: a defect of some particle there is, which way soever it be rendered; as the like is, Psal. 89. 1, 2. Nor do I see why there may not the note of similitude, be supplied; that it might be rendered, *as of old*; according to that, Lam. 5. 21. Mic. 6. 14.

*{and we shall be saved*} Or, *by them of old yet we were saved*; or, *for them, yet as of old, we might be saved*: *and*, for, *yet*; as Chap. 42. 25. & 46. 7. the particle is transposed: as chap. 17. 14. 2 King. 2. 14. Job 23. 12. God might still in mercy, either at their intercession, as in times past, (see on ver. 4.) or, in respect of them, or, out of favor to them, be induced to spare us: as Gen. 18. 32. had we any such now among us. See Jer. 5. 1.

**V. 6.** *{But we are all as an unclean thing*} Or, rather, *unclean person*; because the term is masculine. Their present wretched, and forlorn condition, is in this verse, and the next described; as opposed to the state and condition of those, that were before-mentioned, ver. 4, 5. In former times there were such among God's people, that walked uprightly, and were in special grace, and favor with God; for whose sake God conferred many blessings upon them, and that helped, when God was at any time displeased with them, being provoked to wrath by their sins, to make up the breach between him, and them, Psal. 106. 23. but those righteous, and godly ones, are now all gone, Jer. 5. 1. Mic. 7. 2. Psal. 12. 1. there is such a universal corruption of all sorts with us, that the main body of our people seems no other, than a lump of some filthy matter; such unclean stuff, as by the law was to be burnt, or, abandoned, Lev. 13. 55, 57. & 14. 45, 46. or, like some leprous person, one overspread with leprosy, or some other foul, and loathsome malady from top to toe; such a one as is described, Chap. 1. 4. and very unfit therefore to appear in God's presence, deserving rather to be sequestered from his sight; as the leper, and persons unclean otherwise, were shut out of the camp, and secluded from ordinary society with men, Levit. 13. 45, 46. Num. 5. 2, 3. & 12. 14. 2 Chron. 26. 20, 21. of such general defections, see Psal. 12. 3. Jer. 9. 2, 3. Chap. 59. 3, 4. the scope is to show, that it is not to be marveled, if God, who is of so pure eyes, Hab. 1. 13. cannot endure to look upon such polluted creatures; if none be found fit to intercede with him for the rest, when they are generally all so defiled. See ver. 7.

*{and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags:*} There is no small debate about the subject of this proposition, the word, *righteousnesses*: and great variety of opinion, concerning the attribute, the word rendered, *filthy rags*. By the former, to wit, *righteousnesses*, some understand, those legal rites, ceremonies, and sacrifices, in the observation, and performance whereof, they deemed their righteousness to consist, (see Chap. 57. 12.) but were so performed by them, that they found no grace, or acceptance, with God, yea, were very loathsome, and abominable in his sight, Chap. 1. 11–14. & 66. 3. the Jewish commenters give the word a larger extent; the good works, say they, that they did in those times, were done, either out of vainglory, to gain applause, or, out of emulation, to outstrip one another; or out of other like corrupt grounds, and other like sinister ends, which made them such in God's sight, as is here said. Such were the Pharisees' both devotions, and almsdeeds, Mat. 6. 2, 5. & 23. 5. and so some preached the gospel, Phil. 1. 15, 16. See 1 Cor. 1. 3. Many of ours draw it out further, and take in all the best works and actions, even of the best, and in the best manner performed, as not free from some default, and defilement, that might deservedly render them, such as is here implied, in God's sight, if he should look narrowly, into them, and deem of them, according to the exact tenor, and rigor, of his law, Rom. 7. 21. And thus both divers of the ancients, and very many, not Protestant only, but Popish writers also, not a few, do both expound, and apply the place; these latter, with those ancients, giving testimony thereby, unto the truth, herein maintained, by us, against those of their side, that do therein control, and oppose us. Some yet further enlarge the subject matter here mentioned, as comprehending the natural constitution and condition of all mankind, being such, by breeding and birth, as is described, Ezek. 16. 4–6. But herein for the genuine sense of the place, others of ours, and those of chief note, depart both from these, and the former, advisedly observing, that the prophet's intendment here, is to make acknowledgment of such enormous evils, not bare inbred vitiosity, or, defects, of mere infirmity, but vile, and abominable practices, as had incensed the wrath of God against his people, to such a height of heat, as to cast them out of their land, and to leave them unto a long, tedious, and grievous captivity. That which induced those, both ancienter, and late writers, to bring within compass of this doom, in this place, those defects, and defaults, adhering to, and alloying the purest practices of the most sincere, seems to have been; because the prophet says, *our righteousnesses*; as speaking in his own person, and putting himself in among the rest: but they observe not what one of the Jewish doctors suggests, that the prophets, (which, says he, they learned from Moses, Exod. 34. 9.) speak oft in the person of the people, as their mouth to God: and yet withal comprising themselves in what they speak, as members of that body, in whose person they speak, as taking to heart, and affected with the evils, that do generally, either infect, or infest, that body, as if therein they partook with them; albeit they were wholly free from them themselves. So Ezr. 9. 6, 7, 10, 15. Dan. 9. 5, 6, 10, 11. The words may well be understood with those Jewish doctors, (whom some of our best interpreters herein condescend unto) of those outward semblances of holiness and righteousness, that some among them, in those times, might sometime make some flourish of, when they were inwardly full of nothing but filth, and corruption, and their very lives also otherwise very vile and abominable, as it was with some of the Pharisees, Mat. 23. 14, 23–28. Howbeit, I conceive the genuine sense of the place, to be other than is commonly received, and to speak rather of the persons themselves, compared one with another, though in regard of their properties, and practices, than of the properties, and practices of the same persons, collated some of them, with some other: by *our righteousnesses*, therefore I take to be meant, *the most righteous of us*, or *among us*; it is no unusual thing in Scripture, to put the *abstract* for the *concrete*. So, *wisdom*, for, *a man of wisdom*, *a wise man*, Mic. 6. 9. *folly*, for, *a woman of folly*, *a foolish woman*, Prov. 14. 1. *peace*, for, *a man of peace*; *a peaceable man*, Psal. 120. 7. *strength*, for, *men of strength*; *strong men*, Chap. 3. 25. *pride*, for, *men of pride*, *proud men*, Psal. 36. 11. now these abstracts in a plural form, enhance the notion of the word to a superlative degree: as, *wisdoms*, for the *greatest*, and *chiefest, wisdom*, Prov. 1. 20. & 9. 1. and, *a man of understandings*, for, *a man of very great understanding*, Prov. 11. 12. and nearer home yet to our purpose, *desires*, or, *delights*, for, *a man of desires*, or *delights*; (as it is more fully expressed, Dan. 10. 11, 19.) one *very much desired*, or *delighted, in*, Dan. 9. 23. for what is there rendered, *greatly beloved*, is no more in the Hebrew, than, *desires*, or, *delights*: and, the spouse of her love, Cant. 5. 16. *he all*, or, *all of him, is desires*, or, *delights*; that is, *he is altogether most desirable*, or, *most delightful*; (it is rendered, *altogether goodly*;) or, there is nothing but most desirable, or delightful, in him: in like manner here, as *righteousness* is by our interpreters deemed to signify, *a man of righteousness*, or, *a righteous man*, Chap. 41. 2. (but of that, see there) so here, *righteousnesses*, for, *men of righteousnesses*; that is, men of the greatest *righteousness*, *the most righteous* among us; those that seem, or are deemed, the very best among us, are no better than some unclean thing, (as he said, some *unclean person* before) or such as is here further instanced. This exposition I gather from a parallel place of a prophet, coetaneous to Esay, Mic. c. 7. where the prophet having complained of a general defection in the state; *the pious man is perished out of the land; and not an upright one left among men*, vers. 2. subjoins, vers. 4. *the best of them is a brier, the uprightest beyond a thorny hedge*; worse to deal with, he means. See 2 Sam. 23. 6, 7. it is true, there is no more in the text, than *good*, and *upright*: but the words are aright rendered, *best*, and *uprightest*; for these positives with the Hebrews, when they are used by way of collation, if the collation be of one person, or party, with some one other, make up the first degree of comparison, which we call the *comparative*; when with more than one, the second, which we call the *superlative*. So *the great shall serve the little*, that is, *the greater*, or *elder shall serve the less*, or *younger*, Gen. 25. 23. because spoken only of two; and, of *Japhet, the great*, for, *the greatest*, or, *eldest*, Gen. 10. 21. as, of *Cham, the little*; that is, *the least*, of Noah's three, Gen. 9. 24. as Micah therefore says there, *the best*, and *uprightest, among them*; so Esay, here, *the most righteous of us*; speaking of the same people, both the one, and the other.

*{as filthy rags*} He said in general before, of his people, that they were, the whole body of them, as some unclean person, some leper, or the like; he proceeds now to show more particularly, what the very best of them were like. Concerning the notion of the word here used, and not elsewhere read, as also concerning the notation of it, there is great variety of opinions, even among the Jewish critics themselves. Some of them render it, *a coat of patches*, or *rags*; a beggar's coat made up of rags, of old cloth, worn out, and cast away; from a Chaldee word that so signifies. Others, *a garment defiled with blood*; from a word that signifies *prey*, or *spoil*, Gen. 49. 24. for that garments so taken from ravenous beasts, or, by men in fight, are usually such, Gen. 37. 31, 33. chap. 9. 5. See Lam. 4. 14, 15. Others, *a clout of sores*; a clout, or rag, pulled off from some matury sore; from a Chaldee word so signifying, Lev. 13. 2. Others, *the cloth*, or *sheet*, mentioned, Deut. 22. 15, 17. from a term that imports *testimony*. Others, *a birth clout*, or *cloth* used about *childbirth*; from a Chaldee word signifying *to bear*, or *be with child*, Gen. 4. 1. Others, lastly, *a cloth*, or *cloth of separations*, or, *a menstruous cloth*, or *clout*; as coming from a word, that signifies, both in Hebrew and Chaldee, as before, *to put away*, or *to remove and separate*, Prov. 25. 20. Dan. 2. 21. and as having affinity with another word of that notion, Ezek. 7. 19, 20. & 36. 17. and this most pitch upon; the old Latin among others, and our oldest English: nor is the Greek deemed to intend other, when it renders it, of *a sitting woman*, being supposed to have an eye to that of Rachel, Gen. 31. 34, 35. Nor the Chaldee, who renders it an *abominable* thing in general; but has a word, in particular designing this, derived from it. And to some such loathsome and nasty stuff, in all likelihood, does the prophet compare the most righteous among the main multitude of his people. See chap. 30. 22. Lam. 1. 17.

*{And we all fade as a leaf,*} A just consequent of this their sinful and polluted condition: we are thrown all of us down, and carried away into captivity.

*{and*} Or, *therefore*; as chap. 12. 3. & 47. 8.

*{we all fade*} Or, *fall*; or, *we are all faded*, or *fallen*: for though the word here used, be commonly supposed to signify the former only, (whereof yet no proof can be made, because it is nowhere else found in the form here used) yet that root, which it has very near affinity with, and it is by some of the Jewish critics referred unto, does frequently imply both, *to fade*, and *to fall*. See chap. 28. 1, 4. we are, not with the blessed man, like the tree, *whose leaf never fadeth, nor falleth*, Psalm 1. 3. but with those cursed wretches, Jer. 17. 5, 6. like a tree *whose leaves fade, and shed*, chap. 1. 30. or, rather, we are altogether like a company of such *leaves* of trees, that at time of year shed them, as *fade*, and *fall* to the ground, at the beginning of winter, in the eighth month, *Bull*, 1 King. 6. 38. so termed from the word here used; because then the leaves of such trees begin to *fade*, and *fall*; though some from the other root, in regard of the rains that fall then. See Psalm. 37. 2. & 90. 5, 6.

*{and our iniquities like the wind have taken us away.*} We are for our iniquities hurried out of our land, and carried away captive, as such withered leaves: or other such like dry and light stuff, carried away with some blustering gust of wind in a storm. See the like, chap. 57. 13. Jer. 4. 11. Hos. 4. 19.

*{taken us away*} Heb. *taken us up*: but the word withal implies, sometime, having taken up, *to bring away*. So the east wind is said to have *brought in* the locusts, Exod. 10. 13. sometime, having taken up *to carry away*: and so the west wind is said to have *carried them away*, Exod. 10. 19. and in this latter notion is it here taken. They were by the wind of God's wrath for their sins taken up, and carried into Chaldea; as the prophet was sometime by the Spirit of God *taken up* in Chaldea, and carried from thence to Jerusalem, Ezek. 8. 3.

**V. 7.** *{And there is none that calleth upon thy name, that stirreth up himself to take hold of thee:*} Amidst these our troubles, or notwithstanding them, there are very few, or none among us, that seek unto you as they should; or that put out themselves, to endeavor by any means, to pacify your wrath, and procure your gracious return again to us.

*{none*} Not simply none, for some godly in all times; but so few, that they are not seen, they appear not, they are drowned in the multitude. So Psalm 14. 3.

*{that calleth upon thy name*} that addresses himself unto you, for the redress and removal of these evils, Psalm 14. 4. chap. 43. 22. Dan. 9. 13. Hos. 7. 7, 14.

*{stirreth up himself to take hold of thee*} Either to stay you with us; when you threaten departure; (as when he stood on the threshold of the temple, Ezek. 10. 4.) as they pressed our Savior to stay with them, Luke 24. 28, 29. or, to induce you to return in mercy again to us, since you have withdrawn yourself from us, Jer. 12. 7. Ezek. 10. 18, 19. See chap. 59. 11.

*{for thou hast hid thy face from us*} Or, *though thou hast hid thy face from us*, as the particle is used, Psal. 23. 4. chap. 55. 8. Or, as some, *when thou didst hide thy face from us*, as the same particle is used, Job 5. 21. Psal. 75. 2. Joel 2. 20. And this latter reading seems very probable, thus knitting this with the former; *Neither was there any that called upon thy name, nor that stirred up himself to take hold of thee, when thou didst hide thy face from us*. When at first you began to manifest your displeasure towards us, by withdrawing the light of your countenance from us. See chap. 8. 17. & 57. 17.

*{and hast consumed us,*} Or, *didst consume us*; as before. Heb. *melt us*, or *dissolve us*, Job 30. 22. chap. 14. 31. Ezek. 21. 7.

*{because of our iniquities*} That were before said to carry them away. Heb. *in the hand*; that is, *in the room*, or *place of our iniquities*, in the land where they were committed, while we were yet in our own country: so is the word used, chap. 56. 5. or, *by the hand*, that is, *by means of our iniquities* as chap. 62. 3.

**V. 8.** *{But now, O Lord,*} After this doleful deploration of this their sinful and sad condition, follows a pathetical imploration of favor and mercy, which they make way unto, or entrance into, by minding of God, or themselves rather, (thereby to raise within themselves, the better hope of speeding and prevailing with God) of that special relation that God had unto them, as a Father. So the prodigal, Luke 15. 17, 18.

*{But*} Or, *yet*; as chap. 17. 6. though we have carried ourselves thus ungraciously, and unworthily, towards you, Deut. 32. 5, 6.

*{thou art our Father;*} A very pithy and affectionate compellation, by a sweet and compassionate appellation, Psa. 103. 13. so David to Saul, 1 Sam. 24. 11. *See now my Father.* See chap. 63. 16.

*{we are the clay, and thou art our potter,*} Or, *we were clay, and thou wast our potter*, or *the framer of us*; that is, when we were at first but as a lump of clay, a rude mass, without form or shape, a confused multitude, you did mold and fashion us into a state, both civil and ecclesiastical, into a body politic, into a church, chap. 43. 1, 7, 21. & 44. 2, 21, 24. a metaphor taken from the potter's employment; (as those other forms also, though to another purpose, chap. 29. 16. Jer. 18. 6.) but having withal some eye to the manner of God's framing man's body at first, Gen. 2. 7. as also to the fashioning of it, still in the womb, Job 10. 8–12. & 31. 15. Psalm 119. 73. & 139. 13–16. Jer. 1. 5.

*{we all are the work of thine hands.*} Not as we are men only, or of Adam's posterity; but as by your special procurement we are made a people, yea, a peculiar people for yourself, chap. 43. 21. an argument that God himself uses to show, why he would not, yea, could not, forget them, chap. 44. 21. and that his people are wont to press him with, thereby to persuade him the rather to spare them, Job 10. 8, 9. Psal. 138. 8.

**V. 9.** *{Be not wroth very sore, O Lord,*} It will not stand with the tender affection of a parent, to be over-fierce, over-rough, or rigorous, to his child, to scourge him overmuch, or overlong. Heb. *Be not wroth unto much*, or *to extremity*; though you be wroth, because we have given you just cause of wrath by our sins, vers. 5. yet be not over-wroth with us, either overmuch, or overlong; let not your fierce wrath burn and devour like fire forever, Deut. 32. 22. Psal. 79. 5. See on vers. 12.

*{neither remember iniquity for ever.*} Retain not wrath against us forever, in regard of fore-past excesses; a tender parent is not wont so to do, but is very prone, and ready, to pity and pardon, Psal. 25. 7. & 79. 5–8. & 103. 9. Lam. 5. 20.

*{Behold, see, we beseech thee*} Or, *Lo, behold now*, or, *we beseech thee*, see chap. 38. 3. a very pathetical form of speech. So David, *See now, yea, see, O my Father*, 1 Sam. 24. 11. be pleased yet to cast a glance of your eye upon us, to see, in how lamentable a condition we remain; as if the very sight of them, in what plight they were, might of itself be sufficient, to move him unto commiseration of them. See chap. 63. 15. Lam. 1. 9, 20. & 2. 20. & 3. 50.

*{we are all thy people.*} Or, *we all are thy people*: not we are your only people, all the people that you have; though that also, in some sense, was, at that time, true, Exod. 19. 5. Psal. 147. 20. But we all of us, as bad as we have been, or are, and as badly, and basely, as we are by our enemies entreated, are those that you have been pleased to take into covenant with you, and to make your peculiar people, Deut. 5. 3. & 29. 10–19. See chap. 63. 19.

**V. 10.** *{Thine holy cities are a wilderness; Zion is a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation.*} From themselves, and their relation to God, they pass to God himself, his interest, and honor, concerned in this their present condition, and the devastation of their country, those places especially, which himself had made choice of for his peculiar residence among his people, and their solemn attendance on him, and service of him, there; that so, if not for themselves, who had deserved so ill of him, yet in regard of himself and his own concernment, he might be induced unto mercy and commiseration of them, and to wrath and indignation against their oppressors, who so despitefully used, as well him, as them. So Psal. 74. 22, 23.

*{Thy holy cities*} Heb. *The cities of thy holiness*, or rather, *Thy cities of holiness*; as, *Thy mountain of holiness*, Psal. 15. 1. and, *thy city of holiness*, Dan. 9. 24. *Thy cities*, not ours; and, *holy cities*, having special relation to you. Now hereby some understand only *Jerusalem*, and *Sion*, afterward mentioned; and render the words therefore, *the cities of thy Sanctuary*. See chap. 31. 9. But most, rather, the cities of Judah in general, Jer. 10. 22. called *holy cities*, as the whole land, *an holy land*, Zach. 2. 12. because assigned to God's people; *an holy people*, Exod. 19. 6. Deut. 14. 2, 21. to inhabit, chap. 63. 18. & 65. 9. and because they had in them set, and solemn conventions, for the constant service of God, every Sabbath in their synagogues, Psal. 74. 8. Acts 15. 21.

*{are a wilderness*} Or, *are become a wilderness*; have lain so long ruined, that they are become like a mere wilderness. See vers. 11.

*{Zion is a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation.*} Or, *Zion is become a wilderness, Jerusalem a waste*. See chap. 1. 7. & 62. 4. the subject matter rises; not the lesser cities only, but the mother city Jerusalem, and the seat of your royal palace, and of your temple, Sion; and the sentence runs concise and quick. So Micah's prophecy fulfilled, Jer. 26. 18. Mic. 3. 12. Psal. 79. 1.

**V. 11.** *{Our holy, and our beautiful house, where our fathers praised thee, is burnt up with fire.*} The subject matter rises yet a degree higher, as from the lower cities to Jerusalem, and Sion; so from these to the temple; the other were oft surprised and sacked, when Jerusalem and Sion, yet held out and were saved, chap. 5. 7, 8. & 7. 1. & 36. 1. & 37. 35. and Jerusalem might be taken and sacked, and yet the temple saved, 2 Chr. 25. 23, 24. but now, not those inferior cities only, but Jerusalem and Sion; nor those alone, but God's temple also is destroyed together with them, Psalm 74. 3, 6, 7.

*{Our holy and our beautiful house*} Heb. *our house of holiness* (as, *cities of holiness*, vers. 10.) *and of bravery, goodliness, or gallantry*. See chap. 60. 7. *our house*; so they call God's temple, though termed commonly *God's house*, cha. 56. 5, 7. & 60. 7. and set it forth with glorious attributes, thereby to express and testify their affection to it, as not so much affected with the loss of their own houses, as the loss and want of it. So Psalm 84. 1, 2.

*{where our fathers praised thee*} They say, not *we*, but *our fathers*; as scarce daring once to mention their own services there: they had been either so regardless of God's house, chap. 65. 11. Ezek. 8. 16. or in that manner there served him, that their performances there might well (they feared) be most loathsome and abominable to him, chap. 1. 11–15. & 66. 3. Jer. 7. 9–11. but yet minding him, how formerly in better times he had by their ancestors there been served.

*{is burnt up with fire*} Or, rather, *is burnt down with fire*, Psalm 74. 7. Heb. *is become unto a burning of fire*; or, *is become a burning of fire*; because the particle is in such forms oft redundant. See chap. 5. 9. & 13. 9. for the syntax of it, with this word, seems divers, chap. 9. 5. of the burning of the temple, see 2 King. 25. 9. 2 Chron. 36. 19. Jer. 52. 13.

*{and all our pleasant things are laid waste.*} Heb. *all our desires*, or *delights*, for the word is a substantive, as appears by the constant use of it, 1 King. 20. 6. Ezek. 24. 16, 21, 25. but the abstract is here put for the concrete, as before, vers. 6. *desires*, or *delights*, for matters of *much desire*, of *most delight*; that is, *most desirable*, or *delightful*: our *most desirable*, or *delightful*, either *things*, that is, *matters* in general; as it is expressed, 2 Chro. 26. 19. where it is said of the Chaldeans, that *they destroyed all her* (that is, Jerusalem's) *matters of desires*, or *delights*, rendered there, *goodly vessels*: but the word there used is of a far larger extent, than our English *vessel*, and reaches unto any utensil, or other matter of use whatsoever. See chap. 22. 24. & 32. 7. and so is the adjective, or concrete of the same root and notion used, Lam. 1. 7, 10, 11. or, *our most desirable*, or *pleasant places*; as it is supplied, Hos. 9. 6. because of that which follows, *are laid waste*. Heb. *is*, or *is become unto a waste*; as Jer. 7. 24. & 22. 5. as *to a burning*, before. So also, vers. 10. the verb being singular, it would be rendered to answer the Hebrew exactly, *each of our most desirable*, or *delightful*, matters, or places, *is become a waste*; and it may seem to have reference to the king's palace, and the great men's goodly houses, with their appurtenances, orchards, gardens, and the like places of delight and pleasure; which together with the temple, were likewise burnt down and demolished, 2 King. 25. 9. Jer. 39. 8. & 52. 13. the word is sometime applied also to persons; as Cant. 5. 16. whereof see before, on vers. 6. & Lam. 2. 4. Hos. 9. 16.

**V. 12.** *{Wilt thou refrain thyself for these things, O Lord?*} Or, *Canst thou contain thyself at these things?* as one of the Rabbines well renders it. How can you endure to see your cities, synagogues, your temple itself, lie thus waste and ruined, and your own honor thereby so exceedingly impeached and impaired, Psal. 74. 10, 18, 22, 23. See chap. 63. 15.

*{wilt thou hold thy peace*} Or, *canst thou be silent?* How can you endure to forbear, and let them alone that thus wrong you? See chap. 42. 14.

*{and afflict us very sore*} Or how can you endure to afflict us so extremely? Heb. *unto very much*. Or, as some render it, *unto extremity*. So vers. 9. Howbeit, I observe that the form here used, is applicable as well to extent of time, as to intension of degree; and in such use of it, signifies either *overlong*, or, *forever*; so some Jewish critics take it, in those words, Psal. 119. 8. *forsake me not overlong* (as our Geneva version renders it). Or, *forever*; wherein other of their own that control them, to give it some sense fit for that place and passage, are constrained to offer force to the text, & to knit that clause to the former part of the verse, reading the words, *I will keep thy statutes exceedingly*, or *exactly*, (as answering to what went before, v. 4.) *O forsake me not*. But beside that the pauses there oppose them, carrying on unto this clause the word of *forsaking*: there is another place in that Psalm, vers. 43. which cannot be so avoided. *Take not the word of truth out of my mouth for ever*; that is, *Never let the word of truth be taken out of my mouth*; as chap. 25. 8. For it is a very poor and sorry sense, that their version has, who render it, *Take it not much out of my mouth*; nor theirs much better, that render it *utterly*: the Psalmist's meaning sure was, *never*, at any time, or at all. And I conceive therefore, that it may here be so rendered, as those of Geneva have it, in the former place, as well, *afflict us overlong*, as, *afflict us overmuch*, or, *afflict us for ever*, and so the Chaldee here renders it. See Psalm 79. 5. & 88. 5.

### CHAPTER 65

**Vers. 1.** *{I am sought of them, that asked not for me;*} This chapter the Jewish commenters annex to the former, supposing that God, in the first words of it, returns an answer to the prayer of the captive people, conceived in the latter part of the chapter foregoing. But it seems rather to contain a new sermon divers from the former. And in it we have a clear prediction, both of the conversion, and coming in, of the Gentiles; and of the rejection of the Jews, with a relation of their particular sins, and their obstinacy in them, for which they were to be rejected. Howbeit a remnant of them to be reserved, whom God would prosecute with special favors in the times of the Messiah especially, when his church should be renewed.

*{I am sought of them, that asked not for me*} In these words the Jewish doctors conceive that God, in way of answer to the former complaint of his people, concerning his harsh usage of them, and the continuance of the captivity, does render a reason why it so fared with them, to wit, for the obstinate carriage both of their forefathers, and themselves; who albeit he had from time to time called upon them by his prophets, to return from their wicked ways, and rebellious courses, and come in to him, yet had stood out still against him, and rejected his gracious invitations and offers. So that they understand this whole passage, vers. 1, 2. of their own people, and tell us, it is all the same thing four several times told over, in divers terms, to add the more emphasis to it. But from the apostle's allegation of it, Rom. 10. 20, 21. it evidently appears, that the former part of it, speaks of the Gentiles; the latter part, only of the Jews: the Jewish critics, to draw this Scripture their ways, are mightily puzzled about the signification of the first word: for there seems, say they, a contradiction in the text; *I am inquired of, and they ask not*: and this to assoil, they render the words, some, *I was ready to be inquired of*, entreated by, and reconciled to your forefathers, when they had offended me, had they sought me in their afflictions, but *they asked not* after me. So say they, is the word used, Psal. 111. 2. *The works of the Lord are ready to be sought*, and found out. Others, giving the passive reciprocal notion, as oftentimes it has (see chap. 26. 20.) *I made myself to be sought*; that is, offered myself to be sought unto by them; according to that, chap. 63. 5. *thou didst meet*, that is, prevent them with mercies unasked. Others, taking the word as a potential (of which, see on chap. 63. 12.) *I might have been sought* of them, if they would; but they had no mind to it. Others, as spoken by way of interrogation; *Should I offer myself to be sought* of those that *ask not* after me? Ours, divers of them somewhat strain themselves needlessly about it. Some render the word *I am exposed* to those that *asked not*: and the word indeed in the Rabbinical language is commonly used for *to expound*; whence *midrasses*, or *expositions*, are so termed: but that suits but sorrily with this place, or the notion here intended. Others, because the apostle seems so to render it, *I am sought*, say they, that is, *I am found*; *seeking*, put for *finding*, as Eccles. 3. 6. *a time to seek*, that is, *to get*; because the one is the end, and usual consequent of the other: Mat. 7.7. Luk. 11.10. so Prov. 13.9. *He that covereth a fault, seeketh love*, i.e. finds, gets, gains it, and so on the other side, finding, for seeking, Gen. 19.11. *they wearied themselves with finding*, (that is, seeking) *the door*. But the word of finding, used by the apostle (with whom the two branches are transposed) has reference, not to this word, but to the word following, which the ancient Greek also so renders. This word, both that version, and the apostle retaining it, renders, *I am manifested*, or, *I have been made manifest*; and these strains all seem needless. The old Latin, which some, without cause, here control, telling us, that the word is here passive, gave the right sense of the text, *They seek me, that before asked not of me*, word for word, *I am sought to, by those that have not asked*, to wit, aught of me; that is, I am now inquired of, sought unto, called upon, (so the word is commonly taken: see Chap. 55.6. Ezek. 36.37.) by those, who in former times, having no notice at all of me, Chap. 52.15. & 55.5. Rom. 15.20,21. had not been wont to ask aught of me, that is, to seek to me for aught. So is the word most frequently used, 1 King. 3.5,10,11. Chap. 7.11. & 58.2. Hos. 4.12. Zach. 10.1. and I rather choose therefore to make the supply of me, than for me. See Rom. 10.14. It is apparently spoken of the Gentiles, converted by the ministry of the gospel. The speech is concise and quick; a defect both of the antecedent, and relative, before the latter verb, as Chap. 64.5. and so in the next branch: of the pronoun after it, as Chap. 45.3. & 50.2,4. in the next branch expressed.

*{I am found of them that sought me not*} I prevented their seeking of me, by sending and seeking of my own accord to them, 2 Cor. 5.20. Eph. 2.17. Which some of the Jewish authors would again turn aside unto Terah, and those before [unclear] him; that had not sought God, before God sought them, Josh. 29.2,3.

*{I said, behold me, behold me, unto a nation that was not called by my name*} The Jews to pervert this passage, miserably wrest these words, expounding them, *a nation not called by my name*; that is, a nation that so carry themselves, as if they were none of mine. But to leave them to their forced interpretations. Nor are some of ours, so clear in their expositions of this passage: for some take them, as spoken in way of invitation to the Gentiles, as if God did thereby call upon them, to look after him, and come into him, as Chap. 45.22. or tender, and offer himself unto them, (as the prophet of God, Chap. 6.8.) being ready to entertain them, and make them his people, which before they were not, Deut. 32.21. Hos. 2.14. Rom. 9.25. and this way our version seems to incline. Others, as directed, and delivered, at departure to the Jews; *Behold me, behold me*, now leaving you, and passing to a nation that were none of mine before, according to that of the apostle; *Behold, we turn to the Gentiles*, Act. 13.46. The words run in the Hebrew, *I have said*, or *I say*, (so would it be rendered to fit with the former) *Lo I, lo I*; or, as it is frequently rendered, *Here am I, here am I*; Gen. 22.1,7,11. & 27.18. Chap. 6.8. and it is the voice of God returning a gracious answer unto the suits and supplications of those that seek to him by prayer; here am I at hand, ready to hear and help. So Chap. 58.9. *when thou shalt cry, he will say, Lo I*; or *here I am*: and it is doubled, to intimate his forwardness, to hear, and grant their requests: whereof see, ver. 24. The latter words, some render, *unto a nation that did not call upon my name*, as Chap. 64.7. Jer. 10.25. and this sense would well suit, both with the terms of the first branch, and with the former member of this, if the words of the text would bear it: but this word of calling here, is not a participle active; but a verb, in a weighty form passive: and there is but a vowel difference between either, which caused the mistake. Our version renders it aright, *that was not called by my name*, as Chap. 63.19. that had not in times past borne my name; had not been called, or accounted my people; there is a defect of the relative, as Chap. 64.3,4. This whole verse, some interpreters render all in the future; *I shall be sought to; I shall be found; I shall say*; because it is a prophecy of future times. But the prophet's manner is not unusual to speak of things to come, as past, or present: so Ch. 13.4,5. & 19.1. Rev. 1.7.

**V. 2.** *{I have spread out mine hands all the day unto a rebellious people*} Here we close with the Jewish commenters, and with good warrant from Rom. 10.21. agree unto them, that the speech is of them, and their nation, whom God had long labored with from time to time, to reduce and reclaim; but in vain: and for their willful obstinacy therefore was now resolved to reject, and to receive the Gentiles in room of them, Rom. 11.11–24.

*{spread out my hands*} As the manner is of those that require audience, Act. 26.1. or desire acceptance, Prov. 1.24.

*{all the day*} Continually, constantly; as Chap. 63.6.

*{unto a rebellious people*} Or, *a refractory people*, Jer. 5.23. that would by no means be reclaimed, ver. 12. Chap. 66.4. Jer. 7.13. & 11.7,8. for that exposition of the word, that a Rabbine gives on the place, *a people gone out of the way*; though it suit well with what follows, and the word may be deduced from that which signifies, *to go aside*, Exod. 32.8. yet it does not so fully express what the word usually imports, and is commonly therefore to another root referred.

*{which walketh in a way that was not good*} Heb. *that walk* (for the word is plural, because the word people, collective; so ver. 3.) *the way not good*; that take no good course: or, *in a way* (the particle supplied: as Neh. 9.19.) *that is not good*; that it may answer the present walk: or, if we retain was, then, as some, *that walked*; not good: a form of diminution, for, evil, very bad, stark naught: as 1 Sam. 2.24. Psal. 36.4. Prov. 24.23. & 28.21.

*{after their own thoughts*} Following, not the motions, and directions of my word, and Spirit; but led by their own minds and lusts, Num. 15.39. 1 King. 13.33. Psal. 81.11,12. 2 Pet. 3.3.

**V. 3.** *{A people that provoketh me to anger continually to my face*} Heb. *that provoke me*, or, *provoked me*; as before, ver. 2. See Chap. 3.8.

*{to my face*} That is, either simply, in God's sight, as Exod. 20.3. Deut. 5.7. & 31.29. as if a servant should do things directly cross to his master's known mind and command, to his face: so David aggravates his own sin, Psal. 51.4. or, as some, in God's own house, in his sanctuary; of which, Psal. 42.2. and of their grievous profanations of God's temple, see 2 King. 16.10–15. & 21.4,5,7. & 23.4,6. 2 Chr. 36.14. Jer. 7.10,11. & 11.15. Ezek. 8.3–16. & 43.8. But the former sense seems the more familiar.

*{that sacrificeth in gardens*} Heb. *that sacrifice* (as before) *in the gardens*: such as they have set apart for idolatrous services, and dedicated to their idols. See Chap. 1.29. & 66.17. the reason, says one of the ancients, why Naboth would not part with his vineyard, to be converted, by Ahab, into a garden, that it might not be so abused: but that is a groundless conjecture. Howbeit, some understand it of their groves; whereof see on Chap. 17.8. & 27.9.

*{and burneth incense upon altars of brick*} Heb. *and burn incense* (as before) *upon bricks*: who leaving God's house, and his altar, ver. 1. sacrifice, and burn incense to idols of their own choosing, in places of their own designing, upon altars of their own erecting: which, in contempt, he calls bricks; (so the word properly signifies, Exod. 1.14. & 24.10.) from the matter whereof they were made; as Ezekiah the brazen serpent so abused, brass, 2 King. 18.4. Some expound it, of such stones, with figures engraved upon them, whereof mention is made, Lev. 26.1. & Numb. 33.52. But this seems a groundless conjecture. Others, of the tile-stones, wherewith their houses were covered, on the tops whereof being flat-roofed, they were wont to sacrifice, and burn incense to the idols. See Jer. 19.13. this is more probable than that; but the first carries most likelihood.

**V. 4.** *{Which remain among the graves*} Heb. *who sit in*, or, *on, the graves*: but *to sit*, is oft used, for *to stay, or abide*; as 2 Sam. 7.18. Jer. 39.14. and the particle, *in*, or, *on*, is sometime used for *among*; as Chap. 57.6. that abide among the graves, to consult with spirits, that haunt such places; or, to have dealings with the dead, Deut. 18.11. 1 Sam. 28.6,11. Chap. 8.19. Mar. 5.5. The Chaldee renders it; *that dwell in houses built of the dust, or, molds, taken from graves*.

*{and lodge in the monuments*} That is, *in their idol-temples*, as the old Latin has it, or, *in caves, underground*; or, *cut out in rocks*, as the Greek, there to expect dreams from their imaginary deities; which was a usual practice among the pagans, as appears from Aristophanes, Aristides the Sophist, and others; and Jerome on this place testifies to have been practiced by them, in his days. The word here used is ambiguous; it signifies properly, *places kept, or observed*. Whence it is rendered, Chap. 1.8. *besieged*: and so it signifies, Ezek. 6.12. some would have it here to signify such horrid places, as people therefore are wont cautiously to observe, for to shun and avoid. See on Chap. 1.8. Others, *secret, hidden, places*: as *hidden things*, Chap. 48.6. which agrees well with those secret vaults, caves, and closets, wherein the heathen had been wont to have private commerce with their gods. Others, and this way the Jewish critics most go, render it *wasted, desolate places*; such, say they, as are oftentimes haunted with devils, Mat. 12.43. and so they would have the word taken, Chap. 49.6. but of that there: or, as some of them, *among the corpses, that are kept in the graves*, and there held as in prisons, or holds, Chap. 14.18. Ezek. 32.23. or, *with the corpses, for superstitious purposes, reserved and kept by them*. Some late writers of note, *that lodge with the kept ones*. So, say they, in derision, are their idols here termed; because they were kept carefully for fear of being stolen, as oftentimes they were, Gen. 31.19,30. Judg. 18.18,24. being not able to keep, or save themselves, much less those, that served them, by whose care and provision, they were to be kept from miscarrying, Chap. 41.7. and 46.1,2,7.

*{that eat swine's flesh*} Forbidden by God's law then in force, Lev. 11.7. Deut. 14.8. Chap. 66.3,17.

*{and broth of abominable things is in their vessels*} Or, *and in whose vessels the broth of abominable things is*: the demonstrative, for the relative; as Chap. 54.5. and a defect of the particle in, as Chap. 57.8. there is here a twofold reading. Some read the first word *merak*, which signifies broth; so used, Judg. 6.19,20. and nowhere else found. So the Chaldee, Greek, and old Latin, render it; and the Jewish critics do most follow this reading: and they conceive the word following, to signify the carcass of any unclean creature, from Ezek. 4.14. and consequently, such broth meant here, wherein the flesh of any such had been boiled: but some other read it *perak*, that signifies a fragment, or, part torn off; from a word, that signifies, to tear, or break, off. Exod. 32.2. Nah. 3.1. and those that follow this reading, expound the word following, from Lev. 7.18. & 19.7. where the same is used of the flesh of some sacrifices reserved till the third day, deemed then to be abominable: and of such *fragments*, or *parcels*, of flesh, contrary to the law so reserved, would they have the words here to be understood; but no clear place appears for this use of the former word: and the other reading is the more received; and the rather, for that the latter word, where it is used of such remainders so reserved, seems to have some reference unto such unclean flesh, as implying, that being so reserved, they should be no more accepted, than any such flesh, in its kind unclean.

**V. 5.** *{Which say, Stand by thy self, come not near to me*} These persons as impure and profane, as they were, yet would seem to be holier, than others, and counted all unclean, and polluted, beside themselves. So the Pharisees, in Christ's time, Luk. 5.30. & 7.39. & 18.11,12. and the Samaritanes anciently, Joh. 4.9. as the stories of them relate; and the Jews, and heretics, in Jeromes time, yea to this day.

*{Stand by thy self*} Heb. *Approach*, or, *Draw near, to thy self*: keep apart by yourself; so the Jewish, and most of ours: though some, *Get thee to thine*; that is, to others like yourself.
