*{Come not near to me*} *Touch me not*; as the Samaritanes are reported to have cried usually to others, not of their way, as fearing to be defiled by them: this is supposed also to have been the reason why the Pharisees used to wash so, when they came home from the market; as having contracted some defilement by the touch of others there, Mar. 7.4. See Luk. 7.39.

*{for I am holier than thee*} So the Chaldee render it; and the Jewish commenters unanimously expound it. Heb. *I sanctify thee*: and because the word, *sanctify*, is in Scripture used, sometime, for to set apart for some sacred use, Levit. 17.5. 1 Sam. 16.5. or, for slaughter, Jer. 12.3. Some render the words, *I will sanctify thee*; that is, I will make a sacrifice of you; I will slay you: and they suppose the words to have been spoken to the prophet, repairing to them, when they were busied about some of their abominable services, or sacrifices, to reprove them for the same, as giving him warning to keep aloof off, and let them alone, otherwise threatening to make a sacrifice of him. Others, because the word, *Kadesh*, is sometime used, for some *unclean*, vile, and abominable person, Gen. 38.21. Deut. 23.18. 1 King. 14.24. & 15.12. Hos. 4.14. and it is so rendered, Job 36.14. would therefore have the verb here to be taken in that sense, and render it, *I pollute thee*; that is, I account you a polluted, and unclean person; as Acts 10.15. & 11.9. *Do not thou pollute*; that is, account polluted, or unclean: and the old Latin renders it, *Thou art unclean*: to which purpose, some apply that, Lam. 4.15. some color might this interpretation seem to receive, from what is spoken of these persons, Chap. 66.17. where it is said of them, that they *sanctify themselves in the gardens*: if the word *sanctify*, might be taken there for, *to pollute*; as certain it is, that their sanctification was no other than a gross pollution; and the word *sanctify*, might by a kind of antiphrasis, be used for *to defile*, or *unsanctify*: as the word *to bless*, sometime, for, *to curse*, Job 1.5. 1 King. 21.13. but the words following there, carry it another way; nor is any place produced, where this verb is so used. We return therefore to the first, and most generally received interpretation; wherein all the matter of doubt, or difficulty, arises from the defect of a particle, or preposition, such as in the affixing of pronouns to verbs, is oft-times omitted; this supplied, it would be, *I am holy from thee*: of this kind of defects, see on Chap. 28.15. & 47.8. & 48.20. & 49.24. of this particle in particular; Jer. 10.20. *my children are gone out me*, for, *gone out from me*. Now this preposition in Hebrew, as *παρὰ*, in Greek; *præ*, in Latin, has a peculiar use, in comparative notions: so *good from*, or *above*, as it is, sometime, not amiss rendered, Judg. 5.24. Psal. 45.7. is, *better*, Prov. 22.1. Eccl. 7.1. *wise from*, or *above*, is, *wiser*, 1 King. 4.21. Ezek. 28.3. and, *holy from*, or, *above*, is, *holier*. But an exact, and full instance of the like defect of the same particle, in the same use, we find, Jer. 20.7. where the prophet speaking to God, says, *thou art strong me*, for, *strong from*, or *above, me*; that is, *stronger than I*, as it is well rendered here: and it may be, would as well be, *holier than thou*, here. The ancient Greek renders it, *I am clean*; but they take not notice of the pronoun affixed.

*{these are a smoke in my nose, a fire, that burneth all the day*} These are a continual provocation, and vexation, unto me, (see Chap. 63.10.) like smoke, that rising from green wood, or other like wet fuel, is most grievous and offensive to man's nose, and eyes, Prov. 10.20. See Chap. 3.8. or, as some; These will I in mine anger (as Chap. 9.21.) dispel, and disperse, like smoke, Psal. 68.2. and make fuel of them, matter for the fire, Chap. 1.31. & 9.18. As others, My wrath incensed by them, shall smoke against such, and burn everlastingly against them, Deut. 29.20. & 32.22. Psal. 18.8. & 37.20. & 104.32. & 144.5. Chap. 14.31. & 30.33. & 34.9. & 66.24. The first seems most natural.

*{all the day*} Or, *all day long*; continually: their continual provocations of him, opposed to God's continual invitations of them, ver. 2. So Hos. 11.2.

**V. 6.** *{Behold, it is written before me*} Or, *is written, and lieth before my face*: a defective form of speech; of which kind, see on Chap. 38.21. These their courses are upon record with me; and this record lies always open before my face, (as was before said of their sins, ver. 3.) that I may not forget them: a metaphor taken from the manner of men, great ones especially, that keep books, or records, wherein they enter such matters, as they would not have to be forgotten, Ezr. 4.15,19. & 6.2. Est. 6.1. So Deut. 32.34. Psal. 56.8. Jer. 3.22. Hos. 7.2. Mal. 3.16.

*{I will not keep silence*} I will no longer forbear, as hitherto I have done, Psal. 50.21. & 83.1. See Chap. 42.14. and 64.12.

*{but will recompense, even recompense into their bosom*} Or, *will repay, yea, repay* (as Chap. 44.15. Heb. *and*; as Chap. 56.5,7.) *into their lap*: as it is rendered, Prov. 6.33. that is, abundantly, largely: a figurative form of speech, borrowed from those, that deliver not, what they give out, by tale, measure, or weight, but pour it forth into the receiver's lap, without any regard how much they give of it. So Psal. 79.12. Jer. 32.18. Luk. 6.38. the word is redoubled; to put the doing of it out of doubt. So Deut. 32.41. Chap. 59.18. Jer. 51.56. Ezek. 21.7.

**V. 7.** *{Your iniquities, and the iniquities of your fathers, together, (saith the Lord)*} Some interpreters repeat here, from ver. 6. *I will recompense*, or *repay*; and insert it into the text: but that is needless; for the former words of this verse, have an immediate dependence upon those words in the former verse: and our version therefore closes that verse only with a comma; that neither verses, nor chapters, are always exactly distinguished, was before observed, Chap. 58.3. & 64.1.

*{Your iniquities*} Or, *their iniquities*; a change of the person: as Chap. 1.29.

*{and the iniquities of your fathers together*} The meaning is that when God should set upon it, the sins of that nation being come to their full height, (as of the Amorites he speaks, Gen. 15.16.) he would remember, as well their ancestors' sins, (which he had upon record, ver. 6.) as their own; and would take vengeance for, both together; that which no way impeaches the justice of God: who although he lay nothing upon any person, but what his own particular sins deserve, yea, what comes indeed far short of what is due to them, Ezr. 9.13. Job 37.23. yet he has an eye oft in inflicting judgments, on notorious wicked ones, descended also from such, unto the sins of their ancestors, and either enhances, or lengthens, their afflictions, to make their sufferings the more exemplary, that men may observe how execution of vengeance, though for some time delayed; yet even here falls, at length oft, with a full storm, on the race of the wicked. So 1 Sam. 3.12. Jer. 2.5. Lam. 5.7. Matth. 23.32,35,36. and 27.25. 1 Thess. 2.15,16.

*{which have burnt incense upon the mountains, and blasphemed me upon the hills*} Or, *reproached*, or *dishonored, me*, Chap. 37.4. Psal. 89.51. for it is no verbal, or vocal; but a real, and actual reproach, that he charges them with; to wit, their idolatrous services on such places frequently exercised, Chap. 57.7. Jer. 3.1,6. Ezek. 18.6,11. & 22.9. Hos. 4.13.

*{therefore will I measure their former work into their bosom*} Or, *I will, I say*, (Heb. *and I will*, as Chap. 58.10. & 59.17.) *mete out the reward of their former work* (Heb. *first*, for, *former*, or *forepassed*; as Chap. 41.22. & 42.9. and *work*, for, *reward of work*, as Chap. 49.4. & 61.8. & 62.11.) *into their lap*; as ver. 6. a threefold repetition, to assure the certainty of it; as Ezek. 21.14,27. and an interchange of persons, as Chap. 1.29. & 64.4.

**V. 8.** *{Thus saith the Lord*} God's sorest, and surest menaces, have yet always some matter of grace, and mercy, mixed with them, for the support and comfort, of the few faithful: that which is here therefore annexed, and subjoined, to this dismal doom, concerning a remnant still to be spared, and reserved, for the propagating of his church.

*{As the new wine is found in the cluster, and one saith, Destroy it not, for a blessing is in it*} Or, *As when* (see Chap. 17.5. and 64.2.) *wine* (as Chap. 62.8.) *is found* (as Chap. 13.15.) *in a cluster, one saith*, (or, *it is said*, men use to say, Jer. 3.1. Mal. 1.4.) *Destroy it not, for a blessing is in it*. As when a vine being blasted, or otherwise decayed, is grown so bad, and so barren, that scarce any good cluster of grapes can be discerned on it, (Jer. 8.13.) whereby it may be deemed to have any life left in it, or any likelihood conceived of its recovery, and ever becoming fruitful again; and the husbandman therefore is about either to stub it up, or to cut it down by the ground, if one chance to espy on some branch of it, some one cluster that has grapes with liquor in them, whereby it may appear, that there is life yet, in some part of it, and some hope therefore, that it may, by good husbandry, the dead branches of it being cut away, grow fruitful again, he may thereby be induced to forbear the utter rooting out, or hewing down, of it. This seems to be the genuine sense of the similitude: for the old Latin rendering it, *a grape in a cluster*; has led interpreters aside unto another similitude, of saving a cluster for a sound grape, or two, among many withered, or rotten ones: applying it unto the saving of those, that had any matter of sound grace or goodness, in them, notwithstanding the generality of the judgment, to be put in execution upon the main body of the profane, and rotten-hearted, Chap. 17.6. & 24.13. but that seems to be besides the prophet's scope in this place; in this comparison, at least.

*{a blessing is in it*} That is, according to some interpreters, some good liquor in it, through God's blessing upon it; all things conducible to the sustentation of man's life, being in Scripture termed *blessings*, Deut. 28.4,5. Joel 2.14. but by *blessing*, I rather suppose here to be meant, not so much the liquor in the cluster, a matter of small moment, as the life, and sap, that it argued to be in the plant; whereby it might give hope of recovery, and growing fruitful again. See Chap. 44.3,4. & 61.9,11. Psal. 65.10. & 67.6.

*{so will I do for my servants sake, that I may not destroy them all*} Heb. *not to destroy all*. The meaning is, that for those his sincere servants, that remained yet among them, he would not destroy the whole nation, (see Mat. 24.22.) but reserve a remnant for posterity, as he did with Noah, and his family, (whom the Chaldee here instances in) in the flood; though some also in his family, it may be, none of the best, Gen. 7.1. & 9.22,25. See Chap. 63.17. See Jer. 30.11. Amos 9.8.

**V. 9.** *{And I will bring forth a seed out of Jacob*} Or, *But*; as Chap. 61.6. I will reserve a remnant of Jacobs posterity, which I will bring back again, out of the Babylonian captivity; a type, as oft before, of the spiritual delivery from the servitude of sin and Satan, Chap. 9.20–22. & 43.5,6. Psal. 22.30.

*{a seed*} A small number, that shall be as a seed, which though small, yet is apt to grow, both numerous, and great, Gen. 15.5. & 26.4,12. Mat. 13.31,32. See Rom. 9.27,29.

*{and out of Judah, an inheritor of my mountains*} Heb. *a possessor*; a certain number of Judahs posterity, that shall possess the mountains of Judea. See Chap. 14.23. Ezek. 36.1,8. and 38.8.

*{and mine Elect shall inherit it, and my Servants shall dwell there*} Or, *my choice ones* (as Psal. 106.23. Chap. 43.4. & 45.6. & 48.10.) *shall possess it*, (to wit, their own land again) *and my servants* (those faithful ones, for whose sake, I forbear to destroy the whole, ver. 8.) *shall dwell there*, Psal. 102.28.

**V. 10.** *{And Sharon shall be a fold of flocks, and the valley of Achor a place for herds to lie down in, for my people that have sought me*} The country shall not only be peopled again, with men, but replenished with cattle. See Jer. 31.27.

*{Sharon*} A pleasant, and plentiful quarter, having good store of pasture-grounds, 1 Chron. 27.29. See Chap. 33.9. & 35.2.

*{a fold of flocks*} Or, rather, *a pasture for smaller cattle*: as the word is rendered, Ezek. 34.14. for that seems but a nicety, that some, retaining the former, would have the meaning to be; that that whole region should be as full of lesser cattle, as *a fold* is wont to be of sheep.

*{the valley of Achor*} A very rich vale near to Jericho: so called, from the execution done on Achan, and his there, who by his transgression had disturbed the whole state, Josh. 7.24,26. promised, as here; so Hos. 2.15. as *a door of hope* to God's people upon their return; of the enjoyment of their whole land again, because it seems to have been the first ground that they set foot on, after their passage through Jordan, Josh. 3.16. And Esay might well here have some eye to that of Hosea.

*{a place for herds to lie down in*} Heb. *a lodging*, as Chap. 35.7. *for neat*, or *oxen*; as Chap. 11.7. though I conceive that to be groundless, that, from the former term, some would gather, that the whole vale should be as full of beasts, as a stall is wont to be; for the term is used very commonly of beasts, lying down, and lodging, in those places abroad, where they usually feed, Psal. 23.2. Chap. 13.20. & 27.10. Ezek. 34.14. Now because these two places were situate at either end of the land of Canaan, Achor, eastward, near Jordan; Sharon, westward, near to Joppe, hence some suppose, that the repossession of the whole country is hereby implied, and here intended.

*{for my people that have sought me*} Or, *unto my people, that seek to me*: as ver. 1. See Chap. 64.4. Jer. 29.13,14. Lam. 3.25. Ezek. 36.37.

**V. 11.** *{But ye are they, that forsake the Lord*} Or, *But ye*, or, *As for you, that have forsaken the Lord*. Heb. *And ye*: But so, Chap. 57.3. a place parallel to this. For as there, so here, having related what God would do for the better sort of them, he proceeds now, returning to the main body of the wicked ones, of whom before, ver. 2–4. to illustrate the blessed, and comfortable estate of the one, by the cursed, and dismal condition of the other.

*{that forsake the Lord*} Or, *have forsaken*: as Chap. 1.4,28.

*{that forget mine holy mountain*} Heb. *my mountain of holiness*: as Chap. 56.7. mount Sion, whereon the temple was situate, Chap. 2.2. that regard it not, think not of it, have no mind to it; as Jer. 2.32. Hos. 8.14. contrary to that practice, and profession of those faithful ones, Psal. 102.14. & 137.5,6. See Chap. 62.6,7.

*{that prepare a table for that troop*} Or, *that spread*, or *furnish, a table*. So Prov. 9.2. Psal. 23.5. Chap. 21.5. As God's people had certain solemn feasts, wherein they feasted before God, Deut. 16.14,15. Psal. 68.3. so had the idolaters, in imitation thereof, such like feasts, which they kept in the places where they worshipped their idols, held as for them; because in honor of them, Judg. 9.27. Ezek. 18.6,11. Amos 2.8. 1 Cor. 8.10. & 10.21. And this way, the word of *spreading*, or *furnishing*, used commonly of *tables*, does rather carry it, than the way of those, who by *table*, here, would have an *altar* meant; because God's *altar* is sometime found termed his *table*, Ezek. 41.22. Mal. 1.7,12.

*{for that troop*} Or, *for the troop*: so the word seems to signify in the speech of Leah, at the birth of Gad, whom she therefore so named, when she said, as it is there rendered, *A troop cometh*, Gen. 30.11. and Jacob, alluding to his name, *Gad, a troop shall betroop; but he shall betroop them at last*, Gen. 49.19. and from the same root indeed, comes the word there rendered, *a troop*, as very commonly also elsewhere: but the word Gad, save in that speech of Leah, is nowhere else found. Those that take it here, in that notion, understand by it, either the multitude of their idols, which they so doted upon, that they thought they could never have enough of them, Judg. 10.6. Jer. 2.28. & 11.13. and are said therefore to be in their whoredoms unsatiable, Ezek. 16.24–26,28,29. & 23.40–44. so the Chaldee seems to take it: or, the host of heaven, the celestial bodies, which they worshipped instead of the maker both of themselves, and them, Jer. 7.18. & 8.2. and so some of the Rabbines upon this place. But the most of them hold it to be the name of a particular star, or an imaginary deity, to wit, *Luck*, or *Fortune*, in Arabic so termed; and in effect both fancies come home to one: for they that make a star of it, which some affirm to be the planet *Jupiter*, say, there is no star, for luckiness, where it favors, like to it; and they tell us withal, that in old time, they used, in every house to have *a bed*, or, *a table*, (for on beds they tabled anciently) continually spread for this idol; which was commonly called; *Good luck's table*, or *bed*. And Jerome relates, that in Alexandria, and other cities of Egypt especially, on the last day of the year, there used to be a table spread and furnished, with variety of dishes, and delicacies, both of meat and drink, for this idol, either in way of thankfulness, for the prosperity and fertility of the year past; or to procure and obtain from it the like for the year ensuing.

*{and that furnish the drink offering*} Heb. *that fill mixture*; that is, *wine*: at first so termed, because they used in their ordinary use of it, to mix it with water, to abate the strength of it: but from that use in process of time, both in Hebrew, and other languages, the Greek especially, the word of *mixture*, came to be used for *wine*; or, any such *liquor* as wine: so Psal. 75.8. the cup in God's hand is said to be *full of mixture*; that is, of strong *liquor*: and to take us off from fancying some mixture there intended, Rev. 14.10. the *wine* in that cup is said to be (word for word) *mixed unmixed*: which may seem to imply a contradiction; but is well rendered, *poured out* (or, if you will, *poured in*) *without mixture*; for the verb *to mix*, or *mingle*, is from the same ground used commonly, both in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin; for *to pour in, pour out*, and *serve out*, wine, or other liquor, simply, without respect had to any mixture; and so would it be rendered, Prov. 9.2. where it is said, of *Wisdom, she hath poured out her wine*; to wit, into cups, ready to be served out: where they render it amiss, *she hath mingled her wine*; that is hucksters' fashion, alluded to, Chap. 1.22. not hers. So Prov. 23.30. it is said of wine-bibbers, that *they go out to seek mixture*; that is, *wine*, or *liquor*; where also it is ill rendered, *mixed wine*: for it is the *mere*, not the *mixed*, that they affect, and look after; and no less absurd is one of the Jewish doctors' note here, *mixture*; that is, *wine mixed with water*: they would not in likelihood deal so with their deities, especially when they intended, as for the most part they did, to drink most of it themselves: another of them much better expounds it, *a drink offering*, as our version also renders it; but the word signifies, as has been said, and showed; and *to fill wine*, or, *fill out wine*, or other *liquor*, is a form of speech with us also not unusual.

*{unto that number*} The word here used is commonly deemed to spring from a root, that signifies *to number*, Gen. 13.16. Num. 23.10. 2 Sam. 24.1. Dan. 5.23,26. Whence some render it by *number*: and of these some suppose it to be meant of pouring out a certain number of cups, either according to the number of their idols, unto which they performed those rites; or of those persons that joined together in the service. Some again, of their own, drinking by number: For thus, as sometime at their carousing feasts, they used to drink healths, according to the number of letters in the party's name, that they drank the health to: so in the solemn feasts of *Anna Peranna*, one of their idols, they were wont to drink, in honor of her, as many cups, as they desired years, to have their life prolonged by her, by which means sometime their days came to be abridged of what otherwise they might have been. Of the former, see Martial, lib. 1. Epigr. 12. Of the latter, Ovid, in his *Fast*, lib. 4. Others render them, as our version has it, *unto that number*, or, *unto the number*; that is, as before, to the numberless number, either of their idols, or of the celestial bodies: though some more specially to the seven planets, or the constellations, which the astrologers have reduced to a certain number. Others, lastly, render it, as our margin exhibits it; *unto Meni*, or *unto Mani*, which they suppose to be the name of one of the planets; that which we call *Mercury*, and to be the merchants' God, so termed from *numbering*, or casting up of accounts, a business, about which they are much conversant; and from the word *Maneh*, in Hebrew, *Mna* in Greek, and *Mina*, in Latin, for *a pound*, has its name. And of this name, that an idol was anciently in Armenia and Phrygia, worshipped, is by a learned man out of Strabo, and Jamblicus, reported: Whereunto may be added, that *Armenia* is supposed to have been termed, as some, from *Armani*, and *Minni*, or *Menni*, as the Latin renders it, mentioned Jer. 51.27. or, as others, of *Har*, and *Minni*, as the mountainous part of *Minni*, which *Minni* being the ancientest appellation of that country, may probably be deemed to have been the name of some great man that there ruled, and was after his decease (as the manner was) deified by his posterity. See the like, Chap. 46.1. Jer. 50.1.

**V. 12.** *{Therefore will I number you to the sword,}* Heb. *And*; Yet sometime the copulative is put for the relative, as Chap. 47.8. & 63.12. But it may well be here an expletive only, as oft it is, Ezr. 1.1. Ezek. 17.22. Jon. 1.1. *I will number you to the sword*; or, if some emphasis be deemed in it, *I will even, or in like manner, number you to the sword*: Because the word before-going, had either a notion of *numbering* in it, or a near affinity in sound, at least, with the Hebrew word, that so signifies; God, by the prophet, takes occasion to deliver their doom, in these terms, as if he had said; I will also in no small number, set you apart for the sword; or I will deliver you up to it (that is, as the next words show, I will design you to slaughter) by number and tale, so that none of you shall escape. See the manner of setting out some in that sort, that may seem here alluded to, 2 Sam. 8.2.

*{and ye shall all bow down to the slaughter*} As you used to bow yourselves down before your idols, Chap. 44.15,17. or like those beasts, which you used to knock down, to sacrifice to your idols. See the use of the word, Judg. 5.27. Chap. 10.4. & 46.1,2. and like allusions, Chap. 1.29,30.

*{all*} Not some, but all of you: I will not stand to tithe you out, as in execution of multitudes is usually done, or sever and single out, as well some to be saved, as others to suffer, as David did with the Moabites, 2 Sam. 8.2. but deliver you all out to slaughter, and that by tale also, that none of you may escape.

*{because when I called, ye did not answer; when I spake, ye did not hear*} Or, *Ye would not answer; ye would not hear*; to express more pregnantly their willful obstinacy. Heb. *because I called, and ye answered not; I spake, and ye heard not.* But the like syntax is frequent, as Chap. 44.14. & 53.2. & 59.16. and the indicative in a potential, or spontaneous notion, as common: and so it is well rendered, Psal. 81.11. Jer. 36.25. and would also be, Prov. 13.1,8. Jer. 7.24,26. Zach. 1.4. See Prov. 1.24,25. Chap. 50.2. & 66.4. Jer. 7.13.

*{I called—spake*} In, and by my prophets, whom you refused to hear, and obey, Zach. 7.7,11,12. 2 Cor. 5.20. & 13.3.

*{but did evil before mine eyes*} Or, *did that which was evil in my sight.* (See Chap. 57.1.) that is, that that is displeasing to me, as 2 Sam. 11.27. chap. 66.4. See ver. 3.

*{and did choose that wherein I delighted not:}* Or, *which I would not*, to wit, have to be done, as 1 King. 13.33. Psal. 40.6. with Heb. 10.5. but expressly forbade, and utterly abhorred. See chap. 66.3,4.

**V. 13.** *{Therefore thus saith the Lord God, Behold,}* *Behold*, intimating a strange alteration, as chap. 51.22. & 62.11. four several times repeated, to make the deeper impression.

*{behold, my servants shall eat, but ye shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but ye shall be thirsty;}* Or, *when my servants shall eat, ye shall be hungry; when my servants shall drink, ye shall be thirsty*, or, *my servants shall eat, when ye shall be hungry; my servants shall drink, when ye shall be thirsty.* Heb. *and ye shall be hungry, and ye shall be thirsty*: the same syntax with that ver. 12. Those that have been loyal and faithful to me, ver. 9. whom you have vilified and abused, ver. 5. Chap. 66.5. shall enjoy plenty, and live cheerfully, when it shall be far otherwise with you, Psal. 37.11,19,20. and 68.1,3–6. Eccles. 9.7.

*{behold, my servants shall rejoice, but ye shall be ashamed.*} Chap. 66.5. Dan. 12.2. the syntax, as before.

**V. 14.** *{Behold, my servants shall sing for joy of heart; but ye shall cry for sorrow of heart, and shall howl for vexation of spirit*} A further enlargement of the last branch of the verse foregoing. See Psal. 68.3. Prov. 29.6. Luk. 6.20,21,24,25.

*{joy of heart.*} Heb. *goodness of heart*, as Deut. 28.47. so, *a good heart*, for, *a merry, or a cheerful heart*, Est. 1.10. Prov. 15.15.

*{vexation of spirit.*} Heb. *breach*, or, *brokenness of spirit*; as, Prov. 15.4. *a breach in the spirit.* See Chap. 61.1.

**V. 15.** *{And ye shall leave your name for a curse unto my chosen.*} Your very name shall be accursed, and used in cursing, as when men say, *God make thee like such an one.* See Chap. 43.28. Jer. 24.9. & 29.22. & 34.9.

*{for a curse*} Because unto solemn oaths were execrations usually annexed; *Let that befall me, that befell such an one, if I fail, or break my faith*, Num. 5.21. 1 King. 19.2. Neh. 10.19.

*{my chosen*} See ver. 9.

*{for the Lord God shall slay thee*} Heb. *and*; (as Chap. 64.4.) *Adonai Jehovah shall slay thee*: a change of the number; as Chap. 64.5. See ver. 12.

*{and call his servants by another name:}* Heb. *shall to his servants call another name*; as Deut. 2.11,20. chap. 47.1. By *name*, is one’s state, or condition, in Scripture, commonly implied; and by change of name, is an alteration of state ordinarily intimated. Hereof see, chap. 62.4. by *another name* then, is here meant, either another state, than they were formerly in, in regard whereof other terms should be given them, and speeches used of them, than heretofore had been, Hos. 1.6,9. & 2.1,23. Rom. 9.26. 1 Pet. 2.10. or, a divers state and condition from the wickeds, before spoken of; such as should be used, not in cursing, but in blessing. See Gen. 28.3,4. & 48.20. Ruth 4.11. and this way the Jewish commenters go. Howbeit, divers interpreters here maintain debate about this *other name*, or *new name*; (as it seems termed, Chap. 62.2. as, *other tongues*, and *new tongues*, are one, and the same, Mar. 16.17. & Act. 2.4.) And dispute much what particular name it should be; and some here would have it to be the name, of *a stable people*; or, *the people of the true God*, ver. 16. Others, the name of *God’s children*, Joh. 1.12. Gal. 3.26. & 4.4–6. Others, the name of *Christians*, at Antioch first given them; now an honorable title, whereas the name of a Jew is grown reproachful and odious, Act. 11.28. 1 Pet. 4.16. But that of the Rabbines seems most agreeable to the course and current of the context.

**V. 16.** *{That he who blesseth himself in the earth, shall bless himself in the God of truth; and he that sweareth in the earth, shall swear by the God of truth.*} So that men, in blessing, and swearing, shall make use of your names; as in cursings, and execrations of theirs, ver. 15. Though some suppose, that by *blessing*, and *swearing*, is here intended the whole worship of God, as Chap. 19.18. Jer. 4.2. and the meaning to be, that all religious worship, shall be given generally to the true God, and not, as formerly, to idols, chap. 45.23. But this seems not the scope of the prophet in this place.

*{That*} Or, *So that*: To make the connection of this with the former the more clear.

*{he who blesseth himself*} Or, *that blesseth*, simply, either himself, or any other: he that wishes, desires, or prays for good unto any: for these forms are not always, in notion, or use, reciprocal; as by many instances might be showed. See Gen. 22.18. & 26.4. chap. 66.10.

*{in the earth*} Either *on earth*, as chap. 41.4. Mat. 16.10. & 18.18. or in the land, to wit, where God’s servants abide, as chap. 5.8. & 6.12. & 60.18.

*{shall bless himself*} Or, *bless*, simply.

*{in the God of truth*} God indeed is so styled, *a God of truth*, Psal. 31.5. Jer. 10.10. whereof see there, and the word, *amen*, here used, given unto Christ, expounded, *faithful and true*, Rev. 3.14. but the word is an attribute, not an abstract, and has relation therefore to some subject, which to make the sense entire, therefore must be supplied: it signifies, *firm, faithful, stable, steadfast*: it wants his subject here, (the like whereunto, we have frequently found in this prophet. See Chap. 5.4. & 17.5,10.) which some supply *people*, rendering the words, *shall bless by the God of the faithful, or firm, and stable people*, Psal. 89.36,37. they shall in blessing use the name of God, as having relation to his people, and mention them withal as a people blessed, and established, by him: as they shall bless in God’s name, as craving and expecting the blessing from him: so mentioning God’s people, and their condition, as a precedent, and pattern, of the good that they wish unto any. So Gen. 28.4. & 48.15,16,20. Ruth 4.11. See Zach. 8.13.

*{that sweareth in the earth*} *On earth*, or *in the land*, as before, and as Chap. 66.8.

*{shall swear by the God of truth*} Or, *by the God of the faithful*, or firm, and stable people, that is, they shall in their solemn oaths, mention together with him, his goodness to them, and their blessed estate, and settled condition, by reason thereof. In solemn oaths, they used, as execrations and cursings, if they meant not truly, or should deal unfaithfully: so blessings also, and expressions of desire to live and thrive, do well and prosper, as their intentions were sincere, and their performances should be faithful. So the apostle, 1 Cor. 15.31. *by our rejoicing which we have in the Lord Jesus*; that is, *so may I have joy together with you in the Lord God*; and as we use to say, *So help me God.* The meaning then is, that in conceiving oaths, they should use such forms as these, or the like; *The Lord that blessed such, and such his servants, bless me, and mine, in like manner, and no otherwise, than as I shall deal sincerely and faithfully, in that, which by oath I now oblige myself unto.*

*{because the former troubles are forgotten*} Or, *when* (as Job 3.22. & 5.21.) *the former afflictions shall be forgotten*: When former matters, both your sins (as Chap. 43.25. Jer. 31.34. say some) and your sorrows and sufferings (as Chap. 54.4. which all agree in) shall no more be minded, than as if they never had been. See Zach. 10.6.

*{and because they are hid from mine eyes.*} Or, *and when they shall be hid from mine eyes.* This some (as was before hinted) understand of their sins, the procuring causes of their former afflictions and sorrows; which as they are said to lie open to God’s eye, so long as men after the committing of them continue obstinate and impenitent, ver. 3,6. so, upon man’s repentance, they are said to be *covered*, and *hid* from God’s sight; he regarding them no more now to take vengeance, or cast off, for them, than if he neither saw, nor knew them, Psal. 32.1. & 85.2. Chap. 38.17. Mic. 7.19. But because there is no mention at all of sins, in the text; Others therefore understand this also, as the former, of their sufferings and afflictions, that God out of his tender affection to his children, that had been long in straits and difficulties, as not able to endure longer to see them in that misery, should utterly remove them now out of his sight, by delivering his people out of them, and putting a full period to their grievous pressures, Exod. 3.7,8. Num. 23.21. Psal. 106.44,45. Chap. 16.4. & 26.17. & 60.18. See Chap. 63.15. & 64.12.

**V. 17.** *{For behold,}* A further more strange alteration, subjoined, to give further assurance of the change formerly mentioned, not without a multiplied iteration of this note of wonderment, ver. 13,14. See the like of our Savior, Joh. 5.25,28.

*{I create new heavens, and a new earth:}* Or, *I am creating a new heaven* (as Chap. 1.2.) *and a new earth*; I am even now about it, as Chap. 3.1. and so ver. 18. I am making of a new world; I am about so to alter and change the face and state of all things, that the whole frame of the creature shall seem not to be the same, that before it was. This applied to the external state and condition of God’s people, may bear that interpretation, that some here have given it; the sky not cloudy and gloomy, as hinting God’s wrath, and expressing his frown, Joel 2.2. Amos 5.18. but clear and fair, and lightsome, and seasonable, Chap. 30.26. and 60.1. the ground not horrid, and waste, and shapeless, and fruitless, Jer. 4.23–26. but pleasant, delightful, fertile, and fruitful, Chap. 4.2. or that which some other have, that the change of their condition shall be so great, their prosperity such, in regard of their former afflictions and adversity, that coming suddenly out of the one into the other, they shall seem to be in a new, in another world. See Psal. 126.1. But, being spiritually understood, is applicable to the state of the church, in the times of the gospel, under the kingdom of Christ, in regard of those plentiful endowments of spiritual graces, that therein should abound, the mysteries of salvation, being much more clearly revealed, and the service and worship of God in a more spiritual way settled, those former types and shadows, being taken away and removed, Joh. 1.16,17. & 4.21–24. Act. 2.17,33. 2 Cor. 3.6,18. Heb. 9.1–12. & 10.1–9. and hereunto do the apostles apply this renovation of the church, in this world then to be inchoated, 2 Cor. 5.17. to be consummated in the next, 2 Pet. 3.13. Rev. 21.1,5. and thus also do some of the Jewish doctors expound it. See Chap. 66.22.

*{and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.*} Heb. *ascend into the heart*; as Jer. 3.16. 1 Cor. 2.9. and it seems a form of speech taken from those vapors, or steams, that being sent up from the stomach, and possessing the brain, are wont to produce fantasies and dreams; as if it were said, they shall not so much as be once dreamed of. The meaning is, that the spiritual excellency of the church in those times, shall so far exceed that, which in former time it had been, that the consideration of the one, shall seem to drown and abolish the memorial of the other, Jer. 3.16. 2 Cor. 3.7–10.

**V. 18.** *{But be ye glad, and rejoice for ever, in that which I create:}* Or, *am creating*; as ver. 17. a defect both of antecedent, and relative; as ver. 1.

*{be glad, and rejoice*} This some of the Jewish commenters conceive to be spoken, as that which should be the constant and continual language of those times, inciting one another to cheerfulness and joyfulness, such as the condition of the times required. So it should be like that, *Let us rejoice, and be glad*, Psal. 118.24. Rev. 19.7. But it is rather the speech of God himself, as calling upon his people, to rejoice in the good intended by him, for them, in the restitution of his church, Chap. 66.10. so withal assuring them, that howsoever it fared with the wicked ones, ver. 12–15. yet it should go well with them, Chap. 3.10. they should not want just matter, and occasion of joy; and withal, that this matter, and occasion of joy in them, should not be momentany, and fading, suddenly come, and soon gone, like Jonas his gourd, Jon. 4.10. but should be permanent, and perpetual, Chap. 35.10.

*{in that which I create*} Or, *am creating*; restitution and renovation, especially for the better, is deemed as a creation, ver. 17. Psal. 104.30. So Psal. 51.10. Eph. 2.10. & 4.24.

*{for behold, I create Jerusalem a rejoicing, and her people a joy.*} Heb. *I am creating*, as ver. 17. the word of creating here implying not a bare restitution only, but a restitution in a glorious and magnificent manner: for of such kind of works also is the word used, Gen. 1.26,27. Deut. 4.32. chap. 40.26. I am repairing her, and restoring her to so glorious a condition, as will minister matter of abundance of joy, both to her, and them, and all that are well affected unto either. I am about the doing of that, that I have been so much, and so long solicited for, by my servants, chap. 62.7. Heb. *for rejoicing*, and *for joy*; as, *for a blessing*, Psal. 37.26. Prov. 10.7. or, *a blessing*, simply; and *joy*, and *rejoicing*, for matter of mirth and joy; as *praise*, for matter of praise, chap. 60.18. & 61.11. *for rejoicing*, and *for joy*, that is, *to be matter of rejoicing*, and *of joy*; as, *for a curse*, that is, *to be matter of a curse*, ver. 15.

**V. 19.** *{And I will rejoice in Jerusalem, and joy in my people:}* They shall rejoice in me, chap. 61.10. and I will rejoice in them, chap. 62.5. as it is much matter of joy unto an affectionate parent to see his children do well; and to a gracious sovereign to see his people prosper and flourish, Psal. 35.27. Jer. 32.41. 1 Thess. 2.19,20. & 3.8,9. 2 Joh. 4. 3 Joh. 3,4.

*{and the voice of weeping shall be no more heard in her, nor the voice of crying.*} See the like promises, chap. 35.11. & 51.11. Jer. 31.12. Rev. 21.4. for those Jewish doctors narrow the text overmuch, that restrain *weeping*, and *crying* here, to the mourning for persons, either slain, or taken away by immature death; because of that which follows, ver. 20. Howbeit, it is well observed, both by some of them, and other learned, that in these, and the like predictions and promises, the terms, *no more*, and *for ever*; as they concern the state and condition of this present life, have in them a notion of diuturnity; as they have reference to the life to come, a notion of perpetuity: as also that for the subject matter of them, or the things therein propounded, or promised, as they concern the former, they import a degree only of eminency; as they have relation to the latter, a pitch of absolute perfection. In this manner are we to understand, as these, and the ensuing passages; so also those, chap. 54.9. & 60.18. and other the like.

**V. 20.** *{There shall be no more thence an infant of days, nor an old man, that hath not filled his days: for the child shall die an hundred years old; but the sinner being an hundred years old shall be accursed.*} Albeit, there be no such great difficulty in this passage; but the literal sense of the words, (as I conceive) if the Hebrew forms, used in it, be advisedly weighed, will appear to be obvious enough, and familiar: Yet it is strange to see what a number of far-fetched senses have been forced upon it; so that among that multitude of interpreters, that are commonly in hands, scarce any, very few, at least, found, that hold out the genuine sense of the place. The Jewish doctors understand it of the length of years, that their nation shall attain to, in the days of the Messiah; to wit, that then they should live as long as the fathers did before the flood; and that therefore a man at an hundred years should be counted but a *boy*, or *child*, still; and one that should die at these years should be deemed some accursed creature, as having his life shortened by God for his sins. Others, run out to moral, and mystical senses. Some, that whereas in former times, they had many gray heads, with green wits; many ancient for years, but of babish disposition, and childish behavior, there should now be none such among them; but their old men should be grave, sound, and discreet, able to fulfill, and perform all offices required of them, at that age, in their places: and as for those boyish, or childish old men, for behavior and carriage, they should, as accursed wretches, be consumed and worn out, in the time of the captivity. Some, that whereas God did formerly threaten, that if the magistrates did not duly perform their duty, in doing justice upon delinquents, he would himself do it, by taking away persons so spared, by untimely and issueless death, Lev. 20.4,5,20,21. as he did Er, and Onan, Gen. 38.7,10. that now should not be, it should not need: for that the magistrates should now be very strict and exact in the execution of justice, not sparing any for age, though he were an hundred years old. Some, that whereas the law, as a petty schoolmaster, kept men like children, and infants, in their first elements, or rudiments, unto their old age, the gospel should bring them unto maturity and perfection, Gal. 3.24. & 4.3. Heb. 7.19. Others, that in the times of the gospel, all true believers should be continually growing up in grace, until they came to a full growth, in which then they should continue forever, Eph. 4.12–16. Others, that a child in the kingdom of Christ, shall be happier, than an old man in the kingdom of the world: for a child in the kingdom of Christ, shall attain to an happy perfection of life; whereas in the kingdom of the world, a sinner, even then when he seems to have attained a perfection of life, shall be accursed. Others, refer it all to the resurrection, and the life to come, wherein there shall be no difference of old and young, but children shall rise in a perfect stature, and old men shall be raised in youth-like vigor and strength. Some few have discovered, that long life is here promised, after their return from captivity, to God’s people: but in opening of the words, they have gone somewhat wide. For the better conceiving whereof aright, we are to consider that length of life, is, in Scripture, frequently promised, as a blessing, Exod. 20.12. Deut. 4.1,40. & 6.2. Psal. 21.4. & 61.6. & 91.16. Prov. 3.2,16. Eph. 6.2. and, on the other side, the shortening of men’s lives mentioned, and threatened, as a curse, 1 Sam. 2.32. Job 15.32,33. Psal. 55.23. & 94.23. & 102.24. Eccl. 8.13. God therefore, among other blessings which he would confer upon his people now refined, and restored, promises this, as one ordinarily much desired, that none among them, young or old, should be taken away by untimely death, but should live to the utmost of that, which in the course of nature they might reach; and others of their condition, and constitution, are (where not impeached by any cross occurrent, from within, or from without) wont usually to attain. See ver. 22. Zach. 6.4. Howbeit, that the wicked, such as remained still unreformed among them, (as some few yet, even in those times might) though their lives in those times of public peace and tranquility, might be prolonged; yet a curse of God should pursue them, and at last seize upon them, they should be but accursed creatures, Psal. 140.11. Eccl. 8.12,13. But we shall discuss the terms apart as they lie in the text.

*{There shall be no more from thence*} There shall not hereafter, as in former times, go out, or be carried out, to wit, unto burial, *from thence*; that is, from Jerusalem, ver. 19. but put here for the whole land and state of Israel; because the head city of the kingdom: and thus far the Jewish commenters go along with us. See Eccl. 5.10. So must the words, *from thence*, be understood, as with a notion of place; not, as some, *from thenceforth*, in a notion of time: the word is nowhere found so used.

*{an infant of days*} The word, here used, seems by a late learned scholiast, to be taken for an *embryo*, or child conceived & contained as yet in the womb: for he renders the text, *a youngling, or little infant, that shall not fulfill, or accomplish his days*; that is, says he, the days required, for the birth of it with life. So this branch of the promise, should be equivalent with that, Exod. 23.26. that none among them going with child, should miscarry, or, be abortive. And it is true indeed, that a word of near affinity to this, and whereby the Jewish commenters here expound this, is used of such, Job 3.19. *as infants that never saw light*; as also that, Gen. 33.13. a word deemed to be of the same kindred with this, is rendered, *great with young*. But this, I suppose, here, to have been this learned man’s singular conceit, and so leave it. That word wherewith these Jewish masters here render it, is supposed commonly, to signify a *sucking-child*, or a *suckling*; but we find those two distinguished, the one from the other, 1 Sam. 15.3. & 22.19. Jer. 44.7. Lam. 2.11. See on chap. 49.15. and as that, so this seems to be used more generally for *a child*, or *boy*, though of some bigness; for as of the one it is said, *the children ask bread*, Lam. 4.4. so of the other, *boys despise me, & speak against me*, or *prate of me*, Job 19.18. which of sucking children, can neither of them fitly be said. But by *a child*, or *a boy of days*, what should be meant, is further questioned; and here some would have the meaning to be, one *of many days*, as Josh. 23.1,2. *gone in days*, is used for *stricken in age*: & Dan. 10.14. *the vision is for days*, that is, for many days, as our English well renders it; and so *a boy*, or *a child of days*, should be one, that has lived a long time, many days, is far stricken in years, and yet continues still a child, childish, or boyish. Others would have it, *a child of days*; that is, *of few days*: as, *a number*, for a small number. See chap. 10.19. But to let pass these needless supplies; *a child of days*, here signifies, as the words simply and properly import, *a child for days*; one in regard of days, or age, but a child: and the opposite word, *old man*, joined with it, does evidently evince that to be the true notion, both of the word, and form, here used. So that the meaning of the words, *no child that shall not fulfill, or accomplish his days*, is, that their children should not come to untimely ends, as formerly, having their brains dashed out by the enemy, 2 King. 8.12. Psalm 137.8,9. Jer. 9.20. or being starved for want of food in the siege of the city, Lam. 2.11,12,22. but should live and attain to their just growth, and full stint of years; and herein also the Jewish critics accord.

*{nor an old man that hath not filled his days;}* Heb. *and an old man*: but the copulative, is here in a discretive, or disjunctive notion; as, *father and mother*, for, *father or mother*, Exod. 21.15. as, *the child*, and *the old man*, are here opposed: so *the old man*, and the *full of days*, are distinguished, Jer. 6.11. and the Jewish masters here, are somewhat curious in their explication of these terms: a man, say they, is deemed an old man at sixty, but is not said to be *full of days*, or to *have filled his days*, until he reach unto *seventy*, the stint of man’s life, Psal. 90.10. so it is said of *David*, that he died *full of days*, 1 Chr. 29.28. and yet he lived not beyond *seventy*; for he began to reign when he was *thirty* year old, and reigned *forty*, 2 Sam. 5.4. but, say they, now they were to live hundreds of years, as they did before the flood: had they said *an hundred years*, they had not spoken much amiss: for the words following imply as much but their computation is with the nicest, & their assertion too hyperbolical; a man is then said to have *filled, or accomplished his days*, when he has lived so long, as in course of nature, he might well reach, being not, by any casualty intervening, debarred from attaining thereunto.

*{for the child shall die an hundred-years old:}* The *child*, or *boy*, or *lad*, or *youth*, or *young man*; for it is not the word that was before used, but another, which in Scripture seems to comprehend, *infancy, childhood, & youth*: and sometime also to take in men of middle age. Some would stint it at *twenty years*; and it is given to *Joseph* at *seventeen*, Gen. 37.2. but to Benjamin, when he is deemed to have been above *thirty*, Gen. 43.8. this *child*, or what you please to call him, *the son of an hundred years shall die*; so the words lie, and are word for word in the text. Hence those Rabbinical fictions of men living so many years, that at an *hundred* they should seem to be but *children* and *boys*. And on the other side the fancies of those, who have out of this form, coined us a proverb, *A child of an hundred years old*, for *an old doter*, or *a fool*, styled therefore afterward, say they, *a sinner*: Whereas the syntax is familiar, and as clear as the daylight, or sunshine; *the child, or youth* (that now is) *shall die the son of an hundred years*; that is, shall be an hundred years old when he dies. So Gen. 11.10. *Sem, the son of an hundred years, begat Arphaxad. And Abraham was the son of an hundred years when Isaac was born to him*, Gen. 21.5. in the same form run all those genealogical reckonings, Gen. 5.32. & 7.6. & 12.4. & 16.16. & 17.1. & 25.20,26. & 37.1. & 41.46. & 50.26. and very frequently elsewhere: neither young, nor old, shall die, until they have made up a complete age; such as an *hundred years* has anciently with Greeks and Latins, been deemed to be; whence their *ludi seculares*, held solemnly every *hundredth year*: a form of speech here used to express length of life.

*{but the sinner being an hundred years old, shall be accursed.*} Heb. *and the sinner, the son of an hundred years shall be accursed.* Where because the word rendered *a sinner*, comes from a verb which, in the first place signifies *to miss the mark.* So Judg. 20.16. hence some would here also have it so to be taken, and this branch thus rendered, *he that misseth* (or falleth short) *of an hundred years, shall be accursed*, that is, shall be deemed so to be; but this sense cannot be made out from the words, without manifest wringing and wronging the text. Others taking this word aright, run as wide in the later: for because it is said, Deut. 21.23. that *he that is hanged on the tree is accursed*; would have the meaning to be this, that wicked men, as well old as young, shall be, by execution of justice done on them, made exemplary, & so deemed, as accursed; and that such become sometime matter of a curse, in proverbial phrases and bywords, appears by Jer. 29.22. See v. 15. But this is but to step out to fetch fire, or water, abroad, when we have either of them under our noses, at home. The genuine sense of its own accord offers itself to us. That amidst all this prosperity & tranquility, all this flourishing estate & condition of God’s people, the man that lives among them unreclaimed, and unreformed, continuing still in a sinful course of life, shall be never a whit the more happy for all that felicity, though through God’s patience his life be never so long prolonged, but shall at length prove a cursed wretch. See Job 21.7–20. Psal. 37. & 73. Prov. 1.32. Eccles. 8.12,13. chap. 3.10,11. & 48.22. & 57.20,21. It seems to be not much unlike that, Rev. 20.6. *Blessed is he* (not that lives in the times of the *first resurrection*; that is, in the times of the restitution of the church to its purity and peace, but he) *that being holy, hath his part in the first resurrection*, through a spiritual change wrought in his soul, in raising him from the death of sin, to the life of grace, Joh. 5.25. I shall add only a small punctilio, if I may so term it, which yet, as to me seems, might conduce to make the connection of this clause, with the rest of the context, a little clearer, to wit, if that the copulative here were rendered, by, the discretive, *though*: and the whole clause put into a parenthesis, (*though the sinner an hundred years old be accursed*) because in the very next words, he goes on in relating what benefits, together with this long life, the godly party should enjoy.

**V. 21.** *{And they shall build houses, and inhabit them, and they shall plant vineyards, and eat the fruit of them.*} They, to wit, my servants, v. 13,14. shall live to possess quietly, the houses built by them, and to receive and enjoy the fruit of their labors, v. 9. See Psalm 128.2. Jer. 29.5.

**V. 22.** *{They shall not build, and another inhabit; they shall not plant, and another eat*} To wit, the fruit of what they plant; as in the former branch, inhabit the houses by them built; both to be understood from v. 21. not only for that the curse threatened, Deut. 18.30,39. should now have no place; they should not build, or plant for an enemy to possess and enjoy, ch. 62.8,9. but that they should not build or plant for posterity alone, but should survive long, to enjoy whatsoever, in either kind, they had taken pains about themselves: and this to be principally here intended, appears, both by what went before, v. 20. and by what here follows.

*{for as the days of a tree, are the days of my people*} Or, *shall the days of my people be*; as of a lasting tree, that continues for many ages: not as of a fading leaf, as formerly, that at time of year, sheds, chap. 64.6. it is well known of what continuance oaks and elms are, to omit all others: nor need we therefore have recourse here with the Jewish doctors, therein following the Chaldee paraphrast, wherewith the Greek also concurs, to *the tree of life*, Gen. 2.9. which, say they, lasted *five hundred years.* See Psalm 128.3,6.

*{and mine elect shall long enjoy the work of their hands*} Or, *my choice ones* (as vers. 9.) shall live long to spend themselves; and even to *wear out*, (so the word properly signifies, Job 21.13.) what by their labors they have gotten and gathered, Psalm 128.2,6. so rather, than, as some other, *they shall make their handy work durable.* See chap. 23.18.

**V. 23.** *{They shall not labor in vain*} As those do that cannot enjoy the fruit of their labors; but others eat what they have tugged and toiled for: or whose labors prove fruitless for want of a blessing from above, Lev. 26.16. Deut. 28.30. Jer. 51.58. Hab. 2.13. Hag. 1.6. 1 Cor. 15.58.

*{nor bring forth for trouble*} Or, *unto trouble.* Their issue shall enjoy the like quiet and prosperous condition together with their parents, having no occasions of mourning ministered unto them, by the untimely death, & loss of parents, or their dismal occurrents; which in times of public calamity do so frequently fall out, that the issue of those that live in those times, may seem bred to nothing, but to sorrow and grief; as in times of pestilence, for the grave; in times of war, for the sword: and they are wont therefore to be deemed happy, that are in such times without issue. See Deut. 28.4. Hos. 9.12,13,14. Mat. 24.19.

*{for they are the seed of the blessed of the Lord, and their offspring with them.*} To wit, *is blessed*: God’s blessing is entailed upon them: it takes in their issue together with them, Exod. 20.6. Psalm 37.25,26. & 115.13,14. See chap. 61.9.

**V. 24.** *{And it shall come to pass, that before they call, I will answer*} *And it shall be* (as chap. 2.2.) *before they call, and I will answer*; as chap. 57.11. I will be more forward to grant, than they to crave; more ready to answer, than they to ask. See instances hereof, Psal. 32.5. Dan. 10.12. Luke 15.18,20.

*{and whiles they are yet speaking, I will hear*} By gracious acceptance of their suits, and granting to them, what they are speaking, and suing for, Dan. 9.20–23. So Act. 10.44. & 11.15. See chap. 58.9.

**V. 25.** *{The wolf, and the lamb, shall feed together;}* That is, say some, justice shall be so strictly and severely executed, that there shall be no murders, nor robberies committed, as in former times, chap. 1.21,23. See Deut. 13.11. But the meaning rather seems to be, that such as had been of a fierce and savage disposition formerly, should now be so altered and changed, that they might seem to be transformed out of wolves into sheep; so altered, at least, as if a wolf were grown so tame, that he might safely be trusted with sheep, and suffered to go among lambs, contenting himself to feed quietly, and harmlessly, not on them, but with them. See chap. 11.6.

*{together*} Heb. *as one*; so this form is used, Ezra 2.64. & 3.9. & 6.20. Neh. 7.66. so also, Psal. 82.7. which there not observed, has caused a mistake in the meaning of the place.

*{and the lion shall eat straw like the bullock*} Not prey upon cattle, as in times past. See chap. 11.7.

*{and dust shall be the serpent’s meat.*} He shall rest content with the food, by God, assigned him, Gen. 3.14. and not fasten on man, or beast, nor feed on, or hurt at all any other creature; all shall be harmless. See chap. 11.8.

*{They shall not hurt nor destroy in all mine holy mountain, saith the Lord.*} Or, *none shall hurt, nor destroy, in all mine holy mountain.* Heb. *mountain of holiness*, as vers. 11. throughout my whole church, among my people, chap. 2.2. Psal. 15.1. & 24.3. Sion, for Jerusalem; because the chief part of it, wherein God’s temple, and the king’s palace, stood; and Jerusalem for the whole land; because the mother city. See on verse 20. *from thence.* Of the whole passage, see chap. 11.9.

### CHAPTER 66

**Verse 1.** *{Thus saith the Lord;}* This chapter, though it seem a distinct sermon from that next before-going; yet is much of the same subject matter, and argument with it, and has many forms and expressions, the same that we there had: it consists of various passages, interwoven the one within the other, of mercies and comforts to the godly, of judgments to the wicked: together with prophecies concerning the strange, sudden, and unexpected restitution of the church, and the dilatation of it into all parts.

*{The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool:}* Because the carnal Jews confided much in the material temple, and the external services, and sacrifices, therein performed, Jer. 7.4,10. when as neither their hearts were upright with God, nor their lives otherwise conformable to the rule of his word; God, by the prophet, endeavors to beat down, and raze the grounds of this their vain confidence; in the former, in this verse; in the later, vers. 3.

*{Heaven is my throne:}* That is, the place of his majestical presence, where, in most glorious manner, he manifests himself unto the blessed spirits, as a king sitting in his royal robes, on his throne, Psal. 11.4. & 103.19. Mat. 5.34.

*{the earth is my footstool*} So is the earth in general termed; because the lowest part of the world, which he fills with his powerful presence, Psal. 110.1. Mat. 5.35. but in a more special manner the ark, as a place on which he seemed to rest, as men’s feet do on a footstool, 1 Chr. 28.2. Psal. 99.5. & 132.7. Lam. 2.1. See ch. 60.13.

*{where is the house that ye build unto me?*} Or, *where is there an house, that ye should*, or *can, build for me?* the pronoun demonstrative, put for the verb substantive: as 1 Sam. 9.18. Job 39.19,24. Psal. 25.12. Chap. 50.1. and the verb taken potentially, as chap. 49.15. & 64.11. when as I fill heaven and earth with my presence, Jer. 23.25. what house can you build, that should hold, and contain me? Do you imagine, that I am included in, or confined unto, my temple, as one of your idols, unto some cell, or house, that you have framed for it? Chap. 44.13. See 1 King. 8.27. 2 Chr. 6.18. Acts 7.47–50. & 17.24.

*{and where is the place of my rest?*} Or, *or* (the copulative for the disjunctive; as Gen. 2.6.) *where is there a place* (as before, & Job 38.19.) *for my rest?* or, as some, *what place* (so the old Greek renders it, and so Luke, Acts 7.49.) *is my rest?* *rest*, for a *place of rest*; as Psal. 95.11. & 132.14. such a place for me to rest and repose myself in, as if I could not find rest anywhere else, but there; as the dove in the deluge, Gen. 8.9. Howbeit, in some respects the temple, in regard of the ark, termed *God’s footstool*, is sometime called *God’s rest*, or his *resting place*, Psal. 132.8. as a type of his church, wherein he is pleased to rest, and repose himself, by his Spirit, Cant. 1.7. chap. 11.10. See chap. 60.7,13.

**V. 2.** *{For all those things hath my hand made*} Or, *Since that* (Heb. *And*; as Job 19.28. & 21.22.) *my hand hath made all those things*: (as ver. 8.) to wit, heaven & earth, (v. 1.) and whatsoever is contained in either of them; even whatsoever you see and behold, above, or below, in the sky, or on the earth, chap. 40.26. Gen. 1.1. & 2.1. Psal. 146.6. Joh. 1.3. Acts 7.50. Heb. 3.3,4. & 11.3. for they seem to go aside from the true sense of the text, who expound them of the temple, and the sacrifices, as being all God’s creatures, 1 Chr. 29.14,16.

*{and all those things have been, saith the Lord*} Or, *are*; that is, have their being, Acts 17.25,28. and subsist, Col. 1.16,17. or *are*; that is, *continue*, as the word is used, Dan. 1.21. So Psal. 119.89,91. they continue in being, as supported by him, Heb. 1.2,3. they *are*, to wit, by my hand; thus rather than as some, *have been*, that is, had a beginning: or, as some other, *were*, to wit, the work of my hands: though that was in the former branch intended. Since that all things, both heaven and earth, with all the contents and furniture of either, have had their being at first from him, and are still upheld by him, he has no need at all of them; but can well be without them: as he was also before they were; much less has he need of any house to receive him, or of any service of man therein to be done him, Psal. 16.2. & 50.10,11. Acts 17.25.

*{but to this man will I look, even to him that is poor, and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word*} Or, *yet*, (Heb. *and*: as chap. 60.10. & 63.11.) *to this man do I look; to one afflicted*, or *humbled, and smitten in spirit, and that trembleth at my word.* Albeit, that I am so infinitely high and great, and so all-sufficient of myself, yet will I look after, regard, and take notice of any one that is of an humble mind, and of a penitent spirit, and that does sincerely fear me, Psal. 33.18. & 34.18. & 138.6. & 147.11. such are they that I desire, and delight to abide with, the hearts of such are the house that by my Spirit, I am willing, and well content, to inhabit, Prov. 8.31. 1 Cor. 3.16. & 6.19. Eph. 2.22. as also these affections, and dispositions, are the sacrifices that he accepts of, and takes delight in, Psal. 51.16,17. See chap. 57.15.

*{poor*} To wit, *in spirit*, Mat. 5.3. or rather, here, at least, *afflicted*, or *humbled*; for that the word properly signifies, and is well so rendered, Psalm 18.27. & 22.24. & 88.15. Prov. 15.15. & 22.22.

*{of a contrite spirit*} Heb. *contrite of spirit*; as some: supposing it to come from a word that signifies *to grind*, or *to vex*, Ezek. 13.22. & to be the same with that, which, from thence derived, is found, Pro. 15.13. & 17.22. & 18.14. rendered sometime, *a broken*, sometime *a wounded spirit*: but though in sound it come near to it, and be in substance the same with it, yet it seems to come from another root, and to signify properly *smitten*; and by smiting, *weakened*: used elsewhere of the body, 2 Sam. 4.4. & 9.3. here applied to the mind, and signifies one *smitten in heart*; as it is, Psal. 102.4. or, *dejected in spirit*, as sometime it is used also for *an abject*, Psal. 35.15. Instead of these two, chap. 57.15. we have two others; though in root and sound different from them, in notion near them, to wit, *contrite*, and *low of spirit*: but two of the same, not notion only, but notation also with them, chap. 53.4.

*{and trembleth at my word*} Or, *and that trembleth*; for the relative is wanting, as c. 65.1. a note of one that truly fears God, to stand in awe of his word, and with due reverence receive it, Esr. 9.4. & 10.3. So 2 King. 22.11,19. Psal. 119.131. chap. 50.10. Jer. 36.16.

**V. 3.** *{He that killeth an ox, is as if he slew a man:}* As this people confided much in their temple, so in their sacrifices, and other external services therein performed, no less, 2 Chr. 13.10,11. God therefore in these words acquaints them, how he esteemed of those performances, where those inward affections and dispositions of soul & spirit are wanting; no better than as oblations consisting of such abominable things as the heathen offered to their idols; yea, no better than as the committing of the heinousest crimes, that may either against God or man be committed, such as were *murder*, the heinousest offense in the second table inhibited, and *idolatry* in the first. See Prov. 15.8. & 21.27. chap. 1.11–14.

*{he that killeth an ox*} To wit, for sacrifice; as in the next branch, of *a sheep*.

*{is as if he slew a man*} Heb. *killing an ox, smiting a man*; or *a slayer of an ox, a smiter of a man*, that is, *a murderer* of him: such a one as God would have by force haled from his altar, and put to death, Exo. 21.14. for the term of *smiting* is used oft-times for *slaying*, as Num. 35.11,15,30. Jer. 40.14,15. God, by the prophet so speaks, as putting no difference at all between the one and the other; between their slaying of an ox for sacrifice, & the murdering of a man; between the sprinkling of his altar by them, with the blood of a beast, and the polluting of it with the gore blood of one of their children, that they slew and sacrificed to their idols, Psal. 106.37,38. that which they make offer of unto God sometime to do for him, if he would accept, & give them leave to live as they listed, Mic. 6.6,7. yea, and acted sometime on the very selfsame day, whereon they tendered him their sacrifice, Ezek. 23.38,39. the note of similitude is wanting; as Gen. 49.10. chap. 47.3. & 58.3. which yet makes the speech the more emphatical. See on chap. 40.6,7.

*{he that sacrificeth a lamb, as if he cut off a dog’s neck*} Heb. *a sacrificer*, or, *a slayer*, (as Exod. 12.4.) *of a sheep*; for so the word signifies. See chap. 53.7. *a necker of a dog*, or *one that necketh a dog*; that is, beheads him, or cuts off his head by the neck; as the word is also used, Deut. 21.4. for the verb is derived from a noun that signifies the hinder part of the neck, on which, in the beheading, of man or beast, the executioner’s stroke is wont to light: and hence also in the Jewish Talmud, *the neck*, is termed, *the house*, or *place of slaughter*; because in slaying of beasts for sacrifice, they gave, the deadly stroke there. See Jer. 2.27. *to neck*, for *to cut off by the neck*: (though sometime also *to break the neck.* So it is rendered, Exod. 13.13. & 34.20. (as, *to root*, for, *to pluck up by the roots, to root out*, Job 31.12. Psal. 52.6. and *to tail*, for, *to curtail*, or, *to cut off the tail*, or hindermost part of aught, or party of some troop, Deut. 25.18. Hos. 10.19. See the like, chap. 10.28. & 22.25. here the beheading, or killing of a dog, by necking, or knetching of him, is mentioned as a matter intended for sacrifice, a thing by the ritual law, then in force, so vile and abominable, that whereas some other beasts, as the ass, though unclean, & secluded from being made matter of sacrifice, or the firstlings thereof, to be tendered for an oblation, yet might be redeemed, and somewhat accepted in lieu of them, Exo. 13.13. there was solemn provision made, in express terms, that *no price of any dog* should be brought into God’s house, Deut. 23.18.

*{he that offereth an oblation*} Heb. *maketh an oblation to ascend*, or, *a maker of a meat*, or *meal*, or, *corn-offering to go up*; as 1 Sam. 7.10. Jer. 33.18. See chap. 1.13. & 57.6. & 60.7.

*{is as if he offered swine’s blood*} There is no more in the text, than *swine’s blood*: the rest is supplied from the former member of the sentence, and as in the other branches. See the supplies from foregoing members, Gen. 1.16,30. 2 Chr. 10.11. Prov. 15.15. chap. 58.13. *swine* were unclean, and their flesh not to be eaten, or so much as touched, Lev. 11.7,8. much less their *blood* to be offered on God’s altar, as was the blood of beasts allowed for sacrifice, Exod. 23.18. See chap. 65.4. verse 17.

*{he that burneth incense, as if he blessed an idol:}* Heb. *a remembrancer of incense*, (that is, one *that with incense makes a memorial*: as Lev. 2.2.) or, as some, *a celebrater*, or *praiser* (of God) *by incense*; one that, by such means, would seem to praise God, and express his thankfulness to him. See Psal. 141.2. chap. 1.13. Mal. 1.11. (and of this use of the word here used, see chap. 12.4.) *a blesser of vanity*, or *vexation*: so is an *idol* here termed; because no other than *vanity*, Jer. 10.15. and matter of mere *vexation* and *affliction*, unto all those that serve them, observe them, and rely on them. See ch. 41.29. & 46.1. and of the signification of the word, ch. 1.13. & 10.1. Howbeit the Chaldee paraphrast, whom some of the Jewish doctors follow, expound it another way; *he that makes a memorial with incense, as if he blessed me with some rapine*; that is, as if he presented me (for, *a blessing* is used for *a present*, Gen. 33.13.) with somewhat gotten by oppression, which I profess to abhor, ch. 61.8. but the former sense seems genuine; and the meaning to be, that their incense-offerings were so far from being any grateful savor unto him, that they did but vex him, as much by presenting him with them, as they could by praying to, praising of, and tendering themselves, and their service to some idol. See Ezek. 20.39. where God expressly professes, that he would rather they should go serve any the vilest & basest idols, being such as they were, than perform any service in his house to himself; as deeming himself more profaned and dishonored by this later, than by the former.

*{yea, they have chosen their own ways,}* Or, *because*, or *since that they chose ways of their own.* Heb. *also they*, or *they also*, that is, say some of the Jewish commenters, both their fathers, and they also, as ch. 65.7. but these particles are of very various use; and this in particular, as it is an illative, Job 7.11. so it seems here to be a causal; and *gam* to be put for *sheggam, because*, Gen. 6.3. and so also one of the Jewish critics here expounds it; affirming, that in these words God renders a reason, why he so deemed, and esteemed of their services; to wit, because their persons, and their practices were such, so detestable, and so directly contrary unto that which he required. See the same reason of the like rendered, Ezek. 20.39. Jer. 7.21–28. Some render the words, *they choose these things* (to wit before-mentioned) *in their ways*: which reading, were it admitted, the former might seem to bear a far other sense, than has been given of it; to wit, *they that sacrifice an ox*, or *a sheep*, or, *bring an offering*, or *burn incense*, are such as are withal, *murderers* and *sacrificers of dogs, and swine*, and *idolaters*: but this misreading, and misrendering here, arises from a supposition, that the particle *beth*, should here signify *in*, as it oft does: whereas indeed it is but a bare note of the verb’s government of the noun: whereunto it is prefixed; which as it is in the syntax of divers other verbs, so in that of this very frequently, as may be seen, Deut. 7.7. & 14.2. & 18.5. & 21.5. 1 Sam. 10.26. & 16.8,9,10. as also, chap. 14.1. & 44.1,2. and hereafter again twice, vers. 4. yea, very seldom otherwise: it is therefore aright rendered, *Ye choose your own ways*, or *ways of your own*: such as yourselves have devised, and your hearts hang after, but are none of mine, but directly repugnant to what I require. See chap. 65.2. & vers. 4.

*{and their soul delighteth in their abominations.*} They have no delight in aught, but such abominable practices as they have made choice of, and betaken themselves unto. Of the word rendered *abominations*, see on vers. 17. *their soul*, for *themselves*; as Psalm 3.2. & 33.20. & 107.18. & 124.7. yet the phrase makes it more emphatical; as Psal. 11.5. Zach. 11.8. Heb. 10.38. *their abominations*, as before, *their own ways*.

**V. 4.** *{I also will choose their delusions, and bring their fears upon them:}* One of the Jewish masters finding two *gams*, or *alsoes*, here; the one, in the verse before; the other, in this, would have them rendered, that they may the one answer the other, *both they have chosen, and I also will choose*; as the like, says he, is found, Deut. 32.25. Num. 18.3. Eccles. 9.1. though scarce any of these places are parallel to this. But I suppose rather, that the former *gam*, was there used as a causal; this here, as an illative; *because they have chosen, therefore will I choose*; and may well have a twofold reference; as to their impiety before-mentioned; so to their obstinacy therein, hereafter subjoined. Howsoever, there is in the word thus repeated, an implication of a retaliation; as if he had said, *They have made their choice, and I will make mine: they have taken the courses that they pleased with me, and I will take what course I please with them.* See the like, Lev. 26.27,28. Psal. 18.26. chap. 65.12. Jer. 34.17. The Jewish critic before mentioned, would have somewhat here supplied from vers. 3. to wit, *I will choose*, and delight *in their delusions*: it may be the rather, because of the particle *beth*, here again found; but of that before: and though as much may be implied, yet the supply is not necessary.

*{their delusions*} Or, *devices*, or *designs*: the word is nowhere found, but here, and ch. 3.4. from which place, together with some other, where the verb it comes of is used for, in contumelious manner, *to mock, & abuse*; as Judg. 19.25. 1 Sam. 31.4. Jer. 38.19. some interpreters here render it, *delusions, illusions, petulancies*, or *mockeries*; and this some take actively, or subjectively, *their illusions, petulancies*, or *mockeries*; that is, the abuses, indignities, & dishonors done by them, and offered to God’s sacred majesty; and these put for the reward of them, or the reward for the same due unto them. Others passively, or objectively, *their illusions*, or *mockages*, that is, the reproachful & disgraceful usages, that they shall be exposed unto, undergo, and endure; and this I take to be the genuine sense of the place: so, *my wrong*, for the wrong done, not by me, but to me, Gen. 16.5. and, *my violence*, for the violence offered to me, Jer. 51.35. and this well suits with what follows, *their fears.* So the meaning will be, As they have made choice of such ways and courses as please not me; so will I make choice of such things for them, as they shall find small pleasure in; such as shall bring nothing, but reproach and derision, dread and distraction upon them, that shall expose them to shame, and terror, Jer. 18.16. & 19.8. & 24.9. & 25.9,18. & 39.18. Howbeit, because a word of the same alliance with this, is used sometime for *devices*; sometime, *designs*, and that usually in the worse part, for *evil devices*, and *evil designs*, Deut. 22.14. Psal. 141.4. Ezek. 20.43,44. & 21.24. & 24.14. the greatest number of interpreters, would have this word also to signify, here; by *devices* and *designs*, understanding the due and deserved reward of them; as chap. 65.7. But the use of the word is without example. The Jewish commenters have hints of either.

*{and will bring their fears upon them*} Such terrors and affrightments as they shall sustain, and be distracted with; as Psal. 34.4. Jer. 20.4. Some conceive the meaning to be, that God would bring upon them those evils, which at present they feared, and by betaking themselves to those idolatrous services, and practices hereafter mentioned, v. 17. hoped to avert, according to that, Prov. 10.24. *The fear of the wicked*, (that which he fears, and out of fear, seeks by evil courses to avert, or avoid) *shall befall him.* See Jer. 42.16. Ezek. 11.8. and pregnant instances hereof, 1 King. 12.26–30. with 13.34. and Joh. 11.48–50. with Luke 19.43,44. & 20.24–26. But the people in likelihood, at the time of this prophecy, were rather possessed with security, than surprised with fears.

*{because when I called, none did answer; when I spake they did not hear:}* Or, *none would answer, and would not hear.* Heb. *I cried, and there was no answerer; I spake, and they heard not.* See chap. 65.12.

*{but they did evil before mine eyes*} Or, *that which was evil in my sight*; that is, displeasing to me. Heb. *and*, as chap. 29.13. and, *the evil in mine eyes*, as chap. 65.12. Jer. 7.30.

*{and chose that in which I delighted not.*} Made choice of such courses, and walked advisedly therein, as I detested and abhorred, vers. 3. See chap. 65.12.

**V. 5.** *{Hear the word of the Lord, ye that tremble at his word:}* You that truly fear God v. 2. for to them he now turns his speech; as chap. 50.10. & 51.1,7. partly, to encourage and strengthen them, against the reproachful, disgraceful, and despiteful usages, which at present they sustained at the hands of their own profane & ungodly people: and partly, because they only, and such as they were, had right to, and were to share in those favors, and mercies, that God promises here to bestow upon his church, in, and after the restoration of it.

*{your brethren*} In name and profession, but false and counterfeit ones, 2 Cor. 11.26. Gal. 2.4. and this term seems the rather here given them, to aggravate their harsh and unbrotherly demeanor toward the godly, as Ezek. 18.18. Obad. 10,12. 1 Joh. 3.15.

*{that hated you, that cast you out, for my name’s sake,}* Or, *that hate you*, &c. that malign and oppugn you for your sincere service of God, and cleaving close to him; or, as one of the Rabbines, not amiss, for their *trembling at his word*, Psalm 38.20. Cant. 1.6. vers. 2.

*{cast you out*} So some of the Jewish critics, according to that, Job 18.18. and so it should imply, that censure of *casting out*, the lowest degree of excommunication in the Jewish church, called *Niddui*, by a word from that root; or, *put you off*, or *far* from them; as others of them, conceiving the word here used, to come from another, but near neighbor term, that signifies, *to remove*, or *put far off*, Amos 6.2. and they refer it to the wonted speeches of those, Chap. 65.5. and Lam. 4.15. who, though most vile themselves, shunned others truly pious, as persons polluted, and such as should pollute them, if they came near them. The two roots are so near akin, that among the critics it is questioned, whether the term *niddah*, that has a notion of separation for uncleanness, comes from the one, or from the other; and the meaning here is, those that either by unjust censure, under pretense of a legal proceeding, cast you out, as persons unworthy of communion with God’s people; or that shun you, as persons so polluted, and defiled, that there is no dealing with you, without being defiled by you. See Joh. 9.34. & 16.2.

*{for my name’s sake;}* As Mat. 10.22. & 19.29. Luk. 21.17. Joh. 15.21. that is, *for my sake; for me*, for your loyalty to me, Psal. 44.22. & 69.7. Mat. 5.10,11.
