Mar. 10.29. and thus most, both annex, and expound, this clause, which yet some of the Rabbins, with whom one of ours, an interpreter of prime note, concurs, knit unto the words following, and make part of these presumptuous ones’ words, *By*, or *through my name, God is glorified.* But the phrase to me seems uncouth; and I leave it therefore to the judgment of others.

*{said*} Or *say*, to wit, when they do thus express, and manifest their malevolent, and malignant affection, and disposition towards you.

*{Let the Lord be glorified:}* An Egyptian Rabbine, of no small note among his countrymen, interprets these words far otherwise than we read them, as, if, in them, this ungodly people should complain, that God was over-heavy, and burdensome to them, in requiring of them, such a strict observation of his rites and precepts; and renders the words, *The Lord is burdensome*, or *heavy*, alleging 2 Sam. 13.25. and affirming withal, that in that form, wherein it is here used, it does never signify otherwise: but herein another of his own coat controls him, and points him to a place, Job 14.21. where, in the same form, it signifies, *to be honored*, or *had in honor*. And these, either of theirs, or ours: that thus render it, as the most do, expound it, some of them, as spoken by them in way of justification of their ways and courses in general, to wit, that they honored God more, by serving him in so many places, and with such variety of all sorts of sacrifices, than those did, that confined his service to one place only, and restrained his sacrifices to a small number of creatures, see Chap. 36.7. or, of this particular act of theirs, in casting out of his servants, or sequestering themselves from them, as pretending that they had very good, and just ground, and cause so to do, and that they did a service very acceptable to God, and such as much conduced to the honor of his name, in so doing. So Joh. 16.2. and they render the words, *the Lord is glorified*; to wit, by us, in what we do. But others rather conceive it spoken, in way of derision, *Let God be glorified*, or *appear in glory*; as Chap. 2.11. 2 Thess. 1.10. Tit. 2.13. let him manifest his might, and majesty, in doing some remarkable matter for you, if you be so dear to him, and are so deep in his books, as you deem and pretend yourselves to be; as deriding, and jeering them, for their vain (as they counted it) confidence in God, and hopeful expectation of his glorious appearance, to redress and right their wrongs. So chap. 5.19. Psal. 22.7,8. Mat. 27.43. 2 Pet. 3.3,4. and this suits fitly with what follows.

*{but he shall appear to your joy, and they shall be ashamed.*} Or, *but he shall appear to your joy, when they shall be ashamed*; as Chap. 65.13. See Psal. 50.1–5. 2 Thess. 1.7–10. Heb. *and he shall appear*: whence some take occasion to annex the former member of this branch, at least, if not both, to the words foregoing, making it part of those profane ones’ speech; some rendering them; *and let them be seen to your joy.* Others, *and let us see*, or *that we may see*, somewhat done that may minister matter of joy to you, and such as you are: but the copulative, in a discretive notion, is frequent, chap. 60.10. & 61.6. and these readings do too much disjoint the text: nor can I concur with those, who, though severing this branch from that speech of theirs, render it; *but we* (that is, I and you together) *shall see* (as Chap. 41.23.) *your joy*: for the syntax will not bear it; after the verbs of *sight*, the particle is not wont to be vacant.

**V. 6.** *{A voice of noise from the city; a voice from the temple; a voice of the Lord that rendereth recompense to his enemies.*} Some would thus hang this verse upon the foregoing passage; *they shall be confounded* by *a voice of noise*, &c. Others, disjoining this verse from that, yet so as to carry on the context, prefix some words, and render the text; *For there shall be heard a voice*, &c. But I concur rather with those, who conceive that the prophet abruptly, on purpose, breaks out into these words, as if, in a prophetical rapture, he heard the noise of that *voice*, or those *voices*, that here he speaks of. See the like, Chap. 13.4. Jer. 50.22,28. & 51.54. and it seems not fit or safe, to enervate, and diminish, the force and emphasis of prophetical strains, by any unnecessary additions. But what manner of voice this should be, or when uttered, and heard, is much questioned. Some would have it *a voice* of triumph, and joy, of shouting in the city, of thanksgiving in the temple, upon Judas Maccabeus his recovery of the city, and restitution of the temple, after the spoil and pollutions, by Antiochus, of either, 1 Maccab. 4.52–58. The Jewish most refer it to the Messiah his days, at what time such *a voice* should go forth, to set forward the expedition, against Gog, and Magog, Ezek. 38.21,22. The most of ours refer it to the surprisal of Jerusalem, and the destruction of the temple, either by the Chaldeans, as some, 2 King. 25.4,9. or, by the Romans, as others, Mat. 24.2,13. & 23.38. Luk. 19.43,44. & 21.20,22. This last is most likely.

*{a voice of noise*} Or, *of tumult.* So the Chaldee; that is, a tumultuous noise. So Chap. 13.4.

*{from the city*} To wit, Jerusalem; of people, upon the surprisal of it by the enemies’ forces, running to and fro in the streets, like persons distracted, and like blind men, falling foul one upon another. See Zeph. 1.10,17. Lam. 4.14,15.

*{a voice from the temple.*} Of people fled thither for succor and safeguard; or of the priests, and other officers, as much distracted and distressed, as the people; or, of both crying to heaven, but in vain then, for help. Hither some refer what Joseph the Jew relates, in his *Jewish war*, l. 7. c. 31. of the temple doors flying open suddenly of themselves: and a voice heard, at the feast of Pentecost, by the priests from the inner sanctuary, after a noise of some stirring, or shuffling within, saying; *Let us depart hence*; as also of one Jesus Bar-Annas; that at the feast of Tabernacles, went up and down the city, crying, *A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds; a voice against Jerusalem, and the temple, a voice against all this people*: all which prodigious occurrents, are reported to have been not long before the destruction of that city, and temple, by the Romans. Howbeit, they seem not to be the cry intimated, and pointed to, in this place. For the Jewish masters seem to swerve from the true sense of the text, who because *Heaven* is sometime called *God’s temple*, or *palace*, (for the word imports either) Psal. 11.4. would have the *temple* here to be *Heaven*; and the *voice*, God’s thundering voice, Psal. 29. by storm, and tempest from heaven: as Josh. 10.11. Judg. 5.20. discomfiting the forces of Gog, and Magog, Ezek. 38.21,22. See Rev. 20.8,9. But the material temple on earth, built in that city, seems rather, here specified; and that the rather mentioned, to control their vain confidence in it, as implying, how little relief, or safeguard, they should then receive from it. See ver. 1. Lam. 2.20.

*{a voice of the Lord*} Not his still and gracious voice, speaking now by his prophets, and calling upon them for repentance, with tenders of mercy upon their repentance, which they refused then to hear, ver. 4. but his roaring voice of vengeance now to be executed upon them, for their manifold excesses, and refusal to be reclaimed by the former, Ezek. 9.6,7. & 24.21. So Joel 2.11. Amos 1.2. the word *voice* repeated, has no small emphasis in it; which they seem to lessen, who by variety of terms express it.

*{that rendereth recompense to his enemies*} Heb. *repaying a retribution*, or *reward, to his enemies.* But who these enemies are, the question is. Some would have them to be strange nations, the enemies and oppressors of his people, Chap. 59.18,19. Jer. 50.15,28. Others rather, the obstinate wicked ones amongst his people, whom he justly styles his enemies, as here, so elsewhere, Chap. 1.24. of whom he uses the very same terms, Chap. 65.6,7. and to whose confusion he threatened to appear, ver. 5. See ver. 14.

**V. 7.** *{Before she travailed, she brought forth; before her pain came, she was delivered of a man-child*} The most interpreters, both Jew and Christian, understand these words, of the strange, sudden, and unexpected delivery of the remainders of God’s people, out of the Babylonian bondage, by Cyrus; whereof see Chap. 43.18–21. and this as it seems to be a collation of dissimilitude, compared with their deliverance out of Egypt, which was not without much tugging and struggling, effected, Exod. 3.19. & 5.9,19,21,23. & 6.9. whereas this was done without any labor, or travail at all on their parts, upon Cyrus his proclamation only sent out, 2 Chron. 36.22,23. Ezr. 1.1–3. Psal. 126.1. So it is not unfitly deemed, by a comparison of similitude, to have some glance at the speech of the Egyptian midwives, concerning the Hebrew women, that they were so vigorous, and quick, in their travail, that they were usually delivered ere the midwife came at them, Exod. 1.19. Sion is compared to a teeming woman; the people of Israel, to such an one’s children; which she is said to be delivered of, without pain, or throes, in such case ordinary: as Varro reports of the Illyrian women, who being at harvest work in the field, when they were near their time, would but step aside, and return again, bringing a child with them, as if they had found it, behind the hedge; Varro, *of husbandry*, l. 2. c. 10. Howbeit, divers interpreters understand it of the restitution and restoration of the church, under the ministry of the gospel, when so many thousands were so soon, and so suddenly converted, without any great labor, or painstaking about them, of those by whom they were converted, Act. 2.41. & 4.4. and both these expositions conceived, as subordinate the one to the other, may very well be admitted. But as for that groundless fancy of Popish writers, expounding these words, as spoken of the Virgin Marie’s delivery of Christ without pain; not unlike that their fiction of the *ox*, and the *ass*, in the stable with her; from Chap. 1.3. I let it pass, as scarce worthy the mentioning.

*{she was delivered of*} Heb. *she hath delivered.* So the word properly signifies, Chap. 31.8. but it is applied to delivery of children, by birth here; as to the delivery of a fowl’s young ones, by hatching, Chap. 34.15. and the reason of the phrase is; because they seem to be *delivered*, by birth, the one, by hatching, the other, out of those straits wherein they were formerly, being enclosed and pent up, the one in the womb, the other in the shell: and on the other side, with us, the woman is said to be *delivered*, because she is rid of the burden that she went with before.

*{a man-child*} As Gen. 4.1. Joh. 16.21. *a man.* Heb. *a male*; as Rev. 12.5. as noting both the more might of it: as Rev. 12.5. See Psal. 105.37. and the more joy for it, as Joh. 16.21. for the female is deemed the feebler sex, 1 Pet. 3.7. and less joy usually at its birth: but, that which is more; the term here, seems to be taken collectively, *a male*, for, *males*: as Gen. 2.7,9. for multitudes are here intended at one birth. See ver. 8. and to draw it to Christ, said to be formed in the hearts of believers, Gal. 4.19. seems somewhat harsh. Of the joy at the return of the people from captivity. See Psal. 126.1,2. Chap. 60.4,5. at the conversion of people unto Christ. See Act. 2.46. & 8.8. & 11.18,23.

**V. 8.** *{Who hath heard such a thing? who hath seen such things? Shall the earth be made to bring forth in one day? or shall a nation be born at once?*} Was it ever known, heard, or seen? (see Chap. 64.4.) or is it a thing possible, that a whole country of people should be born in one day; or, that a woman should be delivered of a whole nation at one birth?

*{such a thing*} Heb. *as*, or, *according to this*; and would therefore be rendered more fully, *such a thing as this*; and so afterward, *such things as those*, or, *as these*; as ver. 2.

*{shall the earth be made to bring forth in one day?*} According to this version, the meaning may seem to be, as if the question were, whether the whole earth, or all a whole country, that is, all the women in the world, or, all of some country, should be made to bring forth, together, in one day; or, as some, whether the earth be able, in one day, to bring forth the seeds of herbs, and plants, committed unto it, and laid up in it, as at the first, without any such sowing, it did, Gen. 1.11,12. or, whether it can bring forth (which is more than so) such living wights of all sorts, in one day; as in the sixth day of the creation it did, Gen. 1.24. because the old Latin has it; *shall the earth bring forth in one day?* But the words would rather be read, *Can a land, or, a country, be brought forth in one day?* So the Chaldee, *Is it possible, that a land should be made, or, produced, in one day?* and one of the Rabbines more fully; Is it possible that a woman should in one day be delivered of children enow, to fill a whole land, or a country? Verbs indicative used in a potential form, are common in Scripture. See on Chap. 49.15. & 64.12. and *earth*, for, *land*; no less rife. See Chap. 26.1,10. & 65.16. yet the word, of itself ambiguous, might here the rather be used, with some glance, at the production of both heaven and earth in one day, Gen. 1.1. as implying God’s power, that he, who at first produced the whole earth, and heaven together with it also, in one day, is no less able to make his Sion bring forth children enow in one day, not to people some one land only, but to fill the whole world. See Chap. 27.6. The verb here used, signifies in its first form, *to be grieved*, or, *to be in pain*, generally, Jer. 5.3. more particularly, *to be in travail*, as women are wont to be near unto their time of delivery, Chap. 23.4. & 26.18. in its other forms, it has a notion of *framing, forming, producing*, or, of *being framed, formed, produced*, in general, without special relation to any *pain*, or, *travail*, Psal. 51.5. & 90.2. Prov. 8.24. & 25.23. and it is observed by one of the Jewish critics upon this place, that the active form of the term, here used, is taken sometime in a transient notion, for *to make to travail*, or *bring forth*, or *be in pain*: as Psal. 29.8. but that very seldom: sometime, yea, most commonly, in a standing sense, for *to be in travail*, Chap. 26.17. and here, ver. 7. and by consequence, because *birth* usually follows *travail*, (returning to a transient notion; but in another kind,) *to bring forth.* See Chap. 45.10. and the passive form here accordingly, *to be produced*, or *brought forth*.

*{or shall a nation be born at once?*} Or, *can a nation be born at once*, as before; the disjunctive, inserted, is needless: there is a particle indeed in the text, that commonly signifies, *if*; but is here no other, than a mere interrogative note, as Job 6.5. and here again, ver. 9. The meaning is; Is it possible, that a woman should have as many children at one birth, as were enow to constitute a nation? as if he should say, in the course of nature it is not: for as for those stories related by John Aventine, in his *Bavarian history*, the one; and by Thomas Fazel, in his *Sicilian history*, the other; of two German countesses of Henneburg, Margeret, and Maud, the one whereof should have 364. the other, 1414. children at a birth, they are deservedly deemed fabulous; and may justly challenge the whetstone. But that of the multitudes of those that returned to Jerusalem, after Cyrus his edict of liberty published, to wit, 42360. at once; besides 7337. servants, and maidens, see Ezr. 2.64,65. which might well be deemed a nation brought forth in one day: as also that, whereunto some apply this of those multitudes of converts in the primitive church, 3000 at one time, and 2000, if not 5000. at another, Act. 2.41. & 4.4. may well have place here.

*{for as soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her children.*} Or, as others, *that Sion is in travail, and withal bringeth forth her children.* And because there may seem some contradiction in this, to what was before said of delivery without travail: Some answer, that the meaning was in the former place, before she was scarce in any travail; in this place it is, that some travail she should have, but that so light, and short, that it might well be deemed, in a manner, as none, Chap. 26.20. The Hebrew is, word for word, *that Zion*, or, *yet Zion* (as the particle is taken, and rendered, Job 5.7. Esay 9.1. & 31.4. & 49.25. which those mistake, that render it, *as soon as Sion*) *hath travailed, yea, brought forth her children*; to wit, *at once*, or, *in one day*: for that is the thing intended, and intimated, and is from the former part of the verse, to be supplied, in the application of it unto Sion; for therein the miracle (as one of the Rabbines has well observed) consists, that she should be delivered of so many sons so suddenly, as in one day: and the word of *travail* seems rather in this place, to design the time of travail, than the pains, or pangs of it; she both came near to childbirth, and was delivered of her children, at once, in one day: her burden, or children, stuck not at the breach, or the birth, to put her to any pain. See Chap. 37.3. Hos. 13.13. vers. 9.

**V. 9.** *{Shall I bring to the birth, and not cause to bring forth, saith the Lord*} Or, *Should I bring to the womb’s mouth, and not cause to bring forth?* Some of the Rabbines would have it, *should I bring upon the stool?* to wit, that mentioned, Exod. 1.16. that is, say they, should I cast my beloved wife, Sion, into childbearing pangs, and throes, by bringing in Gog and Magog upon her, Ezek. 38.9,16,17. and not withal afford her deliverance? resembled here by birth. But of the word, which the verb here used, has relation unto, see on Chap. 37.3. and another of them rather reading it, as it was before rendered, expounds it well; Shall I set upon a work, and not go through with it; cause the children to come to the very opening of the womb, and not enable them to come forth, or not afford strength to bring them forth? Some of ours, *Should I open other women’s wombs*; or, *should I that open the matrice* to others: (and make them fruitful, Gen. 29.31. & 30.22.) *not* myself *beget*, or *breed*; (as Gen. 11.27. but remain issueless) or *not cause my Sion to bring forth?* But the former sense being obvious, and such as the words of themselves freely afford, I see not why we may not rest therein.

*{shall I cause to bring forth, and shut the womb; saith the Lord*} Heb. *Am I he that cause to bring forth? and shall I shut*, or, *restrain?* that is, as the Jewish commenters, Am I he that have conferred upon mankind the power of propagation, Gen. 1.28. and that have caused people in all parts of the world to propagate? and should I now deny this blessing to my Sion? But the Hebrew may as well be rendered; *Am I he that begat?* (so the word is expressly rendered, Jer. 16.3. *their mothers that bare them, and their fathers that begat them*) *and should I restrain*, from bringing forth? for that is the first, and native notion of the word. So Gen. 16.2. *God hath restrained me from bearing.* Should I that have begotten children upon Sion, restrain her from being delivered of them? it is true, that the same word is used in that phrase, of *shutting up the womb*, Gen. 20.18. but that is meant of restraint from conception, not from birth; for whereas divers render it, *shall I be restrained?* they depart from the constant use of the word, which is never other than active; there is only in the text, a defect of the pronoun demonstrative, *her*, (as Deut. 25.12.) relating to *Sion*, mentioned, vers. 8.

**V. 10.** *{Rejoice ye with Jerusalem, and be glad with her, all ye that love her*} An exhortation directed to all Sion’s well-willers, inciting them to rejoice with her, as friends and allies are wont to do, at the childbirth of one, that has been long barren and childless, Luk. 1.14,58. or upon the restitution, or recovery of one, that had formerly been decayed, and ruined, in his estate, Job 42.11.

*{be glad with her*} Heb. *of her*, or *in her*; or, *for her*: as Psal. 9.14. & 31.7. for of, or, in God’s goodness showed unto her; yet is the particle sometime rendered *with*: as Psal. 2.11. but then denoting the manner how; not the company with whom. See Chap. 65.19. and hereafter, ver. 13.

*{rejoice for joy with her, all ye that mourn for her*} The same thing in other terms. Heb. *rejoice with joy*; that is, *be exceeding joyful*: as Chap. 61.10. Mat. 2.10. 1 Pet. 1.8. *all ye that mourn for her*, or, *that mourned for her*; formerly, in the time of her afflicted and dejected condition. See Chap. 61.3. Zeph. 3.18. the Hebrew term is in a reciprocal form; but of that, see Chap. 65.16.

**V. 11.** *{That ye may suck, and be satisfied with the breasts of her consolations:}* Or, as the Chaldee renders it, *for that*, or, *because*, (for the particle has oft a causal notion, 2 Chron. 21.7.) *ye suck*, or, *ye shall suck, and be satiated*; that is, *suck your fill*, (as, *they shall eat and be satisfied*; that is, *eat their fill*, Psal. 22.26.) *with the breasts*; or, *of the moisture* that comes from the breast. See Chap. 60.16. that you may partake with her of those blessings, both temporal and spiritual, that God shall very largely endow her with, and bestow upon her; and as her foster children being nursed by her, 1 Thess. 1.2,7. 1 Tim. 4.6. may receive abundance of refreshments and comforts from her, Psal. 36.8. Ezek. 14.22,23. 2 Cor. 1.4–6.

*{that ye may milk out, and be delighted with the abundance of her glory*} Or, *because ye shall milk out*, &c. much the same, in other terms, with the former.

*{milk out*} Or, *wring out*; as Chap. 16.4. Prov. 30.33. for the proper notion is the same, though the forms divers: as the Jewish critic here well observes; the word itself is nowhere else found.

*{and be delighted*} Or, *delight yourselves; take your pleasure*, as Psal. 37.11.

*{with the abundance of her glory*} As Psal. 37.11. *in abundance of peace*, or *prosperity*: but the terms here and there are divers; the word here used, is not in the like notion anywhere else found: the Jewish critics will have it signify *splendor*, or *brightness*; the rather in regard of a Chaldee word of that notion, coming very near to it: and this fits well with what we had, Chap. 60.1–3.

**V. 12.** *{For thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the Gentiles like a flowing stream*} I am resolved to bless her with abundance of prosperity; and to make her glorious by the access of the Gentiles to her, with whatsoever from them may help to grace and adorn her. See Chap. 60.5–14.

*{Behold, I will extend to her*} *Lo I am extending to her*, or *bringing in upon her.* Of the form, see on Chap. 65.17.

*{peace like a river*} Or, *prosperity*, (as Psal. 72.3,7.) *as a flood*, Chap. 48.18. See Chap. 59.19. as Euphrates, says the Chaldee. So Psal. 72.8. Zach. 9.10.

*{like a flowing stream*} Or, *an overflowing stream*, or *river*: as Chap. 30.28. as Nilus, the river of Egypt, Chap. 27.12. See Jer. 47.2.

*{then shall ye suck*} Heb. *and ye shall suck*; and there is the middle distinction in the text; as you shall suck kings, and queens, Chap. 60.16. so you shall suck her, ver. 11. or, *ye shall suck it*; that is, part of that prosperity and glory, that shall flow in upon her, and from her, be conveyed and imparted unto you, ver. 11.

*{ye shall be borne upon her sides,}* Heb. *side*: in her arms on the one side, as children use to be carried. See Chap. 49.22. and 60.4. Psal. 90.12. yet some, because the Latin renders it, *Ye shall be carried at her breasts*, or *teats*; would make it to have relation to infants that hang upon the teat: but that seems somewhat more forced.

*{and be dandled upon her knees.*} The word here used signifies *to take much delight* in aught: the psalmist oft uses it, to express his *delight* in God’s law, Psal. 119.16,24,46,70,77,92,142,144. and of the comforts and refreshments, which from thence his soul received, Psal. 94.19. it is used of children, *playing* and sporting themselves, Chap. 11.8. and some therefore here render it; *ye shall play upon her knees*; as alluding to children that sit playing in their mother’s lap. Howbeit, it seems not amiss rendered, *dandled*: for in such dandlings, children much delight: and it is implied, that they should be as *darlings, children of delights*, Jer. 19.20. (where this word also is used) and, *children of dandlings*, as they seem termed. Lam. 2.20. it has reference unto the manner of parents, that are wont to have their young ones, their darling ones, especially, whom they take most delight in, frequently in their laps, and on their knees, Gen. 30.3. & 50.23. Ruth 4.16. According to the received reading, there should be here a defect of the pronoun possessive *her*; as Chap. 27.22. Howbeit, the words may be read well enough without it; *Ye shall be borne in arms, and dandled on knees*; that is, you shall be carefully, and curiously, or tenderly, and delicately, nursed up, as darling children, of great ones especially, are wont to be, that are almost perpetually, either in the arms, or on the knees. See Num. 11.12.

**V. 13.** *{As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you:}* He says not, as a man comforts his wife, or his spouse (though the church be so to him, Hos. 2.19,20.) as it is said, that *David comforted Bathshebah*, after the decease of her little one, 2 Sam. 12.24. But because the tender affection of mothers to children, is by common experience well known, (See Chap. 49.15.) to express therefore his compassionate disposition, and tenderness of affection to his people; As a mother, says he, comforts her child. As a mother, when her child weeps and cries, having taken some hurt by a fall; or the like accident, does by all tender and gentle usage, bemoaning it, hugging it, and affectionate speech to it, seek to quiet and still it again; or, as when upon some wanton, or waspish carriage of the child, she has showed herself displeased with it, and it may be has withal chastised it, or carried herself strangely toward it, and perceives that the child takes it to heart, and is troubled not a little therewith, she cannot rest, nor be at quiet, until she have reconciled herself again to her child; (See David’s affection toward Absolom, 2 Sam. 13.39.) and by all fair and sweet insinuations, and expressions of renewed love and affection, endeavors therefore to cheer it again: In like manner will I cheer up, and comfort the dejected spirits of my people again, whom I had for a while put to some heaviness, by chastising them for their sins, Chap. 12.1. & 14.1. & 51.3. & 54.7,8. & 57.15,17,18. & 61.2,3. See Psal. 94.19. Act. 9.31. 2 Cor. 1.3–5.

*{as one*} Heb. *as a man*; though a child be intended; as Gen. 4.1. Joh. 16.21. or, *a man*, for, *any one*; as Chap. 40.26.

*{and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem.*} Beholding God’s goodness towards her, rejoicing in it, and enjoying of it together with her, ver. 10,14.

**Ver. 14.** *{And when ye see this, your heart shall rejoice,}* Heb. *ye shall see this* (supplied, as Chap. 59.15.) *and your heart shall rejoice*; you shall rejoice heartily: so Psal. 105.3. or, *For when ye see this, your heart shall rejoice*; as rendering a reason of, or, further confirming, what was delivered in the close of the verse foregoing. The like syntax, see Chap. 53.2. & 59.16. & 65.12.

*{and your bones shall flourish like an herb:}* Or, *as the tender herb*; as it is rendered, Deut. 32.2. or, *the tender grass*; as Prov. 27.25. or, *the green grass*, as Psal. 23.2. your strength and vigor shall revive, and recover verdure again, as grass and plants do in the spring, that in wintertime were withered, and seemed as dead, Chap. 26.19. & 44.4. & 61.11. when the vigor and strength of man’s body is decayed and consumed, *his bones* are said to be wasted and withered, or broken and shattered, or disjointed and dislocated, or dispersed and scattered, Job 33.19. Psal. 6.2. & 22.14. & 31.10. & 32.3,4. & 53.5. & 102.3. & 141.7. Prov. 12.4. & 14.30. & 17.22. Chap. 38.13. Jer. 50.17. Lam. 3.4. Hab. 3.16. and on the other side, when vigor and strength is recovered again, the bones are said to revive, and to be refreshed, and to be filled with moisture and marrow again, Job 21.24. Psal. 51.8. Prov. 3.8. & 15.30. & 16.24. Chap. 58.11. In like manner did God’s people deem of themselves in the time of the captivity, that they were no other than, as a company of dead and dry bones, that lay dispersed and scattered, here and there, without regard; Ezek. 37.11. but God tells them, that those their dead and dry bones, should revive, and grow moist, and recover life and vigor again; as those in the vision, Ezek. 37.1–10.

*{and the hand of the Lord shall be known towards his servants*} God’s goodness; his good hand, his power manifested for the good, of his loyal, and faithful people (Chap. 65.13,14.) shall evidently appear, Ezr. 6.7,9. & 8.18. Chap. 62.2.

*{and his indignation towards his enemies.*} Heb. *and* (or, *but*; as Chap. 65.11.) *he will have indignation against*, or, *be wroth with his enemies*; or, as some would have it rendered, *he will detest*, or *defy his enemies*; as it is rendered, Num. 23.7,8. But I conceive it may very well be rendered, as it is, Zach. 1.12. *he will have indignation towards his enemies.* Our translators seem to have taken the verb for a noun. The deliverance of God’s servants, and the destruction of his, and their enemies, go frequently together. See Chap. 1.27,28. & 14.1. & 61.2. & 63.4. God will, in the restoring of his people, make a difference to be seen between the one, and the other; as Deut. 4.3,4. so Mal. 3.17,18. & 4.1,2.

**V. 15.** *{For behold the Lord will come with fire.*} God will come to execute judgment, and take vengeance on the wicked, in most terrible manner; for nothing is more fearful, or formidable, either to man, or beast, than fire: nor were fireworks also anciently unusual, in warlike expeditions; and devastations thereby most frequently effected, Josh. 6.24. & 8.19. Judg. 9.49. & 20.40. Jer. 38.28. & 52.13. that which is alluded unto in this, and the like expressions, Psal. 50.3. & 97.3. Dan. 7.9,10. Amos 7.4. though some of the Jewish doctors expound it; *with hellfire.*

*{and with his chariots like a whirlwind;}* Or, *and his chariots* shall be, or shall come, (supplied from the former clause) *like a whirlwind*; as Chap. 5.28. Jer. 4.13. of *God’s chariots*: See Psal. 68.17.

*{to render his anger with fury*} Or, *to put in execution his anger with fervor*, Ezek. 18.18. Mic. 5.15.

*{and his rebuke with flames of fire.*} Or, *fiery flames*, or *flaming fire*; as Psal. 29.7. & 105.32. Chap. 29.6. & 30.30. Of his *rebuke*, see Chap. 50.2. & 51.20. & 54.9. This vengeance of God was in part executed on the wicked of his own people, at the destruction of Jerusalem, Jer. 1.15,16. & 39.2,8. and, in part, on the oppressors of them, at the ruin of Babylon, Jer. 50.18,31,32. but shall fully be accomplished at the last day, in the general judgment that shall then be, 2 Thess. 1.8. 2 Pet. 3.7,10,12.

**Ver. 16.** *{For with fire, and with his sword, will the Lord plead with all flesh:}* God will no longer debate in words with men, as formerly he did, by his ministers and messengers, the prophets, Mic. 6.1,2. but he will now plead with fire and sword, the ordinary instruments of hostility, such as men in armies are wont to plead, and decide matters with. So Ezek. 38.22.

*{with fire*} As before, ver. 15.

*{with his sword*} No ordinary one. See Chap. 27.1. *sword*, for all manner of warlike weapons; as Gen. 27.40.

*{plead*} Heb. *be judged*, or *tried*; as Psal. 37.33. & 109.7. or, *plead*, and *debate*, the matter; as Chap. 43.26. Ezek. 20.36. or, *execute judgment*; as 2 Chron. 22.8. or, *proceed in judgment*; as Jer. 2.35.

*{with all flesh*} Either with the main body of the wicked Jewish people; as Mat. 24.22. and these of all sorts and ranks among them; as Chap. 1.5,6. if that particular judgment be in these words intended; or, with the generality of wicked ones, throughout the whole world, if the last ecumenical judgment be designed, Act. 17.31. Rom. 3.19,20. See Chap. 34.1,2. Jer. 45.5.

*{and the slain of the Lord shall be many.*} The Lord’s purpose is to make a great slaughter. See Jer. 25.33. *the slain of the Lord*, for, those that are slain by him; as, *the slain of the sword*, for, such as are slain by it, Chap. 22.2. Lam. 4.9.

**V. 17.** *{They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens.*} He proceeds more particularly, to design who the persons be, against whom he is resolved thus to proceed: by the description of whom, it evidently appears, that the judgment here denounced, does in a more special manner concern the wicked ones of the Jewish nation, before deciphered, Chap. 65.4,5.

*{that sanctify and purify themselves*} That use superstitious rites of expiation, supposing themselves thereby to be made holy and pure. Thus rather than as some, that first *pollute*, and then *purify themselves* with water, like Pilate, that by washing his hands, thought he might discharge himself of the guilt of Christ’s blood, Mat. 27.24. See chap. 65.5. *that sanctify and purify themselves*; that think they do so, when they do nothing less; as, *that blesseth himself*, Deut. 29.19.

*{in the gardens*} Set apart for idolatrous services, chap. 1.29. & 65.3. in the pools, or lavers, that there they had for such uses; or, *for the gardens*, to prepare and fit themselves for the exercise of their idolatry in them: so is the particle used, 1 Sam. 1.27. Ezek. 6.9,11. as among God’s people, the manner was, after any legal uncleanness contracted, to purify themselves, by aspersion of pure water upon them, or by dipping themselves therein, before they repaired unto God’s sanctuary for the performance of any holy duty, Numb. 19.7,8,13,19,20. alluded to Psalm 26.6. so in imitation thereof, both heathen people, and these idolatrous Jews did, by such like washings, deem themselves cleansed from the soil of their sins, and made fit for their idol-service; but it is more likely, that in those gardens, than out of them, they did so purify themselves for the services to be acted in some other part of them, or in some temple thereunto adjoining; as the heathen had their *delubra*, or holy *lavers*, near to their temples.

*{behind one tree in the midst*} This passage has no small variety of notions by interpreters fastened upon it. The Greek renders it, *in the porches*, or *entries, before door*, or *without door*: The old Latin clean contrary; *behind door within*, as chap. 57.8. that is, say some expositors, in secret, where they might not be seen, or taken suddenly, in the manner, Jer. 2.26,27. but as the former has no footing at all in the text; so this later very little. The Chaldee, which some of the Rabbines follow, renders it, not simply *one after another* as some cite him, and some of ours render the text; but, *company after company*; one company of them after another, until the whole society of them be sanctified. Others of them, which our version admits *behind* some *one tree*, or other, in the grove, or in the garden, Jer. 3.6. Whereunto some of ours add, as a thing not unlikely; that as every one of them had a god of his own, so each of them had his peculiar tree, whereat he did service to that his idol. Others, *behind* some *one fountain*, or pool; for they observe here a double reading; the one of a masculine, the other of a feminine form; and they supply terms accordingly correspondent to either. Some of ours would have it rendered, for some *one strange* god; that purify themselves in the gardens, for the service of some strange god: But the word that they render *strange*, is not found so to signify in the form here used. Others therefore, give it otherwise in terms, but in effect to the same notion, *after* some *one* false god, or other, which they follow and serve. Others, lastly, which to me seems most probable, conceive the word *achad*, or *echad*, or as it is not unusually pronounced, *ahad*, and *ehad*, rendered commonly, here *one*, to be, in this place, a proper name; yet not a name of God, as some superstitiously would have it to be, Job 31.15. Zach. 14.9. but of an idol *Ahad*, or *Ehad*, whom also by a gemination of the final consonant, they termed *Adad*: for so Macrobius in his *Saturnales*, lib. 1. c. 23. reports, that the Assyrians called the chief God that they worshipped, *Adad*, by a word, says he, that signifies *one*; whence also he gathers, that by this name, they understood *the Sun*, who is but *one*, and ever *one*, otherwise than *the Moon*. And this some learned suppose to be the same with *Hadad*; which seems to have been a name very common among the kings of *Edom*, or *Idumea*, Gen. 36.35,36. 1 Chron. 1.46,47,50,51. 1 King. 11.14,17,25. but grew afterward much more common with the kings of *Aram*, or *Syria*, 2 Sam. 8.3,5,8. & 10.16,19. 1 King. 11.24. & 15.18,20. & 20.1,33. 2 King. 6.24. & 8.7,15. & 13.3,24. See Jer. 49.27. & Joseph’s *Antiquities*, l. 7. c. 6. Howbeit, because these two names differ in the initial letter, I conceive them not to be the same. But to return to those that understand the word here of that Assyrian, rather than Syrian idol, though it might be common to them both; Some of them render the words, *after Ahad*, whom *they go after*, that is, follow and adore; as Jude 2.11,12. Others, *behind Ahad*, that is, behind the temple of Ahad, amidst the walks and gardens adjacent.

*{in the midst?*} That is, say some, *openly, publicly*, in open view, shamelessly acting such things in their impious rites, as were most unseemly. But I find not where this form is so used in Scripture. Others therefore expound it of those fountains, or lavers, in those gardens, wherein they purified themselves, which were usually situate in the midst of them: though we need not to drive it so near home, as to say, with some Jewish critics, that their groves were at the either end of the gardens, and these fountains, or lavers in the midst, having the one grove before them, and the other behind them, as the men of *Ay*, had the Israelites, Josh. 8.22.

*{eating swine’s flesh,}* Or, *eaters of swine’s flesh.* See Chap. 65.4.

*{and the abomination*} Heb. *the shekets*, which some suppose to be the name of some particular kind of unclean creature; and one of the Jewish doctors seems to intimate as much, when he says, *There are some nations that eat the sheket, and the mouse*: and the placing of it here between two other distinct kinds, may well be deemed to imply no less. And if place may be afforded for conjecture, the joining of *choled*, or *holed*, commonly rendered *a weasel*, with that which is deemed *a mouse*, Lev. 11.29. may afford some suspicion, that *shekets* here may be the same with that *choled*, or *holed* there. Howbeit, the word is used more generally, for *abomination*, or *any abominable thing*, Lev. 11.10,11,12,20. Ezek. 8.10. as also is another word derived from it, Dan. 9.26. & 11.31. compared with Mat. 24.13. the plural whereof we had before, vers. 3. as also Jer. 4.1. & Ezek. 20.7,8.

*{and the mouse*} Some having rendered the former *abominable creatures*, (See Zach. 9.7.) render this, *as the mouse*; and the copulative is sometime put for the note of similitude; as Job 21.33. & 34.3. but seldom, I suppose, in that manner, as here. The *mouse*, is, among other unclean creatures reckoned up, and expressly inhibited for man’s meat, Lev. 11.29. Yet that *mice*, some kind of them especially, were commonly eaten, in many places, among other people, and that reputed also as a dainty dish, does, by authors of good note and credit, appear; for Varro in his *Treatise of Husbandry*, l. 3. c. 15. relates, how for *dormice*, one kind of them, they made warrens for the breed of them, and coops for the fatting of them; and Pliny, l. 8. c. 47. reports, that in the laws sometime made to restrain excess in diet, the use of *dormice*, together with some *shellfish*, and *foreign fowl*, was inhibited. The name some would have given them, from a word, that signifies *to disturb*, or *trouble*: whence *Achor*, chap. 65.10. because they are wont to disturb and trouble the house, by gnawing; the fields, by digging; both by devouring and destroying things of use, 1 Sam. 6.5. And we read indeed of an island called *Gyarus*, in the midland sea, to have been so infested with *mice*, that the inhabitants were enforced to quit it, Pliny, l. 8. c. 29,57. And Eustathius on Homer, from ancient writers, reports, that in some places, by the name of Smintheus, they worshipped Apollo, for ridding their grounds of this kind of vermin, if mice may, at least, be properly so called. But the notation of the word, in regard of the letters of it, seems not very probable: and I have some doubt, which I shall only propound, and leave to the learned, whether the word here used, signify *a mouse*, or no: and the ground of my doubt is; because the creature here mentioned, is ranked among *creeping things*, Lev. 11.29. and I see little reason, why the *mouse*, or the *weasel*, or the *ferret*, should go under that name, more than the *hare* or the *coney*, (which some also render, *a mountain mouse*,) Lev. 11.5,6,26. or why they should not be comprehended under the general head of *Beasts*, before mentioned, Lev. 11.2. and come within the general rules concerning beasts there delivered, ver. 4,5. the rather, for that I find *creeping things* still distinguished from beasts, Gen. 1.24. & 7.14,21,23. I incline therefore to think, that the creature here, and elsewhere, mentioned, is some *creeping thing*, not unlike the *scorpion*, as they differ not much in name; the one termed *Acbar*, the other, *Akrab*, Deut. 8.15. and that divers sorts of creeping things, as *lizards*, and *locusts*, (for they are reckoned also among the *creepers*, and are not forbidden food, Lev. 11.21,22.) and the like, were with many people in times past, not unusually eaten, (as *frogs*, and *snails*, and *tortoises*, also are, in many places at this day) is not only, by divers other authors, but of some of them, to wit, the *Locust*, by Scripture itself testified, Mat. 3.4. Mark 1.6. yea of others, beside the divers sorts of *locusts*, under the names of the *soleam*, and the *chargol*, or, *hargol*, and the *chagab*, or *hagab*, with their several kinds, Lev. 11.21. which it had been in vain to allow for meat, had they not been fit for food, or not usually eaten. But hereof let others further consider, and deem, as themselves shall please. The word is nowhere found in Scripture save here, in that place of Moses, and the story of the Philistines, with such kind of creatures annoyed, 1 Sam. 6.4,5,11,18.

*{shall be consumed together, saith the Lord*} See chap. 1.28.

**V. 18.** *{For I know their works, and their thoughts*} Heb. *And I their works, and their thoughts.* Which sundry interpreters supposing to contain an entire sentence, but with suppression of some word, or words, (as in passionate speeches it oft falls out) conceived, do some supply, as our version, and some Greek copies, *I know*, as Hos. 5.3. Amos 5.12. and the Chaldee, *they are revealed*; or *lie open, before me*: which some of the Jewish commenters expound of the *thoughts* of Gog and Magog, the enemies of God’s people, Ezek. 38.10. that God knew their thoughts, though they little dreamed of his, as Mic. 4.11,12. To which purpose also others of them, with whom, some of ours also concur, render it, *I am with them.* It is I that bring them together, and cause them to come up, and camp against Jerusalem, Ezek. 38.4,8. Zach. 14.2. Others supply, *I will visit*, or take vengeance upon them, for their courses, and their counsels; as chap. 65.6,7. which would well suit with the clause foregoing. Others again, reading the words by way of interrogation, with a kind of indignation, *And their works and their thoughts*, should I endure? not unlike that, Jer. 5.9. & 9.9. But I rather here accord with those, that knit these words together in one sentence, with those that come after, reading the text thus; *As for me, when their works and their thoughts are come*, (that is, when the time of taking vengeance for them, shall come:) *I will gather all nations*, &c. or, as others, *As for me, since their works and their thoughts are such*; or, *because of these their works, and these their thoughts, it shall come to pass that I will gather all nations.* Since that this people do take such courses, and go on obstinately in the same, vers. 3,4. I will execute judgment upon them, and casting off those, that thus persist in their impieties, take in the Gentiles to me, in their stead, Rom. 11.11,12,15,17.

*{For I*} Heb. *And I*; or, *As for me*: the word is put absolutely, as 1 Chron. 28.2. See chap. 65.11.

*{their works*} Or, *for their works*; as, *for the fear*, Mal. 2.5.

*{thoughts*} As chap. 65.2.

*{it shall come*} Or, *it shall come to pass*; or, the time *shall come*.

*{that I will gather*} Heb. *and I will gather together*; so the copulative is used, chap. 65.24.

*{all nations, and tongues*} People out of divers nations and languages, Acts 2.8–11. Rev. 7.9.

*{and they shall come, and see my glory*} Or, *that they may come and see my glory*; the particle used, as before. That being brought into the church, they may have revealed, and imparted unto them, that gracious and glorious presence of God, in his sacred ordinances, which the Jewish people alone did formerly enjoy, Psalm 97.6. Chap. 40.5. 2 Cor. 3.18. & 4.6. Ephes. 3.6. The Jewish doctors expound it, of the nations of the world, being brought to see God’s glorious might, declared in the Messiah his days, in the destruction of Gog and Magog, Ezek. 38.23. & 39.6,7.

**V. 19.** *{And I will set a sign among them,}* What this sign should be, and where it should be set, is much questioned. The Jewish commenters would have it to be, the rotting of the flesh, and eyes, and tongues of those, that served under Gog and Magog, against Jerusalem, Zach. 14.12. Ours, (to pass by the superstitious conceits of some Popish writers, concerning the sign of the cross; to which they apply that also, Matth. 24.30. and some other far-fetched, and ever-strained expositions) do most of them pitch upon one of these two notions: the one, of *a sign*, or *ensign*, erected to to call and gather people together; as chap. 11.12. & 49.22. & 62.10. that which some expound of Christ himself, said to be *set, for a sign*, chap. 11.10. Luke 2.34. Others, of the ministry of the word, and other external signs of Christian profession, together, with the miraculous works accompanying the same, erected first among the Jews, for the conversion of the elect among them, and the bringing in of the Gentiles unto them; and afterward also among the Gentiles. Some expound this branch of the erecting of it among the Jews, chap. 2.2,3. Mark 16.15–20. Luke 24.47,49. Act. 2. & 5.12–16. Some, of the setting it up among the Gentiles, Gal. 2.1. whereof, see on the next branch: and though the word used for a sign in those other places of this prophet, be divers from that here used, nor does the word here used, ordinarily so signify; yet it is so taken, Psalm 74.4. in those words, *they set up their ensigns for signs*, or, *as signs*; to wit, of conquest, and triumph. The other notion is of *a sign*, or *mark*, whereby one may be descried and discerned from some other: as it is said, *God set a sign*, or *a mark, upon Cain*: and so some render the words here; *I will set a sign*, or, *a mark*, not *among them*, but *upon them*; as the same particle is used in those words, Neh. 9.10. *thou didst set*, or *show signs and wonders upon Pharao, and upon his servants, and upon the people of the land*; and they understand it of a privy *note*, or *mark*, that God would set upon his elect, whom he would have reserved, whereby to mark them out for salvation, as temporal here, in the times of execution to be done upon the wicked crew, among whom they were mixed; so eternal hereafter: alluding to that sign, of distinction between the Hebrews & the Egyptians in Egypt, for the saving of the one, amidst the destruction of the other, Exod. 12.7,13,22,23. See the like, Ezek. 9.4,6. Rev. 7.3. & 9.4. and of sealing and marking for life eternal, 2 Cor. 1.21,22. Eph. 1.13,14. & 4.30. 2 Tim. 2.19. & this exposition, the word of *escape* following, seems to confirm. Now the text thus read & rendered, the word *them*, must be restrained unto God’s faithful *servants* before mentioned, vers. 14. which because it is somewhat remote, I suppose we may well retain the received version, *among them*; as the particle is rendered, Psal. 18.49. ch. 57.6. & 65.4. and hereafter, vers. 19. So it may well include the mixed body of the people, among whom those faithful ones abode, upon whom alone this saving mark was to be set. And I conceive that the copulative has the notion of a causal in this place; as chap. 53.2. & 65.15. and the text might better be rendered; *For I will set a sign among them, and send those that escape of them, unto the nations*, as showing by what means that should be effected, which was before mentioned, concerning the coming in of Gentiles, vers. 18.

*{and I will send those that escape of them, unto the nations*} Heb. *I will send of them*, or, *from them escaped ones*, (that is, *some of them, that do escape*) *unto the nations.* This the Rabbines understand of those Gog’s and Magog’s forces, who though not slain, yet with their flesh wasted, and tongue and eyes eaten out, should, as spectacles of God’s wrath and vengeance, being dispersed into remote places, publish without speaking, God’s powerful proceedings, and miraculous dealing with those foreign forces that had invaded his people’s land, Ezek. 39.11. Zach. 14.12,16. But our writers expound it generally of the reserves of the Jewish nation, chap. 37.31. Jer. 44.14,28. Mat. 24.22,24. Rom. 11.5,7. the apostles, and other faithful, by whom the word and glad tidings of salvation by Christ, was carried abroad and divulged among the Gentiles in all parts of the then known world, Mat. 28.18. Mark 16.15. Luke 24.47. Acts 8.1,4. & 10.45. & 11.18,23. & 13.46–49. & 15.7,14. Rom. 10.15,18. & 15.19,20. Eph. 2.17. Col. 1.23.

*{to Tarshish*} That is, as some, *to the sea.* So the Chaldee and the old Latin. Which some expound of people coasting upon the Arabian & Persian gulfs. Others, *to the Ocean*: as if it were said, that they shall go carrying about the gospel both by sea and land, unto the parts hereafter named. See chap. 60.9. yet others among whom the Greek interpreters take it, for the name of a particular place, whether *Tarsus*, in Cilicia, as some; or *Tartessus* in Spain, as others, see on chap. 2.16. & 23.1.

*{Pul*} This some suppose to be the same with *Put*, or Phut, mentioned, Jer. 46.9. & Ezek. 30.5. and both indeed are deemed to be regions situate in Africa; but to be distinct and divers places. An interpreter of prime note would have this *Pul*, or *Phul*, to be *Cyrene*, lying between Egypt & Tunis, taking the ground of this his conjecture from the name of a king, that sometime there reigned, called, as he supposes, *Aphulla*; but by Justine, l. 22. corruptly, *Ophellas.* But herein a late learned writer controls him; showing, that king’s time to be many hundreds of years too young to give this name to that place, whatever it was, that is here so called: as also from Diadore, l. 20. and others, that that king’s right name was not *Aphulla*, but *Ophellas*, or *Opheltes*; the man himself a Grecian, and the name a Greek term. He would have it to be *Phile*, an island, with a city therein of the same name with the island situate amidst the stream of the river Nilus, about some hundred furlongs above *Sciene* and *Elephantine* in the confines of Ethiopia and Egypt, whereof Strabo, Heliodore, Pliny, and many other, as being a place of some note: and he supposes it to have its name from the same ground, with *Elephantine*; (*Phile* and *Elephantine*, being two cities, for size and fashion, bigness and beauty, so near matches, nor in situation far distant, that some authors have confounded them, and taken the one for the other) and to have been so called of the word *Phil*; which with Syrians, Chaldeans, Arabians, and Ethiopians, is used for an *Elephant*; that Esay instead of *Phil*, gives it *Phul*: the like change being found in many other proper names in Scripture, as in *Pau*, Gen. 36.39. & *Pai*, 1 Chron. 1.50. *Tou*, and *Toi*, 1 Chron. 18.9. & 2 Sam. 8.9. *Perudah*, and *Peridah*, Ezra 2.54. and Neh. 7.57. But it may be doubted, whether the word *Phil*, for an *Elephant*, be in those languages so ancient, as to give the name either to this *Pul*, or to that *Phile*; and whether it came not from the Greeks into those languages; as to the Greeks in likelihood by the Punic, from the Hebrew *Eleph, an ox*; by them applied to the *Behemoth*, that *eateth grass, like an ox*, Job 40.15. nor had the Latins at first any other name for them, than *oxen*, as by some old bywords, in common use among them, appears; until they had that of *Elephants* from the Greeks: besides, it appears not that this *Phile*, situate thus in the midst of the river, had any large territory belonging unto it: nor is it very probable, that two cities, no further distant, possessed both by the same nation, sometime wholly, and in part constantly, and having in notion the same name, should the one be so called by an Ethiopian term; the other by a Grecian: and if the names of ancient kings be deemed to be a matter of any moment, to afford light of conjecture, for the finding out of places, as bearing their names; it might be supposed, that this *Pul* should rather be some place in or about Assyria; since that *Pul*, and *Pil*, are in Scripture records, found to have been anciently, even before Esay’s time, in the names of the kings of Assyria. See *Pul*; 1 Chron. 5.26. & 2 King. 15.19. and *Pil-eser* or *Pilneser*, 2 King. 16.7,10. 2 Chr. 28.20. and from this Assyrian *Pul*, or *Phul*, may some of those *Πύλοι*, or *Pylisi*, in Peloponnesus, whereof Strabo, and Pausanias, have had their name; as also that *Φύλλος*, or *Phyllus*, in Thessaly; whence Apollo had a surname, as Strabo, l. 9. and *Φλυὸς*, or *Phlyus*, whom they feigned to be *a gegénes*, or *a giant*, one of those whom the earth bore; some one of those ancient *Puls*, or *Phuls*, in likelihood. See Pausanias in his *Messeniakes.* Besides that I find *Asshur* and *Elam*, whereof more anon, mentioned in a place parallel to this, among those regions, out of which God’s people were to be gathered. See chap. 11.11. Howbeit, if the conjecture concerning this Assyrian *Pul*, shall to the learned seem light, I am well content that it so pass, desiring only to see some other more likely.

*{and Lud*} *Lud* was the name of one of Sem’s sons, brother to *Asshur*, and *Aram*; the one the father of the *Assyrians*: the other of the *Syrians*, or *Aramites*, Gen. 10.22. from him it is generally deemed, that *Lydia*, situate in that part of Asia, which we now commonly call *Anatolia*, his posterity there seating itself, had its name: it was the kingdom sometime of *Gog*, or *Gyges*, (as *Bozra, Byrsa*, chap. 63.1.) See Herodote, l. 1. and of this *Lydia*, and these *Lydians*, (for the name of the country is put for the people) interpreters, with one consent, understand this place, nor otherwise do most understand that in Ezekiel, 27.10. where *Peres, Lud*, and *Put*, are joined together, as affording soldiery to Tyre. Howbeit, because it is said, Gen. 10.13. that *Mitsraim begat Ludim*; and that *Cush*, and *Put*, and *Lud*, are mentioned among those that were in league with Egypt, Ezek. 30.5. and that as *Pul*, and *Lud* here; so *Put*, and *Lud* there, are joined together, as neighbors: as also, that as *Lud* here; so the *Ludim*, Jer. 46.9. are commended for archery: hence, that learned writer, before mentioned, concludes, that the *Lud*, both here, and in Ezekiel spoken of, as also those *Ludim*, (the same in likelihood with these) are not the Lydians, so commonly called, but the Ethiopians, neighbors to Egypt, and their confederates; and, in ancient records, renowned for their skill at the bow. Concerning which, I shall not much contend, only the arguments, some of them, seem not so weighty; since that it appears, by Herodote, l. 1. not only that the Lydians were, in ancient times, deemed one of the *strongest*, and *valiantest* people in all Asia; but that they were also in confederacy with the Egyptians, whom Cræsus therefore had thoughts of sending to, for aid against Cyrus: and for the joining of them together, with *Put* elsewhere, with *Pul* here; it is no good proof of neighborhood between *Lud* and *Put*; no more than between *Peres*, and *Lud*. and beside, that the site of *Pul* here, is uncertain, the reason of the copulative, here inserted, may be, because this member of the sentence ends with an attribute annexed to them, of *handling the bow*; whereof further anon.

*{that draw the bow;}* Heb. *drawers of bow*, (as Jer. 46.9.) *handlers, treaders* (or, *benders*) *of bow.* These, says one of the Rabbines, are the Turks: but who the ancestors of the Turks, whom we now so term, were; or how in those times they were styled, or where they abode, is uncertain. The like character of expertness in the use of the bow, is given by Jeremy, as well to Elam, Jer. 48.35. (where he gives him the *bow*, as our prophet does the *quiver*, Chap. 22.6.) as to *Ludim*, Jer. 46.9. and it may well be questioned, whether this attribute of *drawing the bow*, being in the plural number, whereas *Pul*, and *Lud*, are both singular, be the character of the latter only, or rather common to both; and that rather the reason of the copulative, than the neighborhood of the nations. Our translators seem so to have deemed; and the Hebrew points which they exactly here follow, seem to carry it this way: that which adds some strength to my former conjecture concerning *Pul*, as either in, or appertaining to Assyria; for that *Elymais* (which all grant to be *Elam*) is by Strabo, l. 16. assigned to the *Assyrians*, as part of *Aturia*, (which indeed is no other than *Assyria*) and the *Elymeans* noted for skillful archers.

*{to Tubal*} The old Latin here, has *Italy*; as also Joseph the son of Gorion, places *Tubal* in *Tuscany*: and it was a groundless surmise therefore of a learned writer, to imagine, that some Hebrew copies, had anciently *Ital*, for *Tubal*: for this seems to have given occasion of that erroneous opinion. Tubal we find to have been one of the sons of Japhet, Gen. 10.2. whose posterity therefore bore that name: where their seat was is questioned; for to pass by some of the ancients, who assign them *Thessaly* in Greece, wherein none, I suppose, now follow them. Some place them indeed in Europe, and would have them to be the *Spaniards*, or the *Iberi* in Spain, at least: for though that name did more specially belong to the people, inhabiting one part of that vast country, bordering upon the river *Iberus*; yet the Romanes, as Strabo testifies, used anciently, to call the whole country *Iberia*. But others with more probability place them in Asia, where *Iberi* are also found; supposed by Strabo to have passed thither out of Europe; and unto these, Joseph the son of Matthias, whom most of ours therein follow, in his *Antiquities* refers them. Nor does that learned late writer step far from him, who seems to have precisely discovered both their place, and their name, out of the monuments of antiquity yet extant. For of *Tubal*, says he, have the Greeks made *Tibar*; as of *Picol, Phicor*; of *Belial, Beliar*; whence the region *Tibaris*, Diodore, l. 4. and the people, at first *Tibari*, and then *Tibareni*; who dwelling in part of Pontus, were near neighbors both to the *Chalybes*, men of special note for ironworks, from whom, *steel*, in Latin, has its name; and to the *Moschi*, with whom, in Herodote’s story, the *Tibarenes* are commonly joined; as in Scripture also *Tubal* is with *Meshec*, being the posterity of *Meshech*, brother to *Tubal*, Gen. 10.2. See Ezek. 27.13. and 23.26. and 38.2,3. and 39.1. Besides, that some prints of the name of *Tubal*, or *Thubal* remain in *Thabilaca*, a city, by Ptolomy, reported to be about those parts, so called. Howbeit, some suppose this nation to have had the name of *Tubal*, from *Tubal-Kain*, (whence the Latins had their *Vulcan*) the son of *Lamec*, one of *Kain’s* posterity, the first inventor of smithery, Gen. 4.22. not as some of his race (for that perished in the flood) but because of his trade, which they were generally addicted unto.

*{and Javan*} *Javan* was likewise one of Japhet’s sons, brother to *Tubal*, and *Meshec*, Gen. 10.2. Those of his posterity were termed by the Greeks, and Latins, *Iones, Iaones*, and *Iades*; which, though it cleaved most constantly to those Greeks that were seated in Asia, and came to be peculiarly appropriated unto them; yet the title of *Javan* anciently took in all Greece, and Macedonia also with it: whence it is, that Alexander is termed *the King of Javan*, Dan. 8.21.

*{to the isles afar off*} Or, simply, by way of apposition, *the isles*, or *those isles afar off*; or, *those remote countries*, (as the word is oft used in this prophecy. See Chap. 20.6. & 49.1.) such especially, as were beyond the sea, or coasted, and bordered upon the sea. See Chap. 11.11. to those, with whom the Jewish people had little commerce in times past.

*{that have not heard my fame,}* Or, *the report of me*; as Chap. 53.1. where Christ had not been named, Rom. 15.19. where the gospel had never been preached before, Chap. 52.15. & 65.1.

*{neither have seen my glory;}* In that manner, as his own people had done, Psal. 27.4. & 63.2. & 106.5.

*{and they shall declare my glory among the Gentiles.*} Or, *that they may declare my glory among the Gentiles*; as ver. 18. fulfilled in the apostles, and other of the faithful, sent out from the Jews, to publish the glad tidings of the gospel, concerning the glorious riches of God’s grace, in the salvation & inheritance purchased by Christ. See before on the first branch of this verse. See also, Rom. 10.14–18. & 16.25,26. Eph. 2.17–22. & 3.8,9.

**V. 20.** *{And they shall bring all your brethren for an offering unto the Lord, out of all nations,}* They shall bring home into the church of God, the converts of the Gentiles, and present them there as an offering unto God. See Chap. 60.9. The Jews understand it of the remainder of their nation, that had not yet returned home, thus to be sent into their country in great honor and state, after the discomfiture of Gog, and Magog: And a late writer of the dismission, and setting free of the Jews, taken captive in the Macedonian and Syrian wars, after Judas the Maccabee his prosperous successes. but the bringing in of the Gentiles, seems rather to be described here, as elsewhere; with special eye, and reference, to the return of the Jews from the Babylonian captivity, together with the accommodations of several nations, at Cyrus his command, afforded unto them, for the more easeful and commodious conveyance of them into their own country. Ezr. 1.1–6. See Chap. 45.9,22. & 60.4,9.

*{your brethren*} The convert Gentiles, made, by faith, the seed and children of Abraham, as well as you, Rom. 4.11,12. Gal. 3.16,29. yea, the children of God, as well as you, Joh. 1.12,13. & 11.52. Gal. 3.26,28.

*{for an offering to the Lord*} Consecrate to him and his service, Rom. 12.1. & 15.16. Phil. 2.17. the word, *for*, is supplied; as Gen. 4.3.

*{out of all nations.*} See ver. 18.

*{upon horses, and in chariots, and in litters, and upon mules, and upon swift beasts.*} Various means of conveyance heaped up, to intimate a plentiful affordance of all gracious helps requisite for the bringing of God’s elect home unto Christ. See other expressions looking the same way, Chap. 60.9. ver. 12. Of *horse*, and *chariots*, see on Chap. 24.7. Gen. 50.9. nor need we, with the Jewish commenters, suppose *iron chariots*, though such were used in war, Judg. 4.3. these being intended only for travel.

*{litters*} The Jewish critics are much divided about this word, being found nowhere in this notion, but here, and Num. 7.3. there in the singular number; here in the plural. Some of them, would have it signify *panniers*, or *dossers*, or the like, fastened together, and so laid upon a beast’s back, to carry necessaries in, and to ride, if need be, between them: but what should such implements do with *wains*, or *wagons*, wherewith it is there joined. Others therefore render it *wains*, or *wagons yoked*, drawn with a yoke of oxen each of them, which might well suit with what follows of *twelve oxen*, for *six wagons*, could any good reason be rendered of such signification of the word. Others tell us, the right is, that it goes for some beast; and we find a creeping creature indeed so termed, Lev. 11.29. but very unfit sure to be used about *wagons*: Our interpreters well render them, *their covered wagons*; that is, *close wagons*, as some term them: the word, in its first notion, signifies, *a tortoise*, though the Greeks render it, *a crocodile.* Now from the swelling up (for it has very near affinity with a word that signifies *to swell*, Num. 5.21,22,27.) or, rising shield-fashion (whence *a shield* also is, in Latin, so termed) of the tortoise’s shell, both in Latin, and other languages, were *arched*, and *vaulted roofs*, or works of any sort so called; and from that fashion of covering, were those *wains*, or *wagons*, so termed, being appointed to carry the materials of the tabernacle; and it may well here be rendered, *coaches*, or *litters*, such being usually much of that making. And that learned man therefore seems to have spoken himself without ground, who denies any ground to be found in the Hebrew, for the rendering of them *arched*, or *covered wains*, or *wagons*, as some interpreters of prime note have done: his rendering them *narrow wains*, or *wagons*, because the like Ethiopic term is used for *narrow*, Mat. 7.13. to me seems less probable, and further fetched: but thereof, let others deem.

*{mules,}* On these, great ones, kings’ sons, yea, kings themselves used to ride, 2 Sam. 13.29. & 18.9. 1 King. 1.33. and with *horses*, and *mules*, in great store, besides *camels*, and *asses*, for carriage, were those furnished, that went up, first, after the dissolution of the Babylonian deportation to Jerusalem, Ezr. 2.66. Neh. 7.68.

*{swift beasts*} To the same purpose, most of the Jewish doctors, affirming the word to signify a kind of *camel*, swifter than ordinary (see on chap. 16.1.) such as the *dromedary*, chap. 66.6. so called, say they, of a word that signifies *to skip*, or *dance*, 2 Sam. 6.14,16. because they have a kind of skipping or jumping pace; though some from the same place and ground, would have it rendered, *pacing beasts*, or *amblers* that keep a measure in their pace, and seem to dance as they go; as the word is in that place rendered. The Chaldee renders it *with hymns*, or *praises*; and one of the Rabbines following him, *with mirth and dances*; as David conveyed the ark to Sion: and another, *with sheep*, for sacrifices, expounding this, by that, which in sound of letters comes near it, Chap. 16.1. and indeed the word rendered *dancing*, seems to have its original from the manner of *sheep*, *rams* especially, sporting themselves in their pastures; the word *car*, signifying as well *pasture*, as *sheep, ram*, or *wether*, Chap. 16.1. and thence the word, *carcar, to skip*, and *sport*, as they use to do, Psal. 114.6. The ancient Greeks render it, *with shades*, or *umbellaes*; such as travelers use to carry in those hot countries on the top of a cane, made on light stuff, and spread circlewise, for shadow. Some other of the Greek, and so the old Latin, which some of ours also follow, *in caroches*, or *coaches*; supposing it to be another sort of receipts, for carriage, distinct from the former. The ambiguity is the greater, because the word is nowhere else read: I suppose the first most probable, because it sorts best with the root, whence the word seems to arise.

*{to my holy mountain Jerusalem, saith the Lord,}* Heb. *upon*; or *unto*, (as 1 Sam. 1.10. & 2.11.) *my mountain of holiness* (as chap. 65.11,25.) *Jerusalem*; either by apposition simply, *Jerusalem*; so termed, because it stood, though in a plain, yet on a knoll. See Jer. 17.3. or, *to my holy mountain*, the hill of *Jerusalem*, as Chap. 10.32. or, *at Jerusalem*; as Psal. 68.29. to mount Sion, a type of the church, Chap. 56.7.

*{as the children of Israel bring an offering in a clean vessel, into the house of the Lord.*} That is, say the Jewish masters, they shall bring them in goodly apparel, and rich raiment, such as is fit to go unto God’s house with, Zach. 3.4,5. and as *a gift*, or *offering*, that was not to be redeemed, Lev. 27.28,29. The meaning is, that as nothing, which was not pure, or holy, might be brought into God’s house, Chap. 52.11. Ezr. 8.28. Psal. 93.5. so these Gentile converts should no longer be deemed profane, or impure, and secluded, and sequestered, therefore, from access unto God’s house; but as persons purified, by faith in Christ, should be admitted into the body of God’s church, his house, 1 Tim. 3.5. and have society in it with the saints, Act. 10.15. & 11.8,18. & 15.9. & 26.18. Eph. 2.19. See Chap. 56.3,7.

*{into*} Or *unto*; the particle is wanting; but to be supplied; as Chap. 13.2.

**V. 21.** *{And I will also take of them for priests, and for Levites, saith the Lord.*} The Jewish doctors are somewhat puzzled about these words. Some of them say the meaning is, concerning these only now brought, whereof some might be of the priestly lineage, and some of the Levitical progeny; that albeit, they had stayed long behind their brethren, in foreign parts more remote, insomuch that they were grown now out of remembrance; yea, had peradventure also lived after the fashion of those heathen, among whom they abode, or had been in servitude, and put to base employments among them, which might be deemed to make them unfit for, and uncapable of returning to such offices again: yet upon their return, God would take them again, such of them as were of the priestly race, for priests; and such as were of the other Levitical families, for Levites, and for Levitical employments. But some of them go a step further, and say it is meant, as well of the Gentiles that bring them, as of those that are brought by them, that God would take them into office. That which others startle at, as if some Gentiles then should be admitted into such places; And this to avoid therefore, some of them expound the text, *I will take of them for the priests, and for the Levites*; that is, say they, not *to be priests*, or *Levites*, but to do service unto them; to be as the Gibeonites, *hewers of wood*, and *drawers of water*, for the service of the sanctuary, and of them, that either as priests, or Levites, should minister therein, Josh. 9.23,27. To which purpose also they would force in that of Zach. 14.21. *In that day the Canaanite*, (that is, say they, *the Gibeonite*) *shall be no more in the Lord’s house*: for these Gentile proselytes shall then serve as they did. They might more seemingly have alleged that passage, Chap. 61.5,6. But of that see there. Meanwhile you may observe, how poor souls, they shut their eyes against the light that not shines only, but blazes and flashes full in their faces. They shall be brought, says God, in state, as holy ones, home to my house; and *I will also* (as speaking of a further, and higher degree of honor) *take of them*; what to do with them? think we; to account them as *accursed* ones, and to make *bondslaves* and drudges of them? as Joshua speaks of the Gibeonites. No, nothing less, but to advance them to honorable places, to make *Levites* and *priests* of them; as most of them expound the words of the text: even he himself, among the rest, who relates the other, as his father’s opinion. And it were a fond thing to say, that God would take of them for priests and Levites, that were so born, and such already. Of the convert Gentiles, though *aliens by birth*, therefore the place is clear, whom God elsewhere promises, that he will not only *bring to his house*, but as he says of the eunuch (for the promise alike concerns either) *give a name, and a place, in his house, and within his walls*, Chap. 56.3–7. The only difference between that place, and this, is, that the office, or place there-mentioned, is that spiritual priesthood, which all true Christians share in, and is therefore there promised unto every one of them in general: of which, 1 Pet. 2.9. Rev. 1.6. & 20.6. whereas here under the name of *priests*, and *Levites*, is intimated the ministry of the gospel, the office of *pastors* and *teachers*, whose calling, and employment is, to teach, instruct, and edify God’s people, Jer. 3.15. Eph. 4.11,12. 1 Tim. 3.2. & 4.13,16. 2 Tim. 2.24,25. & 4.1,2. that which was the office of the *priests*, and *Levites*, in times past, Deut. 33.8,10. 2 Chron. 17.7–9. & 19.8–10. & 30.22. Mal. 2.6,7. and it is not therefore said here, *I will take them all*, as in that other place: but *of them*, not *all*, 1 Cor. 12.28,29. Eph. 4.11. Heb. 5.4. but some of them, as Timothy, Act. 16.2,3. Titus, Gal. 2.3. and others. Howbeit, I suppose they are a little over-curious, that would have *bishops*, or *presbyters*, and *deacons*, Act. 6.2–3. Phil. 1.1. 1 Tim. 3.2,12. here intended, as answering to the *priests*, the one; to the *Levites*, the other.

**V. 22.** *{For as the new heaven, and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me, saith the Lord; so shall your seed and your name remain.*} Here again, do some of our Jewish masters strain their wits. For they will needs have the former part of this collation, to be understood of the frame of *heaven* and earth, at first created, Gen. 1.1. and the *heaven*, say they, is called *a new heaven*; because it continues in that newness in which it was at first; nor is it grown old, but it is still as it was at first, Psal. 119.89,91. and the *earth* is termed *new*, because it still continues as at first it was; howsoever, the race of those that are upon it alter and decay, go and come, Eccl. 1.4. But they forget what God had promised before, Chap. 65.17. to wit, that he would *create a new heaven, and a new earth*, unto which these men, did they not willfully wink, might easily see, that this passage has a manifest and clear relation. It is true indeed, that God does sometime illustrate his constant purpose of the continuance of his church to the world’s end, by collations taken from the constant, and continued course, and intercourse of the creature, from the first constitution of it unto the world’s end, Jer. 31.35,36. & 33.25,26. But it is apparent, that he here speaks of *a new heaven*, and *new earth*, that was to come in the kingdom of the Messiah, Heb. 12.28. unto whose times also, the most of them refer that prediction; and, under whom, the face and state of the church should be so renewed, that is, should seem to be a new world, 2 Cor. 5.17. See on Chap. 65.17.

*{new heaven, and new earth*} Not the same, or such as are, or were formerly; but such as never was before; as, *a new thing*, Num. 16.30. Jer. 31.22.

*{which I will make*} Not have already made. Heb. *am making*, or *am creating*, Chap. 65.17. am about to create, and make.

*{shall remain*} Or, *abide.* Heb. *stand*; as Chap. 10.32. Psal. 33.11. Jer. 32.14. not be altered again; as the former state of the church was, Heb. 8.13. & 9.9,10. & 12.27,28.

*{before me*} Or, *in my sight*: who have mine eye constantly on it, to protect it, and support it, Chap. 27.3. Zach. 1.5,8.

*{your seed*} A seed of faithful ones, Jer. 31.36. & 33.26.

*{your name*} See Chap. 65.15. but here, as the Rabbine well observes, *seed*, and *name*, are but under two distinct notions, and two divers terms, in substance the same thing, 2 Sam. 18.18. Psal. 83.4.

*{remain*} Heb. *stand*; that is, continue forever; as before, Mat. 16.18.

**V. 23.** *{And it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another, and from one Sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me, saith the Lord.*} The constancy of the faithful, under the gospel, in frequenting the service, and worship of God at their church meetings, is here foretold; described in terms borrowed from, and alluding unto, the solemn manner and set times of conventions, to that purpose, which were in ordinary use formerly among God’s people, Psal. 110.3. See the complement, Act. 2.42,46.

*{it shall come to pass, that*} Heb. *it shall be*, that; as Chap. 4.3.

*{from one month to another, and from one Sabbath to another,}* Heb. *from month in*, or, *to his month*; or, *from new moon in*, or *to his new moon*; *and from Sabbath in*, or *to his Sabbath*; that is, as the Jewish commenters well expound it, *every month*; or *new moon* constantly; and so, *every Sabbath.* So oft as new moon, or Sabbath, shall come. So 1 Sam. 7.16. 2 Chron. 24.5. & Zach. 14.16. a place parallel to this, *from year in*, or *unto year*, that is, constantly *every year*, or *year by year*; as Neh. 10.35,39. one of the Jewish critics draws hither that, Exod. 5.19. *the matter of the day, in its day*; to which might be added, somewhat nearer to this, *the matter of the year, in*, or, *within*, or *by the year*, 2 Chron. 9.24. but the forms are not the same with this; that, of any other, comes nearest to it; *from day to day, and from month to month*, Est. 3.7. Again, one of them would have the lengthening of the former preposition, by a syllabical adjection, to imply the constancy of their access, without omission of any of those times. And true it is, that in some forms, the word so used, seems to have some emphasis; as 2 King. 4.8. where, *from his passing by*, is not amiss rendered, *so oft as he passed by*; as also, 1 Sam. 18.30. *from their going forth*, might as well be rendered, *so oft, as they went forth.* Howbeit, because that adjection is ordinarily, in other forms of speech, where no such matter is intended; as Chap. 28.19. Exod. 36.5. as also it is found, in like manner, used, with other particles, Judg. 6. 5. Jer. 51. 28. nor are the forms alike to this, in the places produced, in which also the phrase seems to have such force from the preposition itself, rather than from that adjection; the one seems to me, to be of no great weight: the same author would have the words read disjunctively; *from month to month*, or *from Sabbath to Sabbath*. The one, for those that were more remote from Jerusalem, and therefore could not come above once a month thither: the other, for those that were nearer at hand, and might repair thither every Sabbath: but then the *Sabbath* should rather have been set in the first place, *every Sabbath, or every new-moon*, every moment at least: and this therefore seems a mere needless nicety.
