These set-times are mentioned, because the most frequent solemnities, the *new-moon* coming every month, Num. 10. 10. Psal. 81. 3. the *Sabbath* every week, Lev. 23. 2, 3. See Amos 8. 5. There want not of ours, that expound the words, as understood, not of coming to worship, *month after month*, or *Sabbath after Sabbath*; but of a continual service of God, without intermission, all the time between new-moon, and new-moon, and between Sabbath, and Sabbath, (as intimating the observation of a perpetual Sabbath) and not at set-times and seasons only, as it was with the Jewish people, Rom. 14. 5. Gal. 4. 10. Col. 2. 16. But the constant use of the phrase does sufficiently confute them.

*{all flesh*} All sorts of men: all people and nations indifferently, without exception, exemption, or exclusion of any; as well Gentiles, as Jews, ver. 20. Chap. 40. 5. & 56. 7. Joel 2. 28, 32. Rom. 10. 12, 13.

*{come to worship before me.*} Or, *in my presence*. Heb. *to my face*; as Psal. 42. 2. in the assemblies of God's people; where God is, by his ordinances, in special manner, present, as sometime in his tabernacle and temple: for they Judaize too much, that restrain this to the Gentiles repairing to worship in the outer court, whereunto sometime they had free access, 1 King. 8. 42, 43. See Joseph *of the Jewish war*, l. 6. c. 14.

**V. 24.** *{And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcasses of the men, that have transgressed against me;*} From the mercies and favors wherewith God would so abundantly endow and dignify his faithful servants, the prophet returns to those heavy judgments, that God would execute upon those wicked and disloyal ones, whom he had threatened to be avenged on before, ver. 15, 16. of which he would have his faithful ones, whom they had scorned and wronged, to be spectators and eyewitnesses, Psal. 58. 10.

*{they*} Those added to the church, ver. 23. Act. 2. 47.

*{go forth*} Come out of their graves, say some of the ancients, understanding it, of the resurrection, Joh. 5. 28. come out of the world, say some late writers, and joining themselves to the church; go out of Jerusalem, say some of the Rabbines: and it is not improbable, that an eye might be unto some such occurrents concerning that people, wherein, having been straitened by sieges, or inroads, upon the defeat of the adverse party, they regained liberty to look freely abroad. See Chap. 33. 17.

*{and look upon*} Or, *to see*; as John. 14. 9. some exemplary judgments of God, inflicted and executed on the wicked, for their contempt of the gospel, their profaneness, idolatries, and other impieties. See Rev. 6. 4, 8. & 8. 7, 9. & 9. 5, 6, 18, 20. & 16. 2–10, 21. & 19. 20, 21. for that seems too harsh of those, who would here expound, *seeing*, by *hearing*, the torments of hell preached: nor that of others so fit, that refer it, to the real sight of hell, and persons there in tormented, after the last day, Rev. 14. 10. though I deny not, but that by the hideous spectacles here-mentioned, those torments are here typified.

*{the carcasses*} Of those of Gogs and Magogs forces, that shall lie slain upon the mountains near unto Jerusalem, say some of the Rabbines, Ezek. 39. 4, 5, 9. or lying, as others say, *in the valley of Jehoshaphat*, Joel 3. 12, 14. and others, again, in *Tophet*, in the vale of *Gehinnom*, Chap. 30. 33. Jer. 7. 31–33. and it is not unlikely, but that some respect might be had in this passage, either to the carcasses of those that lay slaughtered for some time in the former place, after that they had dispatched one another, in the reign of Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 20. 23, 24. or, of those Assyrians in Sennacherib's camp, destroyed by the ministry of an angel, Chap. 37. 36. whom that latter place of Tophet concerns. Apparent enough it is, that this execution of God's wrath on the wicked, is here described, by a resemblance taken from dead bodies, that after great slaughter made of them, lie a long time above ground unburied, either as deemed unworthy to be at all interred; or, because in regard of the multitude of them, it cannot suddenly be effected. See Ezek. 39. 12.

*{for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched;*} Or, *how their worm dieth not, nor is their fire quenched*; as the particle is sometime used. See on Chap. 51. 2. The prophet, in this clause, pursues the allegory taken from corpses unburied: and this the Jewish doctors, some of them, taking notice of; but withal taking it literally, say, this shall be part of the strange sign, ver. 19. that should be shown upon Gogs, and Magogs army, that though the judgment inflicted on them, be by fire, Ezek. 38. 22. yet the worms, that bred in their carcasses, lying many months unburied, Ezek. 39. 9. shall live in the fire: which fictions, others to shun, say, that the *worm* has reference to the bodies unburied; the *fire*, to their cities burnt down with fire from above, Ezek. 39. 6. See Rev. 20. 8, 9. But such salves need not: the *worm* has reference to such vermin, as is wont to breed in, and feed on, dead corpses; such carcasses especially as lie so long above ground, until they rot, and become as dung, or carrion, Job 12. 14. & 21. 26. Psal. 83. 10. Chap. 14. 11, 19, 20. the *fire*, to the burning of such bodies, not fit now to be stirred, or removed, but to be consumed by fire, in the places where they lie, Chap. 9. 5. & 30. 33. Ezek. 39. 9. So that the resemblance is taken from the bodies that lie rotting on the face of the earth, till they crawl all over with worms and maggots, and in regard both of their unfitness to be managed, and the multitude of them, it is a long time, ere they can be consumed with fire; and because the sight of such must needs be a very loathsome spectacle, it is therefore added;

*{and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh.*} Or, *are a loathsomeness*, or *most loathsome unto all flesh*; unto every creature; or to all those that behold them, one or other; as ver. 23. the word here used, is nowhere else found, but, here, and Dan. 12. 3. where it is rendered, *contempt*: but might better be, *loathsomeness*, or *detestation* there; *most loathsome*, or, *most detestable* here: (*loathsomeness*, being put for *extreme loathsome*; or, *detestation*, for *most detestable*: as *abomination*, for *most abominable*, Jer. 44. 4. *desolation*, for, *extreme desolate*, chap. 64. 10.) for *contempt*, is a term of too low an alloy. The ancient Greek renders it, here, *a sight*, or, *a spectacle*, clipping off its first letter: the old Latin, *a satiety of sight*, which came from the Chaldee, who cut it asunder, and unadvisedly made two words of one. Some of the Jewish critics say, it comes from a word, that signifies, *a worm*: they all herein agree, that it imports somewhat very loathsome, and detestable. By the whole similitude, or allegory, that dreadful, direful, and detestable condition is expressed, that shall, at first, or last, befall all obstinate wicked ones, sometime in exemplary judgments executed upon them in this world; partly, by inward torture of mind, Dan. 5. 6. partly, by corporal pains, 2 Chron. 21. 18, 19. Act. 12. 23. and ignominious usages, Chap. 22. 17, 18. Jer. 22. 18, 19. amidst which, this also is one part of their misery, that they are, generally, rather abhorred, than pitied, Psal. 52. 5–7. & 64. 7–9. but ever, if they do escape vengeance here, after this life, immediately in their souls; and at the last day, in soul and body joined together again; which the Jewish writers also grant to be here principally intended: at what time their condition shall be everlastingly such, as if carcasses swarming with worms, feeding on them, and committed unto the fire, could be sensible of either, and should always so live and continue, with those worms incessantly gnawing of them, and that fire unquenchable, forever tormenting them; for thus are the torments of hell, in Scripture, deciphered, wherein wretches are to abide eternally, without either end, or ease, with some relation therein had to Tophet of *Gehinnom*, where corpses lay continually rotting, or fire was constantly burning for the consuming of them. See Ch. 30. 33. Mat. 3. 12. & 10. 28. & 18. 8, 9. & 23. 41, 46. Mar. 9. 44. Jam. 5. 3. Rev. 14. 10, 11. & 19. 20. & 20. 14, 15.

The Jewish masters out of a superstitious fancy, because they would not have this prophecy conclude with such dismal terms, as this last verse ends in, repeat again the foregoing verse after this, as thereby to salve and avert the evil presage of it. But that is a ridiculous, as conceit, so device and practice of theirs. Well it would be, both for them, and others, so to order their ways here, that they might not meet with such a dismal close, or pass unto such a direful condition, when they depart hence. See the like at the end of the Lamentations of Jeremy.
